title: kv-store
text:
最适合做购物车主存储的是？
The stem gives four deciding conditions: whole-object access by key, sub-millisecond reads at high QPS, no cross-entity transactions, and tolerance for losing the last second or two of edits in an extreme failure. An in-memory KV store fits all four; PostgreSQL could work but costs more latency and write-scaling effort while its transactional strength is explicitly not needed; Neo4j and Elasticsearch don't match this access pattern. If the cart must never lose data or must be strongly consistent with inventory, a durable database should be the primary store.

title: relational
text:
最安全的主存储是？
Account balances are money, so they need ACID transactions and row-level locking to prevent lost updates, which a relational database provides.

title: wide-column
text:
最合适的存储是？
A feed write store needs masterless horizontal write scaling and tolerates eventual consistency, which is exactly what a wide-column store like Cassandra offers.

title: taxonomy
text:
以下哪些是关系型 (SQL) 数据库？（多选）
PostgreSQL and MySQL are classic relational databases, and CockroachDB is distributed SQL, while Cassandra is a wide-column NoSQL store.

title: consistency
text:
补全 ACID：
ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability—the four guarantees behind relational transactions.

title: wide-column
text:
相比单主关系型数据库，Cassandra 在写密集负载下的主要优势是？
Cassandra is masterless so every node accepts writes, giving near-linear horizontal write scaling—traded off against joins and strong consistency.

title: consistency
text:
你给用户资料更新选了最终一致 (eventual consistency)，最主要的代价是？
Under eventual consistency, replicas take time to converge, so a read right after a write may return stale data—mitigated with read-your-writes routing.

title: search
text:
最合适的组件是？
Full-text relevance ranking with typo tolerance needs an inverted index and scoring, which is what Elasticsearch is built for.

title: blob
text:
文件本体应该放在哪？
Large media belongs in object storage like S3 with a CDN, while the database only keeps metadata and the file URL.

title: capacity
text:
经验数量级：单个 Redis 实例大致能处理多少 ops/秒？
Under these assumptions, a single Redis instance handles on the order of 100k ops/sec—a common anchor for deciding whether to shard. It is not a fixed ceiling: pipelining can push it toward a million, while large values, slow commands, or cross-region networks drop it sharply; real capacity should be measured with redis-benchmark on your own workload.

title: capacity
text:
经验数量级：SSD 一次随机读的大致延迟是？
Memory access is about 100 nanoseconds, an SSD random read about 100 microseconds, and a disk seek about 10 milliseconds.

title: consistency
text:
强一致 vs 最终一致，本质上是在权衡哪两者？
By CAP and PACELC, strong versus eventual consistency trades consistency against availability and latency.

title: kv-store
text:
最合适的结构是？
A Redis sorted set keeps members ordered by score with O(log n) updates and native top-N range queries, making it ideal for leaderboards.

title: time-series
text:
最合适的存储类型是？
Time-series databases are optimized for time as the primary axis, with high write rates, time partitioning, downsampling, and retention built in.

title: graph
text:
最合适的存储是？
Multi-hop relationship traversal is expensive with recursive joins, so a graph database like Neo4j, which treats relationships as first-class, is a better fit.

title: caching
text:
补全缓存的代价与缓解：
Adding a cache introduces staleness, which is typically bounded with TTL expiry or write-time invalidation.

title: caching
text:
应选哪种缓存写策略？
Write-through updates the database and cache synchronously on the write path, so the cache holds the new value right after the write and the next read hits it, at the cost of a slightly slower write. Cache-aside usually deletes the key on write, so the next read misses and reloads; write-back writes the cache first and persists later, violating the "not cache-only" constraint; no cache gives up read performance. The two writes in write-through are not atomic, so failures or races still need retry/invalidation as a backstop.

title: caching
text:
Cache-aside（旁路缓存）什么时候把数据写进缓存？
Cache-aside lazily loads data into the cache on a read miss, rather than on every write.

title: kv-store
text:
最顺手的做法是？
For a fast expiring edge dedupe check, Redis SETNX with a TTL is useful, but final payment idempotency still needs a durable idempotency table or database uniqueness.

title: taxonomy
text:
DynamoDB 的数据模型最准确的描述是？
DynamoDB is a managed key-value and document store accessed by partition and sort keys, with single-digit millisecond latency and no joins.

title: partitioning
text:
在分片(sharded)数据库里，一个「名人/爆款」热 key 会导致？
A hot key sends all traffic to one partition, creating a hot partition and skewed load—mitigated by adding a random suffix or handling hot keys separately.

title: newsql
text:
最合适的选择是？
Wanting both relational strong consistency and horizontal write scaling points to distributed SQL such as CockroachDB or Spanner.

title: taxonomy
text:
补全 SQL vs NoSQL 的取向：
"ACID" is anchored by "transactions and rich queries"; "horizontal scaling" is anchored by "distributed NoSQL." Use this as a first split, then refine by requirements: NewSQL covers strong consistency plus write scaling, and DynamoDB/MongoDB also offer transactions and strongly consistent reads.

title: caching
text:
把「为什么加缓存」的决策链排成正确顺序：
A solid decision runs requirement, choice, cost, then mitigation: hot repeated reads lead to Redis, which risks stale data, bounded by TTL and write-through.

title: wide-column
text:
把「为什么给信息流选 Cassandra」排成正确顺序：
Requirement of write-heavy massive scale with eventual consistency leads to Cassandra, whose lack of joins is mitigated by denormalizing tables per query.

title: olap
text:
最合适的存储是？
The key signals are billions of historical rows, wide aggregations, and column scans. This is an OLAP analytics workload: a query scans many rows but often touches only a few columns. Columnar OLAP warehouses read only the needed columns and use MPP to parallelize scans and aggregation across nodes, while a row-store OLTP primary is built for short row-level transactions.

title: scaling
text:
流量继续增长时，最先要警惕哪类上限？
Reads can be spread across caches and more replicas, but every write must go through the single primary's WAL flush, index maintenance, and locking, which replicas cannot share—so write throughput hits its ceiling first as traffic grows. The actual TPS depends on hardware, fsync/synchronous-replication settings, row size, index count, and transaction complexity, and must be measured by load testing rather than assumed as a fixed number.

title: capacity
text:
经验数量级：关系型数据库按主键点查（有索引）大致多快返回？
From the application's view, a same-datacenter network round trip, driver/pool overhead, and occasional SSD reads put a primary-key lookup at roughly one to a few milliseconds. On the server side, a buffer-cache hit can execute in under a millisecond, so a cache mainly helps by offloading the database and avoiding occasional disk reads, not because the database itself is slow.

title: wide-column
text:
Which statement most accurately describes how a wide-column store (e.g., Cassandra, HBase) organizes data?
A wide-column store shards data by a partition key (historically the row key), and a single partition can hold a very large number of entries sorted by a clustering key — that is what makes it "wide." Columns are sparse: unwritten columns take no space. In Cassandra CQL the table still has a declared schema; the "width" comes from a partition holding many clustering-ordered rows, not from each row growing arbitrary columns. It does not do joins and is neither a document store nor a pure in-memory cache.

title: wide-column
text:
相比关系型的行存，Cassandra 宽列模型的关键取舍是？
A wide-column store gives up joins and ad-hoc queries in exchange for masterless horizontally scalable writes, so you denormalize and design one table per query pattern.

title: kv-store
text:
哪条 Redis 命令最适合做这个幂等标记？
Use SET with NX and EX so the write happens only when the key is absent and expires in 24 hours, giving an atomic idempotency guard.

title: kv-store
text:
取「分数最高的前 10 名」（含分数）的命令是？
A sorted set is ascending by default, so use ZREVRANGE with WITHSCORES to read the top ten highest scores.

title: wide-column
text:
哪个建表最匹配这个查询模式？
Partition by user_id and cluster by created_at descending so reads fetch a user's most recent posts efficiently; partitioning by time would create hot partitions.

title: search
text:
哪个 Elasticsearch 查询最合适？
Use a match query with fuzziness AUTO so it analyzes the text, ranks by relevance, and tolerates typos, unlike an exact term query.

title: interview-method
text:
In a system design interview, what does the interviewer really expect during API design?
Most interviewers just want a reasonable API design so you can move on to the harder parts of the system.

title: interview-method
text:
Which statements about the weight of API design in different interviews are true? (Select all that apply.)
API design matters more for frontend, product, and junior roles, but most interviewers only expect a reasonable design, not perfection.

title: api-types
text:
Fill in the three API protocol choices commonly discussed in interviews:
The three interview protocols are REST for standard CRUD, GraphQL for flexible client-driven data fetching, and RPC for fast internal service calls.

title: api-types
text:
Which protocol should be the default choice?
For standard CRUD, REST is the default: resources plus HTTP methods are expressive enough, browsers and mobile clients support it natively, and the tooling is mature. Without signals like flexible fetching or high-performance internal calls, say "REST" and move on.

title: api-types
text:
Which protocol is the interviewer hinting you should consider?
Mentions of flexible data fetching or avoiding over-fetching and under-fetching are a signal to bring up GraphQL.

title: api-types
text:
What is the best fit for this service-to-service link?
checkPermission is an action, so RPC expresses it naturally; gRPC's Protobuf serialization over multiplexed HTTP/2 connections typically cuts serialization and connection overhead for frequent small calls and adds a typed contract. How much faster it is depends on payload size and network latency.

title: api-types
text:
What is the best fit for this push path?
The prompt needs sub-second push without per-second client requests, so the server must push. A persistent SSE (one-way) or WebSocket (two-way) connection fits best; long polling also works but must re-establish a request after each push. A GraphQL query returns once; push needs a subscription, which still rides on a transport such as WebSocket, and a gRPC unary call is likewise one-shot.

title: rest-resources
text:
What is the first principle of REST resource modeling?
REST resources should represent the things that exist in your system, your core entities, not the actions users can take.

title: rest-resources
text:
What naming convention should REST resources use in URLs?
REST resources are conventionally plural nouns like bookings and events, which is easy to get right and worth doing.

title: rest-resources
text:
How should you choose between nested paths and flat paths with query parameters?
Use a path parameter when the relationship is required for the request to make sense, and a query parameter when it is just an optional filter.

title: rest-resources
text:
What endpoint design fits best?
Since you always need the event to ask for its tickets, the event id belongs in the path as a nested resource.

title: rest-resources
text:
What design fits best?
Optional and combinable filters belong in query parameters, so clients can fetch everything or narrow by any combination.

title: rest-resources
text:
Which endpoint best matches REST style?
Create a booking by posting to the bookings collection nested under its event, letting the HTTP method express the action.

title: http-methods
text:
Which HTTP methods are idempotent? (Select all that apply.)
Per RFC 9110, GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent: repeating the same request has the same intended effect as sending it once (responses may differ, e.g. a second DELETE returning 404). POST and PATCH are not guaranteed to be. "Safe" (read-only) is a separate property that only methods like GET have.

title: http-methods
text:
Which statement about POST semantics is correct?
Per the RFC, POST is neither safe nor guaranteed idempotent; it is commonly used to create a resource with a server-assigned id. Without server-side deduplication, a double tap can create two bookings; in practice an Idempotency-Key or a business uniqueness constraint makes retries take effect once.

title: http-methods
text:
What is the key difference between PUT and PATCH?
PUT replaces the target resource with the request content (and may create it if the server allows), and per the RFC it is idempotent, so repeating it causes no additional state change; PATCH applies a partial update whose idempotency depends on the patch semantics.

title: http-methods
text:
Which of these two specific PATCH requests is idempotent when repeated?
RFC 5789 says the PATCH method is not idempotent in general, but a specific request can be: "set the seat list to X" ends in the same state when repeated, while "append a seat" grows the list every time.

title: http-methods
text:
If the first DELETE returns 204 and a retry returns 404, is it still idempotent?
RFC 9110 defines idempotency as multiple identical requests having the same intended effect on the server as a single one. The first call already deleted the resource; after the retry it is still deleted, with no extra state change, so DELETE remains idempotent. A different status code (204 vs 404) does not break idempotency; returning either on a retry is a common implementation choice.

title: http-methods
text:
Why is idempotency so important in production systems?
Networks fail and clients retry, so a non-idempotent POST retry can create duplicate bookings, which is why idempotency matters.

title: http-methods
text:
Fill in the definition and categories of idempotency:
Per RFC 9110, safe methods (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE) plus PUT and DELETE are idempotent and can be retried automatically; POST and PATCH are not guaranteed idempotent by method semantics, so retries need deduplication such as an Idempotency-Key.

title: passing-data
text:
Fill in how the three parameter-passing methods are used:
Path parameters identify the resource, query parameters modify how you fetch, and the request body carries the actual payload.

title: passing-data
text:
Where should notify=true go?
notify doesn't identify the resource, so it doesn't belong in the path (A makes it look like a different resource). It is a business behavior toggle, not request metadata like auth or content negotiation, so a custom header makes the API harder to discover and debug (B). Content in a DELETE request has no generally defined semantics and may be dropped by intermediaries (D). A query parameter is the safest place for an optional modifier. On a POST that already has a body, a body field would be equally reasonable.

title: passing-data
text:
Where should this data go?
Complex business payloads belong in the request body, but the payment field should be a token or payment_method_id, not a raw card number or CVC.

title: passing-data
text:
What is the syntax for query parameters in a URL?
RFC 3986 says `?` starts the query component; under the web-wide application/x-www-form-urlencoded convention (WHATWG URL Standard), key-value pairs are joined by `&`: /events?city=NYC&date=2024-01-01&limit=20. In A, an extra `?` isn't illegal URI syntax, but it becomes part of the previous value, so parsing is wrong; C's `;` was an optional HTML 4-era form, not treated as a separator by modern parsers; D has no such count limit.

title: passing-data
text:
Which request structure is most reasonable?
The required event id goes in the path, the optional notify flag goes in a query parameter, and the complex booking payload goes in the body. The payment field should be a payment_method_id/token, not raw card data.

title: status-codes
text:
Fill in the common HTTP status codes:
Stick to the common codes: 200/201/204 for success, 400/401/404 for client errors, and 500 for server errors. Successful DELETE often returns 204.

title: status-codes
text:
What is the essential difference between 4xx and 5xx status codes?
Per RFC 9110, 4xx means the request itself appears faulty (invalid, unauthorized, missing resource, rate-limited, etc.), so the client should fix or adjust before resending; 5xx means the server failed to fulfill an apparently valid request, which is what points to our own service. Whether to retry a 5xx depends on the code (e.g., 503 with Retry-After) and on whether the request is idempotent.

title: status-codes
text:
When describing what an endpoint returns in an interview, which two things must you state at minimum?
A full HTTP response is a status line (with the status code), header fields, and optional content (e.g., none for 204). Under interview time pressure, at minimum state the status code and the body shape (usually JSON), and add key headers such as Location after a create or Retry-After for rate limiting when relevant.

title: graphql
text:
What original problem did GraphQL solve when it was created at Facebook in 2012?
GraphQL came out of Facebook's 2012 native mobile app rewrite: the data shape clients needed didn't match fixed server responses, so clients were given a query language to declare the fields they need.

title: graphql
text:
What two bad choices does REST face when different clients need different data?
With REST you either proliferate endpoints for each use case or over-fetch by returning everything, and GraphQL escapes that dilemma.

title: graphql
text:
Fill in the names of the two data-fetching problems:
Yes, this is one of GraphQL's classic motivations. REST endpoints usually have server-defined response shapes; when client needs vary, clients either get too much data, not enough related data, or require new page-specific endpoints.

title: graphql
text:
How is GraphQL's endpoint structure fundamentally different from REST?
GraphQL consolidates everything into a single endpoint where the client's query specifies exactly the shape of data the server returns.

title: graphql
text:
Which query fits best?
The mobile client asks only for name and date and the server returns exactly those fields, nothing more.

title: graphql
text:
Which approach best decouples frontend and backend iteration?
With GraphQL the frontend can request additional fields on its own as long as they exist in the schema, without backend deployments.

title: graphql
text:
What main complexity cost do you pay when choosing GraphQL?
GraphQL adds complexity in query parsing, schema validation, and caching, so prefer REST unless the problem truly calls for it.

title: graphql
text:
What does this linearly growing query count tell you about how resolver lookups should be designed?
Because query count scales linearly with record count, the fix must batch the per-item lookups into one, since more replicas or a faster protocol never reduce the number of queries.

title: graphql
text:
What is the standard mitigation for the N+1 problem?
The fix is batching with a dataloader pattern that groups related lookups into one query, at the cost of extra complexity.

title: graphql
text:
How does GraphQL authorization differ from REST authorization?
REST authorization is usually scoped to endpoints/resources (field-level is possible but needs extra response filtering). A GraphQL query spans many fields and types, so authorization naturally goes down to the field: when each field is resolved, check whether the current user may read it. The GraphQL spec itself defines no authorization; the official guidance is to put the check in the business-logic layer that resolvers call.

title: rpc
text:
What is the most fundamental mindset difference between RPC and REST?
RPC calls remote actions in a function-call style: a service is a collection of methods, each with its own request/response type, and the generated stub hides network details.

title: rpc
text:
Which statements about gRPC are true? (Select all that apply.)
gRPC combines Protocol Buffers binary serialization, HTTP/2 with streaming, and multi-language code generation with compile-time type safety.

title: rpc
text:
Besides gRPC, what well-known multilingual RPC framework came from Facebook and was later open-sourced?
Apache Thrift, originally built at Facebook, is another notable RPC framework supporting many languages and serialization formats.

title: rpc
text:
What is the best fit for service-to-service communication?
Frequent internal calls across Go and Java services with type-safety needs are exactly what gRPC's generated code from proto contracts is for.

title: rpc
text:
Given these constraints, which protocol split fits best?
Externally, browsers and third parties must call directly without a special client, so REST/JSON over HTTP is the most universal (browsers calling gRPC need gRPC-Web plus a proxy). Internally, frequent polyglot calls needing typed contracts match gRPC's protobuf binary serialization, HTTP/2, and code generation. If external clients' data needs diverge sharply, the public layer could use GraphQL instead.

title: interview-method
text:
How should you handle internal service APIs during the API step of an interview?
In the API step focus on user-facing APIs and at most mention that internal services talk over RPC during the high-level design.

title: pagination
text:
What happens if /events returns every historical event at once?
Tens of millions × ~1KB ≈ tens of GB. HTTP itself sets no size limit, but materializing and sending a result set this large overwhelms server memory, bandwidth, and the client, and makes latency unbounded. An interactive list endpoint should paginate; if a full dump is truly needed, use an async export or streaming download. Small, bounded lists can skip pagination.

title: pagination
text:
Which request is correct?
Offset twenty with limit ten skips the first twenty records and returns records twenty-one through thirty.

title: pagination
text:
What is the main problem with offset pagination on large or real-time datasets?
With offset pagination, new records shift the data while you page through it, causing duplicates or missed records.

title: pagination
text:
How does cursor pagination work?
Cursor pagination returns a pointer to the last record, typically an encoded id or timestamp, and the next request continues from that record.

title: pagination
text:
What is the core tradeoff between cursor and offset pagination?
Cursor pagination stays stable as data changes but cannot jump to an arbitrary page, while offset allows jumping but shifts under inserts.

title: pagination
text:
Which pagination approach should you choose?
The cursor stores the last item's (created_at, id) and the next page fetches items strictly after it. New items only land at the head, so they never shift the position already passed, and the id tie-breaker prevents duplicates or gaps at equal timestamps. Offset counts positions, so every insert at the head shifts the rest and causes duplicates.

title: versioning
text:
What is the main benefit of URL versioning such as /v1/events to /v2/events?
URL versioning is explicit and easy: clients see the version in the path and servers route each version to its own code path.

title: versioning
text:
What tradeoff does header versioning have compared with URL versioning?
Putting the version in a header keeps the resource URI stable across versions, matching the REST preference that a URI names a resource while representations are negotiated. The cost is visibility: the address bar can't send custom headers. Note that HTTP itself defines no versioning scheme; Accept-Version is a custom header, and the standards-backed variant is content negotiation via the Accept media type.

title: versioning
text:
What is the safer default choice?
URL versioning is not for end users; it makes the contract version obvious to clients, SDKs, gateways, and backend routing. /v1 can keep serving old clients while /v2 introduces new fields or semantics.

title: auth
text:
What are 'verifying the request is really from john@example.com' and 'checking John can only cancel his own booking' called?
Authentication verifies who the user is, while authorization checks whether that user is allowed to perform the specific action.

title: auth
text:
Fill in the two security concepts:
Authentication proves identity and authorization checks permissions, the first two questions every API must answer.

title: api-keys
text:
What authentication method best fits these two scenarios?
Among these options only an API key is a credential for an application rather than a person: one unique key per client, sent in a header and checked server-side. It fits third-party programmatic access and works for internal calls too, though production service-to-service auth more often uses mTLS or OAuth2 client credentials. Passwords, SMS codes, and cookie sessions are designed for human sign-in.

title: api-keys
text:
Why is this proposal a poor fit for user authentication?
A typical API key is a long-lived credential issued to an application, with no built-in expiry and no binding to a specific user, while the required user session needs exactly both. So user-facing auth uses JWTs or server-side sessions. API keys can be given expiry or user binding; this usage simply lacks them.

title: jwt
text:
What is the core mechanism of a JWT?
A JWT is usually base64url encoding plus a signature, not encryption. Its payload is readable, so it carries non-secret claims such as user_id, role, and exp; the server trusts it only after verifying the signature.

title: jwt
text:
What solution fits best?
JWTs suit distributed systems because any service holding the verification key can validate the token independently without shared session storage.

title: jwt
text:
Which JWT payload field makes the token lapse automatically instead of staying valid forever?
The exp claim is the expiration timestamp. Once an access token expires, the API rejects it; the client usually uses a refresh token to ask the auth server for a new access token.

title: auth
text:
What is the recommended way to handle authentication and authorization in an interview?
JWT is a token format or credential often issued after first-party login, while OAuth2 is an authorization protocol commonly used when a third-party app accesses resources on a user's behalf.

title: rbac
text:
Fill in the RBAC structure:
RBAC assigns roles to users and permissions to roles, so users gain permissions indirectly through their roles.

title: rbac
text:
In Ticketmaster's RBAC design, which role-permission mappings are reasonable? (Select all that apply.)
Customers manage only their own bookings and venue managers handle their own venues. Admins have global management capabilities, but not unrestricted access to raw card data, secrets, or every sensitive field.

title: auth-flow
text:
Put the protected request flow for GET /bookings/{id} in the correct order:
The flow is issue the token at login, send it with each request, verify the signature to authenticate, check ownership to authorize, then return the data.

title: rate-limiting
text:
What are common rate-limiting strategies? (Select all that apply.)
Common strategies are per-user limits for authenticated traffic, per-IP limits for anonymous requests, and endpoint-specific limits for sensitive operations.

title: rate-limiting
text:
Which status code should you return when a client exceeds the rate limit?
When rate limits are exceeded the API should return a 429 Too Many Requests status code, typically paired with a Retry-After header telling the client how long to back off.

title: rate-limiting
text:
What rate-limiting strategy targets the problem best?
Endpoint-specific limits, like ten booking attempts per minute, target scalping on the sensitive endpoint without hurting normal browsing.

title: rate-limiting
text:
Where is rate limiting usually implemented, and how deep should you go in an interview?
Rate limiting is typically implemented at the API gateway or middleware, and in interviews a brief mention is usually enough unless asked for algorithms.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for choosing REST for public APIs in the correct order:
The chain runs from a public CRUD requirement through REST's natural HTTP mapping to its over-fetching cost, mitigated by adopting GraphQL only when client diversity demands it.

title: interview-method
text:
Under this framework, roughly how long should the API step take, and what is the common overrun mistake?
In a 45-minute product-style interview with this framework, the API step typically gets about five minutes: give a reasonable design and move on. In coaching experience, over-investing in the API is a more common failure than under-investing, and this budget decides what's left for storage and scalability. If the question itself is an API-design question, re-plan the budget.

title: http-methods
text:
How do safe and idempotent relate to each other?
Per RFC 9110, safe methods have read-only semantics (GET, HEAD, OPTIONS, TRACE), so a gateway may prefetch them; idempotent methods have the same intended effect when repeated (the safe methods plus PUT and DELETE), so they can be retried automatically after a connection failure. PUT/DELETE are idempotent but change state, so no prefetching; POST is neither and needs an idempotency key to retry safely. Cacheability is governed separately by RFC 9111; safety is a common prerequisite, not the definition.

title: graphql
text:
How do you express the Event-to-Venue relationship in the schema?
GraphQL models a relationship as a field: venue: Venue! is typed as another type, so clients traverse it and get every listed event's venue in one query. D's top-level venue(eventId) can sit in the same query document, but the relationship isn't in the schema and can't be traversed from an event, so for a list the client must know and spell out every eventId. Cost: resolving venue per event in a list causes N+1, which a dataloader batches.

title: caching-basics
text:
Why is an in-memory cache usually faster than database reads?
Here the database working set does not fit in memory, so many reads wait on SSD page fetches while Redis serves everything from RAM; that is the main gap. Redis key lookups also skip SQL parsing, planning, and execution overhead; if the database's hot data were fully in its buffer cache, the gap would shrink considerably.

title: where-to-cache
text:
Which cache layer should you mention first by default?
For a multi-server app, start with an external shared cache because every server can read the same hot data while accepting cache-invalidation complexity.

title: where-to-cache
text:
Which cache layer is the best fit?
Use a CDN when geography dominates latency because edge servers serve static media near users instead of forcing every request back to the origin.

title: where-to-cache
text:
Which cache fits this case best?
For tiny internal config read by the backend on every request, in-process cache avoids even the Redis network hop. A CDN is for users fetching public cacheable content at the edge.

title: in-process
text:
Which statements about in-process caching are true?
In-process cache is fastest because there is no network call, but each instance owns its copy and invalidation does not automatically propagate.

title: in-process
text:
How do Redis and in-process cache differ on sharing?
Redis is shared because it is an external service, while in-process cache is per instance and trades sharing for local speed.

title: numbers
text:
What design judgment does this latency anchor support?
This query measures 50ms versus a 1ms cache hit, so caching these hot reads sharply cuts latency. The 50ms is this join's measured cost — an indexed point lookup is usually much faster. Frequent writes raise invalidation and staleness cost, and caching never makes writes strongly consistent.

title: numbers
text:
What design judgment does this latency anchor support?
The 250ms-to-40ms anchor shows why static media belongs on a CDN: edge hits avoid long cross-continent trips.

title: patterns
text:
Fill in the four core cache read/write patterns:
These names sit on two axes: cache-aside/read-through define who handles read misses, while write-through/write-behind define how writes reach the DB.

title: patterns
text:
Which caching pattern is the default?
With plain Redis (no built-in loader) and no proxy layer, cache-aside is the default for a read-heavy system: read the cache, and on a miss the app reads the DB and fills the cache. It is simple and degrades gracefully, at the cost of slower misses and possible staleness.

title: cache-aside
text:
Fill in the cache-aside read flow:
Cache-aside checks the cache first, and on a miss reads the database, writes the result back to the cache, and returns it.

title: cache-aside
text:
What is the main drawback of cache-aside?
It does not mean querying the DB twice. A miss checks cache, then reads DB and fills cache, so that request pays cache plus DB latency.

title: write-through
text:
Which cache write pattern best matches?
Write-through updates the cache and the database synchronously and acknowledges only after both succeed, which minimizes the post-write stale window; write-behind can lose writes, so it is out. The cost is slower writes, and without a distributed transaction, partial dual-write failures, races, and bypass writes can still cause inconsistency, so retries or invalidation/TTL are still needed.

title: write-through
text:
Besides slower writes, what consistency issue often comes up with write-through?
Write-through still has the dual-write problem: if the cache write succeeds but the database write fails or vice versa, the two can diverge.

title: write-behind
text:
Which cache write pattern fits best?
Write-behind writes only to the cache and flushes to the database asynchronously in batches, giving very high write throughput while risking data loss on a crash.

title: write-behind
text:
What is the biggest risk of write-behind?
Write-behind's risk is losing data if the cache crashes before it flushes the batched writes to the database.

title: patterns
text:
How do write-through and write-behind differ on write latency versus durability?
Write-through trades slower writes for durability, while write-behind trades possible data loss for much faster writes.

title: read-through
text:
In which cache pattern does the app never access the DB directly and the cache fetches from the DB on a miss?
Read-through is a read-side pattern: on a miss, the cache layer fetches from DB. Write-through/write-behind are write-side patterns and can be paired with read-through.

title: read-through
text:
Which real-world example is a read-through cache?
A CDN is a read-through cache: on a miss it fetches from the origin, stores the result, and returns it.

title: eviction
text:
Fill in the common cache eviction policies:
LRU evicts least recently used, LFU evicts least frequently used, FIFO evicts oldest by insertion, and TTL sets an expiration rather than being an eviction policy.

title: eviction
text:
What is the safest default answer?
LRU is the safe default because recently used data tends to be used again, which fits most workloads; exact LRU gets O(1) eviction with a hash map plus a doubly linked list, while systems like Redis use a sampled approximation to cut overhead.

title: eviction
text:
Which eviction policy fits best?
LFU evicts the least frequently accessed key, so it keeps consistently popular items like trending videos or top playlists.

title: eviction
text:
What is the core dimension that separates LRU from LFU?
LRU evicts by recency of access while LFU evicts by frequency of access.

title: eviction
text:
Which statement about FIFO eviction is correct?
FIFO evicts the oldest by insertion time only, ignoring usage, so it may drop still-hot data and is rarely used in real systems.

title: eviction
text:
Which statement about TTL is most accurate?
TTL can delete keys, but it answers when a key expires, not which key to drop when memory is full. Pair it with LRU/LFU for capacity control.

title: ttl
text:
What should you configure first?
When data must eventually refresh, like API responses or session tokens, a TTL is essential so entries expire and get repopulated.

title: problems
text:
What problem is this, and what is the best fix?
This is a cache stampede. Single flight coalesces by cache key: concurrent misses for feed:home share one rebuild, while different keys do not merge.

title: problems
text:
Which statement about cache warming to prevent stampedes is correct?
Scheduled warming relies on knowing the expiry time: Plan A's expiry is predictable, so you can rebuild before it; Plan B deletes right after a write at unpredictable times, so scheduled warming only narrows the cold window and cannot stop the first miss wave — use request coalescing, locks, or stale-while-revalidate. Warming is also commonly used for cold starts (deploys, cache restarts), which is outside this question.

title: problems
text:
What problem follows directly when most systems read from cache but write to the database first?
Because systems read from cache but write to the database first, there is a window where the cache holds stale data.

title: problems
text:
Which common techniques handle stale-cache consistency problems? (Select all)
There is no one-size fix; match each data type's freshness need. The inventory page uses write-time invalidation (most common) plus a short TTL as a backstop if an invalidation is lost; the metrics dashboard already tolerates minutes of lag, so eventual consistency is fine. A distributed lock on every read serializes reads and violates the throughput constraint, so it is not a standard fix.

title: problems
text:
What problem is this?
This is a hot-key problem: one key gets vastly more traffic than others and overloads the single node or shard holding it.

title: problems
text:
Which techniques commonly mitigate hot keys? (Select all)
Hot keys are about spreading one shard's load: replicate the key across nodes behind load balancing and keep a local in-process copy. The scraper share is abusive traffic, so rate-limiting by source sheds it directly. A longer TTL only changes expiry; every hit still lands on the same shard, so it spreads nothing.

title: problems
text:
If Redis suddenly goes down, what should be designed ahead of time so the database is not crushed by instant traffic?
If Redis goes down, requests fall back to the database, so add circuit breakers or rate limits to avoid crushing it.

title: patterns
text:
For cache misses, how do cache-aside and read-through differ on who queries the database?
In cache-aside the application fetches from the database and populates the cache, while in read-through the cache itself does the fetch and fill.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for adding a cache in front of a database in the right order:
A solid decision runs requirement, choice, cost, then mitigation: read-heavy hot reads lead to a Redis cache, which risks staleness, bounded by TTL and write-time invalidation.

title: interview-method
text:
Put the steps for introducing caching systematically in an interview in the right order:
Introduce caching by first identifying the bottleneck, then deciding what to cache, choosing the architecture, setting eviction, and finally addressing the downsides.

title: interview-method
text:
When should you bring up caching in an interview?
Do not jump to caching; first identify a database bottleneck, quantify it with rough numbers, and then explain how a cache solves it.

title: implementation
text:
Which command writes the value and sets a 10-minute expiry?
Use SET with EX 600 to store the value and expire it after ten minutes, bounding staleness.

title: decision-chain
text:
Fill in the reasoning for caching a computed personalized feed:
We cache the computed feed because it is expensive to build, read repeatedly, and tolerant of brief staleness, so a short-TTL cache serves it in about a millisecond.

title: what-to-cache
text:
What should be cached first?
Cache data that is read frequently, changes rarely, and is expensive to fetch, like user profiles, and avoid one-off or strongly-consistent data.

title: where-to-cache
text:
In the caching hierarchy, which layer is this?
Only the on-device layer can still read and write while offline, so this is the client-side layer. Note that runs recorded offline exist only on the device until sync — that is local persistence plus a sync queue, not a disposable cache; only previously synced records viewed offline are true cached copies.

title: interview-method
text:
What overall caching principle should you defend in an interview?
Do not cache everything; show you know when caching is worth its complexity and when a well-indexed database is enough.

title: numbers
text:
Which design judgment does this signal most support?
The CPU is spent recomputing the same queries, and the results may lag tens of seconds, so one cached result serves many reads and removes the repeated work; the savings scale with the hit rate. The queries are already indexed, so more indexes don't remove repeated execution. Scaling up or adding replicas can absorb the load, but every node still recomputes the same results — more hardware rather than less waste.

title: numbers
text:
Given this latency target, what is the realistic design path?
The query is already fully tuned and still costs 30-50ms, several times the budget. Results tolerate seconds of staleness and traffic concentrates on a few hot items, so the hit rate can exceed 99% and p99 lands on the 1-2ms hit path. That depends on the hit rate: if more than 1% of requests miss, p99 falls back to the 30-50ms DB path. There is no tuning headroom left; more concurrency raises throughput but not per-query latency; the SLA is a given hard constraint.

title: problems
text:
What is this third technique and how does it work?
As a key nears its TTL, probabilistic early expiration lets a request rebuild it in the background before the hard expiry, so no single moment forces everyone to miss.

title: write-through
text:
What is the prerequisite to implement this pattern?
Write-through must persist to the DB before acknowledging a write, and Redis has no native support for that, so you need a caching library with a data-store plugin or your own application code.

title: write-through
text:
How does this pairing degrade the cache?
In a write-heavy, read-light workload, write-through fills the cache with entries no one reads again; they occupy scarce memory and evict the actually-hot keys under LRU, so the hit rate drops. Note that eviction depends on configuration: Redis defaults to noeviction, which rejects writes when full instead of evicting.

title: what-to-cache
text:
What is the soundest way to design cache keys?
The cache key is how you look data up, so name it structurally to identify one record — user:123:profile for a profile, trending:posts:global for the global feed.

title: where-to-cache
text:
What is true about modern CDNs (Cloudflare/Fastly/Akamai)?
Modern CDNs cache more than static files — public API responses, HTML pages, and edge logic for personalization and security — but static media at scale is still the safest reason to introduce one in an interview.

title: client-side
text:
What does this client-internal cache buy?
A Redis client caches cluster metadata — the node list and slot assignments — so it can route each operation straight to the right node instead of asking the cluster every time.

title: definition
text:
Fill in the three properties of the CAP theorem:
Precisely, CAP says that in a network that may lose messages, a system cannot guarantee both Consistency (linearizability) and Availability. Partitions cannot be opted out of in a distributed system, so the real trade-off happens during a partition: choose C (some requests fail or wait) or A (return possibly stale data). Without a partition, C and A can both hold. "Pick two of three" is a slogan that Brewer himself called misleading in 2012.

title: definition
text:
What does "Consistency" mean in CAP theorem?
CAP consistency means all nodes see the same data at once, so after a write any subsequent read returns the updated value.

title: definition
text:
What does "Availability" mean in CAP theorem?
Availability means every request to a non-failing node gets a response, without a guarantee it holds the most recent data.

title: definition
text:
What does "Partition Tolerance" mean in CAP theorem?
Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating despite arbitrary message loss or network partitions between nodes.

title: tradeoff
text:
What is the key insight that reduces CAP to a single practical choice?
Since network failures are inevitable, partition tolerance is mandatory, so CAP reduces to choosing consistency or availability when a partition occurs.

title: tradeoff
text:
During a network partition, what does choosing "consistency" mean for system behavior?
Choosing consistency during a partition means returning an error rather than serving data that might be stale.

title: choose-availability
text:
Which should this scenario prioritize?
For viewing a profile, showing a slightly stale name beats showing an error, so prioritize availability.

title: choose-consistency
text:
What should this kind of booking system prioritize?
Seat booking must prioritize consistency to prevent two people reserving the same seat during a partition.

title: choose-consistency
text:
To avoid overselling, what should be prioritized?
E-commerce inventory needs consistency so the last item is not oversold to multiple users during a partition.

title: choose-consistency
text:
What should this platform prioritize?
If the matching engine pairs orders against a stale book, it can fill orders that were already taken or trade at prices that no longer exist — a money-level error — so the matching path needs strong consistency. The market-data view pushed to users is different and may lag by milliseconds to seconds with a timestamp.

title: choose-availability
text:
What should a content platform prioritize in this kind of scenario?
Content platforms can prioritize availability because briefly showing an outdated description is not catastrophic.

title: choose-consistency
text:
In which of these scenarios would brief inconsistency be catastrophic, so consistency should be prioritized? (multi-select)
Seat booking, inventory decrement, and account balances need consistency, while a social avatar update can tolerate staleness.

title: decision
text:
What is the single question you should ask yourself?
Ask whether briefly showing inconsistent data would be catastrophic: if yes choose consistency, if no choose availability.

title: tradeoff
text:
How do CP systems and AP systems differ in how they respond during a partition?
During a partition, a CP system errors rather than serve stale data, while an AP system stays responsive but may return stale data.

title: interview-method
text:
When should CAP be discussed?
The consistency-versus-availability trade-off shapes storage, replication and API semantics, so raise it early in the non-functional phase (a common opener): "Under a partition, does this system favor consistency or availability?" Waiting until APIs or schema are done risks redoing earlier choices.

title: interview-method
text:
If a feature must prioritize consistency, which of these designs/technologies fit? (multi-select)
Prioritizing consistency points to distributed transactions, single-node designs, or strongly-consistent stores like RDBMS, Spanner, or DynamoDB in strong mode.

title: interview-method
text:
If a feature must prioritize availability, which of these designs/technologies fit? (multi-select)
Prioritizing availability points to async replicas, CDC propagation, and AP-oriented stores like Cassandra, while two-phase commit goes the opposite direction toward strong consistency.

title: per-feature
text:
What is the most accurate description of how real large-scale systems handle CAP?
Real systems often mix consistency and availability per feature rather than choosing one globally.

title: per-feature
text:
What is the more sensible CAP split here?
Ticketmaster uses strong consistency for booking to prevent double-booking but availability for browsing event details.

title: per-feature
text:
What is the more sensible CAP split here?
The scenario gives two constraints: a match must be visible to both sides at the same time, so matching picks consistency; stale-by-seconds profile content is harmless, so browsing picks availability. B violates the first constraint, C is reversed, and D makes browsing pay latency it does not need. CAP trade-offs are made per feature, not once for the whole site.

title: consistency-levels
text:
Complete the consistency spectrum from strongest to weakest:
Consistency is a spectrum from strong to causal to read-your-own-writes to eventual.

title: consistency-levels
text:
Which consistency level is required?
Bank balances require strong consistency so every read reflects the most recent write.

title: consistency-levels
text:
Which consistency level does this need?
Causal consistency keeps dependent events (post → comment) in the same order for everyone, which is exactly the requirement. Strong consistency would also satisfy it, but the scenario rules out needing globally latest reads and asks for the cheapest sufficient model, so it overshoots; eventual or no guarantee can show the comment first.

title: consistency-levels
text:
Which consistency model fits best?
The requirement only concerns the writer: read-your-own-writes covers it exactly and is the cheapest, e.g. by session-pinning to the primary or carrying a version token. Strong and causal consistency also satisfy it (causal consistency implies read-your-writes), but they additionally constrain what other users see, overshooting the need at higher cost; no guarantee fails it.

title: consistency-levels
text:
Which consistency model is this?
The scenario only requires eventual convergence after an update: no fresh reads, no ordering of dependent events, and no guarantee that the writer sees its own write immediately. That is eventual consistency. DNS converges as TTL-cached records expire, making it the classic example; many availability-oriented NoSQL stores, caches, and asynchronously replicated systems also use it, but it is not the default for every distributed database.

title: consistency-levels
text:
Which statement about eventual consistency is correct?
Async replication with a few seconds of accepted staleness is eventual consistency: replicas converge once writes stop, but reads may be briefly stale. It is what you accept when prioritizing availability and the default of many AP-oriented stores, though not of every distributed database — Spanner and CockroachDB default to strong consistency.

title: tradeoff
text:
What is the main cost of choosing strong consistency?
Strong consistency requires cross-node coordination before a write returns (typically Paxos/Raft majority replication, adding at least one cross-region RTT per write), so latency rises; during a partition the minority side rejects requests to stay correct, sacrificing availability. B is wrong: data loss is a durability setting, not the price of strong consistency; C is wrong: reads can scale as long as they cannot return stale values (e.g. leader leases / read index).

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the consistency-first decision path for using CAP in an interview into the correct order:
The chain runs from asking whether reads must be fresh, to prioritizing consistency, to picking a strongly-consistent store, and accepting the latency cost.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the availability-first decision path into the correct order:
When reads tolerate staleness, prioritize availability with async replicas and AP stores, accepting eventual consistency.

title: definition
text:
What is true about "CAP consistency" versus "ACID consistency"?
CAP consistency is about all nodes seeing the same latest data, which differs from ACID consistency about preserving database invariants.

title: tradeoff
text:
Where does the single-instance design break first during an on-sale spike?
With one copy there is no cross-node propagation, so double-booking caused by replication lag disappears; concurrent bookings on the same database still need row locks or conditional updates (e.g. `UPDATE seats SET ... WHERE status='free'`), which a single database handles well. The cost is scalability: write throughput is capped by that machine, and capacity is what breaks first under a 100x on-sale spike.

title: tradeoff
text:
What should the default consistency stance be for this feed?
Ask whether briefly stale data would be catastrophic — for a feed with no money or inventory it would not, so you take the majority path of availability plus eventual consistency, at the cost of readers seeing stale titles for a few seconds.

title: tradeoff
text:
What is the correct view of labelling a database as CP or AP?
DynamoDB reads are eventually consistent by default, but setting `ConsistentRead=true` on a request makes it strongly consistent (at double the read cost, within the region); Cassandra likewise lets each operation pick a level such as QUORUM. So an "AP database" label describes the default, not the only behavior. The seat-booking path can use strong reads and conditional writes on that path alone instead of swapping the whole database; the cost is choosing explicitly per access path.

title: problem
text:
What core problem does consistent hashing solve?
Consistent hashing distributes data across a cluster while minimizing how much data must move when servers are added or removed.

title: problem
text:
When one database cannot handle the load, what is the process of spreading data across multiple database instances called?
Sharding means distributing data across multiple database instances, which raises the question of which data lives on which instance.

title: modulo
text:
Fill in the basic modulo-sharding flow:
Modulo sharding hashes the key and takes it modulo the number of databases, which bakes the cluster size into the mapping.

title: modulo
text:
Under modulo sharding, what happens when you scale from 3 databases to 4?
Only keys where hash%3 equals hash%4 stay put (hash mod 12 is 0, 1, or 2 — about a quarter); the other three quarters change database, moving among all instances rather than only into the new one.

title: modulo
text:
What does this modulo example tell us about event #1234 after scale-out?
Under the new modulus this key maps to DB0, so its data must actually be moved from DB1; about three quarters of keys share this fate under modulo sharding. The move itself is usually online — copy, switch routing, then delete the old copy — but someone has to run it; nothing happens automatically.

title: modulo
text:
Under modulo sharding, what happens when a failed database is removed from the pool?
Shrinking has the same disease as growing: going from %3 to %2 only keeps keys with hash mod 6 equal to 0 or 1 (about a third), so about two thirds change database — including the survivors' own keys — right when the system is most fragile. C describes consistent hashing, not modulo.

title: modulo
text:
What direct harm does large-scale data redistribution cause in production?
Mass redistribution spikes database load so users see slow responses or cannot access data at all.

title: hash-ring
text:
What is the key insight behind consistent hashing?
The key insight is to place both data and servers on a circular hash ring so ownership no longer depends on the total node count.

title: hash-ring
text:
Fill in the lookup flow for consistent hashing:
Hash the key onto the ring and walk clockwise to the first node, so membership changes only affect the adjacent range of keys.

title: hash-ring
text:
Which of these looks most like a hash-ring range used in production?
Zero to one hundred is a teaching simplification. Production rings use a space large enough that hundreds of virtual nodes almost never collide: a 32-bit space (about 4.3 billion positions, as in Ketama) is common, and some go bigger — Cassandra's Murmur3 tokens are 64-bit and the Dynamo paper uses MD5's 128-bit space. The point is "large enough", not "always 32 bits".

title: hash-ring
text:
With ring size 100 and nodes at 0, 25, 50, and 75, who owns a key at position 60?
Walking clockwise from sixty, the first node you meet is at seventy-five, so that database owns the key.

title: hash-ring
text:
On the same ring, who owns a key at position 80?
Past the last node the walk wraps around the ring, so a key at eighty belongs to the node at position zero.

title: add-remove
text:
A new DB5 joins at position 90. Which data needs to move?
Only keys hashing between seventy-five and ninety move, since they previously wrapped to the node at zero and now belong to the new node.

title: add-remove
text:
Roughly how much data moves when DB5 joins at position 90?
Only about sixty percent of one node's keys, roughly fifteen percent of all data, moves, versus nearly everything under modulo hashing.

title: add-remove
text:
After DB2 fails, who takes over the key range it owned?
Consistent hashing only decides routing: once DB2 is gone, keys in (0, 25] continue clockwise to DB3. Whether the data is readable right away depends on the replica DB3 already holds, not on consistent hashing itself. Other ranges are unaffected.

title: virtual-nodes
text:
Without virtual nodes, when DB2 fails and its clockwise neighbor DB3 takes over its range, what new problem appears?
With evenly spaced nodes, DB2's whole range goes only to its clockwise neighbor DB3, roughly doubling it to about 140% CPU — an overload — while DB1 and DB4 keep serving their own ranges but share none of DB2's. This is exactly what virtual nodes fix.

title: virtual-nodes
text:
How are virtual nodes implemented?
Hash the node name with different suffixes (DB1-vn1, DB1-vn2, ...) so one physical machine occupies several ring positions interleaved with other nodes. Another common implementation pre-splits the ring into a fixed number of equal partitions that physical nodes claim (Dynamo Strategy 3, Redis Cluster hash slots). C copies keys, which is replication, not virtual nodes.

title: virtual-nodes
text:
With virtual nodes, what happens when DB2 fails?
DB2's 150 virtual positions are scattered around the ring and each segment's clockwise neighbor belongs to a different physical machine, so the failed load spreads roughly evenly across survivors instead of crushing one neighbor.

title: virtual-nodes
text:
What benefit do virtual nodes bring when a new node joins?
Without virtual nodes a new node relieves only its single clockwise neighbor; with them it takes small chunks from many places, so once the data is copied the whole cluster is relieved at once.

title: virtual-nodes
text:
How should you tune the number of virtual nodes for more even load?
The virtual-node count is the evenness knob: more points per server slice and interleave the ring more finely, shrinking load deviation, with diminishing returns and rising ring-table memory and lookup cost.

title: modulo-vs-ring
text:
How much data moves when node count changes: modulo hashing versus consistent hashing?
Modulo hashing remaps nearly every key when the node count changes, while consistent hashing moves only the bounded range next to the change.

title: modulo-vs-ring
text:
Which data-to-node mapping should this distributed cache use?
With nodes frequently joining and leaving, consistent hashing keeps most cache entries in place since only adjacent ranges move.

title: hash-ring
text:
Which lookup logic is correct for consistent hashing?
Correct lookup finds the first node clockwise from the key's position, wrapping to the smallest position if none is larger.

title: hot-spots
text:
What is a hot spot?
A hot spot is a node overwhelmed by disproportionate traffic because some keys, like a Taylor Swift concert, are far more popular.

title: hot-spots
text:
Why can’t consistent hashing, even with virtual nodes, solve hot spots by itself?
Consistent hashing distributes keys evenly, not traffic, so one extremely popular key still lands entirely on a single node.

title: hot-spots
text:
What common strategies do real systems use to mitigate hot spots?
Real systems use read replicas, key salting, and adaptive rebalancing, while more virtual nodes cannot fix a single hot key.

title: hot-spots
text:
What is the first choice for this read hot spot?
Replicating the popular key across multiple nodes and load-balancing reads among them is the most common hot-spot fix.

title: hot-spots
text:
How does key-space salting work?
Salting appends random suffixes so a hot key hashes to several nodes, scattering reads that are then aggregated.

title: hot-spots
text:
What is the key trait of adaptive rebalancing?
Adaptive rebalancing monitors traffic in real time and moves hot key ranges off overloaded nodes, which DynamoDB automates.

title: hot-spots
text:
In interviews, what imbalance do virtual nodes solve versus replication or salting?
Virtual nodes prevent structural imbalance in key distribution, while replication and salting prevent workload imbalance in traffic.

title: hot-spots
text:
Fill in the fixes for the two kinds of imbalance:
Virtual nodes fix uneven key distribution while replication and salting fix uneven traffic.

title: replication
text:
In practice, how is node failure handled if consistent hashing cannot move terabytes instantly?
Data is already replicated across nodes, so when one fails the partition is just one replica short and survivors serve reads and writes immediately — service recovery does not wait on any data copy. The cost is a reduced fault margin, so the system later rebuilds the missing replica in the background, which is when data actually gets copied.

title: replication
text:
How does DynamoDB keep serving through a node failure without first moving data?
Replicas already sit across availability zones, so when the leader replica fails the replication group elects a new leader and keeps serving with quorum acknowledgments, without first moving data; the system then rebuilds the missing replica automatically. The cost is a brief latency spike during the switch.

title: replication
text:
How does Cassandra replicate data on the ring?
Replicas sit on the next N distinct nodes clockwise around the ring (exactly the consecutive N under SimpleStrategy; NetworkTopologyStrategy spreads them across racks and DCs). When a node fails, its range is one replica short while reads and writes continue on survivors, and the replica count should be restored soon.

title: replication
text:
If replicas handle failures, when does data actually move?
Transient failures are absorbed by replicas without moving data; re-replication happens only when membership actually changes — adding capacity, decommissioning, or restoring the replication factor after a node is declared permanently dead. Even then, consistent hashing bounds the fraction of keys that move.

title: real-world
text:
Which of these systems place data with such a hash ring? (select all)
Ring-based consistent hashing covers Cassandra's token ring, the Dynamo paper's ring with virtual nodes, and Akamai-style content-to-cache mapping. Redis Cluster is the counterexample: CRC16 mod 16384 picks a fixed slot — a slot table, not a ring. The managed DynamoDB service is not the Dynamo paper.

title: hash-slots
text:
How does Redis Cluster distribute data?
Redis Cluster divides the key space into 16384 fixed slots using CRC16 modulo 16384 and assigns slot ranges to nodes.

title: hash-slots
text:
Why does Redis Cluster use 16,384 slots instead of 100 or millions?
Every heartbeat carries a slot bitmap at one bit per slot: 16384 slots is 2 KB, 65536 would be 8 KB on every gossip message. On the other side, Redis Cluster is not expected to exceed about 1000 masters, so 16384 slots already splits load finely. That trade-off lands on 16384. (Fourteen bits is just the size of one slot number, not the bitmap.)

title: hash-slots
text:
What is the trade-off between consistent hashing and fixed hash slots like Redis Cluster?
Fixed hash slots are simpler to reason about but need more coordination when rebalancing, a real trade-off against consistent hashing.

title: interview-method
text:
How deeply should you discuss consistent hashing in this interview?
Mature distributed stores already handle placement; the prompt only wants one sentence on scaling, so say they hash-partition by partition key and scale automatically, then spend the time on business design.

title: interview-method
text:
In which questions is consistent hashing a core topic worth explaining in depth? (multi-select)
The three correct options share no central assignment table, stable key-to-node mapping, and frequent membership changes where only a small slice should move or reconnect — exactly what consistent hashing solves. D hides distribution inside the managed service. Note that not every distributed system uses it: Spanner and CockroachDB range-partition, and Kafka's controller assigns partitions to brokers while keys map to partitions by hash mod partition count.

title: interview-method
text:
In an infrastructure interview, what points should you explain about consistent hashing?
Be ready to explain why it beats modulo, how virtual nodes balance load, how failures and hot spots are handled, and how it pairs with replication.

title: real-world
text:
What is the correct scope of consistent hashing?
The "nodes" on the ring need not be databases — cache nodes, brokers, or app servers all work, since it is a general key-to-server mapping. It is not universal, though: range queries call for range partitioning, and a fixed node set can simply use modulo.

title: real-world
text:
Should CDN content mapping use simple modulo hashing or consistent hashing?
A violates the no-central-lookup requirement; C ignores the URL, so content has no stable owner. B and D both compute locally, but assuming a uniform hash, going from N to N+1 nodes under modulo remaps about K·N/(N+1) URLs (nearly 99% when adding one node to 100), while consistent hashing lets the new node take over one arc and moves only about K/(N+1) on average.

title: real-world
text:
What warning does Kleppmann in DDIA give about the term consistent hashing?
Kleppmann separates Karger's original consistent hashing (designed for CDN-style caches) from hash partitioning in databases, notes that many databases use the term inaccurately, and suggests calling it hash partitioning. When pressed in an interview, name the concrete scheme — ring with virtual nodes, fixed slots, or a fixed number of partitions — rather than argue the label.

title: summary
text:
Fill in the one-sentence summary of consistent hashing:
Arrange everything on a ring and walk clockwise, so only the adjacent range of keys moves when membership changes.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain from modulo sharding to consistent hashing plus virtual nodes in order:
Dynamic membership breaks modulo hashing, the ring localizes movement, its neighbor-overload cost is then fixed by virtual nodes.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the reasoning chain for identifying and mitigating hot spots in order:
A wildly popular key overwhelms one node because hashing balances keys not traffic, mitigated first by replication and then by salting or adaptive rebalancing.

title: interview-method
text:
What is the most complete answer path?
Three layers: the ring confines impact to that node's ranges, virtual nodes spread those ranges across several neighbors, and existing replicas take over serving, so no large move is needed at failure time; afterwards the system re-replicates those ranges in the background to restore the replica count.

title: modulo-vs-ring
text:
Scaling a consistent-hashing ring from N to N+1 nodes, how many keys move on average?
Under uniform hashing a new node claims only about K over N plus one keys, while modulo remaps K times N over N plus one — nearly ninety-nine percent at a hundred nodes.

title: interview-method
text:
What does a system design interview expect from data modeling?
In a system design interview you just need a clear, functional schema aligned with the requirements, not a fully normalized diagram.

title: db-choice
text:
For a normal social or e-commerce system, what database should you choose by default?
For ordinary social or e-commerce systems, default to relational, then switch only when access pattern, consistency, scaling unit, or operations clearly point elsewhere.

title: db-choice
text:
What is the safest decision chain?
All three scale, but their sweet spots differ: DynamoDB is managed KV/document access, Cassandra is high-write availability, and CockroachDB is distributed SQL with strong transactions.

title: relational
text:
How is data organized in a relational database?
Relational databases organize data into fixed-schema tables where rows are entities and columns are attributes, with foreign keys and ACID transactions.

title: relational
text:
Which storage guarantee best fits this requirement?
Charging and decrementing stock must succeed or fail together without concurrent overwrites, which is exactly what ACID transactions (atomicity plus isolation) give you; pair them with a unique constraint such as an idempotency key to block duplicate charges from retries, and a conditional update to prevent overselling.

title: relational
text:
What is the key difference between A and I?
Atomicity is about one transaction rolling back as a whole on failure. Isolation is about concurrent transactions not seeing half-finished state or overwriting each other.

title: relational
text:
What are the four guarantees of an ACID transaction?
ACID means transactions commit all-or-nothing, preserve constraints, isolate concurrent work, and survive crashes after commit; its C is not CAP consistency.

title: relational
text:
What risk comes with casually proposing complex multi-table joins in an interview?
Multi-table joins become performance traps at scale, so mention denormalized views, caching, or precomputed results when you bring them up.

title: relational
text:
How should you evaluate the claim that relational databases cannot scale?
Do the math first: 10 million writes a day averages about 120 writes/s, and even a 10x peak is about 1.2k/s, which a single-primary relational database usually handles. Beyond that, read replicas spread reads, sharding spreads writes, and pooling plus caching absorb hot spots, so relational databases do scale. Scaling comes from the architecture around the database, not the database alone.

title: relational
text:
Which of these are relational databases? (Choose all that apply.)
PostgreSQL, MySQL, and SQLite are relational databases, while MongoDB is a document store.

title: document-db
text:
How do document databases store and model data?
Document databases store flexible JSON-like documents, shifting modeling toward nesting related data inside documents instead of normalizing across tables.

title: document-db
text:
What is the cost of embedding a user's posts inside the user document instead of using a separate table?
Embedding gives one-read, join-free pages, but updates and growth all land on one user document: editing a post is a write to a large document (array operators can target one element, yet the engine still writes a new document version), and the document grows with every post toward MongoDB's 16MB limit. Unbounded one-to-many data like posts is usually split into its own collection.

title: document-db
text:
Why do system design interviews rarely need a document database?
Interviews scope requirements tightly so evolving schemas rarely appear, removing the main reason to pick a document database.

title: document-db
text:
Which database type best fits this profile store?
Very different shapes, fast-changing fields, and deep nesting point to a flexible schema; because recruiters also filter on fields inside the profile, a key-value store that only fetches a whole value by key is not enough, while a document database can index and query nested fields. A fixed-schema relational design would need many tables and joins.

title: document-db
text:
How does data modeling change once you choose a document database?
With documents you denormalize aggressively, embedding related data to avoid cross-collection lookups, trading storage and update complexity for read speed.

title: key-value
text:
Which storage type best fits this session lookup workload?
Sessions, caching, and feature flags only need exact-key lookups, which is exactly what a key-value store does fastest.

title: key-value
text:
Why is 'key-value replaces SQL' misleading?
In practice you use both: SQL as the source of truth with a key-value cache like Redis in front for hot data.

title: key-value
text:
How does schema design change after choosing key-value storage?
Key-value stores have no joins, so each access pattern needs its own key: session_id is the primary key, and listing by user_id needs either a GSI keyed on user_id (DynamoDB copies the data and keeps it eventually consistent) or an app-maintained user_id → sessions copy. Reads are fast; the cost is duplicated data—manual copies must be kept in sync by you, and a GSI can briefly return stale results.

title: key-value
text:
Which of these are key-value stores? (Choose all that apply.)
Redis and Memcached are classic key-value stores, and AWS positions DynamoDB as a key-value and document database. Cassandra can also fetch by partition key, but it is generally classified as wide-column, with sorted rows per partition by clustering key.

title: wide-column
text:
What is the role of a wide-column database?
Wide-column databases organize data into column families where rows vary in columns, optimized for massive write-heavy and time-series workloads.

title: wide-column
text:
In a wide-column store, how is a new user post written, and why are reads and writes fast?
Writes are fast because of the LSM design: append to the commit log, write to the in-memory memtable, then flush sequentially into SSTables—no random writes. Reads are fast because one user's posts share a partition sorted by created_at, so the latest 20 is a contiguous range; when a partition spans several SSTables, background compaction merges them automatically, not manually.

title: wide-column
text:
Which database type best fits this IoT telemetry workload?
Hundreds of thousands of appends per second, masterless linear write scaling, and scans by sensor plus time range are exactly what wide-column stores target: partition by sensor_id (plus a time bucket) and cluster by time. Aggregates are not computed ad hoc in Cassandra but precomputed into rollup tables. If you need flexible ad-hoc aggregation, a time-series database or a MongoDB time series collection fits better.

title: wide-column
text:
What is the modeling style after choosing a wide-column database?
Wide-column modeling designs around query patterns even more than SQL, duplicating data across column families with time as a first-class citizen.

title: graph-db
text:
What is the safest interview stance on adding a dedicated graph database here?
Friendships are an edge table indexed by user_id for one-hop lookups; the prompt allows PYMK to run offline daily, so a batch job covers the two-hop computation without online deep traversal. That usually rules out the extra query language and ops of a graph database; it is worth discussing only when online multi-hop traversal is a core requirement.

title: graph-db
text:
What usually happens when you proactively choose a graph database in an interview?
Choosing a graph database is a common interview mistake because it sounds sophisticated but adds unnecessary operational complexity.

title: db-choice
text:
Fill in the flagship product most often named for each type:
Know one flagship per type so you can name it in an interview instead of saying "some NoSQL". Other products in each category (Firestore, DynamoDB, HBase, Neptune, etc.) are also valid; the hints in parentheses pin down the one this card expects.

title: requirements
text:
Fill in the three factors that drive schema design.
Everything flows from three factors: data volume, access patterns, and consistency requirements.

title: requirements
text:
Which factor drives the most schema decisions, and how do you derive it?
Access patterns matter most and come straight from your APIs by asking what queries each endpoint needs.

title: requirements
text:
How does data volume affect schema design?
When data no longer fits, you shard or split entities across systems. Shards share one schema but need a shard key and globally unique IDs, and cross-shard joins and foreign keys mostly go away; splitting entities across systems gives each its own schema, with cross-system references held as IDs and enforced by the application. Both must be planned during schema design.

title: requirements
text:
How do the different consistency needs of financial transactions and activity feeds change the schema?
Financial data needs strong consistency in one ACID database, while an eventually consistent feed can spread across systems with schemas optimized per access pattern.

title: requirements
text:
Fill in the interview phrasing that ties a schema choice back to requirements.
Tie schema choices back to requirements, like denormalizing like counts into posts because feeds must load fast and likes tolerate eventual consistency.

title: keys
text:
Should a primary key use a system-generated ID or business data like email, and why?
Use system-generated ids as primary keys because they stay stable even when business rules change, unlike emails.

title: relationships
text:
Fill in the three relationship types.
One-to-many uses a foreign key, many-to-many needs a junction table, and one-to-one is rare and often means the tables should merge.

title: relationships
text:
What does a one-to-one relationship in a schema usually suggest?
A 1:1 split needs a reason: security isolation, large or rarely read columns, very different update rates, and so on. None apply here and the tables are always used together, so the split only adds a join and merging should be considered.

title: foreign-keys
text:
What does the referential integrity protected by a foreign key mean?
Foreign keys enforce referential integrity, preventing orphaned records like a post referencing a user that does not exist.

title: foreign-keys
text:
What is the cost of foreign keys, and how do very large companies handle it?
Foreign keys are checked on every child insert/update (and parent delete) and can take locks on parent rows, which adds up under heavy writes; after sharding, cross-shard foreign keys cannot be enforced by the database at all. So some large companies drop them and enforce integrity in the application—a trade-off, not a rule of scale.

title: constraints
text:
Which of these are database-level constraints? (Choose all that apply.)
NOT NULL, UNIQUE, and CHECK are database constraints that enforce correctness at the cost of write overhead, while GROUP BY is a query clause.

title: relationships
text:
