Which SQL table definition best models likes?
A many-to-many relationship is modeled with a junction table holding foreign keys to both users and posts.

title: indexing
text:
What is the essence of a database index?
An index is a data structure that lets the database find records quickly without scanning every row, like a book's index.

title: indexing
text:
Which index is most efficient for this user-posts query?
The composite key lands you on that one user's contiguous slice, already sorted by time, so fetching twenty posts touches twenty rows — the cost is one more index tree to maintain on every write.

title: indexing
text:
Which index fixes this slow posts endpoint?
The endpoint filters posts by user id, so indexing posts on user id removes the full table scan.

title: normalization
text:
What is the definition of normalization?
Normalization stores each piece of information in exactly one place, preventing anomalies where an update happens in one copy but not another.

title: normalization
text:
What happens if you denormalize username into every post record?
With the username duplicated in every post, a rename must update all of them, and missing one leaves inconsistent data.

title: normalization
text:
What should your default stance be on normalization versus denormalization in interviews?
Start with a clean normalized model and denormalize only when needed, since consistency problems are harder than the performance problems they replace.

title: normalization
text:
When is denormalization a reasonable exception? (Choose all that apply.)
The three exceptions share one trait: the data barely changes after it is written (snapshots, rare updates), or consistency can briefly yield to read speed. D is wrong because of its reasoning: duplication does not make money safer — every extra copy is another place that can drift. Even when a ledger keeps redundant balance snapshots, the immutable entries must stay the single source of truth that can be recomputed and reconciled.

title: normalization
text:
What is the standard way to get denormalized read speed without dirtying the data model?
Keep the source of truth normalized with each fact stored once, and build a separate derived, denormalized view for the read path (a cache, materialized view or dedicated read table all work), refreshed from change events and rebuildable from the source. A puts duplication into the source of truth with manual syncing, which the scenario rules out; C misses the one-read goal; D delays like counts by a day, breaking the within-seconds requirement.

title: sharding
text:
Which sharding key should you choose for this posts workload?
Shard by the primary access pattern: querying posts by user means sharding on user id so a user's posts stay on one shard.

title: sharding
text:
What happens if a write-heavy system shards by time range?
With time-range sharding all current writes hit the newest shard, creating a hot shard, which is an anti-pattern for write-heavy systems.

title: sharding
text:
After sharding by user_id, what problem does a timeline that shows followed users' posts face?
A timeline across followed users spans multiple shards, forcing expensive scatter-gather queries that you should design to avoid.

title: sharding
text:
What is the most important reminder when choosing a sharding key?
Your shard key choice is often permanent and affects every query, so think carefully about primary access patterns first.

title: normalization
text:
What is the core tradeoff between normalization and denormalization?
Denormalization trades update complexity and consistency risk for read performance, while normalization does the reverse.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the schema-design steps in the right order when introducing a database in an interview.
Choose the database type, list the columns, specify keys, pick indexes, decide on denormalization, and finally consider sharding with a matching shard key.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for denormalizing like_count in the right order.
Fast feeds plus tolerable staleness justify denormalizing like counts, whose dual-write risk is mitigated by keeping the truth normalized behind a cache.

title: interview-method
text:
How far should data modeling go at this point?
Data modeling shows up twice in the Delivery framework: name the core entities during requirements, then flesh out fields and indexes in the high-level design.

title: interview-method
text:
How do these core entities relate to the database tables?
Core entities usually map one-to-one onto tables and form the skeleton of the schema, so listing them early already sketches most of your table structure.

title: interview-method
text:
How detailed should the schema be here?
In the high-level design, show just the key fields, the relationships, and one line on how you'd index or partition for the main queries — enough to prove it won't crumble.

title: interview-method
text:
What does a sloppy data model cost you downstream?
A schema isn't just boxes — it's the foundation for your later scaling, consistency, and growth answers, so a sloppy one forces you to redo them all when probed.

title: foreign-keys
text:
When an author is deleted, what protects referential integrity?
MongoDB has no declarative foreign keys or cascading deletes, so deleting a user leaves the referencing posts untouched; application logic (or your own change-stream or cleanup job) has to handle them, and missing that leaves orphaned records. That is the price of the flexible document schema.

title: storage-engine-map
text:
When choosing a storage engine or index structure, what's the first set of questions to ask?
You don't memorize storage choices — you ask five questions: (1) memory or disk, (2) read- or write-heavy, (3) exact-match only or need range/sort, (4) will data exceed RAM, (5) need durability. Three core structures: hash table (O(1) exact-match, in-memory), B-tree (read-optimized + range, on disk), and LSM tree (write-optimized, log-structured). This is the master map behind every index/engine card.

title: indexing-basics
text:
Why is finding a user by email slow in a million-row table with no index?
Without an index the database has no choice but to read about 10,000 pages into memory and compare a million rows to find one record; with an email index it only walks a few index pages plus one data page.

title: storage
text:
How is the main table data usually stored on disk?
Choose heap file. The question is about table data, not the primary-key index: Postgres stores rows in heap pages with no order maintained (space can be reused after VACUUM), while a separate primary-key B-tree points to them. InnoDB's clustered index is the exception.

title: storage
text:
When the needed pages are not in the buffer pool, why must the query load them from disk into memory first?
The CPU can only work on data in memory; when a page is not in the buffer pool it must first be read from disk (usually SSD today) into RAM before rows can be compared. Pages already cached are used directly — that is what the buffer pool is for — and indexes cut how many pages need reading.

title: storage
text:
What is true about random access versus sequential access on SSDs?
SSDs have no mechanical seek, so the gap is far smaller than on HDDs, but small random reads at low concurrency are still noticeably slower than sequential ones. That is the full scan's advantage; an index still wins because it cuts the pages read from thousands to a handful, which far outweighs the extra cost per random read.

title: indexing-basics
text:
What is the core mechanism that makes an index speed up queries?
An index is a separate search-optimized structure that tells the database exactly which pages hold the target data, minimizing pages read from storage.

title: index-cost
text:
Indexes are not free. What costs do they add? (Select all that apply.)
Indexes cost disk space; every insert must maintain each index, and updates to indexed columns must maintain those indexes; more indexes mean more pages and WAL per write, so write throughput drops. Reads are what indexes speed up, so they do not get slower.

title: index-cost
text:
For this table, what is the right indexing judgment?
A write-heavy, rarely-read logging table is the classic case where index maintenance overhead outweighs the benefit.

title: index-cost
text:
What is the most reasonable answer for this tiny table?
For a tiny table a sequential scan is so cheap that maintaining and traversing an index can cost more than it saves.

title: index-cost
text:
Which statement best describes how indexes affect memory usage?
The memory impact is often overstated: the buffer pool is an LRU-like cache that keeps only hot pages, so one more index does not "double" memory. But pages of an index that is maintained on every write (especially with random keys) are pulled into memory too and compete with hot data, so monitor index usage and hit rates and drop indexes that nobody reads but that slow every write.

title: index-cost
text:
Adding an index to a table has real costs — which are they? (select all that apply)
The main costs are slower writes (every insert/update/delete maintains it) and extra disk (a separate B-tree). Memory does not "double": the buffer pool keeps frequently touched pages, though index pages modified by writes are also pulled in, which matters on write-heavy tables. An ordinary index that no query reads and that enforces no uniqueness is pure cost; monitor usage and drop it.

title: index-types
text:
Fill in the common index families interviewers expect you to know:
B-trees are the default, LSM trees serve write-heavy workloads, hash indexes do exact matches, geospatial indexes handle proximity, and inverted indexes power text search.

title: btree
text:
What is the key difference between a B-tree node and a binary-tree node?
Unlike binary trees, a B-tree node can have hundreds of children with an ordered array of keys and pointers, keeping the tree shallow to minimize disk reads.

title: btree
text:
Which structural rules does a B-tree maintain? (Select all that apply.)
Choose A/B/C. A B-tree stays balanced by keeping all leaves at the same depth, keeping nodes roughly half-full or fuller, and using k keys in an internal node to split the key space into k+1 child ranges. D is wrong because keys inside a node must stay sorted.

title: btree
text:
A B-tree node is usually sized to match what unit?
Databases move data between memory and storage in pages; PostgreSQL's page is 8 KB by default (the compile-time BLCKSZ setting, not a hardware constant; InnoDB defaults to 16 KB). Aligning a B-tree node to one page means one I/O reads one full node, the baseline for later LSM and hash-index comparisons.

title: btree
text:
In PostgreSQL, how many disk pages does a B-tree lookup for id=350 usually read?
With integer keys in 8 KB pages the fanout is a few hundred. Ten million rows over a few hundred entries per leaf is tens of thousands of leaves, a few dozen internal pages above them, then the root — height three, so three index pages, plus one heap page fetched by the leaf's TID. Even at hundreds of millions of rows height is about four, so it stays single-digit; in practice the root and upper levels sit in the buffer cache, so physical reads are fewer still.

title: btree
text:
What happens automatically when you create a PostgreSQL table with SERIAL PRIMARY KEY and email UNIQUE?
PostgreSQL automatically creates two B-tree indexes for this table, one for the primary key and one for the unique email constraint.

title: btree
text:
What structure backs a MongoDB index such as db.users.createIndex({"email": 1})?
Even document-model MongoDB uses B-plus trees, a B-tree variant storing all data in leaf nodes, to map indexed values to document locations.

title: btree
text:
Why did B-trees become the default database index? (Select all that apply.)
A B-tree node is usually packed to fit a disk page: one I/O brings in hundreds of sorted keys and child pointers, keeping the tree shallow. It is also sorted and self-balancing, so equality, range, and ordering queries stay predictable.

title: btree
text:
When you are unsure, what is the safest default index answer?
When in doubt in an interview, B-trees are the safe bet because they handle exact matches and range queries efficiently and are what most databases default to.

title: lsm
text:
Which storage-engine index structure fits this workload best?
Choose D. The key clues are hundreds of thousands of writes per second, durable ingestion, and fewer reads that can tolerate higher latency. An LSM first writes sequentially to the WAL and memtable, then flushes batches into SSTables, turning many random small writes into large sequential writes.

title: lsm
text:
Where does a B-tree bottleneck show up at around one hundred thousand writes per second?
O(log n) only means finding which page to modify is fast. The real cost: random UUIDs land each write on a different old page, and with the index far larger than memory those pages must be read from disk/SSD, dirtied and flushed back, with splits adding more writes when pages fill. At 100k writes/s these scattered page operations become a random I/O bottleneck.

title: lsm
text:
What is the fundamental difference between B-trees and LSM trees in how they relate to the table?
The stem fixes how each system is organized: Postgres is a heap plus standalone B-tree indexes, so any column can get its own tree; Cassandra's table itself is an LSM keyed by primary key, fast for key lookups, with other columns needing an extra secondary index. This is a choice these two systems make, not a limit of the structures: InnoDB stores whole tables in B-trees, and MyRocks stores secondary indexes in an LSM.

title: lsm
text:
How should you think about secondary indexes on an LSM-tree storage engine?
Cassandra distributes data by partition key (user_id) and sorts within a partition by clustering key, so primary-key lookups are fast; looking up by email needs an extra structure: a built-in secondary index (queries may fan out across nodes), a materialized view, or most commonly a separate email → user_id lookup table written alongside. Each has different read amplification and consistency than primary-key access.

title: lsm
text:
Fill in the LSM-tree write path:
LSM writes go to an in-memory memtable and a write-ahead log, flush to immutable SSTables when full, and background compaction merges the files over time.

title: lsm
text:
What data structure is a memtable usually implemented with?
Choose C. A write first appends to the WAL for crash recovery, then updates the in-memory sorted map, the memtable. Because the memtable is sorted by key, it can flush into an SSTable; the WAL is only a temporary recovery log.

title: lsm
text:
If a write is already in the memtable, why also append it to the WAL?
Every write is also appended to a write-ahead log on disk for durability, and sequential appends are much faster than random writes.

title: lsm
text:
Which statement correctly describes an SSTable?
When the memtable reaches a few megabytes it is frozen and flushed as an immutable Sorted String Table in one large sequential write.

title: lsm
text:
What does compaction do in an LSM tree?
Compaction periodically merges SSTables in the background, removing duplicates and deleted entries to keep the file count manageable and reads performant.

title: lsm
text:
Why can a key lookup on an LSM tree be slow in the worst case?
A point query must check the memtable, any immutable memtables, and then SSTables from newest to oldest, potentially dozens of files in the worst case.

title: lsm
text:
Fill in the three main read optimizations for LSM trees:
Each tool works at a different level: bloom filters rule out whole files, the sparse index narrows a file down to one block, and compaction bounds how many files a read must check.

title: lsm
text:
What exact promise can a bloom filter make?
A bloom filter can tell you a key is definitely not in an SSTable so you skip it, while a maybe answer still requires checking the file.

title: lsm
text:
You are looking for user_id=500, and an SSTable's metadata says its key range is 1000-2000. What next?
An SSTable is sorted, so its smallest/largest key in metadata bounds its contents; 500 falls outside 1000-2000, so the file cannot match and is skipped with zero I/O. Inside a file, the sparse index then narrows to a specific block.

title: lsm
text:
What is the tradeoff between size-tiered and leveled compaction?
Size-tiered merges once similarly sized files accumulate, so it rewrites less data, but a key may be spread across several overlapping SSTables that a read must check. Leveled keeps key ranges non-overlapping within each level, so a read checks at most one file per level, at the cost of repeatedly rewriting data downward. Leveled does not necessarily have fewer files on disk; it has fewer files per read.

title: lsm
text:
In one sentence, what is the core tradeoff of an LSM tree?
LSM trees fundamentally trade read performance for write performance, which pays off when a system writes far more than it reads.

title: lsm
text:
Which systems are real-world examples of LSM trees? (Select all that apply.)
LSM optimizes writes: a write only goes into an in-memory memtable plus a sequential WAL append; when full it is flushed as an immutable sorted file, and background compaction merges and cleans up. Examples: Cassandra (SSTables), RocksDB, HBase (HFiles). PostgreSQL defaults to heap tables plus B-tree indexes, not LSM.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for choosing LSM storage in the right order:
A write-heavy requirement leads to append-only sequential writes, hence an LSM engine, whose slower reads are mitigated by bloom filters, sparse indexes, and compaction.

title: hash-index
text:
What is the essence of a hash index?
A hash index is simply a persistent hashmap mapping indexed values to row locations, trading flexibility for constant-time exact-match lookups.

title: hash-index
text:
How does this hash index handle multiple keys landing in the same bucket?
In PostgreSQL a bucket page holds multiple entries and chains to overflow pages when full, and buckets are split as the index grows to keep the load factor in check. With a good hash function the average lookup stays O(1). Other systems may use schemes such as open addressing.

title: hash-index
text:
The same structure makes hash indexes fast and limited. Where do they fail?
The same hashing that makes exact matches fast deliberately scatters similar values across buckets, making range queries and sorting impossible.

title: hash-index
text:
PostgreSQL supports hash indexes, but `CREATE INDEX` builds a B-tree by default. Which reason holds up best?
A B-tree's O(log n) is small: assuming a page holds a few hundred keys, even billions of rows are only 3–4 levels deep, and the upper levels usually stay cached, so the real cost is the final disk I/O. Equality lookups are only slightly slower than a hash, while range queries and ordering come for free. This table also has range queries, which a hash index cannot serve, so the B-tree is the safer default. (Since PG 10 hash indexes are WAL-logged and crash-safe, and they can still win for pure equality on long keys.)

title: hash-index
text:
Why is a hash structure the right fit in this case?
Why the winner flips: on disk, I/O dominates and hides hash's O(1) edge, so a B-tree is nearly as fast and more versatile; in pure memory there's no I/O to hide behind, so the O(1) edge finally shows — and this workload is exact-match only, so hash is right. Redis and the MySQL MEMORY engine both default to hash.

title: hash-index
text:
What is the right way to discuss hash indexes in an interview?
On relational tables B-trees handle equality, range and sort, so an explicit hash index adds little; mention it and move on. This is a relational-table conclusion only — KV stores such as Redis or Bitcask use hash structures as their primary index.

title: geospatial
text:
Why does adding separate B-tree indexes on latitude and longitude not solve restaurants within five miles?
Two separate one-dimensional B-trees cannot solve a two-dimensional proximity problem: the latitude range is a strip around the globe, and intersecting both indexes yields a rectangle far larger than the search circle.

title: geohash
text:
What is the core idea behind geohash?
Geohash alternately bisects longitude and latitude, recording one bit per split and interleaving the bits (every two bits is roughly one quartering); every 5 bits become one base32 character, so each extra character subdivides a cell 32 ways. Nearby points usually share a long prefix such as "9q8yyk".

title: geohash
text:
What does the length of a geohash string mean?
A longer geohash is more precise, going from a city at four characters down to a specific block at six.

title: geohash
text:
What existing index structure makes geohash especially elegant?
Once locations become ordered strings, a regular B-tree handles proximity search as simple prefix range scans, plus a few adjacent cells for radius queries.

title: geohash
text:
Which Redis command is currently recommended for radius search?
Use GEOSEARCH with FROMLONLAT and BYRADIUS since GEORADIUS is deprecated, and Redis implements these geo commands with geohash under the hood.

title: geohash
text:
What is the main limitation of geohash?
Locations near each other can get different prefixes if they fall on opposite sides of a major grid boundary, which is why radius queries also scan adjacent cells.

title: quadtree
text:
How does a quadtree organize space?
A quadtree starts with one square and recursively splits any square holding more than a threshold of points into four quadrants, giving dense areas finer resolution.

title: quadtree
text:
Compared with geohash, what is the main extra cost of building a quadtree?
Geohash turns coordinates into strings that the existing B-tree indexes directly; a quadtree needs its own storage, splitting, concurrency and recovery code, and it is unbalanced and maps poorly to disk pages. Databases with built-in spatial indexes mostly use balanced structures like R-trees (GiST), though PostgreSQL SP-GiST does ship a quadtree implementation. Its recursive subdivision idea lives on in in-memory spatial partitioning and map tiles.

title: rtree
text:
What is an R-tree, and what role does it play?
An R-tree does not cut space into a fixed grid; its minimum bounding rectangles grow to fit where data clusters and may overlap, so points and polygons share one index. PostGIS (an R-tree-style index on GiST), MySQL InnoDB and Oracle Spatial use it; other systems take different routes, such as SQL Server's grid tessellation or MongoDB's S2 cells.

title: rtree
text:
What is the core difference between quadtrees and R-trees in how they divide space?
Choose B. A quadtree splits space first, cutting each region into four quadrants; an R-tree looks at the data first and groups nearby points or shapes inside bounding rectangles.

title: rtree
text:
What is one key capability advantage of R-trees over quadtrees?
A single R-tree can index points, delivery-zone polygons, and road networks together because its bounding rectangles simply resize to contain each shape.

title: rtree
text:
What cost comes with the flexibility of R-trees?
Overlapping rectangles sometimes force a search down multiple branches, so implementations balance overlap against tree depth tuned for disk access.

title: spatial-index
text:
How should you decide whether quadtrees or R-trees still apply today?
They are still used, but in different niches: R-tree/GiST for database geometry, quadtrees for in-memory spatial partitioning, and geohash/S2/H3/BKD for moving points or search systems.

title: geospatial
text:
What is the best interview strategy for this geospatial-index question?
Explain why regular indexes fall short, then contrast the hash-based geohash approach with tree-based R-trees to show you understand the trade-offs.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for choosing geohash for restaurant proximity search in the right order:
Proximity search defeats separate lat and lng B-trees, so geohash encodes 2D into prefix-scannable strings, whose grid-boundary weakness is fixed by scanning adjacent cells.

title: inverted-index
text:
Why can a B-tree index not help a LIKE "%database%" query?
A B-tree is ordered lexicographically, so it can seek only when the left side of the pattern is fixed (a prefix match like `'database%'`). With a leading wildcard in `%database%` there is no starting point, so the ordering is useless and every row is scanned. A suffix match `'%database'` cannot use a plain B-tree either unless you add a separate `reverse(title)` expression index; matching anywhere needs a trigram (pg_trgm GIN) or an inverted index.

title: inverted-index
text:
What is inverted in an inverted index?
An inverted index flips the relationship to store each word with the list of documents containing it, like the index at the back of a textbook.

title: inverted-index
text:
Which analysis steps are needed to get this behavior? (Select all that apply.)
Tokenization splits the text into tokens, lowercasing makes DATABASE and database the same term, and stemming folds Databases and database's down to database, so all forms land on the same inverted-index entry. Stop-word removal is optional (the `standard` analyzer keeps stop words by default) and isn't needed here. An inverted index maps term → document list; it is not one B-tree per word.

title: inverted-index
text:
If a user searches for "databas" and still finds documents about "database", which modern search feature is doing that?
Fuzzy matching is the feature that finds close matches like a misspelled word, built on top of the inverted index alongside relevance scoring and phrase queries.

title: inverted-index
text:
What is the main cost of an inverted index?
Inverted indexes need substantial storage and careful updating, since changing a document means updating the entry for every term it contains.

title: composite-index
text:
What is the best index for this feed query?
A composite index on user id and created at lets the database find the user's first entry and scan sequentially, getting both filtering and sorting for free.

title: composite-index
text:
For the feed query above, what extra work does the database do with two single-column indexes?
Each single-column index is ordered by one column only. The optimizer picks one or combines them: fetch the user's rows via idx_user then filter by time and sort; walk idx_time in order but discard other users' rows; or scan both and intersect (PostgreSQL bitmap AND / MySQL index merge) then sort. Every path does more work than one ordered pass over a composite (user_id, created_at) index.

title: composite-index
text:
What does the composite index (user_id, created_at) look like inside a B-tree?
Each B-tree key is effectively a tuple of both columns, sorted by user id first and then created at within each user, turning a 2D query into a 1D scan.

title: composite-index
text:
Does the composite index (user_id, created_at) help a query that filters only by created_at?
Leftmost-prefix rule: the B-tree is ordered by (user_id, created_at), so created_at alone is unordered across the index and would require scanning all of it. Some engines offer skip scan, but it only pays off when the leading column has few distinct values; with millions of user_ids here, build a separate created_at index instead.

title: composite-index
text:
How should the composite-index columns be ordered for this query?
status and user_id are both equality predicates; putting them first makes the matching slice of the index ordered by created_at, so ORDER BY needs no sort. The order between the two equality columns barely matters for this query; if other queries filter by user_id alone, lead with user_id to reuse the prefix. "Most selective first" is only a tie-breaker among equality columns, not the overall rule.

title: composite-index
text:
Fill in common composite-index designs for interviews:
All three follow one pattern: equality columns from the WHERE clause go first, then the ORDER BY columns in order, so each blank is read straight off its query.

title: covering-index
text:
What is a covering index?
A covering index includes every column the query needs, so the database answers purely from the index and skips the expensive table-page lookups.

title: covering-index
text:
How should you position covering indexes in real systems?
A covering index lets a query read every column it needs straight from the index and skip the table lookup, which pays off for high-QPS hot queries that touch only a few columns. The cost is a wider index, extra work on every write, and more storage and cache. So it is a targeted optimization for specific hot queries, not a blanket default for every hot query. In an interview, start with ordinary indexes and bring up covering indexes once a concrete hot query justifies it.

title: interview-method
text:
What is the right default decision flow for choosing an index type?
Default to B-trees, switch to a geospatial index like geohash for lat-lng proximity, and use an inverted index for full-text search.

title: dynamodb-sort-key
text:
How do you model the table so a single-user time-range query becomes a contiguous scan?
Items under one partition key are ordered by sort key, so a fixed user_id plus a sort-key range is one ordered Query whose cost scales with the window. C fails because KeyConditionExpression only works on partition/sort keys, not plain attributes. The sort key must be unique, hence timestamp#messageId.

title: quadtree
text:
Why does returning only the points inside this leaf quadrant miss the nearest restaurant?
Drilling down only covers one cell, and the query circle can cross its boundary, so the true nearest neighbor can fall in an adjacent quadrant hugging the boundary (the leaf may even be empty). So a proximity search runs the full loop: find the target quadrant, check same-level neighbors, then move up or down levels by the search radius. The cost: one query touches several quadrant nodes, not a single lookup.

title: index-diagnosis
text:
What should the first step be to figure out which index to add?
Indexes aren't free — each one adds write amplification and storage, and blind ones may miss the slow query while slowing writes. First use EXPLAIN plus database metrics to find the real bottleneck predicate, then index for it. The cost: one extra diagnosis step, in exchange for not building dead indexes.

title: osi-layers
text:
What is the core value of network layering, or the OSI model, for application developers?
Network layers are abstractions that let developers reason about communication at their own level without knowing how lower layers move the bits.

title: osi-layers
text:
Fill in the three network layers that come up most often in interviews.
Interviews focus on layer three with IP for routing, layer four with TCP and UDP for end-to-end guarantees, and layer seven application protocols like HTTP.

title: network-layer
text:
What is IP responsible for at the network layer, or L3?
IP only handles addressing and routing: each packet is forwarded independently, best-effort, with no reliability or ordering guarantee, so the reordering in the scenario is L4's (TCP's) job. Segmenting application data is TCP's work; IP only fragments packets that exceed a link's MTU.

title: transport-layer
text:
What does the transport layer, or L4, add on top of the network layer?
The transport layer adds end-to-end services like reliability, ordering, and flow control on top of the network layer's raw packet delivery.

title: app-layer
text:
Which group contains only application-layer, or L7, protocols?
DNS, HTTP, WebSocket and WebRTC are application-layer protocols: HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2 and WebSocket run over TCP, DNS usually uses UDP (falling back to TCP for large responses), and WebRTC media runs over UDP. SYN/ACK/FIN are just TCP flags.

title: web-request
text:
Put the browser-to-webpage request flow in the correct order.
A web request resolves DNS, performs the TCP handshake, sends the HTTP request, waits for server processing, receives the response, and tears the connection down.

title: tcp-handshake
text:
Complete the TCP three-way handshake.
TCP opens with a SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK three-way handshake and closes with a four-way FIN and ACK exchange.

title: connection-state
text:
What design consequence follows from TCP connection state living on both client and server?
Because a connection is state both sides maintain, every request repeats the costly setup unless you use keep-alive or multiplexing, which matters for realtime systems.

title: network-layer
text:
Which statement about public IP addresses is correct?
Public IPs are allocated by regional internet registries and are routable, so the internet backbone knows for example that addresses starting with 17 belong to Apple.

title: udp
text:
Which properties does UDP have?
UDP is connectionless with no handshake, offers no delivery or ordering guarantees, and has lower latency precisely because it adds so little on top of IP.

title: udp
text:
Which transport protocol should you choose for this VoIP audio call?
An occasional loss is a small glitch, while waiting for retransmission stalls newer audio behind the old packet. UDP doesn't retransmit; the client absorbs loss with a jitter buffer and loss concealment, gaining low latency. TCP and QUIC reliable streams both retransmit and share the waiting problem.

title: udp
text:
What real-world limitation matters if you want to use UDP for Facebook Live reactions in the browser?
Browsers expose no raw UDP socket to JS; UDP is reachable only through wrapped protocols like WebRTC or WebTransport, which cost more to integrate. A common design: native apps take a realtime UDP stream while browsers fall back to batched HTTP or SSE.

title: tcp
text:
What does it mean that TCP exposes a stream?
TCP gives the application an ordered, reliable byte stream: both sides track sequence numbers and windows, the receiver ACKs, and unacknowledged data is retransmitted. It has no message boundaries; applications add length prefixes or delimiters. TCP is also full-duplex, so a server can send at any time; request-response only is an HTTP restriction.

title: tcp
text:
Which properties does TCP provide?
TCP is connection-oriented with reliable in-order delivery, flow control, and congestion control, while the tiny eight-byte header belongs to UDP.

title: tcp-udp
text:
What transport-layer tradeoff does the UDP/TCP header-size difference illustrate?
UDP's 8-byte header versus TCP's 20-to-60-byte header is a reminder that TCP pays extra bookkeeping for reliability, flow control, and congestion control.

title: tcp-udp
text:
What is the default transport-protocol stance in a system design interview?
Interviewers assume TCP by default, and you earn extra points by correctly making the case for UDP only where it genuinely fits.

title: quic
text:
How should you think about QUIC in interview settings?
QUIC implements reliable streams, congestion control and TLS 1.3 over UDP, cutting handshake round trips and multiplexing head-of-line blocking; HTTP/3 runs on it. It's widely supported at the public edge, but internal service links, L4 load balancers and debugging tools are more mature for TCP, so internal links still default to TCP.

title: tcp-udp
text:
How do TCP and UDP compare on reliability?
On reliability TCP offers guaranteed delivery while UDP is best-effort with no notification of loss.

title: udp
text:
Which signals tell you UDP may be the right choice?
Each option is an independent signal; they don't all have to hold at once. A–C mean waiting for retransmission costs more than losing some data, and D removes a blocker: browsers expose no raw UDP API (only indirectly via WebRTC/QUIC). Modern apps often mix both: TCP/HTTP for signaling and auth, UDP/WebRTC for media.

title: protocol-mix
text:
What protocol mix is typical for a web-based video meeting app?
A web conferencing app typically uses TCP and HTTP for signaling and authentication but UDP via WebRTC for the audio and video streams.

title: http
text:
What does it mean that HTTP is stateless, and why is that useful?
HTTP is stateless because each request is independent, which is good since you want to minimize the stateful surface area of your system.

title: http
text:
Which convention for HTTP methods is correct?
RFC 9110 separates safe (read-only, no server state change) from idempotent (repeating it has the same intended effect as once). GET is both; a GET body has no defined semantics and may be rejected, so it normally has none. DELETE changes state so it is not safe, but deleting once or ten times ends the same, so it is idempotent and a gateway may retry it. POST is not guaranteed idempotent; PUT replaces (or creates) a resource; PATCH applies a partial modification.

title: http-status
text:
Fill in the common HTTP status-code families.
Two hundred means success, two-oh-one created, four-oh-four not found, four-twenty-nine rate limited, and five-oh-two a bad response from the upstream server.

title: http
text:
Why is HTTP content negotiation, such as Accept-Encoding, a useful API design example?
Content negotiation lets clients advertise supported encodings so servers respond with the most efficient one, giving both backward compatibility and graceful degradation.

title: https
text:
What does HTTPS add on top of HTTP?
HTTPS adds a TLS security layer that encrypts communications against eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks, and public websites use it without exception.

title: https
text:
Which security mistake does this scenario expose?
HTTPS protects data in transit, not the trustworthiness of the body. Using the body's userId directly lets an attacker act on another account; identity must come from a server-verified session or token. The other options are real issues, but not the one this scenario describes.

title: rest
text:
Which API style should you use by default in this interview setting?
REST is the recommended default API paradigm for interviews, and you reach for GraphQL, gRPC, SSE, or WebSockets only when REST cannot meet a specific need.

title: rest
text:
What is the core modeling principle behind REST?
REST models everything as resources acted on by HTTP verbs with path conventions, typically exchanging JSON representations.

title: rest
text:
How would REST remodel operation-style endpoints like updateUser or startGame?
updateUser and startGame are operations, not resources: HTTP-based but RPC-like. REST style finds the underlying resource (a specific user, a specific game), addresses it by path, and uses standard HTTP methods: PUT to replace the user, PATCH to set the game's status to started.

title: rest
text:
What is REST's performance weakness, and how much does it usually matter?
Acknowledge the weakness but keep it in proportion: REST doesn't mandate a format, but the common JSON text encoding costs more CPU and bandwidth than binary formats like protobuf; how much depends on payload, language runtime, and benchmark method. Most systems bottleneck elsewhere (database, downstream calls), so find the real bottleneck before tuning the protocol.

title: graphql
text:
What problem does GraphQL mainly solve?
GraphQL solves under-fetching that needs many round trips and over-fetching that returns too much data by letting the frontend query exactly the fields it needs.

title: graphql
text:
When is GraphQL worth bringing up in a system design interview?
Bring up GraphQL only when the problem centers on flexibility or deliberately uncertain requirements, since with fixed interview requirements it is frequently just in the way.

title: grpc
text:
What is gRPC, Google's RPC framework?
gRPC is Google's high-performance RPC framework using HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers, compiling service definitions into client and server stubs.

title: grpc
text:
For the same {id, name} object, roughly how do JSON and protobuf sizes compare?
This JSON carries the field names "id" and "name" plus quotes and colons every time, about 33 bytes; protobuf writes only a 1-byte tag, a 1-byte length, and the value, 15 bytes total. Field names never enter the binary body, so both size and parsing CPU drop — one reason gRPC is cheaper for service-to-service calls. The exact ratio depends on value lengths: the longer the values, the smaller the gap.

title: grpc
text:
Which gRPC features fit large-scale microservices?
gRPC targets large-scale microservices: streaming, deadlines, client-side load balancing, and (in statically typed languages) compile-time checks from .proto-generated stubs. Its weakness is that browsers can't speak native gRPC directly and need gRPC-Web plus a proxy, so it's most common for internal service-to-service calls, while browser-facing APIs usually stay REST.

title: grpc
text:
What protocol combination is recommended for this microservice architecture?
Use gRPC for internal service-to-service communication where performance matters and REST for public-facing APIs whose clients you do not control.

title: grpc
text:
How are RPC and gRPC related?
RPC is the remote-call concept, while gRPC is Google's concrete RPC framework built on HTTP/2, protobuf, code generation, and four call shapes.

title: grpc
text:
How does gRPC server streaming (one call returns a stream) differ from async offload (return a job_id immediately, process in the background)?
Server streaming keeps one call open for a stream of results, while async offload returns a job_id immediately and delivers the result later through another channel.

title: interview-method
text:
Why is over-focusing on RPC protocol choice a mistake here — what is the interviewer actually evaluating?
Interviewers want to see how you think through problems, so beware of hyperoptimizing your RPC protocol choice before handling the substantial bottlenecks.

title: sse
text:
What is Server-Sent Events, or SSE, at its core?
Plain HTTP processes a response only once it is complete; SSE turns one text/event-stream response into a message stream: each event is one or more data: lines terminated by a blank line, and EventSource fires once per complete event.

title: sse
text:
After an SSE connection closes, what recovery mechanism does the standard give the client?
The standard makes EventSource reconnect automatically and send a Last-Event-ID header with the last received event id. Resending missed quotes is the server's own job: it must retain recent events and resume from that id, which is what the one-minute buffer is for.

title: sse
text:
What hidden operational issue does SSE often have in practice?
Some misbehaving networks batch all SSE chunks into a single response, defeating the streaming behavior, a pain anyone who has shipped SSE knows well.

title: sse
text:
What is the best real-time delivery option for this online auction?
SSE is the right fit for pushing auction price updates because the flow is server-to-client only and WebSockets would be overkill.

title: websocket
text:
What capability does WebSocket provide?
WebSockets provide a persistent bidirectional connection with broad browser support, letting the server push data without waiting for a request.

title: websocket
text:
How is a WebSocket connection established, and why is that convenient?
A WebSocket starts as an HTTP upgrade that switches the existing TCP connection's protocol, conveniently reusing session information like cookies and headers.

title: websocket
text:
What is the common infrastructure pain point when deploying WebSocket in the real world?
Every piece of infrastructure between client and server must support WebSockets, and stateful connections at scale demand significant design accommodations.

title: websocket
text:
What requirement mix actually justifies WebSocket?
WebSocket pays off most clearly when traffic is high-frequency, persistent, and bidirectional at once. Plain request-response fits ordinary HTTP, and server-to-client push alone is usually covered by SSE. This is a rule of thumb, not a hard rule: lower-frequency two-way cases such as ordinary chat also commonly use WebSocket, as long as you justify the cost of stateful long-lived connections.

title: websocket
text:
Put the WebSocket workflow in the correct order.
The client initiates a WebSocket handshake over HTTP, the connection upgrades, both sides exchange binary messages, and it stays open until explicitly closed.

title: webrtc
text:
Among these, what two things make WebRTC unique?
Among these six, only WebRTC lets browsers exchange media directly (the server doesn't relay media, so its bandwidth cost can approach zero), and its media defaults to UDP (SRTP); if direct paths fail, ICE can fall back to TCP or a TURN relay. More broadly, DNS and HTTP/3 (QUIC) also run on UDP, so "only" holds just within this comparison set. D is wrong: setup still needs a signaling server, and NAT traversal needs STUN/TURN.

title: webrtc
text:
Fill in the three infrastructure roles behind WebRTC.
Most clients sit behind NAT and don't accept inbound connections: a signaling server exchanges connection info, STUN tells each peer its public-facing address, ICE uses those candidates to attempt hole punching, and TURN relays traffic when direct connection fails.

title: webrtc
text:
Put the happy-path WebRTC connection setup in the correct order.
Clients connect to the signaling server, get their public address from STUN, exchange info via signaling, and then establish the direct peer-to-peer connection.

title: webrtc
text:
What is the safest interview boundary for using WebRTC?
Stick to WebRTC for audio and video calling and conferencing, because most problems do not need peer-to-peer and candidates go wildly off trail trying.

title: scaling
text:
How should you compare vertical and horizontal scaling in interviews?
Vertical scaling means bigger servers and horizontal means more servers, and while modern hardware favors vertical, interviews almost always end up horizontal with load balancing.

title: client-lb
text:
How does client-side load balancing work, and what is its advantage?
In client-side load balancing the client fetches the server list from a registry and picks a server itself, avoiding an extra network hop on every request.

title: client-lb
text:
How does Redis Cluster demonstrate client-side load balancing?
Redis Cluster nodes gossip cluster state, clients hash the key to pick the shard and connect directly, and a wrong node helpfully replies with MOVED.

title: client-lb
text:
How can DNS act as a client-side load balancer, and what classic problem does that help solve?
DNS returns the IP list in rotating order so clients spread across both LBs. Real failover also needs DNS health checks to withdraw a dead LB; recovery is bounded by TTL caching, and some clients retry the next IP on their own.

title: client-lb
text:
In what two situations does client-side load balancing work well?
Client-side load balancing works with a small number of controlled clients like internal gRPC services, or many clients that tolerate slow updates like DNS.

title: client-lb
text:
What hard constraint does DNS TTL create when updating server lists?
TTL lets resolvers everywhere cache answers (good for scale), but it means that after you remove a bad server, compliant caches keep the old record until the TTL expires. TTL is a cache upper bound, not a guarantee that every client switches by then — client caches that ignore TTL and already-open connections can keep using the old IP longer. Fast removal therefore needs an LB / health checks, not just a DNS change.

title: l4-lb
text:
How does a Layer 4 load balancer work?
A layer four load balancer routes on IP and port without inspecting content, acting as if the client had a direct persistent TCP connection to one backend.

title: l7-lb
text:
How does a Layer 7 load balancer work?
A layer seven load balancer terminates connections and routes each application-level request based on its content such as URL, headers, or cookies.

title: lb-choice
text:
Which load balancer type should you choose for WebSocket traffic?
Both L4 and L7 can carry WebSocket: an L7 LB (ALB, NGINX, Envoy) handles the Upgrade handshake and then pins that connection to one backend too. The deciding constraints here are no content-based routing, TLS terminated on the backends, and minimal per-connection overhead, so an L4 LB that never parses HTTP fits best. If you need path/header routing, TLS termination at the LB, or a WAF, a WebSocket-capable L7 LB is the right pick.

title: lb-choice
text:
What is the one-line comparison between L4 and L7 load balancers?
A performance-versus-intelligence tradeoff: L4 looks only at IP/port with low overhead, and a TCP connection naturally stays on one backend; L7 terminates connections and routes on HTTP content at the cost of parsing CPU. Both can carry long-lived connections (L7 also supports WebSocket upgrade with connection affinity), so choose by whether you need content-based routing and can afford the parsing cost.

title: lb-placement
text:
Which statement about where load balancers sit is correct?
Load balancing spreads requests across backend pools, so it applies both at the external north-south edge and on internal east-west service calls.

title: health-checks
text:
How do load balancers implement automatic failover for high availability?
The LB continuously probes backends, stops routing to one after consecutive failures, and adds it back on recovery, with no human needed. Here the hung process still accepts TCP connections, so a plain TCP probe would mark it healthy; you need an L7 probe (e.g. GET /health expecting a 2xx within a timeout) to catch it.

title: lb-algorithms
text:
Fill in the common load-balancing algorithms.
Round robin cycles through servers, least connections picks the server with the fewest active connections, and IP hash maps a client to a consistent server for session persistence.

title: lb-algorithms
text:
Which load-balancing algorithm should you choose for many persistent connections?
For services holding SSE or WebSocket connections use least connections, which prevents one server from gradually accumulating all the active connections.

title: lb-implementations
text:
What forms do dedicated load balancers take in practice?
Three forms: hardware appliances (e.g. F5), software (HAProxy, Nginx, Envoy), and cloud-managed (AWS ELB, etc.). Actual throughput depends on model, connection mode, TLS, and payload, so don't memorize a fixed number. At five million QPS, saying "the LB tier scales horizontally too: DNS/anycast across multiple LBs, or a cloud LB / high-end hardware" brings the conversation back on track.

title: regionalization
text:
What is the availability-zone deployment pattern?
A region contains multiple data centers called availability zones so one building failure cannot take down the service, and the model repeats across world cities.

title: latency
text:
What round-trip latency floor does the speed of light in fiber impose between New York and London?
New York to London is about 5,570 km along the great circle, and light in fiber travels about 200,000 km/s, so one way is about 28 ms and a round trip about 56 ms. Before any routing detours or processing, physics already takes 56 ms — you cannot optimize the speed of light, which is why latency-sensitive apps distribute geographically.

title: cdn
text:
What is the first strategy to reduce latency for globally cached data?
A CDN caches highly cacheable data at edge servers near users, cutting latency dramatically while also reducing load on the backend.

title: regionalization
text:
What architecture should you use when requests naturally only need local data?
First route the request to the city or regional shard, then run proximity search inside that local shard. Geohash is useful, but usually as the second layer.

title: regionalization
text:
What does the data locality principle mean?
Data locality means keeping query data close together and near the user; LA to New York already has roughly a 40ms round-trip lower bound before routing and queueing.

title: failures
text:
Which false assumption about distributed systems did this incident expose, and what mindset should replace it?
Timeouts from a fiber cut expose the first fallacy of distributed computing: "the network is reliable." Clock skew is also a classic pitfall, but it isn't what this incident shows. Robust designs treat failure as normal: timeouts, retries with backoff, graceful degradation, redundant paths.

title: retries
text:
What magic phrase is the interviewer looking for when downstream calls fail transiently?
Interviewers are often looking for the magic phrase retry with exponential backoff, and senior candidates should be ready to elaborate on adding jitter.

title: retries
text:
Why are retries a double-edged sword?
Aggressive retries can hammer an already failing service and make things worse, which is why backoff waits progressively longer between attempts.

title: retries
text:
Why must a backoff strategy include jitter?
Jitter adds randomness so clients do not synchronize their retries into repeated simultaneous bursts hammering the service like a jackhammer.

title: idempotency
text:
How do you prevent a retried $10 charge from becoming $20 or $2,000?
The client generates one unique key per logical payment (e.g. a UUID) and sends the same key on every retry; the server persists the key with its result and returns the first result for any repeat, without charging again. If the actual charge happens at an external processor, pass the same key downstream so it can dedupe too. Do not build the key from business fields like user + date, or a second legitimate payment on the same day will be rejected as a duplicate. The `Idempotency-Key` header is a common implementation (an IETF draft), not a published HTTP standard.

title: circuit-breaker
text:
Put the circuit breaker workflow in the correct order.
A circuit breaker monitors failures, trips open past a threshold, fails fast while open, moves to half-open after a timeout, and a test request decides whether to close.

title: circuit-breaker
text:
What benefits does a circuit breaker provide?
Circuit breakers fail fast, reduce load on struggling services, self-heal by testing recovery, and keep one failure from cascading through the system.

title: circuit-breaker
text:
What pattern prevents this cascading failure during database recovery?
Past a failure threshold the circuit breaker opens, so callers fail fast instead of pushing retries and user requests onto the restarting DB instance; after a cooldown it goes half-open and lets only a few probe requests through, ramping up once the instance holds. That gives the recovering instance breathing room instead of being knocked down again by the thundering herd. More retries or a bigger pool amplify the flood; a faster database doesn't fix being crushed during recovery.

title: circuit-breaker
text:
Where should circuit breakers be placed? (Select all that apply.)
Rule of thumb: any dependency call that crosses the network and can fail or slow down deserves a circuit breaker: third-party APIs, databases, and service-to-service calls all qualify. Pure in-process, in-memory calls have no network failure mode, so a breaker there is only overhead.

title: dedicated-lb
text:
Client-side load balancing or a dedicated load balancer here?
A dedicated load balancer adds one hop per request, but in return gives second-level server-list updates and fine-grained routing by path or user — worth it when the backend churns.

title: user-kernel-space
text:
Put it in user space or kernel space, and what does each cost?
User space is flexible and easy to change but slower; kernel space is efficient but hard to change. Frequently-changed routing belongs in user space — the reason L7 is heavier than L4.

title: graphql
text:
What does GraphQL cost on the backend side?
The flexibility lands on the backend: every nested field runs through a resolver, so deep, wide queries easily turn into N+1 database calls with unpredictable latency and load. The backend needs DataLoader-style batching, query depth/complexity limits, and specially optimized resolvers for hot shapes; you save per-page endpoints, not backend work itself.

title: http2-multiplexing
text:
Which HTTP/2 feature lets these concurrent calls share a few persistent connections without queuing or reconnecting each time?
HTTP/1.1 keep-alive already reuses connections, but each connection carries one request at a time, so high concurrency means queuing or opening many connections. HTTP/2 multiplexing runs many requests as independent streams interleaved on one connection, so a few long-lived connections handle huge volumes of short calls without repeated handshakes or pool bloat. Protobuf only shrinks the payload.

title: tcp-teardown
text:
Why does TCP close with four steps instead of two?
A TCP connection is bidirectional: the client's FIN only says its own send side is done, so the server ACKs first and sends its own FIN once it's finished — each direction closes independently, one more step than the opening handshake.

title: dhcp
text:
Node IPs come from DHCP dynamically at boot — what does that mean for service discovery?
DHCP hands out IPs dynamically at boot, so restarts and scaling events can change an instance's address; a hardcoded or rarely-refreshed server list goes stale the moment that happens — hence the need for dynamic service discovery.

title: health-check-choice
text:
TCP health check or L7 health check here?
A deadlocked app that still returns 500 still completes a TCP handshake fine, so a TCP check misses it; an L7 check actually sends an HTTP request and inspects the status code, catching that fake-alive state at the cost of an extra application-layer round trip.

title: lb-algorithms
text:
Which load-balancing algorithm fits here?
Given a stable client IP and a fixed instance count, IP hash keeps the same source on the same instance, providing session stickiness; the other three only balance load with no such guarantee. Its limit: an IP change or a scaling event moves the user, so cookie-based stickiness or a shared session store is more robust.

title: tcp-flow-congestion
text:
What TCP mechanism handles each of these two situations?
Flow control watches the receiver's buffer so the sender doesn't overrun it; congestion control watches the network path and slows down on loss or delay. They react to different signals even though both throttle the sender.

title: webrtc-udp
text:
Why does WebRTC send audio and video over UDP instead of TCP like HTTP does?
UDP drops delivery and ordering guarantees in exchange for low latency, which is exactly what real-time media needs — a late frame is worse than a dropped one. TCP's retransmission and ordering would stall the whole stream waiting on one lost packet.

title: client-lb-sync
text:
Why don't the new instances receive traffic right away?
The new instances are healthy, registered, and already serving some clients, so the instances themselves aren't the problem (ruling out B/C); the lagging clients' local lists are. Clients either poll the registry on an interval or wait for a push, and either way the update isn't instantaneous: traffic only starts once each client's list refreshes.

title: http-status-4xx
text:
What's the semantic difference between 401 and 403?
401 Unauthorized means the server doesn't know who you are yet; 403 Forbidden means it knows and still says no. A logged-in user hitting someone else's private album is authenticated but unauthorized, so the right response is 403, not 401.

title: http-status-5xx
text:
Where do you look first for a 500 versus a 502?
500 Internal Server Error means the server that generated the response (your application) failed while handling the request; the proxy just passes it through. 502 Bad Gateway means the gateway/proxy got an invalid response from its upstream; here the upstream is your application, so first check whether the app process crashed, isn't listening, or reset the connection. A failure in a dependency your app calls usually surfaces as your app returning 500 (or 502/504 if your app itself acts as a gateway).

title: rest-nesting
text:
Under common REST resource-modeling conventions, how do you express 'a user has many posts'?
The common REST resource-modeling convention expresses ownership with a nested path: GET /users/{id}/posts reads as this user's posts. It's a convention, not a REST constraint itself; server-side filtering like GET /posts?userId={id} is also reasonable. B stuffs the action into the endpoint name (RPC style); C can't be paginated or addressed on its own; D pushes filtering to the client and wastes bandwidth.

title: http-status-3xx
text:
When should you use 301 versus 302?
A 301 tells clients and caches the address moved for good, so use the new one from now on (301 is heuristically cacheable); a 302 says this redirect is temporary, keep hitting the original URL next time. Use 301 for a permanent GET endpoint migration and 302 for a temporary maintenance redirect. For non-GET endpoints like POST/PUT, clients may switch 301/302 to GET, so use 308 (permanent) / 307 (temporary) to preserve the method and body.

title: database
text:
What design decision do these numbers support?
A well-tuned single Postgres handles 20k+ simple writes per second, so 5k WPS does not justify sharding yet.

title: common-mistakes
text:
What is wrong with that judgment?
5k simple writes is well under a tuned single Postgres's ~20k+ reference, so a queue just for buffering is over-engineering; try batching, leaner indexes, and connection pooling first. The reference depends on hardware, payload, indexes, and durability settings. A queue earns its place for reliable delivery, decoupling, or absorbing spikes beyond single-node capacity.

title: database
text:
What design decision do these latency numbers support?
Reference magnitudes: a database read from memory is about 1-5 ms, from disk about 5-30 ms depending on hardware, and an external cache hit about 1 ms. An indexed primary-key lookup already fits the 50 ms p99 target and 1k QPS doesn't stress the database, so a dedicated cache is extra complexity. Add one when read load nears the database's limit or the latency target is much tighter.

title: database
text:
What design decision do these throughput numbers support?
As reference magnitudes that vary with instance size, transaction complexity, and indexes, a single Aurora or RDS primary can reach tens of thousands of read TPS and roughly 10-20k write TPS. 5k reads plus 3k short write transactions fit, so tune a single primary with read replicas before going multi-primary.

title: database
text:
What design decision does this storage ceiling support?
RDS for PostgreSQL and MySQL allow up to 64 TiB per instance and Aurora more (128 TiB or higher depending on version), so 8TB is far below the ceiling and "storage is filling up" isn't a reason to split now; "split at 100GB" is an outdated instinct. Backup-restore and replica-rebuild time at 8TB still deserve a separate look.

title: database
text:
Which signal truly justifies considering sharding?
Sharding is signaled when capacity or throughput nears single-node limits: data approaching the managed per-instance storage ceiling (64 TiB on RDS), or sustained writes approaching the primary's measured limit on this hardware and workload (simple writes reach the 10-20k+ TPS range; complex transactions far less). A few hundred GB, a million users, or JOINs aren't signals; use read replicas, indexes, and caching first.

title: common-mistakes
text:
After doing the size math first, what is the right call?
Ten million times one kilobyte is about ten gigabytes, and about a hundred with the stated 10x for reviews, which fits on one node; since QPS is also within single-node capacity, sharding is unnecessary for now.

title: estimation
text:
Complete the Yelp capacity estimate:
Ten million times one kilobyte is about ten gigabytes, and roughly a hundred with reviews; that fits a single node, and with QPS also stated to be within single-node capacity, there is no need to shard yet.

title: common-mistakes
text:
Where is this reasoning wrong?
Indexed row lookups take sub-millisecond to a few milliseconds, so the latency argument fails, and with read QPS well within capacity a cache just for them is unnecessary infrastructure; high read QPS or expensive joins can still justify caching.

title: caching
text:
What design decision do these throughput numbers support?
For simple commands on small values, a single in-memory cache instance is in the ~100k+ ops/s range, so 60k fits; this is a ballpark that big values, Lua, complex sorted-set work or network bandwidth can lower, so confirm with a load test.

title: caching
text:
What design decision do these latency and memory numbers support?
Same-region cache reads are under a millisecond, and large-memory nodes reach hundreds of gigabytes, so 300GB fits in one instance and full caching often saves engineering time, as long as you leave headroom for forks, replication buffers and fragmentation.

title: caching
text:
What usually becomes the scaling bottleneck first here?
The dataset is stable at about 200GB, far below the roughly 1TB of memory, while request rate is nearing the benchmarked ops/s limit and network traffic is rising, so throughput or bandwidth is the first bottleneck, not memory.

title: caching
text:
Which set of signals is a reasonable trigger to scale the cache?
Scale when hard metrics near this instance's limits: memory (about 1TB on large instances) or throughput (about 100k+ ops/s for simple commands, confirmed by load tests); key count, a high hit rate, or merely using Redis are not signals.

title: common-mistakes
text:
After estimating about 400GB, what is the right conclusion?
100k times 100k times 40 bytes is about 400GB of raw data at most, the same order as a 1TB instance, so sharding isn't the first move; sorted-set overhead makes real usage higher, so verify it before deciding to shard or cache only active contests.

title: message-queue
text:
What design decision do these throughput numbers support?
A Kafka broker's ballpark is about 0.3M to 1M messages per second, heavily dependent on message size, batching, acks and replication; with batched, compressed 1KB messages, 300k doesn't force a large cluster, but load-test it and still run at least 3 brokers for replication.

title: message-queue
text:
What counterintuitive usage does this enable?
Sub-5ms queue latency lets you use queues inside synchronous request flows, gaining reliable delivery without forcing async APIs.

title: message-queue
text:
What scaling decision do these signals support?
The scaling unit is the broker: its throughput equals partitions on it times MB/s per partition, so you add brokers when that nears the benchmarked ceiling or consumer lag keeps growing.

title: app-server
text:
What design decision does this connection-count number support?
A tuned server (raised file-descriptor limits and kernel settings) can hold roughly 100k+ mostly idle connections, so 80k fits; which resource saturates first depends on load, often memory and descriptors for idle connections and CPU for chatty ones, and production still needs at least two servers for redundancy.

title: app-server
text:
In this situation, what is usually the first bottleneck?
The stated signals, high CPU with spare memory, make CPU the first bottleneck here; for many stateless compute-bound services you size machines as QPS times CPU time per request divided by cores and can spend spare memory on local caching, though I/O- or memory-bound services may differ.

title: app-server
text:
What is a reasonable trigger signal?
Scale horizontally when CPU stays above 70-80%, latency exceeds SLA, memory trends high, or network nears instance limits.

title: app-server
text:
What design decision does this container startup time support?
On spare nodes, container instances are typically ready in tens of seconds, depending on image size, app init and health checks, making on-demand scaling a practical alternative to over-provisioning; adding new VM nodes usually takes minutes, which is why the scenario keeps spare nodes.

title: network
text:
What design decision do these network latency numbers support?
Latency is typically under a millisecond within an AZ, around 1-2ms across AZs in a region (AWS says single-digit milliseconds), and 50-150ms across continents, so same-region multi-AZ gives fault isolation with acceptable latency.

title: hardware
text:
What design decision does this memory-size number support?
Memory-optimized instances reach 4TB or even 24TB of RAM, so a 3TB dataset fits on a single machine without going distributed.

title: hardware
text:
What design decision does this storage-size number support?
Local-SSD instances reach about 60TB (i3en) and HDD about 336TB (d3en), so 40TB fits one machine and capacity isn't the reason to distribute; but these are instance stores that lose data when the instance stops or terminates, so archives still need replication, backups or object storage.

title: message-queue
text:
When is a message queue truly worth introducing? (Select all that apply.)
Queues are justified by guaranteed delivery, event sourcing, write spikes beyond a single database, or decoupling, not by a steady 5k WPS.

title: common-mistakes
text:
Before adding a queue for higher write volume, which simpler tactics should you try first? (Select all that apply.)
Before adding a queue, try batch writes, schema and index tuning, and connection pooling.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision steps for whether to shard in the right order:
Decide sharding by stating the scale, doing the math, comparing to single-node limits, and only then sharding if exceeded.

title: database
text:
Does a single database instance automatically mean a SPOF?
No sharding is not the same as a single point of failure: with cross-AZ replicas and automatic failover, a replica is promoted when the primary fails; HA comes from replication plus failover, while sharding is for scale. A truly lone instance with no replica would be a SPOF.

title: cost
text:
What is the right attitude toward cost in a system-design interview?
Interviews care about order-of-magnitude cost sense, not memorized pricing, though obviously wasteful designs still raise flags.

title: cheat-sheet
text:
What scaling judgment do these cache numbers constrain?
These cache numbers are sizing inputs: with a dataset well under 1TB, memory isn't the bottleneck, ops/s or bandwidth usually is, and you add nodes or shards when those approach single-instance limits.

title: cheat-sheet
text:
What sharding judgment do these database numbers constrain?
These database numbers are planning inputs: they help you avoid premature sharding and focus on the limit you are actually approaching.

title: database
text:
What design decision does this concurrent-connection number support?
PostgreSQL's limit is max_connections (default 100, raisable, and managed services derive it from memory), and each connection is a backend process that costs memory and a fork to open, so 3k short-lived connections are wasteful even under the limit; pool them down to tens or hundreds of real connections.

title: message-queue
text:
What design decision do these message size and retention numbers support?
Kafka persists messages in an on-disk log with retention set by retention.ms or retention.bytes, so months of retention works, and 5KB is far below the default ~1MB per-message limit; size disks as write rate times 5KB times three months times replication factor.

title: interview-method
text:
What is the more professional approach?
Use modern hardware numbers, since quoting outdated constraints signals book knowledge without real experience and leads to over-engineering.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the steps for deciding whether high-looking write throughput needs a queue in order:
Quantify the write pattern, compare to the 20k+ WPS single-node limit, try simple tuning first, and only add a queue if truly exceeded.

title: throughput-anchors
text:
Fill in common system throughput anchors:
Read and write ceilings are not identical: relational single-primary writes are lower than reads, Redis simple commands are similar order, and Kafka depends on message size, batching, partitions, and brokers. These are this lesson's first-pass anchors; read ceilings in particular depend on indexes, cache hit rate, and query complexity, and simple point reads often benchmark higher, so capacity planning must rely on load tests.

title: scaling-units
text:
Fill in common storage and queue scaling units:
Name the unit before the number: Kafka uses partitions and brokers; DynamoDB uses physical partitions of about 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU each; CockroachDB splits data into ranges replicated by Raft; ClickHouse scales out by shards, while parts are per-insert data pieces whose count stresses background merges.

title: hardware
text:
What design decision does this capacity fact support?
S3 limits neither total volume nor object count, and petabyte deployments are routine, so "it won't fit" is no reason to build a cluster; the real questions are cost, storage classes, and read latency, with a cache or CDN for hot footage.

title: network
text:
Compute the egress traffic first — what is the right call?
Egress bandwidth equals operations per second times average object size: 150k times 20KB is 3 gigabytes per second, about 24 gigabits, which saturates a standard 25 Gbps instance, so bandwidth drives scaling here, not memory.

title: caching
text:
After the hit rate drops to 65%, what actually happens on the primary database?
With total reads flat, origin traffic equals total reads times the miss rate: 35% over 8% is about 4.4 times. "Memory is not full" does not mean things are fine, because the cache also shields the primary. At 60% memory use, capacity eviction is probably not the cause, so check TTL changes, key changes, mass invalidation, or access-pattern shifts while protecting the primary with throttling or replicas.

title: database
text:
After adding up the commit latencies, what is the right call?
The scenario gives a measured p99 of about 12ms per commit, so three serial commits approach 36ms and leave only a dozen milliseconds for logic and network. One transaction pays a single WAL flush, at the cost of a bigger transaction and longer-held locks. B contradicts the measurement, C ignores that each commit waits for the log flush, and D treats a given SLO as a derived output. Commit latency depends heavily on storage and settings such as synchronous_commit, and can be an order of magnitude lower on local NVMe, so use measured numbers.

title: app-server
text:
Where should this reference table live?
Standard app servers carry 64 to 512 gigabytes of memory, up to two terabytes on high-memory types, so keeping a 2GB table local removes a network hop per request at the cost of one copy per instance to invalidate.

title: estimation
text:
What is wrong with applying the 20k WPS figure directly here?
These figures are starting points for well-tuned systems on specific workloads, not hard ceilings — multi-table transactions, write amplification from too many indexes, cascading updates and competing reads all lower real write capacity, so benchmark your own write pattern.

title: database
text:
Is this a genuine signal to split the database?
Real limits are not only data volume and throughput: with a two-hour RTO and a full-day restore, that gap alone is a reason to split or at least shrink the single database. First check whether incremental snapshots, replica-side backups, or time-based partition archiving bring restore under two hours; if not, split, accepting the lasting cost of cross-shard queries and rebalancing.

title: definition
text:
What is the core definition of sharding?
In system-design interviews, sharding usually means horizontally splitting data across database or storage nodes. Service instances can also scale horizontally, but that is usually called replicas or load balancing, not database sharding.

title: partitioning-vs-sharding
text:
What is the key difference between partitioning and sharding?
In common system-design interview usage, partitioning usually means splitting a table inside one database instance, while sharding stresses spreading data across multiple independent database machines. This is a convention: DDIA treats the two words as synonyms, and Kafka and DynamoDB call cross-machine slices "partitions". So the safest move is to say plainly whether the data lives on one machine or several. Note that replicas also span machines, but each holds the full data set, so that isn't sharding.

title: partitioning-types
text:
Which statements about single-machine partitioning are correct? (Select all that apply.)
Single-machine partitioning stays inside one database instance. Horizontal partitioning splits rows and vertical partitioning splits columns; it can reduce scan and maintenance scope, but it does not add machines or scale writes across machines.

title: when-to-shard
text:
What should you prioritize at this stage?
If the bottleneck is large-table scans, index or maintenance scope, or historical-data cleanup, single-machine partitioning may be enough. It does not add machines, but it lets the database scan less, maintain less, and clean up data more easily.

title: when-to-shard
text:
Put the decision chain for introducing sharding in an interview in the right order.
A good interview answer estimates capacity first, proves one database is insufficient, and only then proposes sharding.

title: shard-key
text:
What properties does a good shard key usually need? (Select all that apply.)
A good shard key has high cardinality, balanced distribution, and matches the dominant query patterns.

title: shard-key
text:
Why is a boolean field like `is_premium` a poor shard key?
A boolean shard key has extremely low cardinality and tends to create only two imbalanced shards.

title: shard-key
text:
If you shard by country and 90% of users are in the US, what is the direct consequence?
A skewed shard key like country can overload the dominant value's shard while others remain underused.

title: shard-key
text:
What is the most reasonable default shard key?
user_id has high cardinality and spreads evenly — 100 million users over 16 shards is roughly 6 million per shard — and user-scoped queries stay on a single shard.

title: time-sharding
text:
What is the common problem with range sharding a constantly growing write table by `created_at`?
Because new rows have created_at close to now, a range router sends almost all inserts to the newest time-range shard. Older shards mostly serve historical reads, while the newest shard carries the write load.

title: range-sharding
text:
How does range-based sharding assign data?
Range-based sharding assigns continuous key ranges to shards, which is simple and supports range scans.

title: range-sharding
text:
Which sharding strategy may fit this case well?
The shard key should align with tenant or company identity; range-based here refers to the distribution strategy, where each tenant receives a continuous ID range that maps to a shard.

title: hash-sharding
text:
