What is the basic routing rule for hash-based sharding?
Hash sharding hashes the shard key and maps the hash result to a shard, often using modulo.

title: hash-sharding
text:
Which strategy would you usually propose first in an interview?
Hash-based sharding is the common default because it distributes many keys evenly across shards.

title: resharding
text:
What goes wrong with simple `hash(key) % N` when scaling from 4 shards to 5?
Only keys where h mod 4 equals h mod 5 stay put — those with h mod 20 in 0–3, about 20%; the remaining ~80% move, so most of the data has to migrate in one night. Consistent hashing moves only about 1/N of keys in expectation when a node is added, which is its selling point.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
What idea should you introduce?
The rule is not hash(key) % N. Compute h=H(key), then choose the first node clockwise on the hash ring. A new node only takes the key range between its predecessor and itself.

title: directory-sharding
text:
What is the core mechanism of directory-based sharding?
Directory-based sharding uses a lookup table or service to map each key to its shard.

title: directory-sharding
text:
What are the typical tradeoffs of directory-based sharding compared with hash or range sharding? (Select all that apply.)
Explicit mappings let you point one tenant at a specific shard; the cost is an extra remote lookup on the request path (the scenario says there is no cache) and the directory becoming a critical dependency — if it is slow or down, healthy data shards are unreachable. Real systems often cache the directory in the routing layer to remove most lookups, at the cost of invalidating the cache when mappings change.

title: directory-sharding
text:
Which approach gives you the finest-grained control?
A directory can explicitly move hot keys to dedicated shards, which formula-based routing cannot do as easily.

title: hotspots
text:
What does a hot spot mean in sharding?
A hot spot is an overloaded shard that receives much more data or traffic than the others.

title: hotspots
text:
Why can normal hash distribution not fully solve the celebrity problem?
Hashing distributes keys, but it cannot split the traffic of one inherently hot key by itself.

title: hotspot-detection
text:
Which metrics help detect a shard hot spot? (Select all that apply.)
Break latency, CPU and request volume down per shard: when balanced, each shard carries roughly total QPS ÷ 16; a shard that stays clearly above its peers and approaches its own capacity is the hotspot. The alert threshold depends on per-shard headroom and your SLO; there is no universal multiplier.

title: hotspot-mitigation
text:
What are common ways to handle shard hot spots? (Select all that apply.)
Three families of fixes: isolate (put the hot key on its own shard so other users stop suffering), spread (a compound key spreads one user's data across shards by date, at the cost of fan-out when reading that user's full history), and split/rebalance (move the other keys off the hot shard). The scenario allows changing the shard key, so B applies. Adding app servers does not relieve a hot database shard.

title: compound-key
text:
Which shard key change can spread one user's load across time?
A compound key like user_id plus date spreads one user's time-partitioned workload across shards.

title: cross-shard
text:
What is a cross-shard operation?
A cross-shard operation touches multiple shards and requires coordinating or aggregating their results.

title: cross-shard
text:
If you shard by `user_id`, which query is most likely to hit only one shard?
With user_id sharding, a single user's profile lookup routes to one shard, while global aggregates span many shards.

title: cross-shard
text:
Why is real-time “global top 10 posts” expensive after sharding by `user_id`?
A global top-ten query is expensive because candidates are spread across shards and must be merged.

title: cross-shard-mitigation
text:
What are ways to reduce the cost of common cross-shard queries? (Select all that apply.)
Trending tolerates minutes of staleness: a cache absorbs repeated all-shard queries and a background job precomputes the aggregate; for order details, denormalize the product name and price snapshot onto the order's shard so one query returns everything, at the cost of extra storage and harder updates. Querying every shard live per request is the pattern to avoid.

title: cross-shard-mitigation
text:
What is the most reasonable handling strategy?
Trending results tolerate slight staleness, so caching or precomputing avoids fan-out on every request.

title: transactions
text:
Why does sharding make formerly simple database transactions more complex?
Sharding is often introduced for capacity or read/write pressure; transaction complexity is a side effect. A single-database transaction covers one database instance, so related writes on different shards need coordination.

title: transactions
text:
What is the main tradeoff of two-phase commit for cross-shard transactions?
Two-phase commit provides atomic commit across multiple databases: either every shard commits or all abort. The cost is extra network rounds, lock waiting, and blocking under coordinator or participant failures.

title: transactions
text:
What is the best direction for transaction design?
The best design keeps related user data on one shard so normal single-shard transactions still work.

title: saga
text:
Put the saga compensation flow for a cross-shard transfer in the right order.
A saga coordinates cross-shard work through independent steps plus compensating actions on failure.

title: eventual-consistency
text:
What consistency model is usually acceptable for this kind of scenario?
A displayed counter can lag a few seconds and converge asynchronously; the price is that two shards may show numbers tens apart at the same moment.

title: modern-databases
text:
How do modern databases usually help you handle sharding? (Select all that apply.)
Modern databases automate routing and balancing work, but they do not remove the need to choose a good key.

title: modern-databases
text:
Which statement about their sharding mechanisms is more accurate?
All three distribute data by key, but the internal unit differs: Cassandra uses tokens/vnodes, DynamoDB uses internal partitions, and MongoDB uses chunks. Do not describe them as one identical consistent-hashing implementation.

title: modern-databases
text:
What is a clear enough way to state the sharding design?
A managed database saves you from writing routing code, but you still choose the partition key. Per AWS docs, one internal partition handles roughly 3,000 RCU and 1,000 WCU, and DynamoDB splits partitions automatically, so what matters is spreading traffic across many key values. user_id has high cardinality and matches per-user access, so it rarely creates a single hot key.

title: capacity-planning
text:
What does this ceiling mean for your capacity plan?
A single managed database cluster has a service storage limit (roughly 256 TiB for Aurora as given; check current AWS docs). At 200 TiB doubling yearly you hit it in about four months, so plan sharding now; archiving cold orders can also buy time. A pricier instance class doesn't raise the storage limit, and dropping indexes only frees a fraction of the space.

title: interview-formula
text:
Complete the three-step interview formula for introducing sharding.
The interview formula is to identify the bottleneck, prove one database is insufficient, and then propose sharding.

title: interview-answer
text:
Put a sharding interview answer for a social app in the right order.
A strong answer chooses the key from access patterns, selects a distribution strategy, then explains tradeoffs and growth.

title: premature-sharding
text:
What is the risk of proposing sharding too early in a system design interview?
Premature sharding adds real operational and consistency complexity before proving the scale requires it.

title: pitfalls
text:
What problems usually come from choosing the wrong shard key? (Select all that apply.)
merchant_id piles the top merchants' orders onto a few shards (data skew), and those shards also take the big merchants' write traffic (hot shard); the dominant query is by user_id, which carries no shard key, so it must fan out to every shard and merge. Sharding does not make the database's own limits disappear.

title: strategy-summary
text:
Complete the keywords for the three sharding strategies.
Range sharding splits continuous ranges of the original key; hash sharding first scatters keys into hash space; directory sharding looks up an explicit mapping. They trade off range scans, balance, and flexibility.

title: routing-flow
text:
Put the routing flow for one hash-sharded read request in the right order.
Hash-sharded routing extracts the shard key, hashes it, chooses the shard, and queries only that shard.

title: final-summary
text:
Which two design decisions should you answer with?
The shard key decides which field groups the data; the distribution strategy decides how those key values map to machines. The same user_id key can be distributed by range, hash, or directory.

title: partitioning-sharding-code
text:
Where do partitioning and sharding happen in this code?
Partitioning happens inside one database: the database places rows into local partitions by created_at. Sharding happens in the application or routing layer: it chooses which database connection to use by user_id.

title: partition-key-examples
text:
Which partition-key choices are usually reasonable? (Select all that apply.)
Choose a partition key from the dominant query pattern and data lifecycle. In SQL, a partition key often enables pruning and retention; in DynamoDB-like NoSQL systems, it is closer to a distribution key that decides the internal partition.

title: shard-key-vs-partition-key
text:
Which statements about choosing the same or different shard and partition keys are correct? (Select all that apply.)
Either can be right. The same key fits per-user or per-tenant locality; different keys are common when user_id/chat_id/tenant_id picks the machine and created_at or a time bucket handles local pruning and retention.

title: cross-shard-merge
text:
What design consequence does this code illustrate?
The shard key defines the fast path. A user_id query hits one shard; a product_id query finds data spread across user shards, so it fans out and merges. Cross-shard writes need saga or 2PC.

title: shard-boundary-smell
text:
What signal is a constant need for cross-shard transactions?
An order and its line items are one aggregate and belong on the same shard; using different shard keys for the two tables is what makes every checkout cross shards. Co-locating by user_id turns checkout into a single-shard local transaction, at the cost of one data migration. B keeps 2PC on the hot path where a coordinator or shard failure stalls the transaction; C only scatters the same checkout further; D distributed SQL can commit atomically across machines, but it still runs 2PC/consensus internally, so the coordination cost does not vanish.

title: scale-read-order
text:
What is the first move when read throughput runs out?
Writes are only at 30% CPU, so the bottleneck is reads; queries already use indexes, so per-query cost cannot drop much further and you need more machines for reads — exactly what read replicas provide. Shard only if replicas still fall short. Cost: with the usual asynchronous replication, replica reads can be slightly stale.

title: partition-vs-shard-throughput
text:
Why can in-instance partitioning not fix this write bottleneck?
Partitioning only splits the table logically, so every partition still shares one machine’s CPU, memory and connection pool and every write still queues behind the same write-ahead log. Sharding gives each shard its own database, so write throughput grows with machine count.

title: shard-key-orders
text:
Which field should be the shard key for this orders table?
99% of requests are scoped to one order; order_id has hundreds of millions of values and hashes evenly, so each request hits one shard. order_status has a handful of values and is badly skewed; created_at is not aligned with the dominant query, so an order-id lookup cannot find its shard (and under range sharding every new order would hit the newest shard); countries are highly skewed. Cost: per-customer history fans out unless you build a customer_id read model.

title: rebalance-trigger
text:
How do the two differ in how a rebalance is triggered?
MongoDB's background balancer notices when per-shard data size differs beyond a threshold and automatically migrates ranges (chunks) to emptier shards (since 6.0 it no longer auto-splits by chunk size); Vitess supports online resharding, but an operator starts the Reshard workflow and switches traffic. Check which model you mean before saying the database scales itself.

title: rare-global-query
text:
How should this global count be handled?
What decides whether to optimise is how often the query runs, not how slow one run is. Three fan-outs a day cost nothing overall, while a cache or counter adds state you have to refresh and reconcile.

title: sharding-layer
text:
How can sharding be introduced while keeping MySQL?
Vitess and Citus sit in front of MySQL or Postgres and take over query routing, cross-shard operations and resharding, so your code keeps speaking SQL. The cost is one more component to run, and cross-shard queries stay expensive.

title: definition
text:
What is the core role of an API Gateway in a microservice architecture?
An API Gateway is the client-facing entry point that routes requests to backend services, not a pure load balancer or a home for business logic.

title: responsibility
text:
When you mention an API Gateway in an interview, what core responsibility is easiest to miss?
The gateway’s primary responsibility is request routing, while authentication and rate limiting are secondary middleware.

title: middleware
text:
Which items are common API Gateway middleware or cross-cutting concerns?
Gateways centralize cross-cutting middleware such as authentication, rate limiting, and CORS handling to avoid duplicating them per service.

title: request-flow
text:
Put a request through an API Gateway in the usual order.
A typical gateway flow validates, applies middleware, routes, waits for the backend response, transforms it, and optionally caches it.

title: validation
text:
Why does an API Gateway usually validate a request before routing it?
Early validation rejects malformed or incomplete requests before they consume backend compute and I/O.

title: routing
text:
Fill in the most common routing key of an API Gateway.
The `/users/*` prefix example only fits the URL path; method, query parameters, and headers are secondary match conditions already listed in the sentence rather than blanks.

title: routing
text:
What component best fits the entry layer?
A gateway fits microservices because it gives clients one stable endpoint while hiding internal service topology.

title: scope
text:
What is the right way to decide whether adding an API Gateway is worth it?
A gateway is most useful for microservices and can be unnecessary complexity for a simple monolith.

title: middleware
text:
Which API Gateway middleware is usually worth mentioning in interviews?
Authentication, rate limiting, and IP allow/block lists are the gateway middleware interviewers expect to hear.

title: caching
text:
How can the API Gateway optimize this endpoint?
Gateway caching fits public deterministic responses where the same input always returns the same output.

title: caching
text:
Which response type is the worst fit for gateway-level caching?
Gateway caching is risky for user-specific private responses because a shared cache entry can leak between users.

title: caching
text:
Which caching strategies can an API Gateway use?
Gateway caching can store whole responses or stable fragments, but it always needs TTL or event-based invalidation.

title: backend-communication
text:
What role can an API Gateway play when client and internal protocols differ?
A gateway can translate between client-facing HTTP and an internal protocol like gRPC when the two genuinely differ.

title: response-transform
text:
Fill in the goal of response transformation at the gateway.
The sentence already states "internals can change without clients changing", and the standard term for that relationship is decoupling. That is the point of response transformation: a stable external API contract while internals evolve freely.

title: scaling
text:
What is the most straightforward way to scale it?
A stateless gateway scales horizontally by adding instances behind a load balancer.

title: load-balancing
text:
What is the difference between client-to-gateway load balancing and gateway-to-service load balancing?
Client-to-gateway load balancing is handled by a front load balancer, while the gateway itself balances traffic across backend instances.

title: global-distribution
text:
How should the API Gateway layer be designed?
For global users, gateways can be deployed regionally with GeoDNS routing and synchronized configuration.

title: global-distribution
text:
What should you consider when deploying API Gateways globally?
Global gateway deployments need regional instances, geo-aware routing, and synchronized configuration.

title: managed-vs-open-source
text:
What is the main tradeoff between managed and self-managed API Gateway options?
Managed gateways (AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management) hand deployment, scaling, and patching to the cloud provider and charge per request — cheap at low volume, potentially pricier than self-hosting at high volume — and customization is bounded by the platform (e.g. custom auth via a Lambda authorizer). Self-managed gateways (Kong, Tyk) allow arbitrary plugins and full deployment control, but the team carries the operational labor. For a five-person team with no SRE, ops capacity is usually the tighter constraint.

title: options
text:
Which options are cloud-provider managed API Gateway or API Management products?
AWS API Gateway, Azure API Management, and Google Cloud API Gateway are fully managed gateway / API-management products where the cloud provider runs the gateway. Kong is an open-source gateway usually deployed and operated by the team (Kong Inc. also sells its own SaaS, but it is not a cloud provider's native product). Note: Google Cloud Endpoints has a managed control plane but you deploy the ESP proxy yourself, which is why API Gateway is used here.

title: options
text:
Which options are open-source API Gateways the team can deploy and operate itself?
Kong, Tyk, and Express Gateway are open-source options a team can self-host, while AWS API Gateway is a managed cloud product.

title: interview-use
text:
What is the best way to introduce the API Gateway in the interview?
In interviews, mention the gateway briefly for routing and middleware, then return to the core system design.

title: interview-use
text:
Complete this concise interview sentence.
A concise interview framing is that the gateway handles routing and basic middleware such as authentication and rate limiting.

title: coupling
text:
What problem do microservice clients usually face without an API Gateway?
Without a gateway, clients become coupled to internal service addresses, protocols, and API details.

title: overuse
text:
What is the main risk of forcing an API Gateway in front of a simple monolith?
Adding a gateway to a simple monolith can add deployment and debugging complexity without a meaningful routing benefit.

title: routing-config
text:
What does this routing configuration do?
The route table maps the /orders path prefix to the order service on port 8081.

title: aws
text:
Which capability set is commonly associated with AWS API Gateway?
AWS API Gateway supports REST and WebSocket APIs, throttling, API keys, Lambda integration, and CloudWatch monitoring.

title: open-source
text:
Which open-source gateway best matches this need?
Kong is built on NGINX and is known for its broad plugin ecosystem.

title: open-source
text:
Which open-source gateway best matches this need?
Tyk's open-source gateway ships built-in GraphQL proxying, so it is the most direct match for "open source plus native GraphQL". Kong OSS can pass GraphQL traffic through, but deeper GraphQL features are mostly enterprise plugins; AWS API Gateway is a managed product, not a self-hosted open-source option. Multi-data-center is not the differentiator: Kong also deploys across DCs, and Tyk's MDCB is a commercial component.

title: open-source
text:
Which open-source gateway best matches this need?
Express Gateway is built on Express.js and is configured and extended in JavaScript, so it is the closest fit to a Node.js stack among these options. Its upstream project has been inactive for years, though, so verify maintenance status before production use; the card tests stack fit, not a current top recommendation.

title: state
text:
Why is an API Gateway usually a good component to scale horizontally?
Gateways usually scale well because they are stateless and each instance can independently handle requests.

title: middleware-placement
text:
Where should these shared entry policies live?
Shared authentication and basic rate limiting belong naturally in gateway middleware to avoid duplicating them per service.

title: service-discovery
text:
Why should a gateway integrate with service discovery?
Service discovery lets a gateway route to healthy backend instances without hardcoding fixed addresses.

title: timeouts
text:
What is the purpose of setting a response timeout at the API Gateway?
Gateway timeouts prevent slow backend calls from tying up entry-point resources indefinitely.

title: logging
text:
Why is the API Gateway a good place to log entry traffic and basic metrics?
The gateway is a good place for entry traffic logs because it sees all client-facing requests in one layer.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for whether to introduce an API Gateway in order.
The decision starts with microservices and client coupling, then adds a stateless gateway for routing and middleware while noting when it is overkill.

title: middleware
text:
Should TLS terminate at the API Gateway or stay encrypted all the way to each backend service?
The scenario says the internal hop need not be encrypted and the gateway must route and authenticate by URL, so terminate TLS at the gateway: forty certificates collapse to one and the gateway sees L7 content. Passthrough (B) hides the URL from the gateway; C duplicates auth forty times; D exposes internal topology. If compliance required end-to-end encryption, you would re-encrypt to backends (TLS/mTLS, e.g. a service mesh), which is not this scenario.

title: middleware
text:
How does it break if you rewrite the response shape in place instead of versioning at the gateway?
The server still returns 200; the break is in the application contract: the old app parses by old field names and types, which no longer exist. The status code hides this, so version at the gateway (/v1 vs /v2) to keep old clients on the old contract, maintaining both until old traffic drains. Purely additive fields usually don't break old clients, which ignore them.

title: caching
text:
Should the gateway's response cache live in each instance's memory or in Redis?
Immediate invalidation, no inter-instance broadcast, and an acceptable 1 ms hop together point to a shared cache: delete one Redis key and every instance sees fresh content, without diluting hit rate across twenty copies. A waits up to ten minutes; C is immediate but is exactly the broadcast machinery the scenario rules out; D gives up caching an identical-for-everyone page at the edge. If the latency budget could not absorb 1 ms, C (near cache plus broadcast invalidation) would win.

title: interview-strategy
text:
On the whiteboard, should the entry LB and API Gateway be drawn as two boxes or one?
A feed interview is decided by storage and fan-out, so collapsing the entry into one box buys time, as long as you can still explain both balancing hops when asked.

title: background
text:
Who originally built Cassandra, and for what use case?
Cassandra was originally built at Facebook to power its rapidly scaling inbox search feature before being open-sourced and widely adopted.

title: positioning
text:
What is the most accurate one-sentence description of Cassandra?
Cassandra is an open-source distributed NoSQL database with a partitioned wide-column model, tunable consistency, and common eventual-consistency/high-availability usage.

title: positioning
text:
Which two classic systems influenced Cassandra's architecture?
Cassandra combines elements of Amazon's Dynamo for decentralized distribution and Google's Bigtable for the wide-column data model.

title: data-model
text:
Fill in Cassandra's data hierarchy:
Cassandra organizes data as keyspace, table, row, and column, where the keyspace defines replication and the column is the actual storage unit.

title: data-model
text:
Besides being the top-level namespace, what does a keyspace control?
A keyspace is the top-level unit that defines the replication strategy for redundancy and availability and owns any user-defined types.

title: data-model
text:
How does Cassandra's wide-column model differ from relational databases in which columns each row has?
CQL columns must be declared up front, but the wide-column store writes per column: a column a row never wrote does not exist on disk, which suits sparse data; in a relational table every row logically has every column, with missing values as NULL.

title: data-model
text:
When two replicas write conflicting values to the same column, how does leaderless Cassandra resolve it?
Each cell carries a write timestamp assigned by the client or coordinator, and replicas reconcile by last write wins on that timestamp, breaking ties by value. The cost is that clock skew can let a truly later write lose.

title: primary-key
text:
Fill in the parts of a Cassandra primary key:
A Cassandra primary key consists of one or more partition keys that place the row and optional clustering keys that sort rows within the partition.

title: primary-key
text:
What does the partition key do?
The partition key is hashed to determine which partition and therefore which nodes store the row.

title: primary-key
text:
What does the clustering key do?
Clustering keys determine the sorted order of rows within a partition, which you choose based on how the app reads data.

title: primary-key
text:
Which CQL primary-key definition is correct?
The inner parentheses group a and b into a composite partition key while c outside them becomes the clustering key.

title: primary-key
text:
What does CQL PRIMARY KEY (a, b, c), without inner parentheses, mean?
Without inner parentheses the first column is the partition key and the remaining columns are clustering keys.

title: primary-key
text:
How does Cassandra's primary key map to DynamoDB's primary key?
Cassandra's partition key and clustering key map almost one-to-one to DynamoDB's partition key and sort key.

title: partitioning
text:
What problems does hash(value) % num_nodes create?
Modulo hashing remaps nearly every key when nodes change, and its fixed 1/N granularity can't weight machines by capacity or rebalance locally. Consistent hashing fixes the first; vnodes (many tokens per machine, more for stronger ones) fix the second.

title: partitioning
text:
How does consistent hashing choose the node for a value?
Consistent hashing maps a value to an integer on a ring and walks clockwise to the first node, which stores the value.

title: partitioning
text:
Under consistent hashing, how much data is affected when a node joins or leaves?
With single-token consistent hashing, the new node takes over only the range just before it, pulling data from its clockwise neighbor—about 1/N of the total—while the rest stays put. With vnodes it takes small slices from many nodes, still about 1/N overall.

title: partitioning
text:
Consistent hashing limits remapping but may still skew load. How does Cassandra smooth it out?
Splitting each physical machine into many vnodes chops its ranges into small, scattered pieces so totals even out, and stronger machines can own more vnodes. Vnodes fix uneven ranges only; a hot partition key needs a key redesign.

title: partitioning
text:
Fill in the terms in a consistent-hashing ring:
Values hash to tokens on the ring, virtual nodes owned by physical machines cover those tokens, and stronger machines take more vnodes.

title: replication
text:
With replication factor 3, how does Cassandra choose the three replica nodes?
Cassandra places replicas by scanning clockwise from the hashed vnode, skipping vnodes that live on a physical node already holding a replica.

title: replication
text:
Why should replica placement skip vnodes on the same physical node?
Skipping vnodes on the same physical machine ensures a single hardware failure cannot take down multiple replicas at once.

title: replication
text:
Which replication strategy should you choose?
NetworkTopologyStrategy is the production-recommended strategy because it is datacenter and rack aware, physically separating replicas.

title: replication
text:
How do NetworkTopologyStrategy and SimpleStrategy differ in awareness of physical topology?
NTS spreads replicas across data centers and racks by reading topology, while SimpleStrategy just walks the ring and ignores where machines physically sit.

title: replication
text:
Which CQL statement is correct?
With NetworkTopologyStrategy you specify a replica count per named datacenter on the keyspace.

title: consistency
text:
What level of transactions and ACID does Cassandra support?
Through 5.0 Cassandra has no relational-style general multi-row ACID transactions. Single-partition writes are atomic and isolated; logged batches make cross-partition writes eventually all apply but without isolation or conditions; CAS/LWT does conditional updates within one partition. A transfer that needs checks and isolation belongs in a transactional database.

title: consistency
text:
Fill in Cassandra's consistency levels:
Reads and writes set consistency levels independently; QUORUM = floor(RF/2)+1, so 2 when RF=3. Use LOCAL_QUORUM for a majority within the local data center.

title: consistency
text:
With replication factor 3, how many replicas must respond for QUORUM?
With three replicas a quorum is two nodes, computed as n over two plus one.

title: consistency
text:
If both reads and writes use QUORUM, what guarantee do you get and why?
With RF=3, W=2 and R=2 give W+R>RF, so the read set includes at least one replica that acknowledged the write; the coordinator picks the newest timestamp and read-repairs, so a successful QUORUM write is visible. Concurrent writes to the same column are still resolved by timestamp LWW.

title: consistency
text:
Under this ONE-heavy setup without LWT, what baseline consistency model does Cassandra provide?
With ONE only a single replica must respond; the others catch up via hinted handoff, read repair, and anti-entropy repair, so the baseline is eventual consistency. That is not true at every level: QUORUM reads and writes (W+R>RF) give read-after-write visibility, and LWT with SERIAL reads gives per-partition linearizability, though neither amounts to multi-row transactions.

title: consistency
text:
What is the best approach in Cassandra?
Consistency is set per operation: QUORUM on both the settings write and read gives W+R>RF so successful writes are visible, while other paths stay at ONE. A local cache only covers the same device and fails across devices.

title: query-routing
text:
Which Cassandra node can receive a client query?
Any node can act as the query coordinator and forward the request to the replicas that hold the data, eliminating single points of failure.

title: query-routing
text:
How does the coordinator know which nodes store the data?
Each node combines gossip-learned cluster state with consistent hashing and the replication configuration to locate the replicas itself.

title: storage-model
text:
What is the core tradeoff of Cassandra's LSM tree versus the B-tree used by many databases?
An LSM tree favors write speed by making writes append-only, at the cost of reads that may consult the memtable and several SSTables.

title: storage-model
text:
How does Cassandra's LSM-based storage engine handle updates and deletes?
Every create, update, or delete is a new appended entry, with deletes written as tombstones and the row state derived from update ordering.

title: storage-model
text:
Fill in the three main components of Cassandra's LSM-based storage engine:
The commit log provides durability via replay after a crash, the memtable holds the latest writes in memory, and SSTables are immutable sorted files on disk — together they deliver high write throughput. Note that in the default periodic mode an ack does not wait for fsync, so a single node can lose its last few seconds of writes on power loss and relies on other replicas; "acked means on disk" requires batch or group mode.

title: storage-model
text:
Put Cassandra's single-node write path in the correct order:
A write hits the commit log first for durability, then the memtable, which later flushes to an immutable SSTable, after which its commit log entries are purged.

title: storage-model
text:
Why must Cassandra write the Commit Log before the Memtable?
The memtable lives in memory and vanishes on power loss; the commit log is a write-ahead log, and in batch mode the ack only happens after fsync, so replaying it on restart recovers the acknowledged write. In the default periodic mode the ack doesn't wait for fsync, so the last few seconds of writes may survive only on other replicas and come back via hints or repair.

title: storage-model
text:
When is a Memtable flushed to an SSTable?
A memtable flushes to disk as an immutable SSTable once it hits a size threshold or after a period of time elapses.

title: storage-model
text:
Put Cassandra's read path for one key in the correct order:
A read checks the memtable first, then uses bloom filters to pick candidate SSTables, reading them newest to oldest.

title: storage-model
text:
What does a Bloom filter do in Cassandra's LSM read path?
Bloom filters let Cassandra skip SSTables that definitely do not contain the key, avoiding wasted disk reads.

title: storage-model
text:
What does compaction do?
Heavy updates and deletes bloat SSTables; compaction periodically merge-sorts several SSTables into new files keeping only the newest version of each key. Tombstones are only purged during compaction once they are older than gc_grace_seconds (default 10 days, leaving a repair window so deleted data doesn't resurrect).

title: storage-model
text:
How does an SSTable index speed up disk reads?
Cassandra keeps index files mapping keys to byte offsets within SSTables so it can seek directly to the data on disk.

title: storage-model
text:
Which storage engine or database style fits better?
Cassandra's LSM-based storage turns writes into appends and batched flushes, making it ideal for write-heavy telemetry workloads.

title: gossip
text:
How do Cassandra nodes share cluster-state information?
Cassandra spreads cluster state peer-to-peer through gossip, with each node periodically exchanging information with others.

title: gossip
text:
Fill in gossip's version-control mechanism:
Generation plus version lets a node compare how fresh information about the same peer is: a restart yields a larger generation and version only grows within one run, so stale state never overwrites newer state and gossip converges to the correct cluster view.

title: gossip
text:
What role do seed nodes play in gossip?
Seed nodes are known addresses listed in configuration (seed_provider, usually static in cassandra.yaml): a starting node contacts them first to learn cluster membership, and each gossip round also contacts a seed with some probability so information doesn't get stuck locally, preventing isolated sub-clusters. Seeds hold no special data and aren't query coordinators.

title: gossip
text:
Which information does gossip track and spread?
Gossip carries cluster metadata: liveness, schema version, and each node's generation/version. When a node sees a peer's schema version differ from its own, it pulls the definition through separate schema-sync messages — a new table missing on some nodes usually means that step hasn't converged. Row data travels over replication and the read/write path, never gossip.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
What mechanism does decentralized Cassandra use to detect node failures?
Cassandra uses a phi accrual failure detector during gossip, with each node independently deciding whether another node is available.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
What happens after a node is convicted as unavailable?
A convicted node stops receiving writes but rejoins the cluster once it starts heartbeating again.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
Why doesn't Cassandra automatically mark a node as permanently down?
Never auto-declaring a node dead prevents intermittent failures or restarts from triggering expensive unnecessary data rebalancing.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
The write returns success to the client; what mechanism lets the offline replica catch up on this write after it recovers?
QUORUM needs only 2 of 3 replicas to ack, so the write succeeds; the coordinator stores a hint for the offline replica and replays it once gossip reports it back. Hints are a short-term, best-effort catch-up mechanism (no longer recorded past max_hint_window), and long-term consistency still relies on repair. With CL=ALL the write would fail outright for lack of replicas, since hints don't count toward the consistency level.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
Which statement about the hint lifecycle is correct?
Hinted handoff is only a short-term catch-up mechanism: once a node has been down longer than max_hint_window, coordinators stop recording hints for it. Three days far exceeds three hours, so most missed writes have no hint, and the returning node needs nodetool repair (or a rebuild); read repair only fixes data that happens to be read and isn't the primary remedy.

title: data-modeling
text:
What is the fundamental difference between relational modeling and Cassandra's query-driven modeling?
Relational modeling is entity-relationship driven with normalization, while Cassandra modeling is query driven and denormalizes as needed.

title: data-modeling
text:
Which capabilities does Cassandra not support?
Cassandra has no joins, foreign keys, or ad hoc multi-table aggregations; it serves single-table queries keyed by partition.

title: data-modeling
text:
Fill in the four major Cassandra data-modeling considerations:
Model around the partition key, worst-case partition size, clustering order, and what data must be denormalized across tables.

title: data-modeling
text:
What is the standard Cassandra modeling move?
In Cassandra you create one table per access pattern and denormalize the data into each, accepting duplication.

title: discord-example
text:
What was Discord's initial primary-key design for the messages table?
Partitioning by channel with messages clustered by descending message id serves recent-message queries from a single partition.

title: discord-example
text:
Why did Discord choose Snowflake IDs instead of created_at?
The key must be unique: two messages arriving in the same millisecond collide on created_at, while a Snowflake ID combines timestamp, worker id, and sequence number, making it globally unique and chronologically sortable.

title: discord-example
text:
What direct query benefit comes from using channel_id as the partition key?
Partitioning by channel lets one partition serve a channel's messages, avoiding slow scatter-gather queries across many nodes.

title: discord-example
text:
What production problem did Discord's first schema hit?
Very busy channels created huge ever-growing partitions, and large partitions in Cassandra hit serious performance problems.

title: discord-example
text:
What was Discord's schema fix?
Discord added a ten-day time bucket to the partition key so even the busiest channel's partition stays bounded and new buckets roll over time.

title: discord-example
text:
What does a fixed ten-day bucket window do for partition size and operations?
Discord bounds each channel's partition by bucketing messages into fixed ten-day windows anchored to its own epoch, so partitions stop growing without any manual migration.

title: discord-example
text:
After adding buckets, when does a recent-message query need to read multiple partitions?
Most recent-message queries hit one bucket, except right after a new bucket starts or for inactive channels whose messages sit in older buckets.

title: discord-example
text:
Put the Discord message-storage decision chain in the correct order:
The requirement of recent per-channel reads led to channel partitioning with descending clustering, whose large-partition cost was mitigated by adding a ten-day bucket.

title: ticketmaster-example
text:
Why is this browse UI a good fit for Cassandra?
The browsing UI tolerates stale availability but must always be up, and the checkout path verifies against a consistent database anyway.

title: ticketmaster-example
text:
What problem does PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_id) create for a hot 10,000+ seat event?
With one partition per event the database repeatedly aggregates over ten thousand seat rows for every popular browsing request.

title: ticketmaster-example
text:
What should the improved tickets table primary key be?
Making event and section a composite partition key shrinks partitions and spreads an event across nodes while matching the section-level UX.

title: ticketmaster-example
text:
What is the Cassandra-style solution?
Denormalizing ticket counts and price floors into an event sections table avoids aggregation, and the stats tolerate eventual consistency.

title: ticketmaster-example
text:
Why is a single event_id partition acceptable for event_sections when reading all sections?
Events rarely have more than about a hundred sections, so a single partition per event easily serves the venue overview query.

title: advanced-features
text:
Which Cassandra feature best fits this need?
SAI (Storage-Attached Index) is a node-local secondary index attached to each node's SSTables. It fits infrequent filter queries that don't justify a separate denormalized table; the cost is that queries without a partition key fan out to all nodes, so they're slower than partition-key lookups. Hot, core queries should still be modeled around the partition key.

title: advanced-features
text:
What is the value of Cassandra Materialized Views?
Materialized views make Cassandra maintain a derived table automatically, so the application no longer writes to multiple denormalized tables itself.

title: advanced-features
text:
What is the right path for full-text search over Cassandra data?
Cassandra's indexes (SASI/SAI) at most offer substring or tokenized matching, with no relevance scoring or typo tolerance. The common approach keeps Cassandra as the primary store and syncs data to Elasticsearch / OpenSearch via CDC or dual writes; the search engine's inverted index serves queries, and details are fetched back from Cassandra by id.

title: when-to-use
text:
Which system traits make Cassandra a good choice?
The first four are Cassandra's sweet spot: high availability, high write throughput, sparse wide columns, and query-driven modeling. CQL tables still have an explicit schema; sparse columns just cost nothing and adding columns is cheap. Joins and ad hoc aggregation are its weak spot.

title: when-to-use
text:
Is Cassandra a good fit?
Strict multi-row transactions plus complex joins hit Cassandra's weak spots: it only offers single-partition LWT (CAS), no general multi-row ACID transactions, and no joins; QUORUM only addresses read/write visibility, not transactional semantics.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the full Cassandra-selection decision chain in the correct order:
High write throughput and availability needs point to Cassandra's LSM and leaderless replication, whose consistency, transaction, and query costs are mitigated by quorum operations and query-driven modeling.

title: decision-chain
text:
Fill in the interview reasoning for choosing Cassandra:
We choose Cassandra for write-heavy horizontally scaling workloads tolerating eventual consistency, paying with no joins or general multi-row transactions and modeling by query instead.

title: data-model
text:
How rich is Cassandra's column type system?
Beyond primitive types Cassandra has list/set/map collections and UDTs, so a nested address can be a UDT column. INSERT ... JSON / SELECT JSON only read and write in JSON format; data is still stored as the declared CQL types, and there is no standalone JSON column type.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
How does a long-offline node recover the writes it missed?
Hints are only stored within the hint window, so a node that returns quickly gets them replayed. Beyond that window, missed writes are recovered by anti-entropy repair (Merkle-tree comparison and streaming of differences), which should run within gc_grace_seconds to avoid resurrecting deletes; read repair only fixes keys that are read and is not the primary mechanism.

title: primary-key
text:
Why make seat_id a clustering key on this table?
The seat order doesn't matter here — seat_id is a clustering key purely so each row under an event_id partition has a unique primary key; without it the tickets would overwrite each other.

title: ticketmaster-example
text:
After partitioning by section, what risk remains for an extreme blockbuster event?
Partitioning by section spreads an event across nodes, but a single ultra-hot section is still one partition on one replica set, so all its read traffic hammers those nodes — that's the Taylor Swift problem the article flags.

title: why-special-structures
text:
Why is it worth knowing specialized big-data structures like Bloom filters in system design?
Specialized data structures matter because they change the shape of the whole solution, making the surrounding system fundamentally different rather than just faster.

title: why-special-structures
text:
In a case where a simple hash table is enough, how would an interviewer read the use of a Bloom filter?
Using a bloom filter where a simple hash table would suffice is a red flag for over-engineering, so keep it simple unless the scale truly demands it.

title: why-special-structures
text:
With limited system design prep time, what should you prioritize?
Master core concepts like caching, load balancing, and partitioning first, because nailing Count-Min Sketch without them still leads to a weak architecture.

title: bloom-filter
text:
Conceptually, a Bloom filter is a probabilistic version of which data structure?
A bloom filter is a probabilistic analog of a set, supporting inserts and membership checks with far less memory than a hash table.

title: bloom-filter
text:
Why is a hash-table-backed set infeasible for membership over trillions of element IDs?
A hash table gives O(1) inserts and lookups but needs memory for every element, which becomes infeasible at trillions of items.

title: bloom-filter
text:
Which answers can a Bloom filter give reliably? (multi-select)
A bloom filter can only say an element is probably in the set or definitely not in it, never that it is certainly present.

title: bloom-filter
text:
Fill in the Bloom filter read/write mechanism:
Each element is hashed k times to set k bits; a lookup checks the same k bits, and any unset bit proves the element was never inserted, so the filter can say "definitely not present".

title: bloom-filter
text:
If all Bloom filter bits for an element are 1, what conclusion is correct?
If all bits are set the element is only probably present, because other elements' hashes may have set those same bits.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What happens as more inserts set more bits to 1 in a Bloom filter?
As the bitmap saturates, the chance that all k bits of an arbitrary element are already set keeps rising, so the false-positive rate climbs; once every bit is 1 the filter answers "maybe" to everything and carries no information. A standard Bloom filter's bit array is fixed at creation and never resizes itself (auto-scaling exists only in variants such as Scalable Bloom Filters, which the scenario rules out).

title: bloom-filter
text:
If more bits reduce saturation, why not make the Bloom filter bit array huge by default?
You size m and k from the element count n and the target false-positive rate (1% here); past that point extra bits barely lower false positives while memory grows linearly, defeating the space-saving reason to use a Bloom filter.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What does this scale imply for deploying a Bloom filter?
A billion-element Bloom filter at a 1% false-positive rate is about 1 GB — bigger than many expect, so it belongs in capacity planning and monitoring like any large in-memory component. A copy per instance isn't forbidden, but 50 instances means 50 GB, which has to fit the per-host memory budget, or else the filter should be centralized or sharded.

title: bloom-filter
text:
How should you describe this memory saving in an interview?
The bloom filter saves about eighty percent versus a hash table, a large win but not several orders of magnitude.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What conditions must hold for a Bloom filter to fit? (multi-select)
A bloom filter fits only when you query set membership, are genuinely space constrained, and can tolerate false positives.

title: bloom-filter
text:
In a Bloom filter, what does a false positive mean?
A false positive means the filter claims presence when the element is absent, while false negatives can never happen.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What is the direct consequence of a standard Bloom filter not supporting deletes?
Standard bloom filters cannot remove elements, so they fit poorly for sets whose items are frequently updated or deleted.

title: bloom-filter
text:
For crawler deduplication, what structure best answers "have we crawled this URL?"
The scenario gives all three conditions: dedup must be shared across machines, storing every URL exactly is too expensive, and an occasional missed page is acceptable — exactly the Bloom filter's sweet spot. It stores no URLs, answering "probably crawled" in small fixed memory; the cost of a false positive is one skipped page, which the scenario accepts.

title: bloom-filter
text:
In crawler deduplication with a Bloom filter, what is the business cost of a false positive?
A false positive makes the crawler believe an unseen URL was already visited, so that page is silently skipped forever.

title: bloom-filter
text:
How should you optimize definite cache misses with a Bloom filter?
A local bloom filter answers "definitely not present" from process memory with no network round trip; keys are registered whenever the cache is written, so a negative lets the request go straight to computation and save those C ms.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What is the latency of one cache miss?
A cache miss costs C plus E milliseconds because you pay the cache check and then still run the expensive operation.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What pitfalls should you call out when using a Bloom filter to short-circuit cache lookups? (multi-select)
The bloom filter degrades as TTL evictions remove entries it cannot forget, and with multiple cache writers it misses hits written by other clients.

title: bloom-filter
text:
Put the Bloom filter choice decision chain in the right order:
The decision runs from a huge membership-query requirement through space and error tolerance to choosing a bloom filter, then owning its false positives and sizing it correctly.

title: bloom-filter
text:
On answer certainty, how do a hash-table set and a Bloom filter differ?
A hash table answers membership exactly, while a bloom filter trades that certainty for memory by answering probably-in or definitely-not.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
What core question does Count-Min Sketch answer?
Count-Min Sketch estimates how many times an item has appeared in a stream, more precisely an upper bound on that count.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
When querying an item in Count-Min Sketch, which value do you return?
You take the minimum across the item's counters, because every counter is inflated by collisions and the smallest gives the tightest upper bound.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
What is the underlying structure of Count-Min Sketch?
A Count-Min Sketch is a two-dimensional array of counters with one hash function per row, incrementing on insert and taking the row-wise minimum on query.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
Fill in what the two Count-Min Sketch size parameters control:
Width controls collision probability and depth controls confidence, and together they give mathematically bounded error.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
What happens at the two extremes: one counter, or one dedicated counter per item?
One shared counter gives a useless bound and one counter per item is exact but saves nothing, so the sketch lives in between with far fewer counters than unique items.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
What is the core tradeoff in Count-Min Sketch?
The key tradeoff is approximate counts in bounded space versus exact counts needing space proportional to the number of unique items.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
What conditions make Count-Min Sketch a good fit? (multi-select)
Count-Min Sketch fits when you query counts for known items under space constraints and can tolerate an upper-bound approximation, never a lower bound.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
In CMS, what does "known items" mean?
After hashing, the sketch cannot tell you which items it has seen, so you must already know the item you are querying.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
For approximate YouTube Top-K videos, what structure combination fits best?
Each view increments the sketch, and the estimated count decides whether the video enters or moves up a small sorted top-K list.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
Put the CMS approximate Top-K flow in order:
A view arrives, the sketch counters increment, the minimum gives the estimated count, and that estimate decides whether to update the top-K list.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
For approximate LFU cache eviction, what is a reasonable approach?
A Count-Min Sketch counts cache hits and a heap tracks the most popular items, making everything else an eviction candidate.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
What is the main problem with using a Count-Min Sketch this way?
A Count-Min Sketch only guarantees the estimate is never below the true count; collisions push counts up, so exact per-click billing would overcharge. Here you should give up the space saving and count exactly. B is wrong: with increment-only updates CMS only over-counts; C is wrong: keys are hashed regardless of type; D is wrong: each write touches d counters, O(d).

title: count-min-sketch
text:
What does Redis actually use to track cache-entry hotness for eviction?
Redis doesn't use a CMS; it reuses a 24-bit field in each object header. Under LRU it stores an approximate access clock; under LFU it splits into 16 bits of last-decrement time plus an 8-bit logarithmic (probabilistically incremented) counter. Combined with sampled eviction, each key carries only 3 bytes of extra metadata.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
By the question they answer, how do a Bloom filter and Count-Min Sketch differ?
A bloom filter answers presence while a Count-Min Sketch answers an upper bound on how many times an item appeared.

title: hyperloglog
text:
What problem is HyperLogLog built to solve?
HyperLogLog performs cardinality estimation, counting the number of unique elements in a very large dataset.

title: hyperloglog
text:
Why not deduplicate billions of users with a HashSet per dimension?
A HashSet stores every element it has seen, so memory grows with cardinality; a hundred thousand dimensions each holding billions-scale sets far exceed tens of gigabytes. HyperLogLog uses a fixed few kilobytes per dimension for an approximate count whose error depends on the number of registers (e.g., Redis's 12 KB implementation has about 0.81% standard error).

title: hyperloglog
text:
What is the coin-flip intuition behind HyperLogLog?
The longest run of leading zeros seen among hashed values estimates how many unique elements passed through, just as longer coin-flip streaks imply more flips.

title: hyperloglog
text:
Fill in the occurrence probabilities for binary prefixes:
Each extra leading zero halves the probability, so observing k leading zeros suggests roughly two to the k distinct values were seen.

title: hyperloglog
text:
Why does HyperLogLog split hash values into buckets?
The first b bits route each hash into one of two-to-the-b buckets, adding redundancy so a single rare hash cannot skew the estimate.

title: hyperloglog
text:
What does each HyperLogLog bucket register store, and when is it updated?
Each register stores only the maximum leading-zero count seen in that bucket, updated only when a new element beats the record.

title: hyperloglog
text:
How does HyperLogLog compute the final estimate from bucket registers?
The estimate is the harmonic mean of all registers with corrections applied at the very small and very large ends.

title: hyperloglog
text:
What do these numbers imply about adding memory for more HLL accuracy?
HLL error scales as 1/√m: going 1.5 KB → 3 KB → 6 KB drops error from about 2.3% to 1.6% to 1.15%, only about 29% each time, with shrinking absolute gains. Size for the error the business actually needs rather than piling on memory.

title: hyperloglog
text:
How does HyperLogLog error change with the number of registers m?
Error scales as one over the square root of the register count, so doubling memory only modestly improves accuracy.

title: hyperloglog
text:
What prerequisites make HyperLogLog a good choice? (multi-select)
HyperLogLog fits when you count unique items in huge data with limited memory and can tolerate small estimation errors.

title: hyperloglog
text:
What are the two main HyperLogLog anti-patterns?
Avoid HyperLogLog when you need exact counts or when the unique set is small enough that a plain hash set is cheaper and exact.

title: hyperloglog
text:
Which common systems have ready-made HyperLogLog implementations you can use directly?
Redis ships PFADD/PFCOUNT/PFMERGE natively; PostgreSQL core has no HLL, but the mature postgresql-hll extension can be installed and used directly. Both are concrete options to name in an interview.

title: hyperloglog
text:
Which modern analytics metrics are good fits for HyperLogLog? (multi-select)
HyperLogLog powers distinct-count metrics like daily active users, unique visitors, distinct search terms, and unique IPs.

title: hyperloglog
text:
What signal best separates scrapers from real users?
HyperLogLog cheaply estimates the share of distinct URLs each IP requests, exposing scrapers that mostly hit never-seen pages.

title: hyperloglog
text:
How can you estimate cache working-set size cheaply?
HyperLogLog answers working-set questions like how many unique keys are accessed without the memory overhead of exact tracking.

title: hyperloglog
text:
What is the fundamental difference between Count-Min Sketch and HyperLogLog?
Count-Min Sketch bounds how often a known item appeared, while HyperLogLog estimates how many distinct items exist overall.

title: quantiles
text:
Why can't you compute an exact P95 under these constraints?
An exact P95 needs every sample retained (whether you sort or use O(n) selection), so memory grows linearly with the count. Under a single-pass, fixed-memory streaming constraint that is ruled out, so you use a bounded-memory approximation. Offline batch computation can still be exact.

title: quantiles
text:
What is the essence of a bucket-based approximate quantile scheme?
Histogram-based quantiles group values into fixed buckets with counts, giving bounded memory no matter how much data flows through.

title: quantiles
text:
What can you read from these latency bucket counts?
Summing buckets in order, 90% finish under 50ms and 98% under 100ms, so the 95th percentile lands in the 50-100ms bucket; the median sits in the 10-50ms bucket.

title: quantiles
text:
Fill in the bucket algorithm's write and read flow:
Each value increments its bucket's counter, and a quantile is estimated by summing counters until the target percentage is reached.

title: quantiles
text:
What tradeoff does cumulative bucket counting make?
Cumulative buckets move the prefix sum to the write path: a value increments every bucket whose upper bound exceeds it, so the worst case is a value in the smallest bucket, which touches every bucket. In exchange, a quantile read just finds the first bucket whose cumulative count crosses the target, with no summing. Prometheus le buckets use this cumulative semantics.

title: quantiles
text:
For a known uniform metric, how should you choose histogram bucket boundaries?
Equal-width buckets are the simplest choice and work well when the value range is known and roughly uniform.

title: quantiles
text:
For wide-range power-law latency, how should you choose bucket boundaries?
Exponential buckets, each a multiple of the previous, keep good relative accuracy across the wide power-law range typical of latency data.

title: quantiles
text:
In this known, stable distribution, why isn't a dynamic histogram (auto-adjusting bucket boundaries) worth it?
Dynamic boundaries pay off for unknown or drifting distributions. Here the distribution is known and stable, so a well-chosen static (e.g. exponential) bucket layout is accurate enough, and periodic rebalancing is pure cost. For unknown or drifting distributions, adaptive structures such as t-digest remain a common choice.

title: quantiles
text:
What determines the error bound when bucket algorithms estimate percentiles?
Quantile error is bounded by bucket width, so a ten-millisecond bucket means the estimate can be off by up to ten milliseconds.

title: quantiles
text:
What requirement mix fits bucket-based approximate quantiles? (multi-select)
Bucket algorithms shine for percentile tracking over big data with bounded memory and real-time streaming, but they discard individual events.

title: quantiles
text:
What are common pitfalls of bucket algorithms? (multi-select)
Common pitfalls are poorly chosen boundaries, unhandled out-of-range data, and reduced accuracy at extreme percentiles.

title: quantiles
text:
How do Prometheus histograms support distributed quantiles?
Prometheus histograms are bucket algorithms whose counts can be aggregated across machines to compute percentiles without centralized raw storage.

title: quantiles
text:
Which call correctly gets P99 latency for an SLO check?
SLO compliance reads the ninety-ninth percentile from the histogram buckets and compares it to the threshold, since averages hide the tail.

title: quantiles
text:
What happens if sub-100ms responses are bucketed into [0-1s, 1-10s, 10s+]?
Coarse buckets like zero-to-one-second lose all precision when most responses are under a hundred milliseconds, so use logarithmic or exponential spacing.

title: structure-selection
text:
Which "structure -> question answered" pairs are correct? (multi-select)
Bloom filters answer membership, Count-Min Sketch gives approximate upper-bound counts rather than exact ones, HyperLogLog counts distinct items, and histograms give quantiles.

title: hyperloglog
text:
Which Redis commands should you use to count daily unique visitors?
Redis PFADD and PFCOUNT use HyperLogLog to count unique visitors in kilobytes of memory with about two percent error.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What happens if each hash sets many bits, making the signature nearly solid?
A dense signature fills the bit array after very few inserts; once most bits are 1 every lookup matches, so false positives approach 100%. That's why each hash sets just one bit.

title: count-min-sketch
text:
About CMS memory, what should you proactively make clear?
CMS is a w-by-d grid of counters whose w and d are sized for the target error and confidence, independent of key count or stream length; it saves versus a hash table but is not free.

title: hyperloglog
text:
Which landing form should HLL take?
A live dashboard needs the current value on demand, so keep HLL as an incremental pre-aggregate: O(1) merge on write, O(1) read; the cost is maintaining that state over time.

title: quantiles
text:
Which histogram signal should auto-scaling and anomaly detection watch?
The SLO is defined on P95 latency, so scaling should watch P95 directly. With mostly fast requests the mean is diluted and barely moves when the tail slows, so scaling comes too late; a single max is noisy and causes flapping; total request count says nothing about per-request latency. Sharp percentile shifts also serve as anomaly signals. (If the goal were resource utilization rather than tail latency, scaling on average CPU is common practice; that is not this scenario.)

title: positioning
text:
Fill in DynamoDB's three positioning keywords:
Each keyword has real meaning: fully managed = operations handled by AWS; highly scalable = horizontal scaling by partition, though a single hot partition key is still bounded by per-partition throughput; key-value (and document) = non-relational, accessed by primary key.

title: positioning
text:
What used to be one of the biggest criticisms of DynamoDB, and how does that stand today?
DynamoDB now supports ACID transactions, neutralizing the old criticism that NoSQL means no transactions.

title: data-model
text:
Fill in DynamoDB's data hierarchy:
Tables hold items, which are like rows capped at four hundred kilobytes, made of attributes that can be scalar, set, or nested types.

title: data-model
text:
DynamoDB is schema-less -- what's the direct consequence of that?
Being schema-less lets items in one table carry different attributes, but pushes data validation responsibility onto the application.

title: data-model
text:
DynamoDB sends and receives data as JSON -- does that mean it's stored as JSON internally too?
JSON is only the transport format, while DynamoDB's actual storage format is proprietary and abstracted away from users.

title: primary-key
text:
What role does the partition key play in DynamoDB?
The partition key's value is hashed to determine which physical partition stores the item, and with the sort key it uniquely identifies the item.

title: primary-key
text:
What is the sort key's role?
The optional sort key orders items sharing a partition key, enabling efficient range queries and sorting within a partition.

title: primary-key
text:
How should the primary key be designed?
Partitioning by chat_id keeps one chat's messages in the same partition so a single Query fetches them; since message_id is given as time-ordered and increasing, using it as the sort key yields chronological order. Choose the partition key around the most common access pattern.

title: primary-key
text:
Why choose a monotonically increasing id over a timestamp?
Timestamps can collide within the same millisecond, while a monotonically increasing ID gives both chronological order and uniqueness.

title: primary-key
text:
Which of these are common techniques for generating ids that are both time-sortable and unique? (select all)
UUID v7, Snowflake, and ULID all put a timestamp in the high bits followed by random bits or machine id + sequence, so many servers can mint IDs concurrently that are globally unique and roughly time-ordered (k-sortable). A per-partition counter only increases within one partition — values repeat across partitions and can't be compared — and it needs atomic updates to a counter item that becomes a hot spot under concurrent writes; UUID v4 is purely random and not time-sortable.

title: primary-key
text:
Why is UUID v7 preferred over UUID v1?
UUID v7 puts the timestamp first so it sorts naturally as a string and avoids exposing the machine's MAC address like v1 does.

title: internals
text:
How does modern DynamoDB's partition-location mechanism differ from the 2007 Dynamo paper?
Conceptually data is still hash-distributed by partition key, but location moved from the paper's peer-to-peer hash ring to a centralized partition metadata service: request routers consult it to find the storage nodes for a partition. That metadata layer also handles automatic partition splits when size or throughput hits the limit.

title: internals
text:
Inside a single partition, what data structure does DynamoDB use to organize data?
Within each partition DynamoDB organizes items in a B-tree indexed by the sort key, enabling efficient range queries.

title: internals
text:
Put the internal steps of 'querying an item by composite primary key' in the correct order:
A composite-key query hashes the partition key to find the node, then traverses that partition's B-tree by sort key to locate the items.

title: secondary-index
text:
What is the definition of a GSI (Global Secondary Index)?
A GSI can use a different partition dimension (or keep the table's partition key with a different sort key); it is essentially a separate internal table with its own partitions and replicas, updated asynchronously, so you can query efficiently on non-key attributes. Option A is the LSI definition: an LSI must keep the base table's partition key.

title: secondary-index
text:
What is the definition of an LSI (Local Secondary Index)?
A local secondary index keeps the table's partition key but uses a different sort key and is co-located on the same physical partitions.

title: secondary-index
text:
How should this query be supported?
Querying by a different partition dimension like user id requires a GSI, since an LSI must keep the table's partition key.

title: secondary-index
text:
What's the most suitable index here?
The query stays within one chat_id partition and only changes the sort dimension, and the table hasn't been created — so you can define an LSI at creation: co-located with the base table, sharing its capacity, and supporting strongly consistent reads. This relies on each group's data (base table + LSI) staying under the 10 GB item-collection limit. If the table is already live, an LSI can't be added — use a GSI (partition key chat_id, sort key num_attachments); also use a GSI if a single group might exceed 10 GB.

title: secondary-index
text:
Which statement about when an LSI can be created is correct?
LSIs must be defined at table creation and cannot be added or removed later, unlike GSIs which can change anytime.

title: secondary-index
text:
On 'consistency support', what's the difference between a GSI and an LSI?
GSIs are eventually consistent only, while LSIs support both eventually consistent and strongly consistent reads like the base table.

title: secondary-index
text:
On 'read/write throughput capacity', what's the difference between a GSI and an LSI?
A GSI has its own separate read and write capacity units while an LSI shares the base table's capacity.

title: secondary-index
text:
How many GSIs and LSIs can a table have at most? What size limit applies to an LSI?
GSIs default to a quota of 20 per table, which can be raised on request; LSIs are capped at 5 per table and must be created with the table. For a table with LSIs, all base-table and LSI items sharing one partition key value (the item collection) cannot exceed 10GB. GSIs have their own partitions and carry no such cap.

title: secondary-index
text:
After a write to the base table, how do a GSI and an LSI each get updated?
GSI updates propagate asynchronously making them eventually consistent, while LSI updates happen synchronously with the base table write.

title: secondary-index
text:
About comparing GSI and LSI, which statements are correct? (select all)
GSIs are flexible global indexes on separate partitions while LSIs serve local per-partition queries co-located with the base table.

title: access-patterns
text:
What is the fundamental difference between the Scan and Query operations?
A scan reads every item in the table while a query reads only items matching key conditions, so scans should be avoided on large datasets.

title: access-patterns
text:
How should the SDK call be written?
Use a query with a key condition expression and bound attribute values instead of scanning and filtering client-side.

title: access-patterns
text:
What is PartiQL in DynamoDB?
PartiQL is a SQL-compatible convenience layer whose statements translate to the same underlying DynamoDB operations.

title: access-patterns
text:
Does returning only some attributes with a ProjectionExpression save read capacity (RCU)?
Projection expressions only reduce network bandwidth because the full item is still read from storage and billed at its total size.

title: data-modeling
text:
How should reviews be stored?
Because reads fetch the whole item, storing reviews inside the business record makes every basic lookup expensive, so reviews belong in a separate table.

title: consistency
text:
At what granularity is DynamoDB's consistency model chosen?
Consistency is chosen per read request by setting consistent read to true, not as a table-level configuration.

title: consistency
text:
Under the default (eventually consistent) read mode, which way does this read path lean in CAP terms?
Default eventually consistent reads can be served by any replica and still return (possibly slightly stale) data when a replica lags — this read path leans AP. Writes still go through the partition leader and need a quorum of replicas, so DynamoDB as a whole isn't simply "an AP system"; you can switch to strongly consistent reads per request.

title: consistency
text:
How much more expensive is a strongly consistent read than an eventually consistent one?
A strongly consistent read consumes 1 RCU per 4KB while an eventually consistent read consumes 0.5 RCU, so it costs twice as much in exchange for reflecting all prior successful writes. Transactional reads (2 RCU per 4KB) are out of scope here.

title: consistency
text:
What's the scope of DynamoDB's ACID transaction support?
Transact write and get items provide serializable ACID transactions across up to one hundred items spanning multiple tables.

title: consistency
text:
When designing an access pattern that needs strongly consistent reads, which index limitation must you keep in mind?
Strongly consistent reads work only on the base table and LSIs, never on GSIs, which constrains access-pattern design.

title: internals
text:
How is an eventually consistent read served under the hood, and why might it return stale data?
Eventually consistent reads can hit any replica (lower latency, half the RCU). A write is acknowledged once the leader and a quorum of replicas (2 of 3) persist it, so the remaining replica may not have caught up — a read that lands on it returns the old value.

title: internals
text:
How does a strongly consistent read guarantee it's always current under the hood?
Strongly consistent reads route directly to the partition leader, which sees every write first and therefore always has the latest data.

title: scalability
text:
How does DynamoDB automatically scale partitions?
When a partition hits its size or throughput limit DynamoDB automatically splits it and redistributes data with hash partitioning keeping load even.

title: scalability
text:
To give users on every continent low-latency reads and writes, which DynamoDB feature do you name?
Global Tables replicate in real time across regions so users read and write locally; the unit you count is regions -- with N regions each write costs N replicated write units, so you trade cost for latency.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
What is DynamoDB's replication topology within a single region?
DynamoDB automatically keeps three replicas across three availability zones per partition, one leader and two followers, with no user configuration.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
Put the underlying steps of a DynamoDB partition write in the correct order:
The partition leader writes a WAL entry, sends it to its peers, and acknowledges the write once a quorum of two out of three persists it.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
Based on public information, how can DynamoDB's per-partition replication group generally be described?
Since DynamoDB is closed source, the safer answer is a leader-based replication group with quorum-backed writes, not a specific protocol name.

title: security
text:
Which statement about DynamoDB's encryption is correct?
Encryption at rest and in transit are separate layers: every table is encrypted at rest by default (with an AWS owned key at no extra charge; choosing a KMS-managed key adds KMS charges), and the SDK uses HTTPS endpoints so TLS protects requests and responses. To truly enforce TLS-only access, add an aws:SecureTransport condition in IAM or VPC endpoint policies.

title: security
text:
Which native DynamoDB mechanisms meet these three requirements? (select all)
Each requirement maps to one mechanism: role-scoped permissions → IAM policies; no public internet → a VPC (gateway) endpoint; encryption at rest → default at-rest encryption. DynamoDB has no native username/password system — authentication goes through IAM.

title: pricing
text:
What's the right pairing?
On-demand per-request pricing suits unpredictable workloads while provisioned capacity is more cost-effective for predictable steady traffic.

title: pricing
text:
Fill in the definitions of the capacity units:
One read capacity unit covers four kilobytes per second and one write capacity unit covers one kilobyte per second.

title: pricing
text:
How will DynamoDB handle this write load under the hood?
A single partition caps out around three thousand RCUs and one thousand WCUs, so DynamoDB automatically splits data across more partitions once demand exceeds that limit.

title: pricing
text:
Storing YouTube view counts in DynamoDB, each write is only a few dozen bytes -- why does every write still cost one full WCU?
Every write consumes at least one WCU because DynamoDB rounds up to the nearest kilobyte, capping a partition at about a thousand writes per second.

title: pricing
text:
Assuming a load of ten million writes per second on DynamoDB (provisioned pricing around $0.00065 per WCU-hour), roughly what order of magnitude is the daily cost?
Ten million WCUs × $0.00065 per hour × 24 hours ≈ $156,000 a day. This gut check shows raw ultra-high write volume can make DynamoDB cost-prohibitive; a common alternative is to aggregate in memory or a stream first and write in batches.

title: dax
text:
What's the most convenient option?
DAX is DynamoDB's purpose-built in-memory cache that delivers microsecond reads without adding a general-purpose cache like Redis.

title: dax
text:
What does adopting DAX require from the application code?
Using DAX means swapping in the DAX client SDK, which is API compatible but not completely transparent.

title: dax
text:
DAX is a read-through-plus-write-through cache, but what's one staleness trap?
Write-through only covers writes that go through DAX; services writing DynamoDB directly leave the item cache stale until TTL/eviction, unless all writes are routed through DAX.

title: dax
text:
