What two caches does DAX maintain internally, and do you have to choose one to enable?
Item cache holds GetItem/BatchGetItem results and query cache holds Query/Scan results; both are always on with no switch to pick one (only their TTLs are tunable).

title: dax
text:
What happens when you issue a strongly consistent read through DAX?
DAX passes strongly consistent reads straight through to DynamoDB and does not cache the results.

title: streams
text:
What is DynamoDB Streams?
DynamoDB Streams is built-in change data capture that lets downstream systems react to item changes in near real time.

title: streams
text:
What are the typical use cases for DynamoDB Streams? (select all)
Streams commonly sync Elasticsearch indexes, feed real-time analytics pipelines, and trigger Lambda functions on data changes.

title: streams
text:
You want to use Kinesis Data Firehose to load DynamoDB changes into S3/Redshift -- what should you watch out for in the pipeline?
Firehose can't consume DynamoDB Streams directly. Two common routes: (1) enable Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB so changes land in KDS and Firehose uses KDS as its source; (2) enable DynamoDB Streams and have a Lambda read and forward records to Firehose. DynamoDB Streams and Kinesis Data Streams for DynamoDB are two distinct features.

title: streams
text:
What's the recommended way to keep them in sync?
Consuming DynamoDB Streams to update Elasticsearch keeps the search index in sync without dual writes from the application.

title: when-to-use
text:
Why is DynamoDB often described in interviews as able to serve almost any persistence layer? (select all)
DynamoDB pairs high scalability and durability with transactions and single-digit-millisecond latency, though it is not free and still ties you to AWS.

title: limitations
text:
In general, which situations should make you avoid DynamoDB? (select all — not limited to this scenario)
Avoid DynamoDB for cost-heavy write volumes, complex query needs, index-heavy modeling better served by Postgres, or when vendor neutrality is required.

title: limitations
text:
What does this signal mean?
Leaning heavily on many GSIs and LSIs signals relational access patterns that a database like PostgreSQL would serve better.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for 'choosing DynamoDB' in the correct order:
Massive scale with no ops burden points to DynamoDB's managed auto-scaling and transactions, whose cost and query limits are mitigated by careful modeling and estimation.

title: decision-chain
text:
Fill in this DynamoDB reasoning about splitting consistency by path:
Critical paths request strongly consistent reads from the leader at double cost while latency-sensitive paths keep the cheap eventually consistent default.

title: internals
text:
On 'in-partition index structure', how do DynamoDB and Cassandra compare?
DynamoDB indexes each partition with a B-tree by sort key while Cassandra relies on an LSM tree optimized for writes.

title: data-model
text:
What type shapes does a DynamoDB attribute support?
Attributes support scalar and set types and can be nested, allowing complex document structures within a single item.

title: pricing
text:
What read-capacity (RCU) cost benefit comes from making most reads eventually consistent?
Eventually consistent reads cost half the RCUs of strongly consistent reads, so routing most read-only traffic through the eventual path directly halves that read cost.

title: scalability
text:
Besides matching the query pattern, what else must you consider when choosing a partition key?
A good partition key both serves common queries and spreads data evenly, since a hot partition throttles at the per-partition throughput limits.

title: positioning
text:
Why can you only go 'so deep' when discussing DynamoDB's internal mechanics?
DynamoDB is not open source, so internals are known only through AWS documentation and the published DynamoDB paper.

title: access-patterns
text:
Which operation fits here?
Scanning is fine when you genuinely need every item of a small table, and only becomes an anti-pattern on large hot tables.

title: fault-tolerance
text:
Fill in DynamoDB's replication and read path:
Each partition keeps three replicas across availability zones, with the leader acknowledging writes at quorum and serving every strongly consistent read.

title: data-model
text:
What happens as the embedded history grows, and how should you model it?
A single item is hard-capped at 400KB (attribute names included), so an ever-growing embedded list eventually gets writes rejected. Store each history entry as its own item sharing the order's partition key with a timestamp sort key, then Query them in order; offloading to S3 with a pointer is for single large blobs.

title: secondary-index
text:
What does each base-table write mean for total write capacity?
Under these assumptions each base write propagates asynchronously to all 3 GSIs, each charging its own write capacity, so total ≈ 1000×(1+3) = 4000 WCU/s. Items lacking a GSI's key (sparse index) don't write to it, and an update that changes a GSI key costs a delete plus a put on that GSI.

title: scalability
text:
What is the main tradeoff when choosing a region?
Region choice trades proximity-driven latency against data-residency law; when they conflict, compliance is the hard constraint and latency the thing you optimize.

title: when-to-use
text:
Which search component should this system add?
Complex search needs like ranking, filtering, and faceting at scale call for a purpose-built engine such as Elasticsearch.

title: documents
text:
In Elasticsearch, what is a document?
A document in Elasticsearch is just any JSON object, the basic unit of data you search over.

title: indices
text:
What does an Elasticsearch index map to in a relational database?
An Elasticsearch index is a collection of documents that searches run against, analogous to a database table rather than an auxiliary index structure.

title: concepts
text:
Fill in the core Elasticsearch concepts from a client point of view:
Documents are the JSON units of data, indices are collections of documents, and the mapping is the schema defining each searchable field's type.

title: field-types
text:
In a mapping, what is the key difference between keyword and text fields?
Use keyword for exact-match fields like an id, and text for fields that need contains-style full-text search.

title: mapping
text:
What happens if a User object has 10 fields but only 2 are searched, and all 10 are mapped?
Every mapped field costs index and memory overhead, so map only the fields you actually search.

title: index-defaults
text:
What are the defaults when you create an index with a simple PUT and no extra parameters?
Since 7.0, a bare index create gives dynamic mapping, one primary shard, and one replica. The replica count is a dynamic setting you can change any time; the primary shard count is static and can only change via split/shrink or reindexing into a new index. Set an explicit mapping when most fields shouldn't be searchable.

title: data-modeling
text:
Which data model is the better fit?
When reviews are rarely updated but frequently queried with books, nesting them inside the book document is the more efficient call.

title: update-api
text:
Which API call should you use?
The update endpoint patches only the given fields without fetching the whole document first, which matters in a distributed, concurrent system.

title: versioning
text:
Reading a document returns _seq_no and _primary_term; writing with ?if_seq_no=N&if_primary_term=M implements what mechanism?
The conditional write only applies if the document's seq_no and primary_term still match what you read; otherwise it returns a 409 version conflict. That's optimistic concurrency control: the client re-reads and retries. The old internal ?version=N form no longer works since 7.0.

title: versioning
text:
What is the main risk of updating a whole document with PUT and no version condition?
A full-document PUT without a condition can silently overwrite a concurrent writer's changes; record _seq_no and _primary_term on read and write with if_seq_no + if_primary_term to prevent it.

title: query-dsl
text:
What is the correct query shape?
Combine conditions with a bool query whose must clause holds a match on title and a range on price.

title: nested-query
text:
What is the correct nested query shape?
A nested query with the reviews path ensures both conditions apply to the same nested review object.

title: response
text:
In search hits, what is _source?
The source field carries the original JSON document you indexed, returned alongside the id and relevance score.

title: api-quirks
text:
What is true about sending a request body with GET /_search?
Elasticsearch responds to GET requests with bodies, and you can fall back to POST or query strings when a proxy objects.

title: geospatial
text:
How do geo_point and geo_shape split responsibilities?
Use geo_point for a single coordinate like a restaurant location, and geo_shape for polygons and lines like delivery zones; a circular area must first be approximated as a polygon (e.g. via the circle ingest processor).

title: geospatial
text:
Which query is the best fit?
The geo_distance query finds documents within a radius of a point and composes with bool filters for multi-faceted local search.

title: geospatial
text:
What structure indexes geo_point coordinates for efficient two-dimensional search?
Geo points are indexed with a BKD tree, a block-optimized k-d tree variant that narrows the search space in two dimensions where separate B-trees cannot.

title: geospatial
text:
What is the most natural search-layer choice?
Location-based apps need geo radius plus multi-facet filtering and ranking in one query, which is exactly where Elasticsearch shines.

title: relevance
text:
How does Elasticsearch sort results when no sort is specified?
By default results are ordered by _score descending; since 5.0 the default scoring is BM25, which refines TF-IDF with term-frequency saturation and document-length normalization. An explicit sort overrides it.

title: relevance
text:
Fill in the idea behind default relevance scoring:
BM25 keeps the TF-IDF idea of in-document frequency times global rarity, but saturates term frequency and normalizes by document length so long documents can't win just by repeating a term.

title: sorting
text:
What Elasticsearch mechanism sorts by a computed value, such as a discounted price?
_script sorting runs a Painless script over document fields to compute the sort value (e.g. doc['price'].value * (1 - doc['discount'].value)). It runs per hit at query time, so it's costly; if you can change the mapping, precomputing a discounted_price field at index time is usually better.

title: sorting
text:
When sorting by a nested field, what do `nested.path` and `mode` in the sort clause each do?
Nested objects are indexed as hidden separate documents, so the parent has no value of its own and the sort must reach in via nested.path. With several reviews per book, mode picks max/min/avg etc. (desc already defaults to max; writing it is for clarity). Without nested, the values are invisible to the parent and the sort silently fails rather than erroring.

title: pagination
text:
At what depth does from/size pagination get blocked by default, and what should replace it for sequential deep paging?
With from/size, every shard must fetch and sort the top from+size hits and the coordinating node merges them, so cost grows with depth; Elasticsearch blocks deep paging with index.max_result_window (default 10,000). For sequential deep paging, switch to search_after (usually with a point in time); raising the cap only postpones the problem.

title: pagination
text:
Why is deep pagination with from/size expensive?
Every shard must fetch and sort its top from+size hits, and the coordinating node merges shards × (from+size) hits before discarding the first from; cost grows with depth. That's why ES caps it by default with max_result_window = 10,000.

title: pagination
text:
Which pagination method should you use?
Search-after starts each page from the previous page's last sort values, staying efficient even for very deep pagination.

title: pagination
text:
Where does the search_after value come from?
Each next page passes the sort values of the previous page's last document, such as its timestamp and id.

title: pagination
text:
Which statements about search_after pagination are correct? (Select all that apply.)
The search_after cursor is just the last hit's sort values, which the client sends back; the server holds no cursor. With no offset concept it can't jump to page N. Without a PIT, writes or deletes during paging can cause misses or duplicates; add a PIT for a consistent snapshot.

title: cursors
text:
Which pagination mechanism best fits this export job?
A point-in-time snapshot combined with search-after gives a consistent view across pages even while the index is being updated.

title: architecture
text:
How do Elasticsearch and Apache Lucene split responsibilities?
Elasticsearch is a distributed orchestration layer over Apache Lucene, which provides the core low-level search functionality.

title: node-types
text:
Which of these are Elasticsearch node roles? (Select all that apply.)
Common node roles include master (cluster management), data (plus hot/warm/cold tiers), ingest (pre-index processing), and ML; every node can coordinate requests, and a node with empty roles is a dedicated coordinating-only node. There's no gateway node.

title: node-types
text:
What is the Master node responsible for?
The master node is the cluster admin, the only node that performs cluster-level operations like adding nodes or creating indices.

title: node-types
text:
What role does a Coordinating node play in the request path?
The coordinating node is the cluster's front end, receiving client requests, routing them to the right nodes, and merging the results.

title: node-types
text:
Which node role handles transformation and preprocessing before indexing?
Ingest nodes transform and prepare incoming data before it is indexed on data nodes.

title: node-types
text:
What is true about deploying Elasticsearch node roles?
A node's roles come from configuration and can be combined, while serious deployments give each role hardware matched to its bottleneck.

title: data-tiers
text:
What determines hot, warm, cold, and frozen tiers for Data nodes?
Data tiers are chosen by how likely the data is to be queried, usually by recency, and whether it can still change.

title: master-election
text:
How is the master chosen when the cluster starts?
Seed hosts only let nodes discover each other; the master-eligible nodes do the voting, and a candidate needs a majority to win, so exactly one master is active while the other master-eligible nodes stand by.

title: search-phases
text:
What two phases does a search request run on data nodes?
Search runs a query phase that identifies matching document ids via index structures, then a fetch phase that optionally retrieves the documents.

title: search-phases
text:
What kind of Elasticsearch query is ideal?
The cheapest query fetches only a few fields for the top-k hits, reading them from doc values or stored fields instead of loading and parsing the whole _source. The fetch phase still runs, but its cost is minimal.

title: storage-hierarchy
text:
Fill in Elasticsearch’s nested storage hierarchy:
An index splits into shards, each shard maps one-to-one to a Lucene index, and each Lucene index consists of immutable segments.

title: sharding
text:
What core capability do shards give Elasticsearch?
Sharding spreads documents and their index structures across nodes so searches run in parallel and the coordinating node merges the results.

title: replication
text:
What are the two main uses of replicas?
Replicas provide high availability and extra read throughput, since the coordinating node balances searches across primary and replica shards.

title: replication
text:
Roughly how much query QPS can this setup handle?
One primary plus Y replicas gives Y+1 query-serving copies; with each on its own node and load spread evenly, read capacity is roughly X×(Y+1). Adding replicas without adding nodes makes them compete for the same hardware, so capacity does not scale linearly, and writes and replication get no such boost.

title: segments
text:
What is the most important property of a Lucene segment?
A segment is an immutable container of indexed data, and all updates happen through new segments, soft deletes, and merges.

title: segment-crud
text:
What does Lucene actually do when inserting a new document?
Writes never touch existing segments: documents enter the indexing buffer and the translog, a refresh (about once a second by default, or when the buffer fills) builds them into a new searchable segment, and a later flush performs the Lucene commit that fsyncs to disk. Batch building is where the high write throughput comes from.

title: segment-crud
text:
What does Lucene do when there are too many segments?
Lucene merges numerous small segments into a new larger one and removes the old segments.

title: segment-crud
text:
If segments are immutable, how is a document delete implemented?
Deletes are soft: the segment marks the document as deleted and hides it from queries, and merges later physically remove it.

title: segment-crud
text:
Why are updates slower than inserts in Elasticsearch?
An update soft-deletes the old document and inserts a new one, adding bookkeeping overhead that lingers until segments merge, which is why Elasticsearch dislikes rapidly updating data.

title: immutability
text:
Which benefits come from immutable segments? (Select all that apply.)
Immutability speeds writes, enables safe caching and better compression, and simplifies concurrency and recovery, at the cost of periodic merges.

title: immutability
text:
What is the main cost of immutable segments?
The price of immutability is periodic segment merging and temporarily higher storage until deleted data is cleaned up.

title: inverted-index
text:
What is an inverted index, and why does it make keyword search fast?
An inverted index keeps a posting list per term: the query locates the term in the dictionary and reads its posting list instead of scanning a billion books. Cost depends on the number of matches, not the corpus size, and it isn't strictly O(1).

title: doc-values
text:
What structure are doc values, and what problem do they solve?
Doc values store one field for all documents in a columnar contiguous layout, so sorting and aggregations read only that column instead of whole rows.

title: doc-values
text:
How do the inverted index and doc values split work in search plus price sorting?
The inverted index finds which documents match, and doc values supply the field values needed to sort those matches.

title: query-planning
text:
When Elasticsearch / Lucene runs a multi-clause query, what decides which clause runs first?
Execution order is decided per shard by Lucene: it estimates each clause's cost (how long the posting list is, how many docs it can match), leads with the sparsest clause, and has the others only verify those candidates. A different order can cost orders of magnitude more.

title: query-planning
text:
For the search "bill nye", with millions of "bill" hits and hundreds of "nye" hits, what is efficient?
Starting from the rare term's few hundred postings and intersecting is orders of magnitude cheaper than expanding the common term's millions.

title: cdc-sync
text:
What is the most common way to connect Elasticsearch in a system-design interview?
In interviews Elasticsearch is usually attached via change data capture to an authoritative store like Postgres or DynamoDB.

title: limitations
text:
What is wrong with using Elasticsearch as the only primary database?
Use Elasticsearch as a search index, not the only source of truth, because it is optimized for search rather than transactional durability.

title: limitations
text:
What is the more reasonable design?
Elasticsearch is built for read-heavy workloads, so rapidly changing counters should be buffered and batched into it rather than written per event.

title: limitations
text:
What consistency fact must you acknowledge when using Elasticsearch?
By default an ES write fsyncs the translog and replicates to in-sync copies before acking, so durability is fine; but it becomes searchable only after a refresh (~1s by default), and CDC adds more lag. A user may not find their just-changed name, so state this and confirm the business tolerates it. C is wrong about immediate searchability; D is wrong because each copy refreshes on its own schedule, so search results can briefly differ.

title: data-modeling
text:
What is the guiding rule for modeling data in Elasticsearch?
Denormalize aggressively since Elasticsearch is not relational, aiming to answer each request with one or two queries.

title: when-to-use
text:
What is the reasonable first step?
For under a hundred thousand rarely changing documents, a simple query on the primary store usually suffices before reaching for Elasticsearch.

title: cdc-sync
text:
What happens if Elasticsearch falls out of sync with the source of truth, and how do you handle it?
Drift means the Elasticsearch index no longer matches the source of truth; repair depends on the primary store or replayable change log, not Elasticsearch magically healing itself.

title: cdc-sync
text:
Put the decision chain for using Elasticsearch with CDC in the right order:
Complex search needs lead to Elasticsearch as a derived search layer, whose staleness and drift are mitigated with change data capture and monitoring.

title: segment-crud
text:
Put the internal Lucene steps for a document update in the right order:
An update soft-deletes the old version, writes the new version into a fresh segment, and relies on a later merge to physically clean up.

title: inverted-index
text:
Fill in the helper structures Lucene uses for an inverted index:
Here, completion means filling the blank, not autocomplete. An FST optimizes the term dictionary: it compactly checks whether a term exists and maps it to the posting-list location.

title: lessons
text:
Even if you do not use Elasticsearch, which design lessons are reusable? (Select all that apply.)
Three transferable lessons: immutable segments simplify caching, compression and concurrency; a coordination layer vs a shard layer (scatter-gather + merge); organizing or duplicating data for query patterns (inverted index, doc values). D is wrong: distribution doesn't give strong consistency for free; under partitions you still trade consistency against availability.

title: search-phases
text:
On read/write responsibility separation, how do Data nodes and Coordinating nodes relate?
Data nodes focus on storage and local search execution while coordinating nodes parse, route, and merge, letting each be optimized independently.

title: pagination
text:
With no unique tie-breaker, how does deep pagination break?
search_after fetches docs after the last sort value of the previous page; with a non-unique sort key, tied docs have no total order, so a cursor landing mid-group may repeat or skip docs. Fix: use a PIT (which adds an implicit _shard_doc tiebreaker) or append a unique field to the sort.

title: architecture
text:
Which layer provides cross-shard faceting/aggregation, one of the core motives for choosing Elasticsearch?
Each shard computes a local aggregation on its own Lucene index (using structures like doc values), and the coordinating node reduces those partial results into a global facet. Lucene can facet within a single index but has no notion of shards spread across machines; cross-shard fan-out and merge belong to Elasticsearch's orchestration layer, which is the core reason to pick it over raw Lucene.

title: mapping
text:
To recall by meaning rather than identical words, which mapping field capability fits?
Recall by meaning needs text encoded as vectors in a dense_vector field for kNN/semantic search. Even with a synonym list, an analyzer only normalizes tokens into the inverted index and covers pre-listed pairs, not meaning in general. Cost: vector recall is heavier and can add relevance noise, so it's often combined with keyword search (hybrid).

title: when-to-use
text:
What is the better choice for this daily click report?
A once-a-day report has day-level latency tolerance, so streaming buys you nothing while adding a full extra ops burden.

title: when-to-use
text:
What is the best fit for this stateless Kafka transformation?
For a trivial stateless transformation, a plain Kafka consumer service suffices and Flink is overkill.

title: state
text:
What does changing from forwarding clicks to counting each user over the last five minutes introduce?
A five-minute window forces the service to remember things across events — state size is roughly active users times one counter each — and that turns a stateless forwarder into a stateful system where recovery, scaling, and ordering all get hard.

title: state
text:
What problems come from implementing a five-minute in-memory counter in a plain service?
A hand-rolled in-memory counter faces three problems: after a crash you must write your own replay-plus-offset-consistency recovery; on scaling you must migrate state between instances yourself; and without watermarks, late or out-of-order events produce wrong counts. Flink takes these over with checkpoints (state snapshotted together with source offsets), keyed-state redistribution, and event-time watermarks. D is unrelated to the DIY approach.

title: dataflow
text:
What does it mean that Flink is a dataflow engine?
Flink is built around a directed dataflow graph where nodes are operators and edges are streams, and Flink arranges the resources to execute it.

title: dataflow
text:
Fill in the terms in a Flink dataflow graph:
In Flink the nodes are operators, the edges are streams, and the entry and exit nodes are called sources and sinks.

title: sources-sinks
text:
Which systems are common Flink sources?
A source turns external data into a Flink stream: Kafka, Kinesis, and file systems all have official or mainstream connectors and are the most common inputs, while a warehouse like Snowflake usually appears as the sink where results land, not as a common source.

title: sources-sinks
text:
What is the role of a sink in a Flink application?
Sinks write data from Flink streams out to external systems such as databases, warehouses, message queues, and file systems.

title: kafka-integration
text:
Why do most Flink interview designs start with Kafka?
Kafka's log can be replayed by offset; Flink stores source offsets in checkpoints and rereads from the same position after a failure, which underpins fault tolerance and exactly-once. A topic's partition count also maps directly onto source parallelism. Note that keyBy still redistributes records by key inside Flink, independent of how Kafka partitioned them.

title: stream-vs-batch
text:
Why is Flink usually not the first pick for pure offline batch processing in an interview?
Flink has a BATCH execution mode and can technically do batch work. Here the job is purely offline with no realtime need and no existing Flink cluster, so a dedicated batch framework like Spark, with a more mature ecosystem and more common discussion, is the cheaper default to explain; if you already run Flink streaming jobs and want unified batch/stream, running batch on Flink is perfectly reasonable.

title: streams
text:
What is the most accurate definition of a stream in Flink?
A Flink stream is a sequence of data elements flowing between operators; this click feed is unbounded, while a bounded stream is what batch processing consumes, and Flink handles both with the same abstraction. It is not a static table, an on-disk log file, or a database connection.

title: streams
text:
What is the key abstraction difference between a Flink stream and a Kafka topic?
A Kafka topic is a durable append-only log with offsets; a Flink stream is just a data edge in the job graph and is not persisted itself. Flink's fault tolerance has two halves: a checkpoint stores operator state and the source's read position, and after a failure the job rolls back to it and rereads from a replayable source such as the matching Kafka offset.

title: operators
text:
What is an operator in Flink?
An operator is a possibly stateful transformation that consumes one or more input streams and produces one or more output streams; you scale one operator by raising its parallel instance count, and its state grows with the number of keys.

title: operators
text:
Which of these are common Flink operators?
Map, flatMap, filter, reduce, window, join, and aggregate are operators you chain in the DataStream API; checkpointing is a fault-tolerance mechanism that periodically snapshots state, never transforms records, and cannot be chained in as a processing step.

title: execution-model
text:
What is the core execution-model difference between Flink and MapReduce?
Flink processes records one at a time in streaming fashion, whereas MapReduce works in batches.

title: operators
text:
What does this Flink code compute for the ad-click job?
It keys the stream by ad id, groups events into five-minute tumbling windows, and reduces each window into an aggregated click count per ad.

title: keyed-streams
text:
What does the keyBy operator do?
KeyBy partitions the stream by a key into a keyed stream, so state and windows are maintained independently per key.

title: state-types
text:
Fill in the state types Flink provides:
Flink offers value, list, map, aggregating, and reducing state, all managed by the framework so they can be checkpointed and restored.

title: state-api
text:
Why put the counter in ValueState registered through getRuntimeContext().getState(descriptor), instead of a normal Java field?
Only state registered with Flink gets checkpointed, restored after failures, and redistributed on rescaling, unlike a plain field.

title: state
text:
Why must state be managed by Flink instead of stored casually in member fields?
Flink can only give scaling and fault-tolerance guarantees for state it manages, restoring it from checkpoints when a node crashes.

title: watermarks
text:
What is a watermark in Flink?
A watermark(t) flows with the data and declares that event time has reached t, so the system assumes no more events with timestamps ≤ t will arrive and can fire windows ending at or before t; it is a heuristic, and events that still arrive later are treated as late events.

title: watermarks
text:
Why can events arrive late or out of order in Flink?
Late and out-of-order events come from network delays, uneven partition speeds, source failures, and varying latencies across the system.

title: watermarks
text:
What three things do watermarks let the system do as they flow with the data?
Watermarks let the system decide when to trigger windows, handle late events gracefully, and keep event-time processing consistent across the cluster.

title: watermarks
text:
Where is this WatermarkStrategy usually configured, and what does its key parameter express?
A WatermarkStrategy should be defined as close to the source as possible: pass it to `env.fromSource(...)` or call `assignTimestampsAndWatermarks` right after the source. The argument of `forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(10))` is the maximum out-of-orderness, equivalent to waiting up to ten seconds for late events.

title: watermarks
text:
How do these two strategies differ?
`forBoundedOutOfOrderness(10s)` emits watermarks at max seen timestamp minus 10 seconds, so windows fire 10 seconds later in exchange for tolerating a few seconds of jitter; `forMonotonousTimestamps()` is effectively zero out-of-orderness tolerance, giving the lowest latency, but the routinely delayed events here become late data that windows drop by default. Note that `noWatermarks()` is for jobs that don't need event time; on event-time windows it means the windows never fire.

title: watermarks
text:
What should a critical business system do with data that arrives beyond the bounded-out-of-orderness wait?
Mission-critical systems augment bounded out-of-orderness with an offline true-up process so even very late data is eventually processed.

title: windows
text:
Fill in the four Flink window types:
Tumbling windows are fixed and non-overlapping, sliding windows overlap, session windows size dynamically by activity, and global windows use custom logic.

title: windows
text:
How does a five-minute tumbling window differ from a five-minute sliding window with a one-minute slide?
A five-minute tumbling window emits every five minutes, while a five-minute sliding window with a one-minute slide emits every minute.

title: windows
text:
Which window should you choose?
Refreshing a five-minute metric every minute is exactly a sliding window with a five-minute size and one-minute slide.

title: windows
text:
When does Flink emit a new result for a window?
Flink emits a window's value when the window ends, with watermarks helping decide when that is.

title: windows
text:
What does the allowed-lateness setting do?
Allowed lateness keeps a closed window open for a grace period so events arriving after the close can still be processed.

title: job-definition
text:
What is the code skeleton of a typical Flink job?
A DataStream job is a StreamExecutionEnvironment plus sources, a chain of operators, and sinks, ending with execute() to build and submit the job graph. B describes querying an external database, not a Flink job (a Flink SQL job declares source/sink tables via connectors and runs INSERT INTO … SELECT, which is not the API in this question).

title: job-submission
text:
After env.execute() submits a job, who splits it into tasks and distributes them to machines?
Flow: DataStream program → StreamGraph → JobGraph (built on the client in session mode) → submitted to the JobManager → the JobManager expands it into an ExecutionGraph, acquires slots, and deploys tasks to TaskManagers.

title: sample-jobs
text:
Which Flink pipeline best fits this dashboard?
Key by page id, aggregate in one-minute tumbling windows, and sink counts to Redis; the unit that counts is the page (page count ≈ group count), not the much larger user count.

title: cep
text:
Which Flink capability best fits this fraud-detection rule?
Complex event processing expresses sequential patterns with time constraints, like a small test transaction followed within five minutes by a large one.

title: sample-jobs
text:
Why does the fraud-detection example write the alert stream to both Kafka and Elasticsearch?
Alerts go to Kafka for downstream automated consumers and to Elasticsearch for querying, showing one Flink job wiring a whole design together.

title: windows
text:
Which window should you use?
Looking back thirty minutes and evaluating every five minutes is exactly a thirty-minute window sliding by five minutes; a tumbling window evaluates only every thirty minutes and misses runs that straddle a bucket boundary, and a session window splits on inactivity gaps rather than a fixed lookback. A per-record KeyedProcessFunction with state could also count precisely, but it fires on every event, while the requirement only asks for evaluation every five minutes, so the sliding window is simpler.

title: cluster-architecture
text:
What are the two main Flink cluster processes and their roles?
The job manager coordinates scheduling, checkpoints, and failures, while task managers are the workers that execute processing in their slots.

title: cluster-architecture
text:
How is JobManager high availability implemented?
High availability deploys multiple job managers and uses ZooKeeper, Kubernetes HA, or a similar quorum/leader-election mechanism to elect one leader.

title: task-slots
text:
What is a task slot, and how is the default count chosen?
A slot splits one TaskManager's resources into shares and is the basic scheduling unit; taskmanager.numberOfTaskSlots defaults to 1 per TaskManager and is commonly set to the cores available to that TaskManager, but slots only divide managed memory and do not isolate CPU, so the core count is just a starting point.

title: task-slots
text:
Can different operators from the same job share a slot?
In the default slot sharing group, subtasks of different operators in one job can share a slot, so the job needs as many slots as its widest operator — eight here, not 8+8+8=24; how many machines that takes depends on slots per TaskManager. Sharing only raises utilisation; each operator keeps its own state and checkpoints, so correctness is unaffected.

title: task-slots
text:
What roles do task slots play?
Slots pre-divide a TaskManager's managed memory so a task doesn't take another's share (heap and CPU in the same JVM are not isolated); the cluster's total slot count caps parallel subtasks, and one TaskManager's slot count caps that machine; slot sharing lets a job's source, aggregation, and sink share one slot. Watermarks move with event timestamps and arrival pace, not slot count.

title: state-backends
text:
Which state backend should you choose?
The RocksDB state backend keeps large working state in local RocksDB/disk while remote storage is typically used for checkpoints or savepoints, at higher latency than memory state.

title: state-backends
text:
What is the core tradeoff between the memory backend and the RocksDB backend?
The memory backend is fast but limited by RAM, while RocksDB supports terabytes of state at higher latency.

title: checkpointing
text:
Which classic distributed algorithm is Flink checkpointing based on?
Flink checkpointing is based on the Chandy-Lamport algorithm for distributed snapshots.

title: checkpointing
text:
How does a checkpoint barrier work?
The JobManager's CheckpointCoordinator triggers a checkpoint and sources inject a barrier into the stream; the barrier flows downstream with the data, each operator snapshots its state to the checkpoint storage once barriers from all inputs arrive (aligned mode) and acknowledges to the JobManager, which marks the checkpoint complete when every task has acknowledged.

title: failure-recovery
text:
Put Flink failure recovery in the correct order:
Flink detects the failure, pauses the whole job, restores from one checkpoint, rewinds sources, and pays downtime to keep state consistent.

title: failure-recovery
text:
In this topology, why must tasks on healthy nodes stop as well?
Flink's default failover strategy restarts only the affected pipelined region. Here the keyBy connects all tasks all-to-all, so the whole job is one region; if healthy tasks kept advancing they'd diverge from the failed branch's input position, so the whole region — i.e., the whole job — rolls back to the latest checkpoint together. A job without shuffles might restart only part of its tasks.

title: failure-recovery
text:
What requirement does source rollback to a checkpoint place on a Kafka source?
Flink stores each partition's offset in the checkpoint and the source rewinds to those offsets on restore; if retention has already deleted that range, the rewind fails.

title: exactly-once
text:
How far does Flink exactly-once cover, and what happens beyond that boundary?
Exactly-once applies to Flink's internal state, so external writes can still repeat after recovery unless you add idempotence or transactions.

title: watermarks
text:
This "past 5:00" watermark arrives at 5:01:15; what is that roughly 75-second gap for?
The stem fixes the out-of-orderness bound at about 75 seconds with negligible ingestion delay, so the 5:01:15 − 5:00:00 gap is essentially the watermark's deliberate wait window, letting late clicks from around 4:59 land in the [4:59, 5:00) window at the cost of a later dashboard. With real ingestion delay, the wall-clock lag would be bound plus ingestion delay.

title: operations
text:
What operational cost does introducing Flink add to a design?
Flink brings significant operational overhead in deployment, monitoring, scaling, and managing state growth and recovery.

title: exactly-once
text:
What posture should you take in an interview about whether you need exactly-once?
End-to-end exactly-once needs a transactional sink and aligned checkpoints, costing latency and throughput. Here duplicates can only land in a store that upserts by click_id, so a replay just overwrites the same row and at-least-once plus idempotence gives correct results. If Flink itself aggregated counts, duplicates would already be in the count and sink idempotence couldn't undo them.

title: interview-strategy
text:
Why should you not model everything in an interview as a Flink streaming job?
Interviewers may not know all of Flink's capabilities and its complexity may not fit the problem, so use it only where it belongs.

title: time-domains
text:
What is the difference between event time and processing time?
Event time is when the event actually happened while processing time is when the system handles it, and separating the two domains is a key Flink pattern.

title: lessons
text:
Which Flink design lessons are useful even when you do not use Flink?
Flink teaches separating time domains, watermark-based progress tracking, local state with checkpointing, and slot-based resource isolation.

title: when-to-use
text:
Put the "why choose Flink" decision chain in the correct order:
Stateful real-time needs lead to Flink, whose operational complexity is mitigated by questioning real-time requirements and keeping simple paths simple.

title: state-enrichment
text:
What is the most direct Flink approach here?
With 50 million accounts and each transaction needing only its own, keying both streams by accountId and connecting them lets each parallel instance hold only its share of accounts with no per-record external calls. Broadcast state would make every instance store all 50 million rows — memory times parallelism — which suits only small dimension or rule tables; synchronous per-record API calls stall on remote latency; skipping enrichment loses key context.

title: windows
text:
Which window type should this velocity-detection job use?
Correct velocity detection needs each transaction attributed to when it truly happened, and only event-time windows with a watermark can pull late, out-of-order events back into the right bucket.

title: watermarks
text:
What is the role of the withTimestampAssigner part here?
Event-time processing has to know which field carries the time, and withTimestampAssigner points Flink at that field so it can advance the watermark and fire windows.

title: sample-jobs
text:
How do you deduplicate the alerts within the stream?
Union merges the two alert streams, keyBy(alertId) routes duplicates to the same key, and a windowed aggregate keeps one per window. The cost is an extra window operator and state, and it only removes duplicates that fall in the same window — boundary-straddling ones need a longer window or keyed state with TTL ("emit first, drop the rest"). Locks can't work because the detectors are independent distributed subtasks with no shared lock; exactly-once prevents replay duplicates, not business duplicates.

title: state-types
text:
As the stream keeps running, how does this state break down?
The root cause is keeping everything: ListState retains every transaction, so state grows linearly; on the heap backend it eventually hits the JVM heap ceiling and checkpoints grow ever larger and slower. Switching to RocksDB only moves the blow-up to disk and checkpoints; the real fix is ValueState, ReducingState, or AggregatingState holding a single accumulator.

title: overview
text:
What is the most accurate way to describe Apache Kafka?
Kafka describes itself as a distributed event streaming platform whose core is a durable, replayable partitioned log. Consumer groups can share that log like a queue, other systems can replay it from any offset, and windowed/stateful computation is done by engines like Kafka Streams or Flink. With proper replication factor, acks=all, and min.insync.replicas, it gives strong durability guarantees.

title: ordering
text:
What goes wrong if match events are randomly spread across queue servers?
Randomly spreading events across queues destroys ordering, so a goal could appear before kickoff, which is exactly why related events must share one partition.

title: partitioning
text:
How should the data be split across queue servers?
Partitioning by game ID keeps every event for one game in the same partition, preserving order while still scaling out.

title: consumer-groups
text:
What assignment does a Kafka consumer group guarantee?
Within a consumer group, each partition is assigned to exactly one consumer, so normally each event is handled once and never split.

title: topics
text:
Which Kafka mechanism separates soccer events from basketball events?
Topics let consumers subscribe only to the category they care about, so the soccer site never even sees basketball events.

title: terminology
text:
Fill in the basic Kafka architecture terms:
Brokers are the physical servers, a partition is an ordered append-only log whose records can't be modified in place once written, and a topic is the logical grouping of partitions.

title: terminology
text:
What is the core difference between a topic and a partition?
A topic is the logical grouping that organizes data, while its partitions are the physical grouping that scales it across brokers.

title: topics
text:
How many producers can write to one Kafka topic at the same time?
Topics are always multi-producer, so zero, one, or many producers can all write to the same topic.

title: queue-vs-stream
text:
What is the key difference between using Kafka as a queue and as a stream?
With classic consumer groups, both usages track progress through each group's committed offsets, and messages are kept by retention rather than deleted on read. The only difference is the consumption pattern: as a queue, consumers in one group share partitions and a message is done once that group handles it; as a stream, many groups read independently and can rewind offsets to replay.

title: message-format
text:
Which fields can a Kafka record technically carry? Select all that apply.
A Kafka record has a value, a key, a timestamp, and headers, and all four are technically optional.

title: partitioning
text:
What is the main purpose of a message key in Kafka?
The key is hashed to pick the partition, so messages sharing a key always land on the same partition and stay in order.

title: ordering
text:
What ultimately determines message order inside one partition?
Ordering within a partition comes from offsets, the append order, not from the timestamp field.

title: partitioning
text:
What do modern Kafka clients do by default when a message has no key?
Without a key, modern clients use a sticky partitioner that batches to one partition then rotates, giving roughly even distribution over time.

title: partitioning
text:
Fill in the default partitioner formula of the Java client:
The Java client hashes key bytes with murmur2, makes the result positive, and takes it modulo the partition count. Partitioning is client-side; other clients (e.g. librdkafka defaults to CRC32) may differ, so mixed-language producers should align partitioners. A bad key causes hot partitions.

title: routing
text:
After the partition is chosen, how does the producer know which broker to send to?
The client sends a Metadata request to any broker, caches the partition-to-current-leader map, and sends the produce request straight to that partition's leader. Brokers do not forward produce requests; a misdirected request gets a NOT_LEADER-type error and the client refreshes metadata and retries. The controller produces and propagates this metadata to the brokers.

title: log-structure
text:
What does it mean to say Kafka is a distributed commit log?
Each partition functions as an append-only log with messages added sequentially at the end, which is why Kafka is called a distributed commit log.

title: log-structure
text:
What benefits does Kafka get from an append-only log design? Select all that apply.
Append-only plus immutability gives three things: replication is just sequential appends (A), sequential writes avoid disk seeks (B), and fixed message positions let a single offset represent progress and enable replay (C). The cost is no in-place edits (D is wrong). Horizontal scaling comes from partitioning, a separate design decision.

title: log-structure
text:
How are messages that were written to a partition eventually removed?
Kafka has no delete-one-message operation. Normal removal is retention expiry or compaction (older versions of a key are cleaned, and a tombstone can eventually remove the key). An admin can also use DeleteRecords to truncate everything before an offset, but that is prefix truncation, not picking one message. Messages are never rewritten in place.

title: log-structure
text:
Why are Kafka's sequential appends more efficient than random writes?
Restricting writes to appending at the end of the log turns random I/O into sequential I/O, minimizing disk seeks, a major bottleneck in many storage systems.

title: offsets
text:
What is an offset?
An offset is a message's sequential position in its partition, and consumers commit it back to Kafka to track their progress.

title: delivery-semantics
text:
What happens if a consumer crashes after processing a message but before committing the offset?
Kafka is at-least-once by default, so a crash after processing but before committing the offset means the message gets reprocessed on restart.

title: delivery-semantics
text:
What does Kafka need to provide exactly-once semantics?
Exactly-once within Kafka relies on transactions: the idempotent producer removes duplicate writes from retries, and a transaction atomically binds "write to B + commit A's offsets", with read_committed consumers seeing only committed data. Defaults (producers are idempotent by default since 3.0) are still not end-to-end exactly-once. External side effects are outside Kafka transactions and need their own idempotency.

title: replication
text:
What is each partition's leader replica responsible for?
The leader replica handles all writes and, by default, reads too, with follower reads only available since Kafka 2.4 for latency optimization.

title: replication
text:
What do follower replicas do during normal operation?
Followers passively replicate the leader's data without serving clients, standing by as backups ready to take over.

title: replication
text:
What happens after the broker holding a partition leader goes down?
The controller promotes a fully synced follower to be the new leader, minimizing both downtime and data loss.

title: controller
text:
What is the Kafka controller?
The controller is Kafka's own role: it keeps the partition-to-leader map, tracks brokers joining and leaving, and elects leaders. Legacy ZooKeeper mode used a broker; since Kafka 4.0 only KRaft exists, a Raft quorum often on dedicated nodes, still part of the Kafka cluster.

title: pull-model
text:
How do Kafka consumers fetch messages?
Kafka consumers pull by actively polling the broker at intervals they control, a deliberate design choice.

title: pull-model
text:
What benefits does Kafka get from a pull model? Select all that apply.
Pulling lets consumers control their rate, simplifies failure handling, protects slow consumers, and enables efficient batching.

title: use-cases
text:
What is Kafka's correct role in this upload workflow?
Asynchronous work like video transcoding is the classic reason to add a message queue so the upload path can return immediately.

title: use-cases
text:
Why is Kafka a good fit for this virtual waiting queue?
Kafka's ordering guarantee is per partition: offsets follow write order inside one partition, and there is no global order across partitions. Keying by show ID puts every request for that show in one partition, so offset order is the queue order. Keying by user ID would scatter requests across partitions and leave only per-user order, which breaks strict FIFO. B, C and D are about storage, parallelism and throughput; none of them gives strict ordering. "First" here means first written to the broker, not first clicked by the user.

title: use-cases
text:
What value does Kafka add between these two microservices?
A queue decouples producer and consumer so they can scale independently, and one service's failure cannot take down the other.

title: use-cases
text:
Which Kafka usage pattern does this click aggregator need?
Continuous immediate processing of arriving data is the stream use case, exactly as in an ad-click aggregator.

title: use-cases
text:
How does Kafka let many downstream systems consume the same data?
Multiple independent consumer groups can read the same retained log simultaneously, each tracking its own offsets.

title: message-size
text:
For interview purposes, how small should one Kafka message stay to avoid hurting memory and network use?
Kafka brokers cap a message at about 1MB by default (message.max.bytes) and reject anything larger; you can raise it, but large messages strain broker memory, replication, and network. Large files like videos belong in S3, with Kafka carrying only a pointer such as the object key or URL.

title: blob-antipattern
text:
How should the actual video file move through the pipeline?
Kafka is built for many small messages; a blob of hundreds of MB far exceeds the default ~1MB message limit and, even if raised, slows replication and the whole partition. The common practice (the claim-check pattern) is to keep the file in object storage and send only its key or URL, which the worker uses to download it.

title: capacity
text:
As a rough order of magnitude, what can one strong Kafka broker handle?
With ~1KB messages and batched writes, a rough single-broker anchor is terabytes of storage (depending on attached disks) and hundreds of thousands to about a million messages per second. It is an order-of-magnitude anchor, not a guarantee: larger messages, no batching, or acks=all with cross-zone replication cut throughput noticeably. If your estimate is far below this, scaling is not the focus of the round.

title: scaling
text:
What happens if you add brokers but change neither the topic's partition count nor its partition placement?
Kafka neither moves existing partitions to new brokers nor splits partitions automatically, so the 3 partitions stay on the original 3 brokers. And with only 3 partitions, even a reassignment could use at most 3 brokers for this topic. To use the new machines you need a partition reassignment, plus more partitions when you need more parallelism.

title: scaling
text:
At what granularity should the partition count be set?
Partition count is a per-topic setting (chosen at creation, can be increased per topic) and caps how many consumers can process that topic in parallel, so it is sized per topic by its own throughput. Cluster-wide disk and network capacity is still planned in brokers, which is a separate question.

title: hot-partition
text:
What problem does this viral ad create for the system?
All clicks for the viral ad hash to the same partition, overwhelming it with traffic and creating a hot partition.

title: hot-partition
text:
Under this premise, what is the simplest hot-partition fix?
Dropping the key lets the default partitioner spread messages roughly evenly, at the cost of an ordering guarantee you did not need anyway.

title: hot-partition
text:
What is this technique for splitting a hot key across partitions called?
Salting appends a random number to the hot key to spread it across partitions, at the cost of more complex consumer-side aggregation.

title: hot-partition
text:
Under this premise, what is the best key design?
A compound key splits the hot key using an independently varying attribute: different regions of the same ad go to different partitions, while one ad in one region stays ordered in one partition. A timestamp key also spreads load but scatters the same ad and region, breaking the ordering requirement; broker number and message size are not business attributes.

title: hot-partition
text:
How does the back-pressure approach work here?
Back pressure means the upstream senses downstream pressure and slows down, at the cost of slower ingestion. Slowing on lag is application-level logic; Kafka's built-in related tools are broker-side quotas (per-client throttling) and the producer blocking when its buffer is full. Dropping loses data, a bigger machine leaves the hot key on one partition, and a standby cluster adds complexity.

title: hot-partition
text:
Put the hot-partition response chain in the right order:
Name the hot partition, explain that hashing pins a hot key to one partition, offer no-key, salting, a compound key, or back pressure, then state the ordering or aggregation cost.

title: durability
text:
What does acks=all mean?
With acks=all the leader waits for every current ISR member to write the message before acknowledging. Combined with min.insync.replicas=2, writes are rejected when the ISR drops below 2, so every acknowledged message is on at least two replicas and survives a leader crash. Without that setting, an ISR shrunk to just the leader makes it behave like acks=1.

title: durability
text:
Fill in the common replication setup:
A replication factor of three means one leader plus two followers, so data survives a single broker failure and a follower can be promoted right away.

title: availability
text:
How should you respond to the question, what if all of Kafka goes down?
A full-cluster outage is unlikely, so it deserves one sentence on mitigation (producer buffering or degradation, replay after recovery) rather than a long detour; the more common and worthwhile case is consumer failure, with offset commits and rebalancing. Avoid saying "Kafka is always available": with default settings Kafka would rather stop accepting writes when replicas are short than lose acknowledged data, which favors consistency.

title: rebalancing
text:
How does Kafka make sure these partitions keep getting processed?
Kafka rebalances the failed consumer's partitions across the remaining group members so every partition keeps being processed.

title: offsets
text:
Where does a restarted consumer continue reading from?
A restarted consumer reads its last committed offset from Kafka and resumes from there, missing nothing though possibly reprocessing a message.

title: offsets
text:
In this scenario, when should the offset be committed?
Commit the offset only after the HTML is safely stored, since committing any earlier means a crash would silently lose that work.

title: consumer-design
text:
What risk comes from making one consumer do too much work, and what design reduces it?
The more work a consumer does per message, the more gets redone on failure, so keep each consumer step small, like splitting crawling into separate download and parse phases.

title: producer-retries
text:
Under this requirement, what else should you do when enabling retries?
When a response is lost or times out, the producer resends a batch that was actually written, creating a duplicate. With idempotence on, the broker drops duplicate batches by producer ID + sequence number within one producer session and partition (and keeps per-partition order when max.in.flight.requests.per.connection ≤ 5). Compression and partition count are unrelated to duplicates; acks=0 waits for no acknowledgment, so retry decisions become even less reliable. Note: Java clients on Kafka 3.0+ enable idempotence by default; it only prevents retry duplicates within one producer session — across producer restarts or end to end you need transactions or downstream dedup.

title: consumer-retries
text:
What native support does Kafka provide for retrying failed consumer processing?
A classic consumer group only fetches messages and commits offsets; it does not know whether your processing succeeded. You can re-read by not committing or by seeking back, but backoff, retry counting, and DLQ are yours to build (or a framework's). The common pattern writes failures to a retry topic consumed by a separate consumer with a retry limit, then to a DLQ, so the main consumer is not blocked. Kafka also never silently skips a failed message for you. (Share groups in Kafka 4.x add delivery counts and redelivery, but they are out of scope here.)

title: dlq
text:
What is the dead-letter queue used for here?
A dead letter queue stores messages that failed too many retries so they can be investigated later without blocking the main flow.

title: kafka-vs-sqs
text:
Which queue choice is easier for this requirement?
SQS ships with built-in retry counting and dead-letter-queue support, which is exactly why the web crawler breakdown chose it over Kafka.

title: performance
text:
What is the first common way to improve Kafka producer throughput?
Batching packs many messages into one produce request, spreading per-request round-trip, header and broker-side costs, and making compression more effective. In KafkaJS you pass a messages array to one send(); the Java client batches per partition in the background according to batch.size and linger.ms.

title: performance
text:
Which compression algorithms does Kafka support, and what does compression save?
Kafka supports algorithms like GZIP, Snappy, and LZ4, trading a bit of CPU for smaller messages that transfer faster.

title: performance
text:
Among these options, which has the biggest effect on Kafka parallelism and load balance and should be discussed first?
The partition key decides which partition each message lands in. Key skew creates hot partitions, and since one partition is consumed by only one consumer in a group at a time, the hot partition caps throughput no matter how many machines you add. Compression (and batching) are real throughput levers but cannot fix skew; client language and field naming matter far less. So among these four, start with the partition key.

title: retention
text:
By default, how long does Kafka retain messages, and what does that mean for your replay window?
This is a default setting, not a computed number: the default seven-day retention already covers a three-day replay need, and only a longer requirement would force you to raise retention.ms at extra storage cost.

title: retention
text:
Fill in the retention policy configuration fields:
Two topic-level configs decide when log segments are deleted: retention.ms by time and retention.bytes by per-partition size, whichever triggers first. Longer retention lets consumers replay older data, at the cost of disk usage and more data to copy during recovery or partition reassignment.

title: philosophy
text:
How does Kafka treat message content itself?
An Apache Kafka broker treats key and value as opaque bytes, persisting them and serving them by offset; producers and consumers agree on serialization. Avro with a Schema Registry is a common practice, but the registry is an external component, not a Kafka requirement; broker-side schema validation is a Confluent commercial feature, not part of Apache Kafka.

title: producer-api
text:
Which kafkajs send call preserves per-user event order?
Setting the key to the user ID hashes all of that user's events onto one partition and preserves their order.

title: consumer-api
text:
How should kafkajs consumers configure groupId?
Different group IDs make each service an independent consumer group that reads the full stream with its own offsets.

title: queue-decision
text:
Put the decision chain for adding Kafka to an upload pipeline in the right order:
Async spiky work leads to choosing a Kafka queue, whose at-least-once redelivery is mitigated by idempotent consumers that commit offsets only after finishing.

title: managed-services
text:
What removes much of Kafka's production scaling and operations burden?
Managed services take over patching, broker replacement, monitoring, and varying degrees of scaling (e.g., MSK storage auto-scaling, serverless/elastic clusters that scale with load), but capacity planning such as partition count and key design is still yours — which is what interviews test. Hand-written scripts are error-prone; self-managed Kafka does not scale itself without configuration; a single node gives up replica fault tolerance.

title: what-is-k8s
text:
What core problem does Kubernetes solve?
Docker builds and runs a single container; once you have many across machines you need an orchestrator for scheduling, self-healing, autoscaling, and load balancing — that is Kubernetes.

title: pod-vs-container
text:
Are a Pod and a container the same thing in K8s?
A Pod is the smallest schedulable unit — a wrapper around container(s). Usually one Pod = one container, but it can hold a few tightly-coupled containers sharing localhost and volumes (e.g. a sidecar). Scaling means adding/removing Pods.

title: core-objects
text:
Fill in the three core Kubernetes objects:
A Node is a machine that runs Pods; a Deployment keeps N replicas (via an underlying ReplicaSet) and handles rolling updates — rolling updates are what a Deployment adds over a bare ReplicaSet; a Service gives a churning set of Pods one stable address and load balances across them.

title: hpa
text:
Which K8s mechanism should you use?
The HPA watches Pod CPU/custom metrics and adds Pods above a target (e.g. 50%), removing them when load drops; it needs a Metrics Server. This is how bursty judge autoscaling is implemented.

title: cluster-autoscaler
text:
What adds machines?
The HPA adds Pods; the Cluster Autoscaler adds Nodes. Every ~10s the CA checks for Pods that cannot be scheduled due to lack of resources and adds machines (removing idle ones). Together: HPA adds Pods → no room → CA adds Nodes.

title: hpa-vs-ca
text:
How do the HPA and Cluster Autoscaler differ and work together?
The HPA scales Pods (by CPU/metrics); the Cluster Autoscaler scales Nodes (by whether Pods are unschedulable). They complement: HPA adds Pods first, and when the cluster is full the CA adds machines; both scale back down as load falls.

title: when-k8s
text:
When is Kubernetes actually worth it?
K8s pays off when you orchestrate many containers across many machines with elastic scaling, self-healing, and rolling deploys. At small scale its operational complexity outweighs the benefit — a monolith or a few containers is enough; do not over-engineer.

title: programming-model
text:
What are the input/output signatures of the user-written map and reduce functions?
Map turns each record into zero or more intermediate pairs. After the framework groups by k2, reduce receives all values for one key and emits zero or more final key-value pairs. The paper often omits the output key and writes list(v3); the complete type is list(k3,v3).

title: execution-flow
text:
What is the correct order of the seven MapReduce execution steps?
The order isn't arbitrary: a reduce worker must finish pulling its whole partition before sorting and grouping, or a key's value list would be incomplete.

title: task-sizing
text:
How should split size, M, and R be chosen? What's the paper's rule of thumb?
Paper §3.5: each map task gets about 16–64MB of input (the same scale as GFS's 64MB chunk, which helps local reads), and M is far larger than the worker count for dynamic load balancing and cheap recovery when a machine dies; R is only a small multiple of the worker count because each reduce task produces a separate output file. Typical setup in the paper: 2,000 workers, M=200,000, R=5,000.

title: master-state
text:
What core state does the MapReduce master maintain?
Paper §3.2: for each map and reduce task the master stores its state (idle / in-progress / completed) and the identity of the worker for non-idle tasks; for each completed map task it also stores the locations and sizes of its R intermediate file regions and pushes them incrementally to workers with in-progress reduce tasks. It keeps only control-plane metadata, never the intermediate data itself.

title: sort-shuffle
text:
In the MapReduce paper, why does the reduce worker sort the pulled data by key before grouping, instead of building an in-memory hash table keyed by key?
Paper §3.1: many different keys map to the same reduce task, so after reading the intermediate data the reduce worker sorts it by key so that same-key records sit together, using an external sort if it doesn't fit in memory. A sequential scan then streams one group at a time to the reduce function, without holding the whole key space in memory, and yields key-ordered output as a bonus (§4.2). This is the paper's design choice; other systems achieve the same grouping with hashing plus partitioned spill to disk.

title: sort-shuffle
text:
Why doesn't this extra sorting step need to be built separately?
Because grouping already forces a per-partition sort, the framework gets an ordered output file as a free side effect, no extra job needed.

title: combiner
text:
What mechanism does local pre-aggregation on the map side to cut this kind of network traffic?
A combiner runs a local reduce-like pass on the map side before sending data, but it only works for commutative, associative functions like sum, not average.

title: partitioner
text:
What fixes the default partition function scattering one host's data?
Paper §4.1: the default partitioning is hash(key) mod R; when keys are URLs but you want grouping by host, you can supply a custom partition function hash(Hostname(urlkey)) mod R, so all URLs of one host land in the same output file. R=1 throws away all parallelism; sorting only orders data within a file and does not choose the reducer; a combiner only merges locally on the map side and does not route, so partitioning still happens. Trade-off: a very large host can make one reducer a hotspot.

title: disk-io-physics
text:
Given that one random seek costs about as much time as reading 1–2MB sequentially, what does that imply for large-block storage like GFS's 64MB chunks?
One seek ≈ the time to read 1–2MB, so on a 64MB contiguous read the seek is only a few percent, while at a few hundred KB seek time is comparable to transfer time. This is a commonly cited physical argument for large blocks (HDFS material uses this arithmetic). The GFS paper §2.5 itself lists three other reasons: fewer client–master lookups, reusable long-lived connections, and smaller master metadata (see mapreduce-012); seek amortization points the same way but is not the paper's stated rationale.

title: gfs-assumptions
text:
Given these premises, should GFS optimize for high throughput or low latency — and why?
The workload dictates the goal: mostly large sequential/append access means maximizing throughput pays off more than any single request's latency, so GFS explicitly trades latency for throughput.

title: master-chunkserver-flow
text:
Should GFS's data plane (the actual bytes) flow through the master? Why does that choice keep a single-master design from becoming a bottleneck?
Clients cache chunk locations and read data directly from chunkservers, so the master's load scales with the number of files/chunks, not with byte throughput — which is why it never becomes the bottleneck.

title: chunk-size-tradeoff
text:
GFS settled on 64MB chunks — what benefits was that trading for, and what cost did it introduce?
Paper §2.5: large chunks cut client–master lookups, let clients keep a persistent TCP connection to a chunkserver, and shrink master metadata (§2.6.1: under 64 bytes per 64MB chunk) so it fits in memory. The cost is that a small file has only one or two chunks and becomes a hotspot when many clients read it at once; the paper mitigates this with a higher replication factor and staggered start times.

title: chunk-location-metadata
text:
Why does GFS deliberately avoid persisting chunk locations, instead re-deriving them by asking chunkservers every time?
Chunkservers are the final authority on their own disks, so state you can re-derive from them — like chunk locations — shouldn't be persisted at the master.

title: record-append-consistency
text:
Who is responsible for cleaning up duplicate records and padding, and how?
Record append guarantees the data is written atomically at least once: if any replica fails, the client retries the whole append, which can leave duplicates; if a record doesn't fit, the primary pads the chunk. GFS doesn't dedup at the storage layer — records carry checksums so readers skip padding and fragments, and unique IDs so readers drop duplicates.

title: mapreduce-intermediate-storage
text:
MapReduce's input and final output both live in GFS — so why does it deliberately keep the intermediate map output on each worker's local disk instead of also writing it to GFS?
Intermediate data is read once by this job's reduce workers, so it skips GFS's replication cost by living on local disk — a lost map task just gets rerun instead.

title: data-locality-scheduling
text:
Why does MapReduce's scheduler prefer to place a map task on a machine that already holds a replica of that data, and why are splits usually sized to fit within one GFS chunk?
Because GFS exposes chunk locations, the scheduler can move compute to data; §3.4 reports most input is then read locally. Sizing and aligning splits to chunks keeps a split on one chunk and one machine — a design choice for locality, not a hard rule in the paper; a split spanning chunks will likely read part of its data over the network.

title: worker-failure
text:
How should the master handle this already-completed map task?
The paper resets completed map tasks on a failed worker back to idle, because their output lives only on that machine's local disk. Option C fails because a reducer that already fetched the data may itself be re-executed later and need it again; the paper re-runs the map task and tells reducers that haven't read yet to fetch from the new machine. Completed reduce tasks don't re-run, since their output is already in GFS.

title: master-failure
text:
When the master process itself dies, what does the paper's implementation actually do?
The paper notes checkpoint recovery would be easy to build, but with only one master and a low failure rate, the shipped implementation just aborts the job and leaves retry to the client.

title: atomic-commit
text:
What mechanism guarantees the final output file reflects only one of the two executions, not a mix?
Both map and reduce write to private temp files and atomically rename to the final name on completion, so if two executions both try to commit, only one rename takes effect.

title: determinism-semantics
text:
If the map/reduce functions are deterministic, does reading the re-executed map output cause the result to diverge from a fault-free sequential run?
With deterministic functions, no matter how many reruns happen, only one atomic commit ever takes effect, so what reduce reads matches exactly what a fault-free sequential run would produce.

title: nondeterministic-semantics
text:
In this situation, how strong is the semantic guarantee the paper actually makes?
Under non-determinism the guarantee weakens: e(R1) may have read one run of M while e(R2) read a different run, so the job no longer corresponds to one single global sequential execution.

title: stragglers
text:
What does the paper call this handful of tasks that delay overall completion, and what typically causes it?
The paper calls this a straggler — a machine unusually slow to finish, from causes like a bad disk (30MB/s dropping to 1MB/s) to a cache-disabling init bug that slowed computation over 100x.

title: backup-tasks
text:
When the backup task mechanism was disabled, what happened to the sort benchmark's completion time?
The paper's sort-benchmark control shows disabling backup tasks makes it about 44% slower — 891 seconds becomes roughly 1283 — while backup tasks themselves normally cost only a few percent more resources.

title: scale-numbers
text:
At what M (split count) and roughly how fast do these two benchmarks actually run?
Grep and sort both split ~1TB into M=15000 pieces on ~1800 machines — grep finishes in ~150s (incl. ~1 min startup), sort in 891s with under 50 lines of code.

title: counters
text:
How does the paper's counter facility gather these numbers, and how does it avoid double-counting?
Counters are user tallies incremented inside map/reduce and periodically reported to the master, which dedupes counts from backup tasks and re-executions — handy for sanity-checking input/output counts.

title: lineage-sstable
text:
Which later storage structure best matches this idea of a sorted output file that supports random lookups by key?
Sorting makes each partition's output ordered by key; add an index and you can look up by key — the same idea as Bigtable's SSTable (sorted, immutable, block-indexed). It's a conceptual echo between the papers, not an explicit prediction.

title: lineage-sstable
text:
Put these six links of the lineage in causal order.
Each link follows from the one before: expensive seeks force big append-only chunks, and MapReduce's sort turns that into physical key adjacency that BigTable indexes into an SSTable.

title: lineage-sstable
text:
Besides lock-free reads, which other benefits of immutable SSTables does the Bigtable paper name?
Bigtable §6: since SSTables are never modified after creation, reads need no synchronization; permanently removing deleted data becomes garbage-collecting obsolete SSTables; and split tablets share the parent's SSTables, so splits are fast. The paper doesn't cite compression (A); there's no format-compatibility requirement (B); LevelDB/RocksDB SSTables are still immutable (D).

title: gfs-fit
text:
Why can BigTable safely be built on top of GFS's loose consistency?
GFS only promises "consistent but undefined" for concurrent overwrites from multiple writers. BigTable avoids that case: the commit log is append-only, SSTables are written once, and each file has a single tablet-server writer (serial writes are "defined" in GFS). So BigTable never needs stronger concurrent-write semantics from GFS.

title: commit-log-design
text:
What does keeping a single commit log per tablet server avoid?
Thousands of per-tablet log files would mean heavy concurrent writes and seeks and break group commit's batching, so BigTable pays for that with a recovery-time sort of the log by (table, row, LSN).

title: lsm-tradeoff
text:
How should you respond to "does sequential I/O still matter in the SSD era"?
SSDs have no seek, but NAND writes by page and erases by block, so small random writes trigger FTL garbage collection, adding device-level write amplification and wear; every I/O also carries fixed command overhead; and on the network-attached block storage given in the scenario, each I/O is a network round trip with IOPS-based limits and pricing. The conclusion holds — only the reasons change from disk seeks to these three.

title: modern-successors
text:
What did Spark/Flink drop from MapReduce, and what did they keep?
Spark/Flink pipeline steps as a DAG instead of writing every step to triple-replicated HDFS, but key-based aggregation still needs a shuffle to redistribute data by key, and Spark's sort-based shuffle and spills still sort — a modern continuation, not an unchanged copy. For fault tolerance Spark recomputes lost partitions from lineage and Flink restores from checkpoints; neither uses synchronous replicas. Both keep locality-aware scheduling.

title: modern-successors
text:
