What best explains this cross-system structural convergence?
The physical fact that seeks are expensive and sequential reads are cheap doesn't care about team or language, so any workload shaped like 'look up a run of values by key' that outgrows memory converges on the same shape.

title: interview-usage
text:
Which signals point you toward a MapReduce-style design?
No single clue is enough — key-based aggregation, data too big for memory, and tolerance for batch latency all have to hold at once before the problem actually matches MapReduce's sort-then-group shape.

title: interview-usage
text:
When you hear "no database allowed", what should your first sentence be?
State the optimization target first — disk locality, one seek plus one sequential read — so any single implementation detail the interviewer pokes at can be swapped without collapsing the whole answer.

title: default-choice
text:
In a system design interview, what is the pragmatic starting point for choosing a database?
PostgreSQL offers ACID, relational constraints, rich queries, JSONB, full-text search, and mature replication; start from this reliable default and let requirements justify a change. D is a poor fit: Redis has RDB/AOF persistence and MULTI/EXEC, but lacks foreign keys and joins, its durability window depends on configuration, and keeping everything in memory is costly.

title: motivating-example
text:
Which social-platform requirements make PostgreSQL a reasonable primary store?
Postgres fits social-style data when relationships, referential integrity, atomic multi-step operations, and rich queries matter.

title: consistency-needs
text:
How do consistency needs differ between a like count and creating a DM thread?
A like count can often be eventually consistent, while creating a DM thread usually requires atomic transactional updates.

title: btree-index
text:
What index type does PostgreSQL use most often by default?
PostgreSQL's default and most common index type is the B-tree index.

title: btree-index
text:
What query shapes are B-tree indexes usually good for?
B-tree indexes work well for exact matches, range filters, and sorting that follows the indexed column order.

title: index-tradeoff
text:
Why should you not blindly add an index to every column?
Every index speeds some reads but slows writes, consumes disk, and may not even be chosen by the planner.

title: multi-column-index
text:
Which index best matches this profile-page query pattern?
A multi-column index on user_id and created_at matches the profile query pattern for a user's recent posts.

title: full-text-search
text:
Which index type does built-in PostgreSQL full-text search usually use?
PostgreSQL full-text search commonly uses a GIN index over a tsvector column.

title: full-text-vs-elasticsearch
text:
What is the pragmatic starting point for this search need?
Every listed requirement—stemming, basic relevance, multiple languages, boolean queries—is covered by Postgres's built-in full-text search (tsvector + GIN), and the data is already there, so there's no need to run a separate search cluster and sync pipeline. Revisit Elasticsearch when fuzzy, typeahead, or faceting needs appear.

title: elasticsearch-when
text:
Which requirements make Elasticsearch a stronger choice?
Elasticsearch shines at search UX and distributed search: tunable relevance scoring, low-latency faceted aggregations at scale, and fuzzy queries plus suggesters for typo tolerance and search-as-you-type. Postgres can do similarity matching with pg_trgm, prefix matching with :*, and facet counts with GROUP BY, but as these needs grow in number and scale, ES fits better. A primary-key lookup only needs the B-tree PK index and is no reason to add ES.

title: jsonb
text:
In Postgres, what keeps metadata flexible while still queryable?
JSONB with a GIN index gives Postgres flexible metadata storage with efficient containment queries.

title: postgis
text:
What capability does PostGIS add to PostgreSQL?
PostGIS adds geospatial types, spatial indexes, and spatial operations such as distance and containment to Postgres.

title: postgis
text:
Which PostGIS function is central to this nearby-post query?
ST_DWithin is the key PostGIS function for finding rows within a geographic distance.

title: gist
text:
What is the intuition behind the GiST index commonly used by PostGIS?
PostGIS uses GiST indexes with spatial strategies such as bounding boxes to accelerate geospatial queries.

title: combined-search
text:
Which capabilities can Postgres combine in one rich search query?
Postgres can combine full-text search, JSONB filters, and PostGIS geospatial predicates in one query.

title: covering-index
text:
What is the purpose of a covering index?
A covering index includes needed columns so some queries can be answered from the index without fetching table rows.

title: covering-index
text:
Which SQL statement looks like a covering index?
Including title and created_at in the user_id index can let Postgres satisfy the query from the index alone.

title: partial-index
text:
When is a partial index most useful?
A partial index indexes only rows matching a predicate, making it smaller and cheaper when queries target that subset.

title: partial-index
text:
Which index is a better fit for mostly active-user queries?
A partial email index on active users is smaller and better matches the common query pattern.

title: read-performance
text:
What design judgments follow from these Postgres throughput anchors?
These are estimation anchors, not SLAs: heavier joins and aggregates need a lower throughput budget; full-scan cost depends first on rows scanned and then on whether data is in memory or on disk, with disk reads being much slower for the same rows. B treats an estimate as a commitment, and D calls the heavier join faster.

title: scale-limits
text:
What design judgments follow from these Postgres scale anchors?
These are rules of thumb, not hard limits. Once the hot working set outgrows memory, cache hit rate drops and more queries hit disk, so add memory or archive cold data; approaching these scales is the time to evaluate partitioning or sharding. B ignores join complexity and indexing, and D treats rules of thumb as hard ceilings.

title: memory
text:
Why is memory king for Postgres performance?
Postgres caches hot data in shared_buffers and the OS page cache. When the working set fits in memory, most reads need no I/O; once it exceeds RAM, cache misses trigger disk reads and latency rises noticeably with more variance—how much depends on the storage medium, access pattern, and the query's own CPU cost.

title: write-path
text:
Put the PostgreSQL write path in order:
Postgres writes modify buffers and WAL in memory, update indexes, flush WAL at commit, and later write dirty pages to data files.

title: wal
text:
Under the default configuration (synchronous_commit = on), why does WAL flush often drive write commit latency?
With the default synchronous_commit = on, commit returns only after the transaction's WAL records are fsynced to disk; WAL writes are sequential and friendlier than random writes, but still synchronous I/O on the commit path. Data pages can be written later by checkpoints and background writers, with WAL replay covering crashes. Setting synchronous_commit = off skips the flush wait and lowers latency, at the risk of losing the last few acknowledged transactions on a crash.

title: write-throughput
text:
What design judgments follow from these Postgres write-throughput anchors?
These are rough benchmarks: the more tables and indexes a transaction touches, the heavier each write and the lower the throughput. Beyond the single-core figure, first use concurrency across cores and batched INSERT/COPY; only when a fully used single node still falls short should you consider sharding. B inflates the scale, and D treats an estimate as a commitment.

title: write-limit-factors
text:
Which factors reduce Postgres write throughput or increase commit latency?
Indexes add maintenance work, synchronous replication waits for replica acknowledgements, and complex transactions add locks, WAL, and checks. PgBouncer usually reduces connection overhead.

title: connections
text:
Why do high-concurrency apps often put PgBouncer or another pooler before Postgres?
Connection pooling matters because Postgres uses a process per connection, so hundreds of direct connections waste memory and CPU.

title: write-optimizations
text:
Which optimization or scaling tactics help when Postgres write pressure rises?
Postgres write scaling is a ladder: raise one-node capacity, reduce commit overhead, offload non-critical writes, then partition or shard when one node is still too hot.

title: batching
text:
For buffered like writes, what is the simplest write optimization?
Batching multiple writes into one transaction improves throughput by reducing per-write commit overhead.

title: write-offloading
text:
What write pattern fits non-critical logs, analytics events, metrics, or last-seen updates?
Side-effect writes like logs and analytics should go through a queue so workers can batch, aggregate, and persist them off the user path.

title: partitioning
text:
How does Postgres table partitioning help large tables?
Postgres supports range, list, and hash partitioning. Once a table is split into physical partitions by a partition key, queries that filter on that key use partition pruning to skip irrelevant partitions, and inserts maintain only the target partition's indexes. With time-range partitioning, old partitions can also be detached or dropped wholesale for lifecycle management.

title: partitioning
text:
Why can time-partitioning a posts table help both writes and reads?
A is wrong: new posts all carry the current timestamp, so live writes land almost entirely in the newest partition—time partitioning concentrates writes rather than spreading them; use hash partitioning or sharding to spread writes. B is right: each partition has its own smaller indexes, so an insert maintains only the current partition's indexes. C is right: with a time predicate, partition pruning skips historical partitions. D is wrong: partitioning is not a cache and does not change the consistency model.

title: sharding
text:
When user-post lookups dominate, what is the better sharding key?
The shard key should follow the dominant query dimension. Since the main query fetches posts by user, sharding by user_id keeps it on one shard; a random UUID or created_at modulo scatters a user's posts and forces scatter-gather; first letter of content is skewed and unrelated to the query. The trade-off is that very large users can create hot shards, which needs separate handling.

title: sharding
text:
What is the main cost of sharding Postgres?
Sharding spreads single-node write pressure, but the design must handle query routing, cross-shard transactions, schema migrations, and multi-database operations.

title: replication
text:
What are the two main purposes of Postgres replication?
Replication is used to scale reads across replicas and provide high availability if the primary fails.

title: sync-vs-async-replication
text:
What is the core tradeoff between asynchronous and synchronous Postgres replication?
Asynchronous replication favors write performance with possible recent data loss on failover, while synchronous replication adds latency for stronger durability.

title: read-replicas
text:
What caveat matters most when read replicas scale Postgres reads?
Read replicas can lag behind the primary, so users may not read their own recent writes.

title: failover
text:
Put the rough Postgres primary failover flow in order:
Failover detects the failed primary, promotes a replica, updates connection routing, and points applications to the new primary.

title: acid
text:
Complete ACID:
ACID stands for Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, and Durability.

title: transactions
text:
What basic guarantee does a database transaction provide?
A transaction guarantees a group of operations either all commit or all roll back.

title: atomicity
text:
For this bank transfer, which database mechanism should you use?
A single transaction ensures both account updates commit together or both roll back.

title: concurrency
text:
Why can concurrent auction bidding still break even if you use a transaction?
A transaction makes a group of operations commit atomically, but doesn't keep the values you read valid until commit. Under the default Read Committed, a plain SELECT takes no row lock, so two transactions can both read the same stale maxBid and both think they are highest. Fixes: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE to take an exclusive row lock on the auction row, a conditional write (UPDATE ... WHERE max_bid < :new), Serializable, or OCC.

title: row-locking
text:
Which concurrency-control approach protects the auction maxBid row?
SELECT FOR UPDATE locks the auction row so concurrent bid checks and updates are serialized.

title: serializable-vs-locking
text:
What is the main tradeoff between row-level locking and Serializable isolation?
Row-level locking is explicit and efficient when you know which rows to lock, while serializable isolation handles complex cases but requires retry logic.

title: isolation-levels
text:
Which distinct isolation behaviors does PostgreSQL actually provide?
PostgreSQL effectively provides Read Committed, Repeatable Read, and Serializable, with Read Uncommitted behaving like Read Committed.

title: read-committed
text:
What is Postgres's default isolation level?
PostgreSQL's default isolation level is Read Committed.

title: repeatable-read
text:
What is notable about Postgres Repeatable Read?
The SQL standard allows phantom reads at Repeatable Read, but Postgres's Repeatable Read reads from one snapshot for the whole transaction, so rows inserted and committed by others midway stay invisible — phantom reads are prevented too. The cost: if a concurrent transaction modifies the same row, this one may get a serialization failure and must retry.

title: serializable
text:
What does Serializable isolation mean?
Serializable isolation makes transactions behave as if they ran one at a time, but conflicting transactions may abort and need retries.

title: occ
text:
With rare bid conflicts, which application-level concurrency strategy can you use?
In OCC, the version is stored on the database row. The client only sends back the version it read, and the UPDATE succeeds only if the row still has that version.

title: when-to-use
text:
Which requirements support choosing PostgreSQL in a system design interview?
Postgres fits complex relationships, strong consistency, rich querying, JSONB, full-text search, and geospatial needs.

title: when-not
text:
Why might a single PostgreSQL primary be the wrong fit here?
Extreme write throughput can exceed Postgres because WAL, index maintenance, and single-primary writes become bottlenecks.

title: extreme-writes-alternatives
text:
Which are reasonable alternatives or side systems?
High-volume event streams that tolerate eventual consistency fit a horizontally write-scalable wide-column store like Cassandra; high-frequency counters fit atomic increments in Redis with periodic write-back. Indexing every column makes each write heavier, and not persisting at all gives up durability.

title: global-active-active
text:
Why is plain Postgres not a natural fit for active-active multi-region writes?
Postgres is not naturally active-active because its single-primary model makes multi-region writes and conflict resolution difficult.

title: global-alternatives
text:
Which alternatives do you consider for global multi-region writes?
Global multi-region alternatives include CockroachDB for global ACID, Cassandra for eventual consistency, and DynamoDB global tables for managed replication.

title: simple-key-value
text:
Why might PostgreSQL be overkill for this access pattern?
For truly simple key-value access, Postgres can be overkill because its transactional and query machinery adds unnecessary overhead.

title: scalability-myth
text:
What is wrong with saying, 'NoSQL scales better, so skip PostgreSQL'?
"NoSQL scales better" is a blanket claim: you first state the read/write ratio, data volume, query patterns, and consistency needs, then check whether Postgres indexing, read replicas, partitioning, or sharding can handle them. Switching technology without those numbers is a weak argument.

title: relational-model
text:
Complete the three relationship cardinalities between entities:
Common relational patterns are one-to-one, one-to-many, and many-to-many, with join tables for many-to-many relationships.

title: foreign-key
text:
What value does a foreign key provide in a relational database?
A foreign key enforces referential integrity by requiring referenced rows to exist.

title: normalization
text:
What is the tradeoff between normalization and denormalization?
Normalization reduces duplication and preserves integrity, while denormalization can speed reads at the cost of keeping duplicated data consistent.

title: acid-consistency
text:
How does ACID Consistency differ from CAP Consistency?
ACID's C means database rules (foreign keys, CHECK, uniqueness) are not broken by a transaction; CAP's C is linearizability: in a replicated system, every read sees the most recent completed write. One asks "is the data valid," the other asks "are replicas up to date."

title: acid-fit
text:
Which paths usually need strong ACID transactions from a database like Postgres?
Financial transfers, authentication state, and inventory/order updates usually require strong ACID guarantees.

title: sql-command-types
text:
Which SQL command categories are matched with the right examples?
DDL defines structure and DML manipulates data, while options 3 and 4 swap the examples for access control (DCL) and transaction control (TCL).

title: index-maintenance
text:
Why is updating the indexed status column much slower than updating an unindexed column?
A Postgres update writes a new row version. If no indexed column changes and the page has room, it can be a HOT update and indexes stay untouched. Changing an indexed column like status rules out HOT, so all four indexes on the table get new entries for the new version, each adding WAL, and the old version waits for VACUUM. That is why indexes should cover only high-value read paths.

title: read-scaling
text:
What is the common way to scale reads in Postgres?
Read-heavy workloads can scale by sending reads to replicas while writes continue to the primary.

title: managed-postgres
text:
How should you describe Postgres high availability in an interview?
In interviews, it is reasonable to rely on managed Postgres for backups, replication, and failover while explaining the high-level failover flow.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the 'choose PostgreSQL and scale gradually' decision chain in order:
A strong Postgres decision starts from relationships and consistency needs, chooses Postgres, then scales with targeted optimizations before adding more complex systems.

title: durability
text:
What mechanism mainly provides Postgres durability?
Postgres durability relies on Write-Ahead Logging, where committed changes can be replayed after a crash.

title: durability-tradeoff
text:
What does relaxing durability with settings like synchronous_commit = off mean?
Relaxing synchronous commit can improve speed but risks losing recent commits on crash or power failure.

title: primary-key
text:
What does PostgreSQL usually create automatically for a primary key?
Postgres creates a unique B-tree index for a primary key to enforce uniqueness and speed lookups.

title: summary
text:
Which statements are a mature way to justify choosing PostgreSQL in an interview?
A strong interview answer treats Postgres as a capable default while explaining concrete requirements, scaling options, and when alternatives are justified.

title: read-vs-write-cost
text:
In this measurement, why are reads about an order of magnitude faster than writes?
Here each insert is its own transaction, so every commit waits for the WAL to reach disk and adds an entry to each of three indexes; a read just follows an index to the row and changes nothing. That is why, on this node and configuration, the gap is about 10x. Batching commits, relaxing durability, or dropping indexes narrows it a lot — the ratio is not a fixed rule.

title: lost-update
text:
After B commits a $95 bid, what inconsistent state is left in the database?
B's INSERT writes the $95 bid; then UPDATE ... WHERE maxBid<95 under Read Committed sees A's committed 100, the condition fails, and 0 rows change. The app commits without checking the row count, leaving an orphan bid. Fixes: roll back when rowcount is 0, lock the auction row first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, or use Serializable with retry.

title: batch-failure
text:
What is the failure mode of this batched commit when the server crashes?
Batching buffers writes in memory and commits them together to cut per-commit cost — but a crash before commit loses the batch, so use it only for retryable writes like likes.

title: sharding-ops
text:
What is the operational reality of sharding on PostgreSQL?
DynamoDB splits and routes by partition key automatically; native Postgres gives you partitioned tables (postgres_fdw can place partitions on other servers, but routing, rebalancing, cross-shard queries, and transactions are on you). So in practice you route shards in the application or use the Citus extension to take that over. It enlarges the ops surface, so it usually comes after indexes, replicas, and partitioning run out.

title: hybrid-replication
text:
To keep committed writes durable while also scaling reads, how do you commonly arrange replication?
Synchronous replicas put committed data on multiple nodes (durability) at the cost of waiting on every write; asynchronous replicas scale reads but lag and may serve stale data. So keep a few sync replicas for durability and let async ones absorb reads. More sync replicas means slower writes, and the default synchronous_commit=on only guarantees the WAL is flushed on the standby, not replayed — read-your-latest from a replica needs remote_apply or reading the primary.

title: error-handling
text:
Which failure must the application handle under each of these two concurrency-control approaches?
Serializable throws serialization failures on a dependency conflict, so you retry the transaction; row-level locking can deadlock, so you handle the rolled-back victim.

title: why-btree-fails
text:
Why can a database answer "find users aged 20 to 25" in milliseconds?
In a B-tree, keys sit sorted and adjacent in leaf pages: read a few levels from the root to find the first age=20 entry, then scan leaf pages sequentially and stop after LIMIT 100; the (age, user_id) index covers the returned column, so no table lookups are needed. Pages read depend on tree height plus rows returned, not on the 100M table size. Without the LIMIT, returning tens of millions of rows is not millisecond-fast, and the planner may switch to a sequential scan.

title: why-btree-fails
text:
How far can the latitude index by itself narrow the candidate rows?
A single-column index sorts by one dimension only: the latitude index narrows candidates to a horizontal strip of matching latitude, whose longitudes can be continents apart. The distance filter can still produce the right final answer, but only after reading and checking every row in that strip.

title: why-btree-fails
text:
Why does a composite index on (lat, long) still fail to solve proximity search?
A composite index still sorts by the first column and breaks ties with the second, so the database falls back to brute-force distance checks row by row.

title: root-problem
text:
Complete the root problem in proximity search:
A one-dimensional sort order cannot preserve two-dimensional closeness, so neighbors on the ground can land far apart in the index.

title: two-approaches
text:
What are the two main production approaches to proximity search?
Production systems either build a custom spatial tree that understands shapes or flatten each location into a single sortable key an ordinary index can handle.

title: candidate-set
text:
With cell- or bounding-box-based spatial indexes like this, what is the common query pattern?
Cells and bounding boxes are squares while the query is a circle, so matched cells always include points outside the radius. These structures cheaply generate a candidate set, and exact distance or geometry math on that set produces the real answer.

title: two-approaches
text:
Which indexing route fits each data type?
Geometric data with polygons belongs in a spatial tree like PostGIS, while constantly moving points belong in encoded cells on an ordinary index.

title: spatial-trees
text:
What trick makes a custom spatial tree work inside a database, not just in memory?
Spatial trees work on disk only when shaped like a B-tree, with balanced page-sized nodes and predictable depth.

title: quadtree
text:
How does a quadtree organize a map?
A quadtree makes the map itself the tree, splitting each overloaded quadrant into four children until every leaf holds few points.

title: quadtree
text:
In a quadtree proximity search, what forms the candidate set?
The candidate set is the points in every leaf whose cell intersects the query circle. The leaf containing the query point is not enough: the nearest point may sit across a boundary, and in dense areas the circle can span several rings of small leaves. Collect all intersecting leaves, then filter by exact distance.

title: quadtree
text:
What does it mean for a quadtree to adapt to data density?
Dense areas like Manhattan grow deep subtrees while an empty lake stays one coarse cell, so no space is wasted subdividing emptiness.

title: quadtree
text:
What is the quadtree "depth problem" at scale?
Splits land at geometric midpoints rather than where data sits, so dense clusters need many levels and the busiest regions become the slowest to query.

title: quadtree
text:
What is the quadtree "disk problem" at scale?
A quadtree is a pointer structure, and on disk every pointer hop risks a random page read, leaving you waiting on the disk after a few hops.

title: quadtree
text:
Where are quadtrees still useful today?
Quadtrees mostly live in memory today: map tiles and collision detection. A is wrong because of the word "default". Mainstream databases usually default to the R-tree family (e.g., PostGIS GiST), BKD (Lucene), or encoded keys on a B-tree (e.g., MongoDB S2). On-disk quadtrees do exist, such as PostgreSQL SP-GiST's quad_point_ops, but they are not the default.

title: kd-tree
text:
On the split rule dimension, how do quadtrees and k-d trees differ?
A quadtree splits both dimensions at once into four quadrants, while a k-d tree alternates one dimension per level in a binary tree.

title: kd-tree
text:
Which statement about k-d trees is correct?
A k-d tree stays balanced by splitting at the median and served nearest-neighbor search for decades, but its pointer structure makes it painful beyond RAM.

title: bkd-tree
text:
What modernization does a BKD tree add to a k-d tree?
BKD packs points into disk blocks, which fixes the random I/O problem of pointer-based trees. The cost is that each tree is bulk-built once and never modified afterward. To support writes, a system keeps several trees and periodically merges and rebuilds them (the logarithmic method in the Bkd-tree paper, segment merges in Lucene). That makes it a natural fit for this bulk-load-heavy workload.

title: bkd-tree
text:
What index backs Elasticsearch geo fields today?
Elasticsearch geo fields use BKD trees, the k-d tree idea repackaged into a disk-friendly block-structured index.

title: r-tree
text:
What was the R-tree's role in spatial-index history?
Disk-based structures for points already existed before the R-tree (K-D-B-tree, grid file). The R-tree's contribution was to index extended objects such as polygons and lines, via minimum bounding rectangles, inside a balanced, paged, B-tree-like tree that supports dynamic inserts and deletes. That made it the foundation of spatial database indexing.

title: r-tree
text:
Why can't county borders and highways fit into the existing point quadtree?
A point index assumes every object has one coordinate. Highways are lines and counties are polygons that span many cells, so a point quadtree cannot decide which node should hold them. Some quadtree variants (MX-CIF, PMR) can store shapes by splitting them across cells, but the usual move is an index that bounds shapes, such as an R-tree.

title: r-tree
text:
How does an R-tree use its core building block, the MBR?
Every object gets wrapped in its minimum bounding rectangle, and nearby rectangles nest inside larger ones all the way up to the root.

title: r-tree
text:
Why can an R-tree work as a database index like a B-tree?
An R-tree stays balanced with all leaves at the same depth and page-sized nodes, splitting and merging pages exactly like a B-tree.

title: r-tree
text:
What performance trap matters most in an R-tree?
R-tree rectangles can overlap, and a query landing in two rectangles must descend both branches, so sloppy insertion that creates overlap drags performance down.

title: r-tree
text:
Which R-tree variant is most commonly adopted to reduce overlap?
Overlap is the R-tree's weak spot. The R*-tree (Beckmann et al. 1990) uses better insertion heuristics plus forced reinsertion to reduce overlap, and it is the most commonly adopted variant, for example in SQLite's R*Tree module and Boost.Geometry's rstar. Some systems use their own split algorithms instead, such as PostgreSQL GiST.

title: r-tree
text:
What should you use?
For real geometry like containment and intersection, R-tree-based systems such as PostGIS on GiST are the standard answer.

title: encoded-keys
text:
What is the core idea behind the encoded-key route?
Encoded keys skip custom trees entirely by turning each location into a sortable key that any ordinary index can use.

title: encoded-keys
text:
What is a space-filling curve?
A space-filling curve threads a single line through two-dimensional space so points close on the map stay close along the line.

title: geohash
text:
How is a geohash string built?
A geohash recursively divides the world into thirty-two cells per level, adding one character per level to zoom in further.

title: geohash
text:
How many geohash prefix characters should coarse candidate filtering and door-level precision use?
Choose precision by purpose: coarse-filter cells should match the search radius, so a 5-character prefix (about 5 km) plus neighboring cells captures the candidates. Using 9 characters for coarse filtering would require querying on the order of a million 5-meter cells to cover 5 km, which blows up query cost. Only the door-level point needs a longer prefix or the raw coordinates.

title: geohash
text:
Why are a geohash string and integer just two readings of the same bits?
A geohash is a sequence of interleaved bits. The base32 string groups every 5 bits into one readable character; the integer is another reading of the same bits. As long as both sides use the same encoding and the bit count is a multiple of 5, the two convert losslessly and work with any sorted index. Caveat: Redis's internal 52-bit geohash uses a different latitude range, and its GEOHASH command re-encodes to a standard string, so you cannot map those bits directly.

title: geohash
text:
What is the "prefix property" of geohash?
Keys sharing a prefix fell into the same cell at every covered level, so a longer shared prefix means a smaller shared box on the map.

title: geohash
text:
Which SQL can use an existing index for coarse filtering?
A LIKE prefix scan on the geohash column is an ordinary B-tree range scan, which is exactly how geohash makes proximity queries run on any database.

title: geohash
text:
How do Redis GEOADD and GEO commands work under the hood?
GEOADD interleaves latitude and longitude into a fifty-two-bit geohash integer stored as a sorted-set score, making nearby queries a range scan.

title: geohash
text:
What is geohash's most dangerous boundary problem?
Space is cut into hard cells, so neighbors on opposite sides of a boundary may share only a short prefix, and at top-level boundaries like the equator or prime meridian, no prefix at all. A naive prefix query misses them. This is inherent to encoded-key schemes and is fixed by also querying neighbor cells.

title: geohash
text:
What is the standard fix for geohash boundary problems?
First choose a precision whose cell side is at least the radius. Then querying the home cell plus its 8 neighbors (a 3×3 block) fully covers the query circle. The ring query guarantees recall, and exact-distance filtering guarantees precision.

title: geohash
text:
Put the "find nearby drivers with geohash" query flow in order:
You locate the rider's cell, expand to the three-by-three ring, fetch candidates by prefix scan, post-filter by exact distance, and return the winners.

title: geohash
text:
Complete the common encoded-key query pattern:
When the cell side is at least the radius, the 3×3 ring fully covers the query circle, so the ring query fixes boundary misses. Post-filtering removes points that are inside the window but too far away. Together they form a complete proximity query.

title: s2
text:
Why does geohash start to fail at global scale?
Geohash treats the globe as a flat rectangle, so cells are fat squares at the equator and thin slivers near the poles.

title: s2
text:
How does Google S2 solve the sphere problem?
S2 projects the sphere onto the six faces of a cube and subdivides recursively, so cells at the same level have roughly comparable areas (within about 2x max/min, far better than a lat/lon grid). It also handles shapes crossing the antimeridian correctly. MongoDB's 2dsphere index is built on S2.

title: s2
text:
What S2 advantage is shown by a polygon crossing the antimeridian at +180/-180 longitude?
Because S2 actually understands the sphere, it correctly handles polygons crossing the antimeridian where flat grids mangle the wraparound.

title: s2
text:
On cell-area consistency, how do geohash and S2 differ?
Geohash splits latitude/longitude into equal-degree rectangles, so a cell's ground area shrinks with cos(latitude) and differs by many times near the poles; S2 projects the sphere onto a cube's six faces before subdividing, which keeps same-level cell areas within roughly a 2x range — roughly similar, not exactly constant. That makes S2 (or H3) the better fit for globally consistent density analysis.

title: h3
text:
What is Uber H3's signature design, and why?
H3 uses hexagons because all six neighbors sit at roughly equal distance, making ring queries and heat maps much cleaner than lopsided square neighbors.

title: h3
text:
How does H3 differ from geohash/S2 on ID ordering versus map proximity?
Geohash and S2 keys lie on a space-filling curve, so a neighborhood becomes a handful of key ranges (up to 9 for a geohash 3x3 sweep, a set of cell ranges for an S2 covering) scanned with BETWEEN; H3 IDs don't preserve map proximity in sort order, so you compute the exact ring of neighbor IDs with grid math and query WHERE cell IN (...). Different query shapes, both cheap.

title: h3
text:
What is the common H3 dispatch pattern?
A driver move is a single integer-column update, candidate generation is a plain IN lookup, and no spatial extension is needed; an exact-distance post-filter removes drivers outside the radius. Actual write throughput depends on how the underlying store is sharded and configured, but each update is cheap enough for a flood of location writes.

title: interview-method
text:
What actually earns points when explaining proximity search in an interview?
What lands is explaining why a plain index fails on latitude and longitude and walking the tradeoffs aloud, not naming the specific library.

title: selection
text:
What is the choice and its cost?
Geometric data with containment queries calls for a spatial tree like PostGIS, paying for a spatial extension and pricier writes.

title: selection
text:
What exactly is the write-side weakness of the spatial-tree route?
Rebalancing R-tree rectangles is real work and the BKD variant is essentially write-once, so neither loves churning data.

title: selection
text:
What is the choice and its cost?
Moving points need cheap writes and fast candidate generation, which is exactly what encoded cells sell: each move updates one integer column on an ordinary B-tree index, and the lost polygon support isn't needed anyway. The throughput ceiling depends on the store and sharding, but each update is cheap.

title: selection
text:
Complete the proximity-search selection rule (answer with category names):
The index only delivers a candidate set, shrinking "check every row" to "check a small patch of map"; whenever the result is defined by exact distance or radius, you finish by computing real distance to drop candidates outside it. Cell-level aggregation such as a heat map is defined per cell and doesn't need this step.

title: selection
text:
Put the decision chain for choosing a location index in order:
Decide by data shape, pick tree or encoded key accordingly, generate a small candidate set, and finish with exact math.

title: numbers
text:
Which design judgment does this scale fact support?
A degree of longitude is about 111 km at the equator and shrinks toward zero at the poles, so same-level geohash cells become thin strips at high latitude and candidate-set sizes vary by city. For consistent global recall, a sphere-based grid like S2 or H3 is the recommended choice since its cells are far more uniform than geohash (though not exactly equal-area); staying on geohash also works if you adjust precision by latitude and query more neighbor cells.

title: numbers
text:
Which set of ID bit widths is correct?
Each geohash character is five bits, Redis stores a 52-bit geohash integer, and S2 and H3 both use 64-bit cell IDs, so a 64-bit bigint column fits any of them.

title: selection
text:
On the cost of one location update, how do PostGIS/R-tree and H3 on a normal index compare?
Both routes write a new row version; the difference is the index. A GiST/R-tree insert may enlarge bounding rectangles or split nodes, which costs more, while H3 is a plain B-tree insert on an integer key — and if the driver hasn't crossed a cell boundary, the cell is unchanged and the index needn't change at all. Geometry trees pay for shape semantics with pricier updates; encoded keys give up shape semantics for cheap ones.

title: quadtree
text:
Which structure fits?
In-memory workloads like game collision detection are where quadtrees still shine, since pointer chasing is cheap in RAM.

title: spatial-trees
text:
Why is "quadtree -> k-d/BKD tree -> R-tree" a repair chain instead of three isolated structures?
Treat them as a learning chain where each fixes one weakness: the quadtree is intuitive but unbalanced → k-d/BKD split at medians and go to disk in blocks → the R-tree wraps shapes in bounding rectangles and supports dynamic inserts and deletes. This is a memory order, not a timeline (the R-tree dates from 1984, BKD from 2003).

title: candidate-set
text:
What goes wrong if you skip exact distance post-filtering?
Skipping the post-filter leaves in corner candidates that fall inside the query ring but are actually farther than the target radius.

title: encoded-keys
text:
Which property of the cell ID makes coarse aggregation cheap?
H3 and S2 IDs are hierarchical 64-bit encodings: the parent is computed with constant-time bit operations (H3 rewrites the resolution field and marks finer digits as unused; S2 clears low bits and resets the trailing marker bit), so you can GROUP BY the parent over the same column with no recomputation. The cost: you only get fixed hierarchy levels, and H3's hexagonal children don't tile their parent exactly, so H3 roll-ups are approximate at edges, while S2 nests exactly.

title: h3
text:
How do you widen the search when one ring isn't enough?
H3 ring queries expand adaptively: if the first ring returns too few drivers, add the next ring's cell IDs to the IN list, at the cost of more candidates to post-filter.

title: basics
text:
What best describes how Redis positions itself?
Redis is an in-memory data structure store written in C, exposing familiar structures like strings, hashes, and sorted sets.

title: threading
text:
What is Redis's concurrency model for executing commands?
Redis executes commands one at a time on a single thread, so every command is atomic without locks even though newer versions offload I/O to helper threads.

title: threading
text:
Which statements about Redis's single-threaded design are correct? (multi-select)
"Single-threaded" mainly means the command executor touches data structures serially, so a single command needs no database-style row locks (multi-step logic still needs MULTI/Lua). GET/SET/INCR cost microseconds of CPU; the docs note CPU is rarely the bottleneck — network or memory usually is — with exceptions for big values, Lua, or large ZSET ranges. Extra cores run I/O threads and background work but never split one SET/INCR.

title: persistence
text:
Fill in Redis's two persistence modes:
RDB takes periodic snapshots while AOF logs every write and fsyncs once per second by default.

title: persistence
text:
If you persist with RDB snapshots alone, what happens to data when the process crashes?
With RDB snapshots alone, a crash loses every write since the last snapshot.

title: persistence
text:
Which design conclusion does this fsync frequency best support?
The once-per-second fsync policy leaves a roughly one-second loss window, so critical writes need per-write fsync or a truly durable store instead of the defaults.

title: durability
text:
Compared to a relational database's default commit-is-on-disk guarantee, what stance does Redis's default persistence take?
Redis deliberately trades durability for speed: the open-source default enables only RDB snapshots with AOF off, so a crash loses writes since the last snapshot; even with AOF on, the default appendfsync everysec leaves about a one-second window, and replication is asynchronous. This is a product stance, not a bug.

title: durability
text:
Given this requirement, what's the best choice?
MemoryDB is a Redis-compatible durable primary: it acks only after the write is in a Multi-AZ transaction log, so failover keeps it. Self-managed Redis AOF only covers single-node disk durability; replication is still async, so the last acked writes can be lost on failover. For rebuildable caches, Redis/ElastiCache is cheaper and faster.

title: data-model
text:
What best describes Redis's logical data model?
Everything in Redis is a value stored at a string key, and the data structure lives inside that value.

title: data-structures
text:
Which of these are native Redis data structures or capabilities? (multi-select)
Redis natively offers strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, streams, and geospatial indexes, but it has no joins.

title: data-structures
text:
What is the status of capabilities like Bloom filters, JSON, and time series in Redis 8?
In Redis 8, JSON, Bloom-style probabilistic structures, and time series are Open Source data types; older versions often needed Redis Stack modules.

title: protocol
text:
What characterizes Redis's wire protocol, RESP?
RESP is the wire format Redis clients and servers speak over TCP: simple, fast to parse, mostly readable, and not HTTP/gRPC.

title: set-commands
text:
Which command should you use?
To ask whether A is in B's set, use SISMEMBER. SMEMBERS fetches all members, SCARD counts members, and SADD writes a member.

title: cluster-slots
text:
Which conclusion does the fixed slot count during cluster operation best support?
Redis first maps a key to CRC16(key) % 16384, then looks up the slot owner; scaling moves slot ownership, not the key-to-slot formula.

title: cluster-routing
text:
How does a Redis Cluster client find the node that owns a key?
Clients cache the slot-to-node map, compute the slot from the key, and connect directly to the owning node because Redis will not forward requests.

title: cluster-routing
text:
What happens when a client sends a request to a node that no longer owns that slot?
The slot has a new owner, so the old node replies MOVED; the client refreshes its map (e.g., via CLUSTER SHARDS) and resends — nodes don't proxy. If the slot were still migrating and the key already moved, the reply would be ASK: the client sends ASKING to the target for that one request without updating its slot map.

title: cluster-gossip
text:
How does every node in the cluster learn the full slot layout?
Nodes share cluster state via a gossip protocol, so every node knows the full slot map.

title: cluster-scaling
text:
After adding the node and rebalancing, what happens to the data?
A newly added Redis Cluster node starts with zero slots; a reshard/rebalance moves a share of slots and their keys (via MIGRATE) to it online. During migration clients follow ASK for individual requests, and after it completes they refresh via MOVED — cluster-aware clients need no code changes.

title: replication
text:
What is the acknowledgment timing in Redis primary-replica replication?
By default Redis replies OK once the primary executes, without waiting for replica acknowledgment; the replication stream goes out asynchronously, so a replica may get it slightly before or after — OK just doesn't imply the replica has it. Low latency, but failover can lose the last acknowledged writes. WAIT reduces that risk but is not a quorum commit.

title: replication
text:
After the primary crashes and a replica is promoted, what is the most typical data consequence?
Redis replication is async by default: OK means the primary applied the write, not that replicas received it. If the primary dies before sending the tail, the promoted replica only has the data it saw.

title: cluster-philosophy
text:
Compared to most databases, what is Redis Cluster's design philosophy?
Redis Cluster hands you primitives instead of solving scaling for you, so structuring your keys is how you scale Redis.

title: hash-tags
text:
What's the correct approach?
In Redis Cluster, multi-key operations including MULTI require all keys in one slot, or you get CROSSSLOT; a shared hash tag hashes only the part inside {}, forcing related keys into the same slot. The cluster must stay, so shrinking to one node is out; a lock can't change slots; splitting the transaction breaks "change together".

title: performance
text:
Which design conclusion do these numbers best support?
A 60k peak against a measured 150k–200k ceiling leaves 2–3x headroom and the data fits in memory, so one primary suffices; sharding adds cross-slot, hash-tag, and ops cost and should wait until load approaches the measured ceiling or memory runs out. Enough throughput is not enough availability, so you still want a replica (rules out D). The ceiling is a benchmark for this workload, not a constant — it shifts with value size, command mix, and persistence settings.

title: performance
text:
Which design conclusion does this latency order of magnitude best support?
Since a command itself costs only microseconds, the number of network round trips dominates perceived latency, which is why pipelining and MGET pay off.

title: performance
text:
Why is the N-plus-one query pattern disastrous on SQL but tolerable on Redis?
N+1 means one list query plus N detail queries. SQL pays planning and index costs per SELECT; Redis commands are lighter, and MGET or pipelining batches round trips.

title: caching-ttl
text:
What guarantee does Redis give for a key with a TTL set?
Redis checks expiry before returning a key; if it is timed out, the command deletes it and returns missing. Background expiration cleans up expired keys that nobody touches.

title: eviction
text:
With no eviction policy configured, what is Redis's default behavior once memory fills up?
Out of the box Redis rejects writes once memory is full, so a cache must explicitly configure an eviction policy like allkeys-lru.

title: eviction
text:
Which eviction policy should you configure?
For a pure cache, allkeys-lru lets Redis evict the least recently used keys to make room since everything is reloadable.

title: eviction
text:
What's distinctive about how Redis implements LRU eviction?
Redis stores recent-access metadata per key. On eviction, it samples a few keys and removes the stalest one in that sample. More samples approximate true LRU better but cost more CPU.

title: caching-ttl
text:
What problem does TTL expiration solve versus what problem does eviction solve?
Expiration handles staleness while eviction handles memory pressure; they solve different problems.

title: distributed-lock
text:
What is the correct command to acquire the lock?
SET with NX and EX atomically creates the lock only if absent and adds an expiry so a crashed holder cannot keep it forever.

title: distributed-lock
text:
What does the NX flag on the SET command mean?
NX makes the SET succeed only if the key does not already exist, which is the atomic lock acquisition.

title: distributed-lock
text:
What failure does adding an EX 30 expiry to the lock key prevent?
Without an expiry, a holder that never comes back (killed process, or long-term loss of contact with Redis) keeps the lock forever and blocks everyone; EX 30 caps the hold time at one TTL. Option C is a different failure: the lock was written on the primary but lost in failover before replicating — a TTL can't fix a lock that vanished, only a lock that can't be released.

title: lock-release
text:
Why store a random token as the lock's value instead of a fixed value?
The random token is the identity of this lock request. When A releases, it first checks the value is still tokenA; if B has reacquired the lock with tokenB, A must not delete it.

title: lock-release
text:
What's the risk of blindly running DEL when releasing a lock?
The token only helps if release reads and compares it; a blind DEL ignores the value. After tokenA expires and B writes tokenB, A's DEL deletes B's lock.

title: lock-release
text:
What's the correct implementation?
Redis runs the whole Lua script as one command on its single thread, making the check-and-delete atomic.

title: distributed-lock
text:
Which concurrency-control style does 'acquire the lock first' belong to, versus Redis's WATCH with MULTI/EXEC?
Grabbing a lock up front is pessimistic because others must wait. WATCH with MULTI/EXEC is optimistic: other clients can still write, but EXEC aborts if the watched key changed.

title: lock-failover
text:
What's the classic way a single-node Redis lock fails during primary-replica failover?
The primary can reply OK before the replica applies the lock. If the primary dies first, the new primary has no lock key and SET NX can succeed again.

title: redlock
text:
What is the core idea behind the Redlock algorithm?
Cluster maps a key to one slot; Redlock sends the same lock key to several independent Redis nodes. The lock is acquired only if a majority SET NX succeeds before TTL expires.

title: redlock
text:
Kleppmann's famous critique of Redlock says that even if the algorithm holds, what can still happen?
Redlock decides who acquired the lease, but after the lease expires a stale holder can wake up and keep writing. Without a fencing token or version check at the resource, an old write can overwrite a newer one.

title: fencing
text:
What's the standard technique to stop an expired lock's holder from corrupting data with a stale write?
An expired Redis lock cannot stop the old worker, so each grant needs a higher fencing token and storage must reject stale tokens.

title: lock-alternative
text:
What's the right attitude to take?
Use Redis locks as a concurrency throttle, but enforce money, inventory, and uniqueness invariants in storage with conditional writes, versions, or fencing tokens.

title: distributed-lock
text:
Put the decision chain for a Redis distributed lock in the correct order:
The chain runs requirement, choice, cost, mitigation: atomic SET NX EX gives mutual exclusion that can break on failover, so back it with fencing or database constraints.

title: leaderboard
text:
What's the most suitable Redis structure?
A sorted set keeps members ordered by score with log-time updates and range queries, a natural leaderboard at scale.

title: leaderboard
text:
Which command is correct?
Rank 0 is the lowest score and -1 is the highest. The range 0 to -6 removes the low end through the sixth-from-top member, leaving the final five highest-score members.

title: leaderboard
text:
What happens when you ZADD a member that already exists in a sorted set?
ZADD sets a member's score rather than appending a row, so an existing member's score is replaced and its rank moves.

title: rate-limiting
text:
What's the most direct Redis implementation?
INCR atomically increments and returns the window's counter, and rejecting when it exceeds N implements a fixed-window limiter.

title: rate-limiting
text:
What goes wrong if a rate limiter calls EXPIRE on every single request?
Calling EXPIRE on every request keeps pushing the reset forward so a steady stream never gets a fresh window; set it only when INCR returns one.

title: rate-limiting
text:
If INCR and EXPIRE are sent as two separate commands and the process crashes right between them, what's the consequence?
If the process crashes after INCR but before EXPIRE, the counter keeps no TTL, so put the increment and first-expire logic in one Lua script.

title: rate-limiting
text:
Fill in the sliding-window rate limiter (one sorted set per user, score = request timestamp):
The sorted set stores requests by timestamp: trim entries outside the window, count what remains, and ZADD the new request only if under the limit (member = timestamp plus a random suffix for uniqueness, score = timestamp). "Add only if under the limit" is conditional logic MULTI/EXEC can't express, so the whole sequence runs atomically in a Lua script to avoid over-admission.

title: geospatial
text:
Which pair of Redis commands directly supports this requirement?
GEOADD stores coordinates and GEOSEARCH queries by center and radius using Redis's native geospatial index.

title: geospatial
text:
What's the underlying implementation of Redis's geospatial index?
Redis GEO encodes coordinates into a geohash-like sorted-set score; it may search boxes or radii, but it is not stored as an R-tree, quadtree, or grid table.

title: geospatial
text:
Why is the linear term N the bounding-box candidate count rather than the in-radius hit count?
GEO stores geohash-encoded coordinates in a sorted set. A query computes a few grid-aligned boxes covering the circle, range-scans the sorted set for every member in those boxes, then computes the real distance for each and drops those outside the circle — every candidate is touched, so the linear term is the bounding-box candidate count N. The log term comes from seeking each score range's start in the sorted set (skiplist), not from filtering.

title: streams
text:
What is a Redis Stream, fundamentally?
A Redis stream is an append-only log similar to a Kafka topic, and consumer groups coordinate who processes what.

title: streams
text:
Fill in the command division of labor for a Stream-based work queue:
The queue loop is XADD to append, XREADGROUP to deliver, XACK to finish, and XCLAIM or XAUTOCLAIM to recover idle pending entries.

title: streams
text:
In a Redis Streams work queue, how does an unacknowledged task recover after the worker that claimed it crashes?
Unacknowledged stream entries stay in the PEL, so another worker can claim an idle entry with XCLAIM or XAUTOCLAIM and retry it.

title: streams
text:
What side effect comes from the XCLAIM takeover mechanism?
Redis cannot tell a slow worker from a dead one, so an entry can occasionally be processed twice and your handler must be idempotent.

title: streams
text:
What must you remember before treating a Stream as a 'reliable log'?
However log-like it is, a Stream shares Redis's persistence trade-offs: defaults use RDB snapshots with AOF off, so a crash loses entries since the last snapshot; AOF everysec still leaves about a one-second window; and asynchronous replication can lose acknowledged writes on failover. A "never lose anything" audit log needs these tightened explicitly, or a system built as a durable log.

title: streams-vs-kafka
text:
When should you switch from Redis Streams to Kafka?
Kafka earns its complexity when you need long retention, replay for many independent consumers, and durable ordered throughput where losing a message is unacceptable.

title: pubsub
text:
In one line, how do Pub/Sub and Streams divide responsibilities?
Streams serve consumers that must catch up on missed entries, while Pub/Sub only delivers to whoever is listening right now.

title: pubsub
text:
What are Redis Pub/Sub's delivery semantics?
Redis Pub/Sub is at-most-once delivery, so a subscriber offline at publish time misses the message entirely.

title: pubsub
text:
The old assumption is 'adding cluster nodes doesn't add Pub/Sub capacity' — what's actually true now?
Normal cluster Pub/Sub still propagates across nodes, while Redis 7+ sharded Pub/Sub routes channels by slot so many spread-out channels can scale, but one hot channel stays shard-bound.

title: pubsub
text:
What setup or creation step do you need before using a Pub/Sub channel?
A channel is just a name that comes into existence when someone publishes or subscribes; there is nothing to create.

title: pubsub
text:
How many connections to Redis does a server subscribed to one million channels need?
One TCP connection to a Redis shard can carry many SSUBSCRIBE channels, so connections scale with involved shards, while subscription state and fanout still scale with channels.

title: pubsub
text:
What's the correct fix?
Pub/Sub only notifies subscribers online right now; offline catch-up must re-read from a durable log (Streams/Kafka) or Message+Inbox tables. An outbox table is a separate concern: it makes "write the message" and "publish the event later" reliable and often pairs with this design, but it is not the catch-up source itself.

title: pubsub
text:
Compared to native Pub/Sub, what are the drawbacks of a homegrown Pub/Sub built on Redis (storing topic-to-subscriber-address sets, with the publisher fanning out directly)? (multi-select)
Native Pub/Sub still uses TCP/TLS, but it reuses established Redis client connections from chat servers to Redis; Redis maintains channel-to-connection state and pushes over those connections. In a homegrown design, Redis only stores addresses, so the publisher fans out itself and owns server-to-server pools, TLS, retries, backpressure, health checks, and stale-address cleanup.

title: pubsub
text:
In native Pub/Sub, what happens when a channel's last subscriber disconnects?
When the last subscriber disconnects the channel vanishes from memory and later publishes to it are simply dropped.

title: hot-key
text:
In a 100-node Redis cache cluster, a single product suddenly goes viral and its traffic hits half the whole site — what happens?
Key hashing fixes ownership: a key lives on one node, so more nodes can't share one key's traffic. ~1M QPS is far beyond the stated per-node ceiling, so that node times out, while the other 99 average ~10k QPS each — underused but unable to help. This is the hot-key problem, shared by Memcached and DynamoDB.

title: hot-key
text:
What's the best mitigation?
The app server process has its own memory, so it can keep a tiny TTL map. Reads check local memory first, then Redis/DB on miss; because the prompt wants most reads to avoid Redis entirely, local hot-key caching fits better than Redis replicas.

title: hot-key
text:
How does the 'key copies' approach work?
Storing copies under suffixed keys spreads them across nodes and readers pick a random suffix, while every write must fan out to all copies.

title: hot-key
text:
What's wrong with this expectation?
Redis replicas do not automatically serve cluster reads; enable replica reads or READONLY explicitly, and remember this helps read-hot keys, not write-hot keys.

title: hot-key
text:
Put the decision chain for handling a hot key in the correct order:
Cache consistency is not just building a cluster. It is the problem of keeping multiple cached copies of the same value from staying stale after an update. Replicating a hot key spreads reads, but writes, deletes, and invalidations must touch more places.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Which signals indicate Redis is the wrong choice for this scenario? (multi-select)
Avoid Redis as a system of record, for working sets too big for RAM, or when you need joins and cross-key queries; sub-millisecond reads are exactly why you would use it.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
What's the restriction on multi-key operations (MSET, a MULTI touching several keys) in cluster mode?
MSET or a MULTI transaction must execute on one node. If the keys map to different slots, they belong to different primaries, and Redis Cluster does not run a cross-node transaction coordinator; it returns a CROSSSLOT error. Use a shared hash tag when those keys must be operated on together.

title: philosophy
text:
Compared to databases with a built-in optimizer and query planner, what's Redis's orientation?
Redis favors explicit data-structure access over SQL-style planning, which keeps commands predictable but pushes joins, secondary indexes, and complex queries into your model.

title: persistence
text:
Which statement about RDB vs AOF is correct?
RDB is a periodic full snapshot that restores fast but loses writes since the last snapshot (minutes under these settings); AOF appends every write for replay, and with `everysec` typically loses about one second (worst case ~2s); `always` loses less but is slower. Both can run together.

title: streams-vs-kafka
text:
For this queue, which statement about Redis Streams vs Kafka is correct?
Both can fan out with consumer groups; for no-drop queues, Kafka's replicated disk log is safer, while Redis Streams is faster but bounded by Redis persistence and retention.

title: lock-correctness
text:
When the lock alone is not enough, how does the downstream ensure only one write takes effect?
A Redis lock only reduces contention; the downstream store must use CAS, version checks, or a fencing token to reject a stale holder's late write.

title: redis-lock-vs-db-lock
text:
Redis lock vs database lock — when do you use which?
A Redis lock is fast but expires, so a hot path needs CAS or fencing (the fencing token must be generated separately, e.g. with INCR; SET NX doesn't provide one); a DB lock is slower but lives in the same transaction as the business write, fitting "lock + write atomically".

title: cluster-failover
text:
How is a new master chosen for this shard?
After most masters mark the old master FAIL, one replica wins majority authorization, promotes, and takes the hash slots; Sentinel is for non-sharded setups.

title: infrastructure-config
text:
Which topology should you deploy?
The deciding constraint is 'fits one node, write throughput is fine, but no downtime allowed' -> pick HA primary-replica: you get automatic failover without Cluster's sharding complexity; the cost is async replication, so a failover can silently drop the last few acknowledged writes.

title: lock-consensus
text:
When a lock failure would break correctness and there's no single data row to conditionally write, what do you use?
A Redis lock expires, and an async-replication failover can hand out the same lock twice. When you need true mutual exclusion or leader election with no row to conditionally write, use a consensus system like ZooKeeper/etcd: it won't issue two locks on failover and provides a monotonic value (zxid / etcd revision) usable as a fencing token. A GC pause past the lease still affects consensus locks too — full safety needs the external system to check that token, or an idempotent action. Cost: an extra cluster, slower and pricier than one DB conditional write.

title: when-to-use
text:
When should you choose a time-series database (TSDB)?
A time-series database is worth adopting once a general-purpose database genuinely bottlenecks on write volume, time-range queries, or retention, not just because the data happens to have a timestamp.

title: scale
text:
What does this write rate and retention imply for the storage engine design?
50k points/s alone might be absorbed by one machine with batched writes; the real problem is ~130 billion points over 30 days: once B-tree indexes far exceed memory, every row insert does random index-page I/O. Sequential appends with batched reorganization (LSM, time-chunked storage) turn random writes into sequential ones — the motivation behind TSDB write paths. It is a design recommendation, not the only option (e.g. a partitioned relational extension with batched COPY is another implementation).

title: postgres-limit
text:
Where does a normal Postgres row table first break down for large-scale metrics stored as timestamp, host, metric_name, and value?
The real bottleneck is repeated label strings in every row plus heavy index maintenance under high write volume, which indexing alone or a smaller numeric type can't fix.

title: examples
text:
Which of these are time-series databases (TSDBs)?
InfluxDB, Prometheus, and TimescaleDB are time-series systems, while ZooKeeper is a coordination service for configuration and distributed locks, not a TSDB.

title: append-only
text:
What is the core idea of append-only storage?
Append-only storage writes new points at the end of files, turning random writes into fast sequential writes.

title: io
text:
For disk I/O, what advantage does append-only writing have over traditional in-place updates?
In-place updates need to locate, read, modify, and rewrite old data, causing random I/O, while append-only writes sequentially at the end and reclaims space later via background compaction.

title: io
text:
Roughly how large is the gap between random and sequential I/O on a spinning disk?
Each random I/O on a spinning disk pays seek plus rotational latency (milliseconds), so small random writes manage only hundreds of IOPS, while sequential writes skip the seek and reach hundreds of MB/s. By bytes the gap exceeds two orders of magnitude; the exact ratio depends on I/O size and drive model. This is why append-only and LSM designs exist.

title: lsm
text:
Put the LSM tree write path in order:
LSM trees write to a sorted memtable, flush immutable SSTables, compact them in the background, and may check multiple files on reads.

title: lsm
text:
Why is the memtable in an LSM tree usually kept sorted?
A sorted memtable flushes into a sorted SSTable, enabling binary search, efficient ranges, and merge-based compaction.

title: lsm-tradeoff
text:
What is the main tradeoff of an LSM tree?
An LSM writes to memory plus a WAL and flushes sorted SSTables sequentially, so foreground write throughput is high; the cost is reads that may merge several SSTables (read amplification) and background compaction that rewrites data repeatedly (write amplification, temporary space amplification). It suits write-heavy metric streams, not every workload.

title: compression
text:
Complete the idea behind delta encoding:
Delta encoding stores differences between adjacent values, which compress well when time-series data changes gradually.

title: compression
text:
What problem does varint, or variable-length encoding, solve in TSDB compression?
Variable-length encoding stores small deltas in fewer bytes instead of always using a fixed-width integer.

title: timestamps
text:
Why is timestamp delta-of-delta encoding especially effective for fixed sampling intervals?
Delta-of-delta compression works well because regular sampling intervals make second-order timestamp deltas mostly zero.

title: floats
text:
What is the intuition behind XOR compression for floating-point values in a TSDB?
XOR compression exploits similar adjacent floating-point values because their XOR contains many zero bits.

title: storage-efficiency
text:
Why can a normal metric point be tiny in raw form but still waste space in row storage?
The actual payload is about 16 bytes; the bloat comes from label strings repeated on every row plus the per-row header (roughly 27 bytes of fixed overhead in PostgreSQL), plus index entries. A TSDB stores per series: labels once, then only compressed timestamps and values.

title: time-partitioning
text:
What does time-based partitioning mean in a TSDB?
Time-based partitioning groups points into time-windowed chunks such as daily or weekly partitions.

title: time-partitioning
text:
What benefits does time-based partitioning provide?
Time partitions localize writes, prune reads by time range, and make retention as simple as dropping old partitions.

title: retention
text:
Why is TSDB retention usually cheaper than deleting old rows from a huge table?
Retention is cheap because old time partitions can be dropped instead of deleting rows from a massive table.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What role does a Bloom filter play in the LSM/TSDB read path?
A Bloom filter lets the database skip SSTables that definitely do not contain a queried series without disk reads.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What are the false positive and false negative properties of a Bloom filter?
Bloom filters can have false positives but no false negatives, so they may cause extra reads but do not miss existing keys.

title: bloom-filter
text:
What order of memory cost and false positive rate is typical for a well-tuned Bloom filter?
A practical Bloom filter can use around 10 bits per key for about a 1 percent false positive rate.

title: downsampling
text:
What problem do downsampling and rollups solve in a TSDB?
Downsampling stores lower-resolution rollups for older data so historical queries scan far fewer points.

title: rollups
text:
What values does a rollup usually pre-aggregate for each time bucket?
Rollups usually store aggregates such as min, max, sum, and count for each time bucket.

title: rollups
text:
Compared with scanning raw 10-second samples, what does a 5-minute rollup change for a past-day trend query on one series?
86,400 s ÷ 10 s = 8,640 points; 86,400 ÷ 300 = 288 buckets; 8,640 ÷ 288 = 30x. Rollups are pre-aggregated at write time or by a background job, so the query reads 288 stored results without recomputing (which is why C is wrong); the cost is losing spikes inside each 5-minute bucket.

title: requirements-negotiation
text:
What is a more mature response?
A strong interview answer negotiates raw retention by keeping fine resolution for recent data and rolling up older data.

title: block-metadata
text:
What is block-level metadata used for in TSDB queries?
Block metadata such as min and max values lets the engine prune blocks that cannot match a query.

title: data-model
text:
Complete the basic TSDB data model:
In InfluxDB, a measurement is like a table name, tags are indexed filter dimensions, fields are the measured values (usually unindexed), and the timestamp places the point in time. Prometheus calls these metric name, labels, sample value, and timestamp; it has no field concept.

title: tags-vs-fields
text:
In this data model, what is the key difference between tags and fields?
In an InfluxDB-style model, tags become part of the series key and are indexed, so they suit common filter dimensions; fields hold measured values, are not part of the series key and are not indexed, so they suit high-cardinality or store-only values without exploding the series count. Note that systems like Prometheus have no fields, only labels, and high-cardinality values generally stay out of labels.

title: series
text:
What usually uniquely identifies a series in a TSDB?
A series is typically the unique combination of a measurement and its tag values.

title: storage-engine
text:
Put the typical TSDB write/storage engine steps in order:
A TSDB often writes to the WAL, buffers points in memory, flushes compressed immutable files, and compacts them in the background.

title: file-format
text:
What does the series index at the end of a TSDB data file usually record?
The file index maps series keys to the block offsets containing their data.

title: query-execution
text:
Put the TSDB query execution path in order:
Query execution prunes partitions by time, finds series via tag indexes, merges buffer and disk data, and streams aggregations.

title: tag-index
text:
What is the intuitive similarity between a TSDB tag index and an Elasticsearch inverted index?
A tag index maps tag values to matching series, much like an inverted index maps terms to documents.

title: multi-tag-query
text:
How would a tag index usually handle a query like region='us-west' AND env='prod'?
A multi-tag query intersects the series sets for each tag predicate before reading data blocks.

title: series-locality
text:
Why is series-oriented storage better suited to metric queries than a normal row table?
Series-oriented storage colocates related points, reducing scattered reads and improving compression for time-range queries.

title: streaming-aggregation
text:
Why does a TSDB query like mean(value) GROUP BY time(5m) usually not need to load all points into memory first?
Aggregations can be streamed by maintaining bucket state such as sum and count as points are read.

title: time-locality
text:
What are the two locality intuitions behind fast TSDB queries?
Time-series databases exploit both time locality and series locality to minimize disk access.

title: cardinality
text:
What does cardinality mean in a TSDB?
Cardinality is the number of unique tag combinations, or series, that the database must track.

title: cardinality
text:
Why should high-cardinality values like user_id or request_id usually not be TSDB tags?
High-cardinality values like user IDs create too many series and can overwhelm the in-memory index.

title: tags-vs-fields
text:
Where should request_id go in a TSDB?
In a tags/fields model, a rarely filtered high-cardinality value should be stored as a field: it is still written and readable, but stays out of the series key and tag index, so it cannot blow up the index. In a labels-only system like Prometheus, such values usually belong in logs or traces rather than labels.

title: assumptions
text:
Complete the key TSDB data assumptions:
Time-series databases perform best when tags are low cardinality, samples are regular, and adjacent values have small deltas.

title: performance
text:
For the target workload, what order of performance gain can a TSDB have over a general-purpose database?
The gain comes from stacked designs: sequential appends, time-partition pruning, columnar compression that cuts bytes scanned, and pre-aggregated rollups. Common benchmarks show 10–100x on time-range aggregations, but that is an empirical range that depends on data shape, query type, and how well the baseline is tuned; if the workload breaks time-series assumptions (heavy random updates, cross-entity joins), the gain disappears.

title: anti-pattern
text:
Should you default to a TSDB just because the data has time?
A time-series database is not automatically a good fit for global Top-K queries across many series.

title: monitoring
text:
Why does a TSDB fit better than a normal row table?
Monitoring metrics fit TSDBs because they are append-heavy, time-windowed, compressible, and often queried by series tags.

title: buffer
text:
Why does a TSDB query usually check both the in-memory buffer and disk files?
Queries merge in-memory buffered points with older disk files because recent data may not have been flushed yet.

title: write-read-design
text:
What does "writes are optimized to assist reads" mean in a TSDB?
TSDB writes organize data by series and time so later reads touch fewer and more contiguous blocks.

title: building-blocks
text:
Which of these are core TSDB building blocks?
Core TSDB building blocks include append-only storage, LSM-style compaction, and specialized compression.

title: building-blocks
text:
Which optimizations mainly help the TSDB read path?
Bloom filters, block metadata, and tag indexes help the read path skip irrelevant files, blocks, and series.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the "should we use a TSDB" decision chain in order:
The decision should start with the workload, validate TSDB assumptions and precision tradeoffs, then choose TSDB or fall back to simpler storage.

title: summary
text:
What data features does a TSDB exploit for performance?
TSDBs gain performance by exploiting time order, compressible adjacent points, and low-cardinality tag filtering.

title: compaction
text:
What exactly does background compaction do to relieve this?
Deletes only append tombstones, so SSTables pile up and reads slow; compaction merges SSTables in the background, keeps only the newest version of each key, and drops data shadowed by tombstones. The tombstone itself can be dropped only once no older version could still need masking (for example, at the bottom level or after a grace period). The cost is write amplification, since data is rewritten repeatedly.

title: lsm
text:
What lets an LSM engine keep sustained writes from being slowed by concurrent reads?
Writes only append to the memtable and WAL, and immutable SSTables are reorganized by background threads, so writes do not contend with or wait for reads. The costs: reads may scan several unmerged SSTables (read amplification), and if compaction falls behind, the engine deliberately slows or stalls writes.

title: rollups
text:
What is the main cost of using pre-computed rollups?
With raw points kept for the full year, rollups are an extra data layer: whether aggregated on the write path or by a background downsampling job, each raw point is aggregated and written into several more buckets, costing extra storage and write amplification in exchange for scanning far less history at query time. (If raw points were kept only briefly and only rollups kept long-term, rollups would save storage instead — a different question.)

title: file-format
text:
Why split timestamps and values into two segments with different codecs instead of storing them row by row?
Timestamps are nearly evenly spaced and adjacent float values are close — two different kinds of redundancy. Splitting lets timestamps use delta-of-delta (mostly zero at a fixed interval) and values use XOR (similar floats XOR to mostly zero bits), each compressing best. The actual ratio depends on how regular the sampling is and how much values fluctuate. Cost: reads must decode the two segments separately.

title: embeddings
text:
What is a vector or embedding in a vector database?
An embedding is a numeric vector representing an object so that similar objects have nearby vectors.

title: dimensions
text:
What design judgment does this embedding dimensionality range support?
At 1536 float32 dimensions, one vector is about 6 KB, so dimensionality directly affects memory and per-query math.

title: similarity-meaning
text:
What decides what similar means for vectors?
The meaning of similarity depends on the embedding model and the objective it was trained for.

title: embedding-models
text:
Which model sources can generate embeddings?
Embeddings can come from text models, image models, or custom models trained for a specific recommendation objective.

title: similarity-metrics
text:
