What does cosine similarity measure?
Cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors and largely ignores their magnitude.

title: similarity-metrics
text:
Which of these are common vector similarity or distance metrics?
Common vector similarity metrics include Euclidean distance, cosine similarity, dot product, and Hamming distance.

title: hamming
text:
What kind of vectors is Hamming distance best for?
Hamming distance counts differing bit positions in binary vectors and can be computed very quickly.

title: knn
text:
What does KNN search mean in a vector database?
KNN just means taking a query embedding and returning the K closest vectors; brute force costs N times D float ops, which is why large N needs an index.

title: exact-vs-ann
text:
What is the core difference between exact KNN and ANN?
Exact KNN compares against every vector, while ANN trades some accuracy for much faster search.

title: exact-knn-cost
text:
Why is naive exact KNN expensive over 1M 1536-dimensional vectors?
A million 1536-dimensional vectors means about 1.5 billion dimension operations before top-K maintenance, so online systems usually need ANN.

title: recall
text:
What does recall measure for ANN search?
recall@K = (number of true top-K neighbors returned) / K. Recall 0.95 means about 9.5 of the true top-10 come back on average. An average similarity score (C) only says how close the results are; it cannot tell you which true neighbors were missed — scores can be high while closer points are skipped. Note: when exactly K results are returned, recall@K and precision@K are numerically equal, which is why ANN benchmarks usually report recall@K only.

title: ann-tradeoffs
text:
When tuning ANN index parameters, which metrics are mainly traded off?
Raising parameters like efSearch or nprobe searches more candidates — recall goes up, latency goes up. Parameters like M, nlist, or quantization bits set index size, affecting memory (and build time). So recall, latency and memory form the tuning tradeoff triangle. Foreign key depth is a relational concept unrelated to ANN.

title: indexing
text:
What is the main purpose of a vector database index?
Vector indexes reduce search cost by skipping most vectors and comparing only a much smaller candidate set.

title: benchmarking
text:
Why is intuition alone not enough to prove one ANN index is best?
ANN index choice depends on real data and query patterns, so benchmark recall and latency on an evaluation set.

title: hnsw
text:
What is the core intuition behind HNSW?
HNSW builds a multi-layer neighbor graph and searches from sparse upper layers down to a dense base layer.

title: hnsw-search
text:
Put the HNSW search flow in order.
HNSW starts at a sparse top layer, greedily walks toward the query, descends layers, and does local search at the base layer.

title: hnsw-tradeoff
text:
What is the main cost of HNSW?
HNSW keeps both the raw vectors and the multi-layer graph edges in memory (roughly M to 2M neighbor IDs per vector, depending on M), so total memory is high; building searches and links every point, and each insert must find its place and update neighbor links, so builds are slow and inserts relatively expensive. It suits read-heavy, low-latency search.

title: hnsw
text:
Why is HNSW often chosen in production vector search?
HNSW is popular because it can hit high-recall, low-latency targets, but it pays with memory, build time, and update cost.

title: ivf
text:
What is the basic idea behind IVF?
IVF clusters vectors around centroids and searches only the closest clusters for a query.

title: ivf
text:
What does the nprobe parameter control in IVF?
In IVF, nprobe controls how many clusters are searched at query time.

title: ivf
text:
In IVF, what do nlist and nprobe each control?
IVF has two phases. Build (offline): k-means splits vectors into nlist clusters, each with a centroid, and each vector is assigned to its nearest centroid — nlist sets the total number of clusters. Query (online): find which centroids the query is near, search only the nearest nprobe clusters, compute exact distances there, and take top-K — nprobe sets how many clusters this query probes. Library analogy: nlist is how many sections the library has (fixed at build), nprobe is how many sections you browse this time. When recall is low but latency has headroom, raise nprobe to browse more sections and recover true neighbors that landed in a neighboring cluster at the boundary — trading latency for recall.

title: ivf-tradeoff
text:
What is the typical tradeoff of IVF versus HNSW?
IVF only trains centroids and assigns vectors to clusters — no full neighbor graph — so it builds faster and uses less memory (large memory savings usually also need PQ). The downside: a query near a cluster boundary may have neighbors in the adjacent cluster, compensated by raising nprobe, so recall at the same latency is often lower than HNSW.

title: ivf-edge
text:
Why should IVF not search only the single nearest cluster?
IVF searches multiple clusters because true neighbors can lie across cluster boundaries.

title: lsh
text:
What is the core idea of LSH?
LSH uses hash functions that make similar vectors likely to collide in the same buckets.

title: lsh
text:
For cosine similarity, how does random-hyperplane LSH create a hash bit?
Random hyperplane LSH hashes vectors by which side of each random hyperplane they fall on.

title: lsh-fit
text:
Why might LSH still be worth considering?
LSH remains useful for fast index builds, streaming data, and Hamming-style similarity, even if HNSW often performs better.

title: annoy
text:
How does Annoy build its index?
Annoy builds a forest of random projection trees and searches candidate leaves from multiple trees.

title: annoy-tradeoff
text:
What are Annoy's key advantage and limitation?
Annoy is mmap-friendly and good for static datasets, but its indexes are immutable and require rebuilds for updates.

title: filtering
text:
What problem does this kind of query add to vector search?
Real vector queries often require filtered search, combining similarity with structured predicates like stock or price.

title: filtering
text:
What is the difference between post-filtering and pre-filtering?
Post-filtering searches similar candidates then filters them, while pre-filtering restricts the set before vector search.

title: filtering
text:
Which filtering strategy is more likely to fit here?
Pre-filtering often wins when a restrictive filter reduces the candidate set to a tiny subset.

title: pgvector
text:
What is the main appeal of pgvector?
pgvector is attractive because it adds vector search to Postgres while keeping ACID transactions, SQL, joins, and familiar tooling.

title: pgvector-filtering
text:
What is pgvector's limitation for filtered vector queries?
pgvector relies on the Postgres planner, which can produce suboptimal plans for awkward filter selectivity.

title: elasticsearch
text:
What is one strength of Elasticsearch kNN for vector retrieval?
Elasticsearch kNN is useful when you already run Elasticsearch and need hybrid keyword plus vector search.

title: pinecone
text:
How do purpose-built vector databases like Pinecone treat metadata filtering?
Purpose-built vector databases often treat metadata filtering as a first-class feature integrated with ANN search.

title: hybrid-search
text:
What does hybrid search usually mean?
Hybrid search combines keyword or full-text retrieval with vector similarity and merges or reranks the results.

title: writes
text:
Why are vector databases usually more read-heavy than small-update-heavy?
Inserting or updating vectors means rewiring HNSW graph edges or cluster assignments, and frequent updates can degrade the index or force rebuilds. Decide between real-time and batch writes; structured fields like price or stock should be updated as metadata without recomputing embeddings.

title: hot-cold-index
text:
What is a common vector index maintenance pattern?
A hot-cold index pattern searches a small recent index and a large stable index, then periodically merges or rebuilds.

title: updates
text:
How are updates usually implemented in a vector database?
Vector updates are commonly implemented as delete plus insert, often with soft deletes until the index is rebuilt.

title: rebuilds
text:
Which strategies reduce the impact of a slow vector index rebuild?
Large vector index rebuilds can be handled with rolling swaps, partitioned rebuilds, or background reindexing.

title: start-simple
text:
What is the most pragmatic starting point here?
If the data already lives in Postgres and the scale is millions of vectors, pgvector is often the pragmatic starting point.

title: scale-threshold
text:
At what vector-count scale should you seriously evaluate a purpose-built vector database?
100M is a rule-of-thumb anchor: 768-dim float32 × 100M ≈ 300 GB of raw vectors, which plus index overhead exceeds one machine's memory, making sharding, filtering, and index rebuilds first-class concerns. The real triggers are memory, QPS, filtering, and update needs, not a fixed number.

title: options-simple
text:
Which options fit starting from an existing database or storage system?
Pragmatic starting options include pgvector, Elasticsearch kNN, and Redis Vector Search when those systems are already in use.

title: options-purpose-built
text:
Which of these are mainstream purpose-built vector databases?
Purpose-built vector database options include Pinecone, Weaviate, Milvus, Qdrant, and Chroma.

title: milvus
text:
How should you position Milvus?
Milvus is an open-source vector database built for serious scale, with the tradeoff of higher operational complexity.

title: qdrant
text:
What is one highlighted strength of Qdrant?
Qdrant is a Rust-based vector database noted for strong filtering support.

title: interview-scenarios
text:
Which system design problems naturally lead to a vector database?
Vector databases earn their place when you need semantic similarity, candidate recall, or near-duplicate detection; an exact ID lookup is just a normal index.

title: rag
text:
What role does the vector database play in this architecture?
In RAG, the vector database retrieves document chunks similar to the query embedding for the LLM to use.

title: architecture
text:
What is the most common vector retrieval architecture pattern?
A common pattern is to use the vector database as a search service returning IDs, then fetch full records from the primary database.

title: two-stage-retrieval
text:
How is two-stage retrieval usually used in search or recommendations?
Two-stage retrieval uses vector search for broad candidate generation and a slower model to rerank the candidates.

title: design-decisions
text:
What design decisions should you proactively explain when adding vector search?
Vector search usually tolerates brief staleness, and the embedding pipeline and filtering strategy shape the architecture. A vector database generally should not be the authoritative transactional store, so D is a decision to avoid, not one to present.

title: consistency
text:
Why can vector search results usually tolerate short staleness?
Vector search can often be eventually consistent because new items usually do not need to be searchable immediately.

title: memory
text:
What design judgment does this single-vector size support?
A 1536-dimensional float32 vector is about 6 KB, so millions of vectors quickly become gigabytes of raw data.

title: memory
text:
What design judgment does this total size support?
1536 × 4 B ≈ 6 KB per vector, × 1M ≈ 6 GB. HNSW stores neighbor links per vector — about M×2 four-byte IDs at the base layer (~128 bytes at M=16) — only a few percent extra at 1536 dims, so for high-dimensional vectors the vectors themselves dominate memory; graph overhead matters more at low dimensions. 6 GB fits on one machine, but the budget must cover vectors, graph, metadata, and headroom.

title: latency
text:
What latency is a common target for a well-tuned in-memory ANN index?
An in-memory ANN index avoids disk I/O and visits only a small fraction of candidates, so a tuned one commonly targets sub-10ms, often 1–5ms. Hundreds of ms is an end-to-end product ceiling; tens to hundreds of ms is more typical of heavy filtering or disk-based indexes. Higher recall means visiting more candidates and higher latency (D reverses this). It is an empirical target, not an SLA.

title: source-of-truth
text:
Why should a vector database not be the transactional source of truth?
A vector database should be treated as a similarity search index, not the transactional source of truth.

title: embedding-drift
text:
What is the main risk of embedding drift after changing models?
Changing embedding models can make old and new vectors incompatible, requiring re-embedding and careful index migration.

title: cold-start
text:
What is the cold-start problem in personalized vector recommendations?
Personalization has a cold-start problem when new users lack behavior history for a reliable user embedding.

title: dimensionality
text:
What is the tradeoff between embedding dimensionality and performance?
Higher-dimensional embeddings can capture more nuance but cost more memory and search time.

title: exact-match
text:
If the requirement is exact lookup by document_id, what should you use?
Exact document lookup should use a normal database or key-value index, while vector search is for similarity.

title: decision-chain
text:
Put the decision chain for whether to introduce a vector database in order.
The decision should start with a real similarity problem, choose the simplest viable vector capability, benchmark index tradeoffs, and only then move to dedicated vector infrastructure.

title: filtering
text:
What happens in Elasticsearch kNN when the filter is this restrictive?
Elasticsearch applies the knn `filter` during HNSW traversal, not afterwards, so as long as at least K documents match it returns K results, at the cost of exploring more of the graph. If very few documents pass the filter, Lucene switches to exact brute-force search over the filtered set, so latency does not grow monotonically with filter strictness.

title: operations
text:
How do you stop a v2 query vector from searching v1 vectors?
Two models produce incomparable vector spaces, so mixing them returns semantically unrelated results while still looking like valid scores — tagging the model version keeps the two indexes separate, at the cost of running both during the migration.

title: architecture
text:
Should embedding generation sit on the synchronous upload path or in an async pipeline?
A fast upload plus a one-minute searchability window together justify moving GPU inference to the background: upload latency no longer depends on inference time, at the cost of a not-yet-searchable window plus retry and status tracking for failed embed jobs. Only if the product required instant searchability would synchronous embedding be worth weighing.

title: similarity-metric
text:
Should you use Euclidean (L2) distance or cosine similarity here?
We care about semantic direction, not length — L2 would push two same-direction vectors apart just because their magnitudes differ, while the cost of cosine is that it discards magnitude entirely.

title: exact-knn
text:
How do you keep exact KNN viable at this scale?
At this scale with perfect recall required, brute force is already viable — you only shrink the constant on the O(n) scan. SIMD lets one CPU instruction process several floats at once (the width depends on the instruction set, e.g. 8 fp32 lanes with AVX2, 16 with AVX-512), and a GPU scores thousands of vectors in parallel; compute still grows linearly with the vector count.

title: ivf
text:
Why is latency flat in the lab but higher in production?
At concurrency one, probes run in parallel and the 4x extra work hides behind idle cores; in production the CPU is already near saturation, so there are no spare cores, the extra probes queue, and the added total work shows up directly as higher average latency.

title: lsh
text:
Why does a single LSH table miss similar vectors, and how do you fix it?
LSH works on the probability that similar items collide, so one unlucky split in a single table separates true neighbors — extra tables with different hyperplanes raise the chance of sharing at least one bucket, at multiplied memory and query cost.

title: lsh
text:
Put the LSH query flow in order.
LSH only uses bucket hits as a coarse filter and still computes real distances on the survivors, so candidate-set size drives query cost — more tables mean better recall but a bigger merged candidate set.

title: lsh
text:
What does adding more tables cost?
A similar vector is retrieved if it shares a bucket in any table, so more tables raise the chance of at least one collision and recall goes up — but every extra table stores another full bucket index, and each query hashes into all tables and merges, dedups and reranks more candidates, so memory and query time rise together. The other knob works the opposite way: more bits per table make buckets finer and lower the per-table collision probability (recall down, precision up), which is why you usually add bits for precision and add tables to recover recall.

title: index-maintenance
text:
How should you handle this cluster drift?
The centroids were trained on the distribution from six months ago; once the data drifts, the partitioning no longer fits — some clusters balloon and many vectors and queries sit near boundaries between clusters, so a fixed nprobe covers a smaller share of the true neighbors and recall slides. Raising nprobe patches it temporarily at higher query cost; the real fix is to periodically re-cluster and rebuild, keeping the old index serving until the new one is swapped in.

title: index-maintenance
text:
What form should the hot index take?
With only a few thousand vectors between merges, a linear scan of the hot set is negligible and not worth HNSW build and memory overhead; queries merge the brute-force hot results with the cold-index results. The cost is that scan time grows as the hot set accumulates, so it must be folded into the cold index by the periodic merge.

title: index-maintenance
text:
Should updates go through real-time upserts or batch plus periodic rebuild?
Every HNSW insert has to locate the vector and rewire its connections, and the graph degrades as inserts pile up, so writing tens of millions one by one is brutally expensive — the price of batching is a full cycle of staleness before data becomes searchable.

title: vector-db-options
text:
What role does S3 Vectors play in this architecture?
When you already lean on S3, the corpus is modest and queries are infrequent, S3 Vectors stores vectors in an S3 vector bucket and serves similarity queries (with metadata filtering) through its query API, so there is no extra vector database to operate; the trade-off is that it targets low-cost, infrequent querying, with higher latency and lower throughput than a purpose-built vector database.

title: applications
text:
What retrieval approach should decide near-duplicates here?
Exact hashing matches nothing when wording differs but meaning does not, whereas geometric distance between embeddings captures exactly that closeness — the cost is a similarity threshold you must tune on real data.

title: capacity
text:
How should you size the retrieval fleet?
Node count = peak QPS ÷ (measured per-node throughput × target utilization) = 200k ÷ 14k ≈ 15 nodes; since each node holds a full replica, QPS spreads linearly across nodes; then add redundancy for a node or zone failure. The 20k per node is a benchmark for this index configuration — change dimension, data size, or recall target and you must re-test.

title: motivation
text:
What problem appears if a chat app stores user-to-server routing in one database table?
A database mapping becomes a single point of failure, adds a lookup to every message, and turns into a bottleneck at scale.

title: motivation
text:
What new problem appears if you cache the user-to-server mapping table?
Caching the mapping creates staleness: a user who reconnects elsewhere leaves other servers routing messages to the old server.

title: motivation
text:
If servers broadcast routing changes directly to each other, what breaks at scale?
Connections ≈ server count × server count (n squared), not channel or user count: full-mesh broadcasting floods the network as the cluster grows.

title: motivation
text:
What classic problem do you hit when you build your own heartbeat-based failure detector?
Heartbeats hit the network partition problem: a live server can look dead to some peers, leaving the cluster with inconsistent views.

title: motivation
text:
Which distributed-systems problems is ZooKeeper designed to solve? (Select all that apply.)
ZooKeeper packages service discovery, configuration sharing, failure detection, leader election, and consensus so you do not build those algorithms yourself.

title: mental-model
text:
What is the best mental model for ZooKeeper?
ZooKeeper is like a shared metadata tree: writes are totally ordered through the leader, every client sees the same update order regardless of which server it connects to (single system image), and catches up within bounded time. Reads are served locally and may be slightly stale; call sync() first if you need the latest value.

title: znodes
text:
Which statement about ZNode data is correct?
ZNodes hold small coordination data under one megabyte each, organized in a large hierarchical tree, not bulk data.

title: znodes
text:
Fill in the three basic ZNode properties (3.5+ also adds container and TTL nodes).
These three basic properties are the raw material of every ZooKeeper recipe: persistent for config, ephemeral for liveness (tied to session expiry, not to a TCP disconnect), and sequential for ordering, locks and election (often combined as EPHEMERAL_SEQUENTIAL).

title: znodes
text:
Which ZNode type should you use?
Configuration like max message size belongs in persistent nodes that survive until explicitly changed.

title: znodes
text:
Which ZNode type should you use?
Ephemeral nodes disappear automatically when the creator's session ends, which is exactly how ZooKeeper detects dead servers.

title: znodes
text:
Which ZNode feature should you use?
Sequential nodes get a monotonically increasing counter appended by ZooKeeper, giving a global order for locks and elections.

title: znodes
text:
Which ZooKeeper command is correct?
The -e flag creates an ephemeral node that vanishes automatically if server two crashes.

title: chat-routing
text:
With ZooKeeper in place, how does Alice on Server 1 route a message to Bob?
Server one looks up Bob's znode to learn he is on server two and routes the message there, with the mapping kept current automatically.

title: scalability
text:
What is the more scalable routing design?
ZooKeeper's write load ≈ server count, not user count: track a few dozen servers with ephemeral nodes for fast failure detection, and hash users to them — user growth is only a secondary cost.

title: ensemble
text:
How should ZooKeeper be deployed in production?
ZooKeeper runs as an ensemble of typically three, five, or seven servers, since odd sizes make majority decisions cleaner.

title: ensemble
text:
How do the Leader and Followers split work inside a ZooKeeper ensemble?
The elected leader processes all writes while followers help serve reads from any server in the ensemble.

title: quorum
text:
In a 5-node ZooKeeper ensemble, how many node failures can it tolerate?
A five-server ensemble tolerates two failures because three remaining servers still form a majority, or quorum.

title: client-connection
text:
What does a ZooKeeper client connection string look like, and why?
The connect string lists every server; the client library connects to one, and if it dies, reconnects to another from the list. As long as it reaches a server that is still part of the quorum within the session timeout, the session and its ephemeral nodes survive. The session timeout and watcher are separate constructor arguments, not part of the connect string.

title: watches
text:
What is the ZooKeeper watch mechanism?
A watch notifies the client when a znode changes, replacing constant polling with push notifications.

title: watches
text:
What happens if every message queries ZooKeeper for routing instead of using watches?
The routing map changes a few dozen times per second but is read hundreds of thousands of times per second: every message pays an extra round trip, ZooKeeper read load scales with message volume, and any ZooKeeper hiccup stalls the whole message path. ZooKeeper reads are not slow — each server answers from memory — the mistake is putting the coordinator on every message's hot path. Cache locally and refresh on watch notifications, so ZooKeeper load tracks the change rate, not the message rate.

title: watches
text:
What key usage pattern do ZooKeeper watches enable?
Servers keep a local cache of ZooKeeper state and update it on watch notifications instead of querying every time.

title: positioning
text:
Why is ZooKeeper a coordination service rather than a database?
ZooKeeper's value is a consistent view, change notifications and coordination primitives like sessions and ephemeral nodes. Its reads are actually fast (each server answers from memory), but the entire dataset must fit in every server's memory, a znode is capped at about 1 MB by default, and every write is broadcast by the leader and waits for a quorum. Profiles and message history are large and write-heavy, so they would exhaust memory and swamp the write path — they belong in a database or KV store.

title: watches
text:
What is the correct way to use watches for routing changes?
Register a watch on the users path and update the local routing table in the callback when a znode changes.

title: capabilities
text:
Which of the following are typical ZooKeeper use cases? (Select all that apply.)
Configuration management, service discovery, leader election, and distributed locks are all built from small znodes, ephemeral/sequential nodes, and watches, matching the four duties in the scenario (option C covers both election and locks). Full-text search needs an inverted index and bulk text storage, which is not ZooKeeper's role.

title: config-management
text:
How would you implement this with ZooKeeper?
Update one znode and every watching server gets notified and changes behavior without restarting.

title: config-management
text:
Which configuration belongs in ZooKeeper, and which does not?
Put dynamic runtime configuration in ZooKeeper and keep static deploy-time configuration in files or environment variables.

title: service-discovery
text:
What is the standard ZooKeeper pattern for service discovery?
Instances register ephemeral nodes, consumers read the children to pick one, and a watch keeps the list current as instances come and go.

title: leader-election
text:
Put ZooKeeper's application-level leader election recipe in the correct order.
Each server creates a sequential ephemeral node, the lowest number leads, everyone watches the next lower node, and when the leader dies the next in line takes over.

title: leader-election
text:
In the election recipe, why does Server 3 watch node-0000000002 instead of the leader node?
Each server watches only the next lower node, forming a chain so a failure notifies exactly one successor instead of everyone.

title: leader-election
text:
Which real systems have used ZooKeeper for leader or controller election?
HBase's HMaster and ZooKeeper-era Kafka's controller were both elected through ZooKeeper: candidates race to create one ephemeral node (/hbase/master, /controller), the creator wins, and when its session dies the node disappears and the rest race again. That is the single-ephemeral-node approach, not the smallest-sequential-node recipe, which adds chained watches to avoid the herd effect. Redis uses its own Sentinel/Cluster voting, Nginx has no leader concept, and Git merges have nothing to do with runtime coordination.

title: distributed-locks
text:
What is the ZooKeeper distributed-lock recipe?
The scenario needs three things: mutual exclusion, automatic release on crash, and no stampede on release with first-come ordering. B uses ephemeral sequential nodes: the lowest number holds the lock, each client watches only its predecessor, a release wakes exactly one waiter, and the numbers themselves are the queue order. A gives mutual exclusion and auto-release too, but every release wakes all waiters at once (herd effect) with no ordering. C confuses ZooKeeper's internal leader with an application lock; D relies on drifting local clocks.

title: distributed-locks
text:
When is a ZooKeeper lock a poor fit, and what should replace it?
Each ZooKeeper lock acquire or release is a leader-plus-quorum durable write that takes milliseconds by itself; when the lock is held only a few milliseconds, the locking overhead is as long as the critical section and all lock traffic is serialized through the leader, which is a poor trade. High-frequency, short-hold mutual exclusion fits Redis locks or plain database transactions / conditional updates better. ZooKeeper locks suit low-frequency, long-held, correctness-first cases. Actual write throughput depends on fsync latency, hardware, and load; there is no fixed ceiling.

title: distributed-locks
text:
Should you choose a ZooKeeper lock or a Redis lock?
Choose ZooKeeper locks when correctness trumps performance and locks are long-lived, since ephemeral nodes detect crashes more robustly than Redis timeouts.

title: zab
text:
Which protocol does ZooKeeper use internally for consensus?
ZooKeeper runs the ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast protocol so all its servers agree on system state despite failures.

title: zab
text:
What are the two main phases of the ZAB protocol?
ZAB runs in two modes. In recovery, it elects the leader with the most up-to-date transaction history and syncs followers to it, filling in every committed write before serving clients — that is what keeps acknowledged writes from being lost or reordered. In broadcast, the leader assigns each write an order and commits it once a majority has persisted it. (The ZAB paper further splits recovery into discovery and synchronization.)

title: zab
text:
How does ZooKeeper's internal leader election differ from the application recipe?
Internally ZooKeeper elects the server with the most up-to-date transaction history, preferring the highest ID on ties, the opposite of the lowest-sequence application recipe.

title: zab
text:
How are ZAB, Paxos, and Raft related?
ZAB predates Raft and differs in implementation, but like Paxos and Raft it achieves distributed consensus.

title: consistency
text:
Fill in ZooKeeper's consistency guarantees.
These five guarantees make ZooKeeper trustworthy as a coordination source of truth. They rely mainly on leader-ordered writes with quorum persistence (ZAB), plus zxid checks on reconnect so a client never sees an older view.

title: consistency
text:
Follower reads can be stale. What should you do when you need the strongest read consistency?
Follower reads can be stale, so clients call sync before reading when they need the most up-to-date view.

title: workload
text:
According to the official ZooKeeper documentation, at what read/write ratio does it perform best?
Reads are served from the local in-memory replica of whichever server the client is connected to (no quorum, possibly slightly stale; use sync when needed), while writes go through the leader and ZAB majority acknowledgment. The official docs say it performs best in read-dominant workloads around 10:1, so read-heavy service discovery fits and write-heavy log collection does not.

title: sessions
text:
What are the key points of ZooKeeper sessions?
Clients hold heartbeat-maintained sessions with a ten-to-thirty-second timeout, and expiry deletes their ephemeral nodes and watches.

title: sessions
text:
What tradeoff does the ZooKeeper session timeout setting create?
A short session timeout causes false failovers on network blips, while a long one delays detecting real failures.

title: storage
text:
How does ZooKeeper make sure acknowledged updates are not lost?
Every change is synced to a write-ahead transaction log before responding, and periodic snapshots speed up recovery on restart.

title: storage
text:
Why is swapping disastrous for ZooKeeper performance?
ZooKeeper executes requests in total order, so one request paging in from disk — about 10ms versus 100ns from memory — stalls everything queued behind it.

title: failures
text:
What does ZooKeeper do when no network partition can form a majority?
Without a majority ZooKeeper refuses writes until the partition heals, preventing split-brain disagreement.

title: failures
text:
Put ZooKeeper's automatic handling of a crashed chat server in the right order.
After a crash the session times out, its ephemeral nodes are deleted, and watching servers get notified and update their routing automatically.

title: ecosystem
text:
Which systems still depend on ZooKeeper today?
ZooKeeper is still common in the Apache ecosystem: HBase uses it for master election and RegionServer tracking, HDFS/YARN HA use it for automatic failover, and Storm and Pulsar use it for metadata by default; ClickHouse replicated tables need ZooKeeper or the ZooKeeper-compatible ClickHouse Keeper. Kubernetes stores cluster state in etcd (an independent project started by CoreOS), not ZooKeeper; most cloud-managed products use their own mechanisms; and claiming nobody uses ZooKeeper anymore is wrong.

title: ecosystem
text:
What trend does Kafka's move away from ZooKeeper with KRaft show?
Kafka's move to KRaft reflects a broader trend toward self-contained systems with built-in consensus instead of external coordination services.

title: alternatives
text:
How is etcd positioned relative to ZooKeeper?
etcd solves the same class of problems as ZooKeeper (configuration, service discovery, leader election, locks), but it uses Raft, a native gRPC API (JSON via a gateway), and is tightly bound to the Kubernetes ecosystem, which fits the Go + gRPC team in the scenario. It is not a rewrite of ZooKeeper, its KV interface stores configuration naturally, and its writes are strongly consistent.

title: alternatives
text:
What is Consul's distinguishing feature compared with ZooKeeper?
Consul goes beyond coordination with service discovery, health checks, and network automation that reconfigures load balancers as services change.

title: limitations
text:
What does ZooKeeper hot spotting mean?
Hot spotting is many clients watching or reading the same znode: every change fans out a flood of notifications, followed by everyone reading back at once, so the traffic concentrates into a bottleneck. The standard election and lock recipes use chained watches (each client watches only its predecessor) precisely to avoid this; naive implementations where everyone watches one node are what create the hot spot.

title: limitations
text:
What are ZooKeeper's main limitations? (Select all that apply.)
ZooKeeper writes are expensive through leader and quorum, capacity is memory-bound with small znodes, and it is simple to use but complex to operate.

title: smart-routing
text:
What role does ZooKeeper play in this live-chat routing design?
ZooKeeper coordinates smart routing by mapping rooms to servers so a gateway can colocate all viewers of a stream on the same server group.

title: infra-design
text:
In a distributed message queue, which responsibilities can ZooKeeper handle as the consensus brain? (Select all that apply.)
Broker registration, topic metadata, partition leader election, and consumer membership/assignment are all small, strongly consistent coordination data that ZooKeeper can handle; message payloads are far too large and belong in the brokers' own logs. For reference, ZooKeeper-era Kafka used ZooKeeper for broker registration and topic metadata, and used it to elect a single controller that chose each partition's leader and wrote the result back to ZooKeeper (cheaper than per-partition elections at thousands of partitions); the old consumer also tracked group membership in ZooKeeper, which moved to the broker-side group coordinator from 0.9 on.

title: hierarchical-locks
text:
Why is ZooKeeper the better fit than Redis here?
When resources have parent-child relationships and locking must respect the hierarchy, ZooKeeper's tree plus child watches are native features. Redis has a flat key space, so hierarchy is a prefix convention, and its keyspace notifications/Pub/Sub are lost on disconnect, which makes reliable hierarchy monitoring hard.

title: interview-strategy
text:
What is the right posture toward ZooKeeper in this interview setting?
Do not reach for ZooKeeper unless you are designing deep infrastructure or need coordination beyond what modern load balancers and built-in service discovery offer.

title: zab
text:
How does a write request, such as registering Bob's ZNode, flow through the ensemble?
A write goes to the leader, which broadcasts it to followers and confirms success once a majority has accepted and saved it.

title: znodes
text:
Under ZooKeeper's default configuration, roughly what is the hard size limit for a single znode's data?
The default jute.maxbuffer is about 1 MB, and larger znode data is rejected; but the docs are clear that ZooKeeper is not a general database or large-object store — znode data is usually bytes to kilobytes, and the whole dataset must fit in memory. A multi-MB JSON belongs in object storage or a DB, with only a reference in the znode.

title: sessions
text:
What is the typical ZooKeeper session timeout range?
Session timeouts are typically ten to thirty seconds, balancing false-positive failovers against how long real failure detection via ephemeral nodes takes.

title: primitives
text:
Fill in ZooKeeper's three basic primitives.
ZooKeeper combines znodes in a hierarchical namespace, a reliable server ensemble, and watches for change notification.

title: consistency
text:
What happens under concurrency if you pass version = -1 to setData?
-1 disables the version check and overwrites unconditionally. ZooKeeper still applies the two writes one after another in the leader's total order, but ordering is not protection: the later write still overwrites the earlier one, so that update is lost. To be safe, pass the version you read (CAS); a mismatch returns BadVersion and you re-read and retry. Option D describes what happens when you pass a real version, not -1.

title: leader-election
text:
Should you use application-level leader election or grab a distributed lock per operation?
Payments and scheduling need one server to own the role long-term, which leader election gives with auto-failover; a lock only enforces per-operation mutual exclusion.

title: consistency
text:
After reconnecting, how does this follower get back to a view consistent with the others?
A lagging follower catches up by replaying the writes it missed before it can serve consistent reads; until it catches up, reads from it can be stale.

title: storage
text:
What happens if you put the transaction log on the same disk as snapshots and other I/O?
The transaction log must fsync before acking, and since ops are totally ordered, one slow write stalls the whole queue — so give it a dedicated disk.

title: core-concepts
text:
What is the difference between core concepts and specific technologies like Redis or Kafka?
Core concepts are technology-agnostic building blocks that interviewers assume you know and will probe when you propose using them.

title: networking
text:
For routine client-server communication, what should you choose by default?
With no real-time push and no extreme performance requirement, default to HTTP over TCP: mature tooling, works everywhere, and needs no justification in an interview. WebSocket is for bidirectional real-time, and neither a custom UDP transport nor FTP has a reason here.

title: networking
text:
What is the key difference between SSE and WebSocket?
Server-sent events are unidirectional with the server pushing down one HTTP connection, while WebSockets are truly bidirectional.

title: networking
text:
For one-way live updates, which real-time approach fits better?
For one-way server push like live scores or notifications, server-sent events are simpler and fit standard HTTP infrastructure better.

title: networking
text:
What design consequence follows because SSE and WebSocket are stateful connections?
A long-lived connection is pinned to one server once established, unlike short requests that can be rebalanced each time. So the load balancer must handle long-lived connections (L4 pass-through or an L7 that supports HTTP Upgrade), and you must plan for uneven connection distribution, draining connections during rolling deploys, and throttling/backing off the reconnect storm when a server with thousands of clients dies. They still scale horizontally and still run over TCP; no UDP needed.

title: networking
text:
For performance-critical internal service calls, what communication option is worth mentioning?
Use gRPC for internal service-to-service communication when performance is critical, since binary serialization over HTTP/2 beats JSON over HTTP.

title: networking
text:
How do L7 and L4 load balancers differ?
L7 understands HTTP content and can route by path or header; L4 just distributes TCP connections without reading content, with lower overhead. Here no path-based routing is needed after the connection is set up, so L4 is enough and cheaper. If you did need to route different WebSocket endpoints to different services, an L7 that supports Upgrade (ALB, nginx) works too.

title: networking
text:
Why is it a common mistake to jump to WebSocket whenever a prompt says real-time?
Proposing WebSockets when long polling or server-sent events would do adds needless stateful-connection complexity at scale.

title: networking
text:
What does the physical fiber propagation floor mean for this deployment?
New York to London is about 5,570 km; light in fiber travels about 200,000 km/s, so the RTT floor is about 55-60 ms and 70-90 ms in practice, already over the 50 ms budget. CPU, compression, HTTP/2, and TCP tuning only reduce processing time or the number of round trips, not the propagation time of one, so serving must move closer to the user.

title: api-design
text:
What does an interviewer usually expect from the API-design section?
Most interviewers don't need a perfect API; they want reasonable endpoints so you can spend time on the hard parts, though sloppy endpoints still signal inexperience.

title: api-design
text:
What is a reasonable pace for the API-design section?
Budget about five minutes: list the few endpoints that carry the core features and move on. A and B burn time on field details that the high-level design and deep dives need; D hides the core objects and main flow from the interviewer.

title: api-design
text:
How should you choose between cursor-based and offset-based pagination?
Offset paging skips the first N rows, so every new post at the top shifts page three and the user sees duplicates. Cursor paging starts after the last item's sort key (such as id), so new inserts don't move it. For lists that rarely change, offset is simpler.

title: api-design
text:
What auth method should each of the two caller types use?
User sessions need a short-lived credential with claims that the gateway can verify without a DB lookup, which is exactly what a signed JWT is for. The internal callers are few and want the simplest long-lived credential that can be revoked per caller, so one API key per caller fits directly. C puts a never-expiring key in the browser and gives the batch services no identity of their own. Note that in production, service-to-service auth also commonly uses mTLS or OAuth 2.0 client credentials (which usually issue JWTs); API keys win here only because the prompt asks for the simplest per-caller-revocable credential.

title: api-design
text:
What API-layer point should you proactively mention for an abuse-prone system?
If the system could get hammered by bots or abuse, mention rate limiting but do not go deep unless asked.

title: data-modeling
text:
Which storage choice fits structured relational data with transactions and complex queries?
Structured data with clear relationships, strong consistency, transactions, and complex queries is the relational home turf. DynamoDB and MongoDB offer transactions too, but ad-hoc multi-table joins are not their strength.

title: data-modeling
text:
Which storage choice fits flexible schema and horizontal scaling without complex joins?
Flexible schemas and horizontal scaling are NoSQL's home turf. Spanner also scales horizontally, but its schema is strictly defined and frequent changes still require DDL; read replicas only scale reads and still need migrations.

title: data-modeling
text:
What does normalization mean, and what does it cost?
Normalization splits data into tables so orders reference a product ID: one rename updates everywhere, at the cost of joins on read, which get expensive at scale.

title: data-modeling
text:
What is the read/write tradeoff between denormalization and normalization?
Denormalization duplicates data to avoid joins and speed up reads, at the cost of updating every copy when the source changes.

title: data-modeling
text:
What is the safer default when you start data modeling in an interview?
In a relational database, normalization gives single-place updates and no duplication; denormalization trades consistency upkeep for read speed and is worth it only once a hot-path read bottleneck is confirmed. (Query-driven NoSQL modeling would start denormalized, which is why the scenario fixes a relational store.)

title: data-modeling
text:
If DynamoDB is partitioned by user_id for fetching a user posts, what happens when you query posts by hashtag?
DynamoDB Query requires an equality condition on the partition key. Hashtag is not a key and there is no GSI, so the only option is a full-table Scan with a filter; making it fast requires a GSI or a separate hashtag-to-post table.

title: data-modeling
text:
Fill in the relational versus NoSQL design bias.
A first-pass instinct: relational databases favor multi-table ACID transactions and joins, while NoSQL favors flexible schemas and horizontal scaling. Strongly consistent reads are not unique to relational databases; DynamoDB offers them too.

title: indexing
text:
On a 10-million-row users table, what does an email lookup mean without an index?
Without an index, finding a user by email scans all ten million rows, while an index lets the database jump straight to the row in milliseconds.

title: indexing
text:
What is the most common index structure, and why is it useful?
The B-tree keeps data sorted so it supports both exact lookups and range queries, which is why relational databases default to it.

title: indexing
text:
What is the core difference between a hash index and a B-tree index?
Hash indexes are faster for exact matches but cannot do range queries, so they are less common than B-trees.

title: indexing
text:
Which index should you build for filtering by city and date?
A composite query filtering on both city and date calls for a compound index on the two columns.

title: indexing
text:
Which combination fits best?
With Postgres as the primary, PostGIS adds geospatial queries without another system; full-text search needs tokenization, inverted indexes and relevance ranking, which is Elasticsearch's job. LIKE and B-trees cannot tokenize or do 2-D distance queries, and plain Redis has no full-text search. This is not the only option: Elasticsearch can also run geo queries.

title: indexing
text:
If an external search index is synced from the primary DB through CDC, what is the direct consequence?
External indexes sync via change data capture and lag slightly behind the primary, a staleness that is almost always acceptable for search.

title: caching
text:
After moving a hot read path behind cache hits, what changes about the database scale-up point?
A cache hit near one millisecond versus twenty to fifty for a database query fully offloads that read traffic, pushing back when you need to shard or scale.

title: caching
text:
Which caching pattern fits?
The bottleneck is reads and the write path is unchanged, which rules out the write patterns. Plain Redis cannot load from the database and the app owns the miss logic, which is exactly cache-aside: check cache, on miss query the DB, fill with a TTL.

title: caching
text:
What is the hardest part of caching, and what strategies handle it?
The hardest part of caching is invalidation, handled by invalidating on writes, using short TTLs and accepting staleness, or combining both.

title: caching
text:
What happens when a hot cache entry expires all at once?
When a popular cache entry expires, many concurrent requests miss at once and pile onto the database, a thundering herd that can take down the system.

title: caching
text:
Which techniques prevent a cache stampede? Select all that apply.
Locking (single-flight) and early recomputation handle the rebuild burst when one hot key expires; jittered TTLs handle thousands of bulk-warmed keys expiring in the same second. A zero TTL sends every request to the database.

title: caching
text:
For a full Redis outage, which defenses keep the database alive? Select all that apply.
If Redis goes down entirely, defend with a small in-process fallback cache, circuit breakers to shed load, and graceful degradation.

title: caching
text:
What is wrong with caching everything?
Cache only data that is read frequently and changes rarely; caching data that changes every request adds latency and complexity for nothing.

title: sharding
text:
Which signals mean you may actually need sharding? Select all that apply.
Sharding is triggered by load numbers: storage nearing a single instance's practical limit, write throughput nearing the primary's ceiling after vertical scaling runs out, or reads that replicas can't absorb. The actual limits depend on hardware, payload, indexes, and durability settings; there is no fixed terabyte or writes-per-second number. User count alone isn't a load signal, and this scenario (500GB, 2k writes/s, spare replicas) hits none of the signals, so it shouldn't shard yet.

title: sharding
text:
What is the most important sharding decision?
The shard key decides how data is distributed and which queries are cheap or expensive. Instagram sharding by user id makes per-user timelines a single-shard query, but a global trending feed must hit every shard and aggregate, which is expensive. That makes it the first sharding decision.

title: sharding
text:
What is the tradeoff between hash sharding and range sharding?
Hash sharding scatters adjacent keys across shards for more even load but loses range locality, so range scans hit many shards. Range sharding keeps locality, but a time-increasing workload like this one, where the last hour is hottest, piles reads and writes onto the newest shard. Hashing only removes hot spots caused by key ordering; a single hot key still lands on one shard.

title: sharding
text:
What is wrong with proposing sharding at 10K writes per second and 100GB of data?
The biggest sharding mistake is doing it too early; at ten thousand writes per second and a hundred gigabytes you do not need it yet.

title: sharding
text:
What new problems does sharding introduce? Select all that apply.
Sharding buys scalability but brings three pains: cross-shard transactions need 2PC or sagas, which are complex, slow, and hurt availability; hot shards; and resharding means mass data migration. Choose shard boundaries so operations like transfers stay within one shard where possible.

title: sharding
text:
What is the right way to explain a sharding proposal in an interview?
Justify why a single database will not work, state your shard key, and explain which queries get fast and which get slow.

title: sharding
text:
Put the Instagram user_id sharding decision chain in the right order.
Outgrowing one database leads to hashing by user id, which makes global queries expensive, mitigated by shard-boundary design and offline aggregation.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
With hash(key) modulo N server assignment, what happens when you add or remove a server?
Modulo placement is extremely sensitive to N: going from 10 to 11 nodes reassigns about 10/11 of keys. For a cache, that means almost every entry misses at once and traffic floods the database; for a storage cluster, most data must migrate. This is exactly what consistent hashing solves.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
How does consistent hashing work?
Consistent hashing places servers and keys on a ring where each key belongs to the next server clockwise, so only a small range moves when nodes change. Typical users: Cassandra's token ring, Memcached clients such as ketama, and the Amazon Dynamo paper; Redis Cluster uses 16,384 hash slots, not a ring.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
In a 10-server cluster adding one server, how much data moves with modulo hashing versus consistent hashing?
Adding one server to ten means moving about ninety percent of data with modulo hashing but only about ten percent with consistent hashing.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
How much detail should you give about consistent hashing in an interview?
In interviews just say you will use consistent hashing to distribute data across nodes; explain the internals only if asked.

title: cap-theorem
text:
What is the accurate statement of the CAP theorem?
Strictly, C means linearizability (every read sees the latest completed write), A means every request to a non-failing node gets a non-error response, and P means the network may drop messages or partition. Since the inter-datacenter link does break, partitions are a given, so the real trade-off only happens during a partition: reject some requests to keep C, or keep responding and accept divergence to keep A. “Pick two of three” is a common simplification that wrongly suggests P can be given up.

title: cap-theorem
text:
During a network partition, how do consistency-first and availability-first systems behave?
A consistency-first system refuses requests rather than serve stale data during a partition, while an availability-first system keeps responding and converges later.

title: cap-theorem
text:
What is the safer default consistency answer for feeds, recommendations, or analytics?
For most systems availability is the right default: users tolerate a slightly stale feed but not a down app, so eventual consistency works.

title: cap-theorem
text:
Which consistency model should you choose for stale-read-sensitive paths?
Choose strong consistency when stale reads cause real business harm, like overselling inventory, fraud, or double-booked seats.

title: cap-theorem
text:
What is the difference between eventual consistency and weak consistency?
Weak consistency only says a read right after a write is not guaranteed to see it, with no further promise about if or when replicas converge. Eventual consistency is a special case of weak consistency that adds one promise: if no new writes arrive, all replicas eventually converge to the same value. DynamoDB's eventually consistent read means exactly this — it may miss a just-completed write, but a read shortly after should return it. So they are not synonyms; eventual adds a concrete guarantee on top of plain weak consistency.

title: cap-theorem
text:
What blind spot in CAP does PACELC cover?
PACELC notes that outside rare partitions the real tradeoff is consistency versus latency, since strong consistency requires coordination before responding.

title: cap-theorem
text:
Put the strong-consistency decision chain for a ticket-booking system in the right order.
Stale reads costing real money lead to strong consistency, whose availability and latency costs are contained by applying it only to critical paths.

title: numbers
text:
What happens if you design with outdated 2010s hardware numbers in mind?
A modern box with NVMe, dozens of cores, and hundreds of GB of RAM can often serve tens of thousands of QPS of well-indexed simple reads (the exact figure depends on payload, query complexity, indexes, cache hit rate, and benchmark method). Estimating with decade-old hardware intuition makes you propose sharding and caching long before the bottleneck exists.

title: numbers
text:
Fill in the latency ladder that shapes almost every design decision.
Each rung is roughly two to three orders of magnitude apart: memory is ~1000× faster than SSD, an SSD read is ~5-10× faster than a same-DC round trip, and a same-DC round trip is ~100× faster than crossing a continent. Cache and multi-region decisions come from these gaps. Exact numbers shift with hardware generations, so remember orders of magnitude.

title: numbers
text:
Roughly how much storage can one Postgres instance comfortably hold, and when should sharding enter the conversation?
On storage alone, a modern single Postgres instance commonly holds a few TB, so sharding at 500GB for storage is premature complexity. But sharding also depends on write throughput, replication lag on a single primary, backup/restore time, and vacuum cost, any of which can force a split earlier.

title: numbers
text:
What database scale anchors and expansion triggers should you remember?
This is a rule-of-thumb anchor, not a spec: a tuned single instance with simple indexed queries often reaches tens of thousands of read TPS and around ten thousand writes; the real figure depends on CPU/disk, payload, indexes, transaction and fsync settings, concurrency, and benchmark method. Watch trends: writes nearing the measured ceiling, rising uncached read latency, or a need for geographic distribution.

title: numbers
text:
What Redis-scale cache anchors and alert triggers should you remember?
With simple commands, a Redis node commonly does 100k+ ops/s at about 1ms client-side latency (server-side is usually sub-millisecond); large values, Lua, big ZSETs, and network bandwidth lower that sharply. Keep per-node memory in the tens of GB and scale data via cluster sharding rather than TB-sized nodes. Scale-up signals are trends: falling hit rate, memory nearing maxmemory with evictions, rising latency; exact thresholds depend on the workload.

title: numbers
text:
What message-queue scale anchors should you remember?
This is a Kafka rule-of-thumb for small, batched, compressed messages; real throughput depends on message size, NIC/disk bandwidth, acks and replication factor, and partition count, and pushing throughput raises end-to-end latency. Watch for nearing the benchmarked ceiling, hot partitions, and growing consumer lag. Other MQs such as RabbitMQ or SQS have different profiles.

title: numbers
text:
When should you do back-of-the-envelope estimation?
Back-of-the-envelope math is a decision tool: do it at forks like whether to shard or whether one Redis suffices, so the numbers back that choice. Crunching everything up front produces numbers tied to no decision and eats architecture time. If the interviewer asks for estimates, do them.

title: numbers
text:
How do you estimate the server count on the spot?
Formula: servers = total rps divided by per-machine rps; rps is requests per second, so 50K over 5K is about 10, plus 20 to 30 percent headroom for spikes and failures, and that count sizes cost and the load-balancer pool.

title: networking
text:
What happens if you expose gRPC directly to browsers?
Browser fetch/XHR don't let a page control HTTP/2 framing or read the trailers gRPC uses to return status, so a browser can't speak native gRPC. gRPC-Web fills the gap but usually needs a proxy like Envoy or server middleware to translate, and it doesn't support client or bidirectional streaming. That's why the common pattern is REST externally and gRPC internally.

title: networking
text:
How do you cut the global latency of static assets?
Cross-continent round trips have a speed-of-light floor that faster processing can't remove, so a CDN caches static content on edge nodes near users to serve locally and dodge the distance.

title: api-design
text:
In this case, what API style should the public API default to?
Default a public API to REST, mapping resources to URLs like /users/{id} and acting via HTTP methods like POST /events/{id}/bookings, because it's universally understood and expected.

title: caching
text:
For data that must be immediately fresh, which invalidation strategy fits?
Freshness drives the strategy: if the next read must see the new value, delete (or update) the cache entry right after the DB write so the next read rebuilds from source; TTL-based options have a built-in stale window. This shrinks the stale window to near zero but isn't an absolute guarantee: a concurrent read can repopulate an old value and the delete can fail, so strict paths add delayed double-delete, versioning, or reads from the primary. The cost is an extra step on the write path.

title: caching
text:
Where should you cache small, rarely changing values like these?
Small, rarely changing, per-request values fit an in-process cache: reads hit local memory with zero network hop, at the cost of no cross-instance sync, so use it only for config-like data that tolerates brief inconsistency.

title: sharding
text:
When is range-based sharding a good fit?
Range sharding fits best when access naturally partitions into contiguous ranges: each tenant's data is one contiguous key range, so queries hit a single shard and whole-tenant moves or scans are easy. Hashing tenant_id also keeps a tenant on one shard but loses range locality. The risk is a hot range, such as one huge tenant or a monotonic time series, piling load on one shard; then you split the range or switch to hash.

title: numbers
text:
What do these signals together mean, and what should you do?
A clear drop from baseline hit rate, memory nearing maxmemory, and spiking evictions mean the hot set no longer fits: entries are evicted and refetched, pushing load back onto the database. Add memory or nodes and review what is cached (cold data, oversized values). Thresholds like 80% are rule-of-thumb alerts; set them from your own baseline.

title: numbers
text:
What do these signals together mean?
With downstream healthy and all three signals crossing in the app tier, the instances are saturated. The servers are stateless, so scaling out is the most direct fix; size it by computing count from both CPU and connections, taking the larger, plus headroom. Scaling up with more cores could ease CPU, but the connection ceiling and single-box risk remain, so scale-out is preferred.

title: framework
text:
What is the most common reason mid-level candidates fail system design interviews?
The single easiest way to fail is not delivering a working system, which mid-level candidates most often misdiagnose as a time-management problem.

title: framework
text:
What is the real issue behind so-called poor time management?
The issue is rarely that you must work twice as fast; usually you just need to focus on the right things.

title: framework
text:
What are the benefits of following the Delivery Framework? (Select all that apply)
The framework keeps you focused on what matters, gives you a track to fall back on when nervous, and helps you build the solution linearly.

title: framework
text:
Fill in the recommended time budget for each Delivery Framework stage:
This is Hello Interview's suggested Delivery Framework budget, with high-level design taking the largest share. The point is not the exact minutes but protecting deep-dive time; pacing varies by company and interviewer.

title: framework
text:
Put the five main Delivery Framework stages in interview order:
The delivery framework runs requirements, core entities, API, high-level design, and finally deep dives, with an optional data-flow step for data-processing systems.

title: functional-requirements
text:
What is the standard phrasing for a functional requirement?
Functional requirements are the "users should be able to" statements that capture the core features of the system.

title: functional-requirements
text:
What is the right way to gather functional requirements?
Gather functional requirements by asking targeted questions as if talking to a product manager, iterating with the interviewer toward a prioritized feature list.

title: functional-requirements
text:
When a real product has hundreds of features, how many core features should you focus on?
Your job is to identify and prioritize roughly the top three core features out of the hundreds the real product has, since that short list has to carry the rest of the interview.

title: functional-requirements
text:
What happens if you list every possible functional requirement?
A long requirements list hurts more than it helps, since top companies directly evaluate your ability to focus on what matters.

title: functional-requirements
text:
Which core functional requirements are reasonable for designing Twitter? (Select all that apply)
For Twitter the core functional requirements are posting tweets, following users, and seeing tweets from followed users.

title: non-functional-requirements
text:
What do non-functional requirements, or NFRs, describe?
Non-functional requirements are statements about system qualities that matter to users, phrased as "the system should be" statements.

title: non-functional-requirements
text:
What is wrong with saying only that the system should have low latency?
Saying the system should be low latency is meaningless; a useful requirement names the part that matters and quantifies it, like search under 500 milliseconds.

title: non-functional-requirements
text:
Fill in the Twitter non-functional requirement examples:
"A few seconds late is fine, failing to load is not" means choosing availability over consistency during partitions and accepting eventual consistency; 200 ms is a quantified latency target for feed rendering. Together they show how to write NFRs: name the CAP trade-off, give a scale number, and give a measurable latency target.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
Which dimensions belong in the non-functional requirement checklist? (Select all that apply)
The checklist covers CAP trade-offs, environment constraints, scalability, latency, durability, security, fault tolerance, and compliance.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
What is the right CAP question when defining non-functional requirements?
Partition tolerance is a given in distributed systems, so the real CAP question is whether to prioritize consistency or availability.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
When evaluating scalability as an NFR, what should you consider besides total volume?
For scalability, consider unique needs like bursty traffic at certain times, event spikes, and whether reads or writes need to scale more.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
What is the textbook contrast for durability requirements across businesses?
A social network might tolerate some data loss, but a banking system cannot, which is the classic durability contrast.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
From the eight NFR checklist items, how many should you finally choose for the system?
Identify the three to five non-functional requirements most relevant to your system.

title: capacity-estimation
text:
What does this framework recommend for early back-of-the-envelope estimates?
This course's framework holds that upfront estimates usually just conclude "it's big" and change no decisions, so tell the interviewer you'll skip them and do the math only when a number actually changes the architecture, such as whether to shard.

title: capacity-estimation
text:
If your storage, DAU, and QPS math only concludes “it is large,” what signal does the interviewer get?
Calculating storage and QPS just to conclude it is a lot gives the interviewer nothing except proof you can do arithmetic.

title: capacity-estimation
text:
When is it actually necessary to estimate during the interview?
Estimation matters when it changes the design, like estimating topic counts in a top-k system to decide between a single min-heap and a sharded one.

title: core-entities
text:
What should you do in the roughly two-minute core entities stage?
Spend about two minutes listing the core entities your API will exchange and your system will persist, framed as a first draft.

title: core-entities
text:
Why should the core entities stage not become a full data model?
You don't know what you don't know yet, so start with a small entity list and add fields once the high-level design clarifies what each request updates.

title: core-entities
text:
Which questions are useful when identifying core entities? (Select all that apply)
Ask who the actors are and which nouns are needed to satisfy the functional requirements, and choose good names for them.

title: core-entities
text:
What is the core entity list for the Twitter example?
For Twitter the core entities are simply the user, the tweet, and the follow relationship.

title: api-design
text:
What is the purpose of the API or system interface stage?
The API defines the contract between your system and its users, usually mapping to the functional requirements and guiding the high-level design.

title: api-protocol
text:
Which API protocol should you choose by default?
Default to REST, which uses HTTP verbs for CRUD on resources, unless you have a specific reason not to.

title: api-protocol
text:
Which API style best fits this case?
GraphQL lets each client declare the fields it needs in one request, so a single schema fixes both over-fetching and under-fetching. Option B (one REST API per client, i.e. Backend-for-Frontend) also solves the field mismatch, but the team doesn't want to maintain multiple backends, so GraphQL fits better here.

title: api-protocol
text:
Which protocol best fits this internal service-to-service case?
Use RPC like gRPC for internal service-to-service APIs where performance is critical, since it is faster than REST.

title: api-protocol
text:
How should you handle real-time features, such as notifications, during the API stage?
For real-time features you will need WebSockets or server-sent events, but design your core API first.

title: api-design
text:
Which endpoint design best follows REST conventions?
Use a plural resource name with POST and put only the tweet text in the body, deriving the current user from the auth token.

title: api-security
text:
What is the risk of letting the client send user_id as the current user?
Never take the current user's identity from the request body; derive it from the authentication token, or anyone can impersonate anyone.

title: api-design
text:
What is the REST convention for naming resources?
The common convention is plural nouns for resource collections (/tweets, /tweets/{id}), with actions expressed by HTTP methods rather than in the path (/createTweet). This is an industry naming convention, not a requirement of the REST architectural constraints themselves.

title: data-flow
text:
What optional step can come after APIs and before high-level design?
For data-processing systems, optionally spend five minutes listing the high-level sequence of actions the system performs.

title: data-flow
text:
Put the web crawler data flow in the correct order:
A web crawler fetches seed URLs, parses the HTML, extracts new URLs, stores the data, and repeats.

title: high-level-design
text:
What is the core output of the high-level design stage?
High-level design means drawing boxes and arrows for components like servers, databases, and caches to satisfy the API you defined.

title: high-level-design
text:
What is the safest way to move through high-level design?
With the API already listed, each endpoint maps to a functional requirement; walking them one by one and adding what each needs means the finished diagram covers every requirement. Data-pipeline systems like crawlers fit a data-flow walk better.

title: high-level-design
text:
What usually happens when you add caches, queues, and other complexity too early?
A very common failure: adding complexity too early burns the clock, and candidates often fail to finish a working design. Call out improvements briefly, note them, and keep building the main path.

title: high-level-design
text:
What should you explain out loud while drawing the high-level design?
Talk through how data flows through the system and what state changes with each request, from the API call to the response.

title: high-level-design
text:
How much schema detail should you write next to the database in the diagram?
Document only the columns that matter to your design next to the database, skipping obvious fields and types the interviewer can infer.

title: logistics
text:
What should you do about interview whiteboard tools like Excalidraw?
Ask your recruiter which whiteboarding software you'll use and practice with it ahead of time so you're not fumbling in the interview.

title: deep-dives
text:
What should you do with the remaining roughly ten minutes for deep dives? (Select all that apply)
Deep dives harden the design by meeting the non-functional requirements, addressing edge cases and bottlenecks, and improving based on interviewer probes.

title: deep-dives
text:
How do junior and senior candidates differ in the deep-dive stage?
Junior candidates can expect the interviewer to point out weak spots, while senior candidates should identify them and lead the deep dives themselves.

title: deep-dives
text:
What is the cost of talking nonstop and covering the interviewer during deep dives?
Talking over your interviewer makes you miss the specific signals they need and hurts your communication and collaboration evaluation.

title: deep-dives
text:
In the Twitter example, what is the most interesting deep-dive problem?
For Twitter the most interesting deep dive is low-latency feed fetching, discussing fanout-on-read versus fanout-on-write plus caching.

title: deep-dives
text:
Fill in the four jobs of the deep-dive stage:
These four jobs define "hardening the design": verify each non-functional requirement, handle edge cases, remove bottlenecks, and improve the design from the interviewer's probes; every NFR should map to a deep-dive discussion rather than a passing mention.

title: high-level-design
text:
When you spot these optimizations, what's the right move?
Flag optimizations with a quick verbal callout plus a written note, then keep building the main path — premature complexity is why candidates never finish a working system.

title: non-functional-requirements
text:
Where should the latency NFR land?
Quantify latency only for requests doing meaningful computation — e.g., Yelp search under 500ms; a blanket 'be fast' on simple reads carries no signal.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
What tradeoff should these environment constraints force in your design?
Environment constraints — battery, limited memory, 3G bandwidth — are hard limits that drive bitrate and caching choices; the design must bend to the device.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
Which three levers make the fault-tolerance NFR concrete?
Fault tolerance becomes concrete through redundancy, failover, and recovery — they decide whether one node's failure takes the system down. Option A lists the levers of the security NFR, which guard against leaks and violations, not crashes.

title: nfr-checklist
text:
Which three areas make the security NFR concrete?
Security becomes concrete across data protection (encryption at rest and in transit), access control (least privilege), and compliance. Option A lists the fault-tolerance levers, which guard against downtime, not leaks.

title: foundation
text:
Put the foundation stages for system design interview prep in the right order:
Learn the interview format first, then pick a delivery framework, and only then fill in the core-concepts knowledge map.

title: foundation
text:
What should be the first preparation step?
If you have never done a system design interview, learn the format and expectations before memorizing full solutions.

title: delivery-framework
text:
Why should your prep include choosing a delivery framework?
A delivery framework gives you a linear roadmap through requirements, API, data model, and deep dives so you don't drift under time pressure.

title: basics
text:
Which high-level foundation materials should a beginner study first? (Select all that apply.)
Core concepts, key technologies, and common patterns form the reusable knowledge base that practice questions build on.

title: active-practice
text:
How should you compare passive reading with hands-on practice in system design prep?
Passive reading helps, but actively designing the system yourself builds far stronger retention and interview performance.

title: practice-loop
text:
Put one recommended practice loop for a design question in the right order:
The loop is choose a question, read the requirements, attempt it yourself, compare against the answer key, and finish with a peer mock.

title: practice-loop
text:
What should you do before reading the answer key?
Trying the design yourself first exposes real gaps that reading the answer key directly would hide.

title: whiteboard
text:
What tool or format should you use when practicing a design question by yourself?
Guided practice or a virtual whiteboard forces you to make requirements, components, and data flow explicit instead of staying in your head.

title: mock-interviews
text:
What should you do next?
Mock interviews train the spoken, time-constrained version of design that silent reading cannot replicate.

title: question-selection
text:
Which starting point is more reasonable?
Beginners should start with easy problems to build the delivery framework before moving into harder designs.

title: writeup-vs-guided
text:
What is the main difference between Common questions and More Practice?
Every common question comes with a written guide; More Practice problems have no written guide and instead offer the same step-by-step guided practice and AI feedback. Both lists span easy through hard.

title: progression
text:
What is the most reasonable next practice target?
A good progression moves from easy framework practice into medium tradeoffs before tackling hard production complexity.

title: practice-rule
text:
Fill in the key rule for practicing system design questions:
The rule turns passive input into active output: attempt first, compare against the answer key, then rehearse it out loud under time pressure.

title: passive-learning
text:
What problem does reading the solution without drawing your own design most often cause?
Reading a solution can create a false sense of mastery because the author already organized the structure and tradeoffs for you.

title: delivery-framework
text:
How should you fix this topic-jumping problem?
A delivery framework keeps your answer linear and prevents scope creep during a fast-paced interview.

title: foundation-benefits
text:
What are the benefits of reading Core Concepts, Key Technologies, and Patterns first? (Select all that apply.)
The foundations give you reusable vocabulary and a tradeoff framework, but they do not replace active practice.

title: target-company
text:
Who is the better person to choose for a peer mock?
A peer from the target company is more likely to give feedback aligned with that company's interview style.

title: reading-vs-speaking
text:
