What is the biggest difference between understanding a write-up and explaining a design in an interview?
Speaking a design out loud requires actively organizing structure, tradeoffs, and communication under time pressure.

title: difficulty
text:
What prep strategy does this problem count and difficulty split support?
Two weeks at one problem a day is about 14 problems — not even all 30, let alone three passes (~90). An interview can land on any tier, so sampling all three covers the real range within that budget.

title: answer-key
text:
What is the most useful way to review the difference?
The useful review compares requirements and tradeoffs behind the difference, not the memorization of one architecture diagram.

title: foundation
text:
Fill in the three foundation steps in the preparation path (the third step covers three knowledge areas):
The foundation is understanding the interview format, choosing a Delivery Framework as your answer structure, and then filling in three knowledge areas: Core Concepts, Key Technologies, and Common Patterns.

title: practice-tool
text:
What is a workable substitute before you have a mock partner?
Guided practice or a virtual whiteboard lets you practice structured output even before you find a mock partner.

title: scope-creep
text:
What problem does a system design answer without a clear roadmap most often run into?
Without a roadmap, answers tend to drift into scope creep and lose time needed for the core design.

title: study-plan
text:
What time-allocation strategy makes the most sense?
With limited time, build the minimum framework quickly and spend most effort on active easy-to-medium practice.

title: end-to-end-plan
text:
Put the full preparation path in the right order:
The full path is understanding the format and framework, filling in the foundations, practicing problems actively, and finishing with mock interviews.

title: what-is-sd-interview
text:
What ability does a system design interview mainly test?
A system design interview mainly tests whether you can turn an ambiguous problem into the infrastructure pieces needed to solve it.

title: what-is-sd-interview
text:
What is the right mindset about standard answers in system design interviews?
Design interviews are not about one right answer — interviewers assess how you weigh trade-offs and communicate your thinking.

title: what-is-sd-interview
text:
How is a system design interview positioned differently from a LeetCode-style algorithm interview?
System design interviews are practical and feel closer to real engineering work than LeetCode-style algorithm interviews.

title: levels
text:
Which statements about level and system design interviews are correct?
Entry-level rarely has system design, it becomes common at mid-level, and at senior level it is the norm with outsized weight.

title: interview-types
text:
What category do most system design interviews fall into?
The overwhelming majority of system design interviews are product or infrastructure design questions like designing Uber or a rate limiter.

title: interview-types
text:
What type of interview is this, and how should you prepare?
Designing class structure, objects, and interfaces is a Low-Level Design interview, which needs its own dedicated LLD guide.

title: interview-types
text:
Which interview type should you prepare for?
The prompt says the interview digs into modeling and feature engineering, which is the core of ML system design, so prepare with the dedicated ML System Design guide. B treats ML as a black box, contradicting the deep modeling focus; C is about class structure and interfaces, D about client state and rendering — neither matches this interview.

title: assessment
text:
What baseline expectation applies to every level in a system design interview?
Every level is expected to deliver a complete, working design that satisfies the requirements, with depth as the only differentiator.

title: assessment
text:
For the same prompt, what mainly separates a mid-level answer from a senior-level answer?
A mid-level engineer nails the fundamentals broadly, while a senior engineer moves through them quickly to leave time for deep dives.

title: assessment
text:
What is true about staff-plus system design interviews?
Staff-level system design interviews differ substantially from lower levels, so you need to adjust your approach accordingly.

title: rubric
text:
Fill in the four themes that Hello Interview identifies as common across most companies' system design rubrics:
Company rubrics are worded differently, but most map onto these four themes (a framework distilled by Hello Interview): problem navigation, solution design, technical excellence, and communication and collaboration.

title: problem-navigation
text:
What is the core skill tested by Problem Navigation?
Problem navigation means decomposing an under-specified problem, prioritizing it, and driving it toward a solution.

title: problem-navigation
text:
Which are common failure modes in the Problem Navigation dimension?
Common navigation failures are under-exploring requirements, focusing on trivial parts, and getting stuck; outdated tech choices belong to a different competency.

title: problem-navigation
text:
What is the most common root cause when candidates cannot make progress in a design interview?
Most candidates stall because they lack structure, which a delivery framework fixes by giving them a track to run on.

title: solution-design
text:
What does the Solution Design dimension evaluate?
Solution design assesses whether you can solve each piece with core concepts and fit the pieces into a cohesive whole.

title: solution-design
text:
Which are common failure modes in the Solution Design dimension?
Solution design fails through weak fundamentals, ignoring scaling and performance, or a tangled spaghetti design.

title: solution-design
text:
What will interviewers usually do if they suspect you are reciting a memorized answer?
Interviewers test for memorized answers by probing your reasoning, expressing doubt, and asking you to walk through trade-offs.

title: technical-excellence
text:
What does the Technical Excellence dimension evaluate?
Technical excellence means knowing current technologies and recognized patterns — such as at-least-once delivery with idempotent consumers to avoid duplicate effects — and applying them to the problem at hand.

title: technical-excellence
text:
Which are common failure modes in the Technical Excellence dimension?
Failures include not knowing available technologies, reasoning from outdated hardware constraints, and not recognizing common patterns.

title: technical-excellence
text:
What is the main risk of relying on system design material from around 2015?
Hardware has advanced enormously in the last decade, so reasoning from outdated constraints makes your design choices look stale.

title: communication
text:
What does the Communication and Collaboration dimension really evaluate?
The communication dimension gauges what you'd be like as a colleague: explaining ideas, taking feedback, and collaborating on the problem.

title: communication
text:
Which are common failure modes in the Communication and Collaboration dimension?
Communication failures include unclear explanations, getting defensive about feedback, and getting lost in the weeds instead of collaborating.

title: communication
text:
What is the best response when the interviewer challenges your design?
Treat pushback as collaboration — respond to the feedback and adjust your design with reasons instead of getting defensive.

title: preparation
text:
What usually happens if you read a lot but never practice applying the material?
A common failure mode is consuming lots of material but stumbling when it's time to apply it, which only practice fixes.

title: preparation
text:
What preparation pace is recommended for someone completely new to system design?
This course suggests a dedicated sprint or three to four weeks for someone new to system design; with the interview a month out, that pace fits. One or two days is too short to build the framework, and "at least six months" exceeds the time available. Experienced candidates often prepare in under a week.

title: preparation
text:
What is the most reasonable first step?
The gap is two whole areas you can't close in a few days, and the recruiter said the date is flexible, so the first step is to ask for a later date. Many recruiters care more about your chance of passing than the original slot; if you only needed light review, keeping the date would be fine.

title: preparation
text:
What should you prioritize when preparation time is extremely tight?
If you're really short on time, master the delivery framework first, skim the key technologies, and spend the rest on core concepts.

title: preparation
text:
Order the study priorities when preparation time is extremely tight:
Learn the delivery framework first for structure, then skim the key technologies, and spend any remaining time on core concepts.

title: problem-navigation
text:
Put the causal chain in order: how lack of structure causes interview failure and how to recover:
An ambiguous problem plus no structure burns time on the wrong things and fails to deliver, which the delivery framework prevents.

title: problem-navigation
text:
Fill in the correct Problem Navigation posture:
Good problem navigation means decomposing the problem, prioritizing the most important pieces, and delivering a working system.

title: rubric
text:
Among that guide's four evaluation themes, which one does it call often the most important and hardest for beginners?
Hello Interview's guide calls Problem Navigation often the most important competency and the one newcomers struggle with most, since poor navigation burns time on the wrong things. This is that guide's view; other companies' rubrics may weight things differently, and the other three themes are still scored.

title: assessment
text:
What happens if a senior-level candidate spends most of the interview on basics and never reaches a deep dive?
A senior candidate who spends the whole interview on basics never gets to show the depth expected at that level.

title: interview-types
text:
What building blocks do prompts like designing Uber or a rate limiter typically use?
Product and infrastructure design questions are solved with pieces like services, load balancers, and databases.

title: solution-design
text:
How does describing only the boxes, never the flow between them, sink your solution design score?
Solution design is judged on whether the pieces fit into a cohesive whole, so with only per-box duties the interviewer can't verify a single end-to-end path.

title: interview-strategy
text:
What mainly determines how deeply an interviewer will probe key technologies?
Interviewers probe technology depth in proportion to your level, so a rough description is fine for mid-level but a senior who cannot explain the inverted index is a yellow flag.

title: interview-strategy
text:
For each building-block category such as queues, caches, and search, what is the right prep goal?
Interviewers rarely care which queueing solution you pick, but you must know at least one option in every key category.

title: core-database
text:
What default database should you bring into the interview?
Pick one database for your interviews: a relational database like Postgres for product design, or a NoSQL database like DynamoDB for infrastructure design.

title: sql-vs-nosql
text:
What usually happens if you volunteer a generic SQL vs NoSQL comparison?
Most interviewers do not want a generic SQL versus NoSQL comparison; talk instead about how your chosen database solves the problem at hand.

title: sql-vs-nosql
text:
Which statements are yellow flags for lack of system design experience? (Select all that apply)
Claiming you must use relational for relationships or NoSQL for scale is a yellow flag because the two technologies overlap heavily.

title: relational-features
text:
Which built-in relational database features matter most in interviews? (Select all that apply)
The three relational capabilities to remember are arbitrary joins, rich indexing (many indexes per table, including multi-column, geospatial, and full-text), and atomic transactions. Postgres doesn't automatically shard writes across machines; that takes application-level sharding or an extension like Citus. More indexes also aren't free, since each one adds write cost.

title: sql-joins
text:
SQL joins are powerful, but what should you watch for in system design?
Joins are powerful for combining tables but can become a major performance bottleneck, so minimize them where possible.

title: indexes
text:
Fill in the key points about relational database indexes:
Indexes let queries skip full table scans. The B-tree is the default relational index structure and handles both equality and range lookups. A table can carry several indexes for different queries, with multi-column and specialized indexes as strengths, but each index adds write cost and engines have concrete limits (InnoDB allows 64 secondary indexes).

title: transactions
text:
If creating a new user and their first post runs in one transaction, what does it guarantee?
A transaction groups operations atomically so either both succeed or both fail, preventing invalid data like a post from a nonexistent user.

title: nosql-models
text:
What are the four common NoSQL data models?
The common NoSQL data models are key-value, document, column-family, and graph.

title: consistency-models
text:
What is the difference between strong consistency and eventual consistency?
Strong consistency promises that once a write is acknowledged, every later read sees it; it doesn't require every replica to update at the same instant, and quorum reads/writes can provide it. Eventual consistency only promises replicas converge once writes stop, with stale reads in between. Like counts usually tolerate a few hundred milliseconds of staleness, so eventual consistency is the common pick.

title: nosql-scaling
text:
Fill in the NoSQL scaling mechanisms:
Horizontal scaling is a core NoSQL selling point: shard by partition key, then decide which machine owns each partition. Cassandra and similar systems use consistent hashing so node changes move little data; HBase and MongoDB can use range partitioning, and Redis Cluster uses hash slots.

title: nosql-choice
text:
For this write-heavy NoSQL scenario, which choice fits most directly?
Cassandra is the most direct fit because the workload is write-heavy, append-oriented, and partitionable, while MongoDB, Redis, and Neo4j optimize for different primary access patterns.

title: blob-storage
text:
How should you split large file bodies from searchable metadata?
The design principle is to split responsibilities: blob storage holds large binary objects cheaply and durably, while the database stores searchable metadata and pointers.

title: blob-storage
text:
Why is S3-style blob storage a poor fit as the primary business database?
Blob storage is excellent for durable large objects, but the business database still needs to handle indexes, permissions, state, pagination, and metadata updates.

title: presigned-upload
text:
Put the presigned-URL large-file upload flow in the correct order:
The client requests a presigned URL, the server returns it and records it, the client uploads directly to blob storage, and a completion notification updates the status.

title: presigned-download
text:
With a presigned-URL architecture, what is the standard path for downloading a large file?
The client asks the server for a download, and the server issues a short-lived CDN signed URL; the client downloads through the CDN, whose edge verifies the signature, serves cache hits directly, and on a miss fetches from blob storage with its own identity. Without a CDN, you can hand out an object-storage presigned URL directly. Either way, file bytes never pass through the app server.

title: blob-cost
text:
If S3 Standard is about $0.023 per GB-month, roughly how much is DynamoDB Standard table storage?
DynamoDB Standard table storage is about $0.25/GB-month, roughly 10x the S3 price of $0.023, which is the cost argument for keeping large blobs out of the database.

title: blob-durability
text:
How does blob storage achieve very high durability?
Blob storage achieves durability through replication and erasure coding so data survives disk or server failures.

title: blob-scalability
text:
In an interview, do you need to design S3 scalability yourself?
S3 has no total storage limit and objects up to 5TB, and the provider handles capacity, so at ordinary volume treat it as a given. Request rate does have a per-prefix baseline (about 3,500 writes / 5,500 reads per second); only at very high QPS do you spread key prefixes or add a CDN.

title: chunking
text:
Which upload method should you use?
Use chunked upload for large files: only failed parts are retried and parts upload in parallel. S3 multipart upload supports this natively and is required above the 5GB single-PUT limit.

title: full-text-search
text:
Why is `LIKE "%term%"` not a scalable full-text search approach?
A leading wildcard can't use a normal B-tree index, so the database scans many rows and compares text one by one; it also has no tokenization or relevance ranking. PostgreSQL's pg_trgm index can speed up substring matching, but full-text search normally uses an inverted index plus relevance scoring.

title: inverted-index
text:
What is the inverted index, the core data structure behind search-optimized databases?
An inverted index maps each word to the list of documents containing it, so a search looks up the word instead of scanning the table.

title: search-techniques
text:
Fill in the three key techniques behind search-optimized databases:
Tokenization splits text into words, stemming reduces words to their root form, and fuzzy search tolerates misspellings using edit distance.

title: search-db-choice
text:
Which component is the best fit?
Full-text search over events or tweets calls for a search-optimized database like Elasticsearch built on inverted indexes.

title: elasticsearch
text:
Which statement about Elasticsearch is correct?
Elasticsearch is a distributed RESTful search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene.

title: search-alternatives
text:
If you want full-text search without adding Elasticsearch, what alternative can reduce the design footprint?
Postgres ships full-text search (tsvector / tsquery) accelerated by GIN indexes, letting you skip a separate search cluster at moderate data volume. Redis also offers a Query Engine with full-text indexing, but in an interview Postgres's built-in capability is the safer pick.

title: api-gateway
text:
What does an API gateway do in a microservices architecture?
An API gateway routes each request to the right backend service and handles cross-cutting concerns like authentication, rate limiting, and logging.

title: api-gateway
text:
What is the recommended move?
In nearly every product design interview, include an API gateway as the first point of contact, but do not dwell on it because interviewers rarely probe its details.

title: api-gateway
text:
What are common API gateway products?
Common API gateways are AWS API Gateway, Kong, and Apigee, and nginx or Apache web servers often serve the same role.

title: load-balancer-l4-l7
text:
Under these constraints, which load balancer type fits best?
The common heuristic is "long-lived connections lean L4, content routing needs L7," but it is only a lean — L7 balancers like ALB and NGINX support WebSocket natively. Here there's no routing need, no TLS termination at the LB, and huge connection counts, so L4 fits best; if you needed path-based routing or edge auth, L7 would win.

title: load-balancer-interview
text:
When drawing an architecture in an interview, how do you show load balancers without overdoing it?
In an interview either omit load balancers and say services are horizontally scaled, or draw a single one at the front as an abstraction.

title: load-balancer-tech
text:
What are common load balancers, and what changes at extremely high traffic?
Common choices are managed AWS ELB and open-source NGINX and HAProxy. At extreme traffic you usually put an L4 tier in front of L7, either dedicated hardware or software L4 balancers like Maglev or Katran on commodity servers; which is faster depends on the implementation, hardware does not automatically win.

title: queue-buffer
text:
Which component is the best one to introduce?
A queue buffers bursty ride requests so the system processes them at a manageable rate without dropping any.

title: queue-buffer
text:
If the system handles 200 requests per second and suddenly receives 1,000, what happens with a queue?
A queue smooths the spike: with ample capacity and no expiry, the 800 excess requests wait and workers drain them at 200/s in about 4 seconds — more latency, no loss. If the queue were bounded and full, or messages had a TTL, the excess could still be rejected or dropped.

title: queue-decoupling
text:
What direct benefit do you get when a queue decouples producers and consumers?
Decoupling producer and consumer lets you scale each side independently and restart services behind the queue with negligible impact.

title: queue-latency
text:
What happens if you put a queue on a synchronous path with a latency target under 500 ms?
Because the endpoint waits synchronously for the consumer, queue wait adds directly to user latency. The scenario says peak backlog reaches seconds, which blows the 500 ms budget; even off-peak, tail latency is no longer under control. The queue's own delivery overhead is usually milliseconds — the problem is waiting in line, not that queues are inherently slow.

title: dead-letter-queue
text:
What is a dead letter queue used for?
A dead letter queue stores messages that could not be processed so you can inspect and debug why they failed.

title: queue-partitions
text:
How do queues scale for higher message volume, and how do related messages keep order?
Queues scale by partitioning across servers, and a partition key keeps related messages in the same partition.

title: backpressure
text:
Capacity can't be raised, yet 300/s keeps arriving and the queue keeps growing. What is the right response?
A queue can hide a capacity shortfall: with 300/s in and 200/s out, the backlog grows forever. If you could add processing capacity, you would scale consumers first; here capacity is capped by the downstream rate limit, so apply backpressure — slow or reject new messages when overloaded, pushing pressure upstream so the shortfall becomes visible.

title: queue-tech
text:
What are the two most common queue technology choices?
The two most common queue choices in SD interviews are Kafka (a distributed streaming platform you operate or buy as a managed service, usable as a queue, ordered within a partition) and SQS (a fully managed AWS queue; FIFO queues keep order per message group). Redis and Postgres can be bent into simple queues, but they are a cache and a relational database, not dedicated queue products; NGINX/HAProxy are load balancers and S3/DynamoDB are storage.

title: queue-decision
text:
Put the “introduce a message queue” decision chain in the correct order:
Bursty traffic that must not be dropped leads to a buffering queue, which costs latency and can hide missing capacity, mitigated by backpressure.

title: streams-vs-queues
text:
What is the key difference between a stream and a message queue?
Unlike queues, streams retain data for a configurable period so consumers can read and re-read from the same position or a past point in time.

title: stream-processing
text:
What architecture makes sense here?
Ingest engagement events into a stream and process them in real time with a system like Flink or Spark Streaming to update the dashboard.

title: event-sourcing
text:
Which pattern and component fit best?
Event sourcing stores every state change as an immutable event, so replaying to a point in time rebuilds any account and gives you an audit trail; a "rollback" is a new compensating event, not an edit to history. The log can be a dedicated event store, an append-only ledger table, or Kafka with long retention and per-account partitioning; Kafka has no per-account conditional append, so concurrency control needs its own design.

title: pub-sub
text:
Which typical stream use case is this?
A chat room stream where every participant subscribes and receives each message simultaneously is a classic publish-subscribe use case.

title: consumer-groups
text:
What problem do multiple consumer groups solve in a stream?
Multiple consumer groups let different consumers read the same stream independently to process the same data in different ways.

title: windowing
text:
What does windowing mean in stream processing?
Windowing groups stream events by time or count, which suits rolling aggregates like mean delivery time per region over the last day.

title: event-sourcing
text:
Fill in the definition and value of event sourcing:
Event sourcing stores state changes as a sequence of events that can be replayed to reconstruct state at any point, ideal for audit trails.

title: stream-tech
text:
What are the common technologies around stream processing?
The most common streaming technologies are Kafka, Flink, and Kinesis.

title: distributed-lock
text:
Why use a distributed lock instead of a database transaction lock?
A transaction lock is released when its transaction ends, but this hold spans several separate user requests over about 10 minutes, so you cannot keep one DB transaction open. You need a hold that lives outside the transaction and expires on its own: a Redis `SET ... NX EX 600`-style distributed lock is common, and a `hold_expires_at` column claimed with a conditional write is a viable alternative.

title: distributed-lock
text:
Which Redis command is correct?
SET with NX acquires the lock atomically only if it is free, and EX six hundred makes it expire so a crashed process cannot hold it forever.

title: lock-expiry
text:
What happens if a distributed lock has no expiration and the holder crashes?
Lock expiry ensures a crashed process cannot leave the lock stuck forever, since it auto-releases after a set time.

title: lock-use-cases
text:
Which are typical interview scenarios for distributed locks? (Select all that apply)
Distributed locks fit checkout holds, ride matchmaking, deduplicating cron jobs, and last-second auction bids, not static content delivery.

title: deadlocks
text:
Process 1 holds lock A and waits for B, while process 2 holds B and waits for A. What happened, and how do you prevent it?
Each process holds one lock while waiting for the other, a circular wait, which is a deadlock. The root cause is inconsistent acquisition order, so the standard prevention is for every process to acquire locks in one global order (e.g. driver before order, or sorted by key); centralizing lock acquisition makes that order enforceable instead of being broken by scattered code. A lock-wait timeout is a useful backstop.

title: redlock
text:
What is Redlock?
Redlock is the distributed-lock algorithm described in the Redis docs: the client locks a majority of independent Redis instances, which tolerates a single instance failure better than one-node locking. Its safety relies on timing assumptions such as bounded clock drift and pauses, and it does not issue fencing tokens, so correctness-critical writes still need fencing or a conditional write.

title: cache-use-cases
text:
What are the three typical uses of a distributed cache? (Select all that apply)
Use a distributed cache to store precomputed metrics, user sessions, and results of expensive queries, not strongly consistent payment data.

title: cache-write-strategy
text:
Fill in the three cache write strategies:
The three write strategies trade off consistency, read performance and write performance: write-through keeps cache and store more easily in sync but pays both latencies on every write; write-around keeps write-only data from polluting the cache; write-back (write-behind) is fastest for writes but loses data if the cache fails before flushing.

title: cache-data-structures
text:
What is the better way to describe the cache design?
Be explicit about the cached data structure, such as a Redis sorted set for retrieving the most popular events.

title: redis-vs-memcached
text:
How do Redis and Memcached differ in supported data structures?
Redis supports many data structures like hashes, lists, sets, and sorted sets, while Memcached only stores strings and binary objects.

title: cdn-basics
text:
How does a CDN work?
A CDN routes each request to the nearest edge server, serving cached content or fetching from the origin and caching it on a miss.

title: cdn-dynamic
text:
Is the statement “CDNs can only cache static assets” correct?
CDNs can also cache dynamic content and API responses, which works well for content accessed frequently but changed infrequently.

title: cdn-tech
text:
What are the most popular CDN providers?
Popular CDNs include Cloudflare, Akamai, and Amazon CloudFront, offering caching plus DDoS protection and web application firewalls.

title: cache-eviction
text:
Which eviction policy fits?
LFU evicts by cumulative access count, so a bursty hot key keeps a high count and survives quiet gaps, whereas LRU looks only at recency and would drop it during the lull.

title: cache-invalidation
text:
What must you do so users don't see the stale venue that's still cached?
The cache keeps serving the old venue because the DB write never touched it, so you must invalidate that key on write and let the next read miss and repopulate from the database.

title: lock-granularity
text:
What locking granularity should you choose?
Match granularity to the smallest sellable unit: since seats sell individually, locking ticket-123 blocks only rivals for that seat while other seats sell in parallel.

title: cdn-invalidation
text:
How do you make edge nodes stop serving the old version?
When the URL cannot change, the stale copies already cached at the edges can only be cleared by active invalidation (a purge), so the next request refetches from origin. TTL expiry means waiting out a stale window; setting TTL to 0 may not affect objects already cached and gives up caching; the CDN does not detect origin changes on its own. Cost: a purge takes seconds to minutes to propagate across edges, does not clear browser caches, and must be triggered on every change. If the URL can change, versioned filenames (cache busting) are the more common approach and need no purge.

title: queue-work-distribution
text:
What is the queue mainly doing here?
Queues serve two purposes - buffering bursts and distributing work - and here, with steady traffic but heavy tasks, the value is even work distribution across a worker pool.

title: search-scaling
text:
How do you scale this search-optimized database?
Elasticsearch scales out via primary shards; replicas only share reads. Adding nodes rebalances existing shards, but the primary count is fixed at index creation, so split, reindex, or roll over.

title: why-patterns
text:
In a time-boxed system design interview, what value do patterns provide?
Recognizing patterns lets you fall back on proven best practices and spot common failure modes ahead of time, which often separates senior from junior engineers.

title: why-patterns
text:
How do common system design patterns relate to each other in an interview design?
These patterns are not mutually exclusive, and a system like a video platform typically combines several of them at once.

title: realtime-protocol
text:
Which protocol should you start with?
Start with simple HTTP polling and only move to server-sent events or WebSocket once polling no longer serves your needs.

title: realtime-protocol
text:
Fill in the three protocol options for realtime updates.
Realtime updates can use simple HTTP polling, one-way server-sent events, or two-way WebSocket, with the latter two trickier to operate.

title: realtime-server
text:
What server-side push architecture is commonly used here?
Pub/Sub services decouple publishers from subscribers for realtime delivery, as in a WhatsApp-style chat system.

title: realtime-server
text:
For realtime push, what are the strengths of Pub/Sub and stateful servers on a consistent hash ring?
Pub/Sub wins on decoupling publishers from subscribers, while stateful servers on a consistent hash ring suit heavier per-session processing.

title: realtime-when
text:
What kind of feature actually needs the realtime-push pattern?
Synchronous APIs simply return a response, while chat, notifications, and live dashboards need updates pushed the moment they happen.

title: long-running-tasks
text:
What is the core move in the long-running-task pattern?
The long-running-task pattern is immediate acknowledgment plus background processing: the web server validates the request, enqueues the job, and returns a job ID in milliseconds (typically 202 Accepted); the client then polls or receives the result via SSE/WebSocket, while a separate worker pool executes the job.

title: long-running-tasks
text:
Put the long-running-task flow in the correct order.
The user submits a task, the server validates and enqueues it, returns a job ID instantly, and workers pull and execute it in the background.

title: long-running-tasks
text:
What three benefits does a queue-plus-worker architecture provide for long-running tasks?
Queue-plus-workers gives fast user responses, independent scaling of web servers and workers, and fault isolation.

title: long-running-tasks
text:
Why is putting work behind a queue from the start often a bad call?
For short-running jobs, returning the result synchronously keeps the architecture dramatically simpler with clearer backpressure and better user experience.

title: long-running-tasks
text:
Besides queues and worker pools, what companion mechanisms must long-running tasks handle?
Beyond queues and worker pools you must handle job status tracking, retries, and dead letter queues for poison messages.

title: contention
text:
What is the nature of this problem, and which pattern should you apply?
Multiple users grabbing the same ticket is a contention problem that needs coordination mechanisms to prevent race conditions.

title: contention
text:
Which techniques belong in the contention-handling toolbox? (Select all that apply.)
Contention solutions range from pessimistic locking and optimistic concurrency control to distributed locks, two-phase commit, and queue-based serialization.

title: contention
text:
What is the recommended evolution path for solving contention?
Most contention problems start with single-database solutions and only scale to distributed coordination when necessary.

title: contention
text:
What happens if you split data across multiple databases too early?
Databases are built around contention; after a split, transactions and locks still work within one shard, but operations spanning shards lose that single-database protection and the application must handle them. Splitting is sometimes right, just not prematurely — interviewers will probe whether you understand the cost.

title: scaling-reads
text:
What read-to-write ratio is typical, and what does it imply for architecture investment?
For consumer apps like photo sharing, read-to-write ratios typically start around 10:1 and often exceed 100:1 — scrolling fires hundreds of queries while you post once a day — so invest in the read path first (indexes, replicas, caches). Write-heavy systems like log ingestion or IoT telemetry don't follow this rule of thumb.

title: scaling-reads
text:
Put the natural read-scaling evolution in order.
Scale reads by first optimizing within the database with indexes and denormalization, then adding read replicas, then external caches like Redis and CDNs.

title: scaling-reads
text:
What should you do first?
Start scaling reads inside the database: the hot queries are doing full table scans, so indexing and denormalization are the cheapest, fastest wins before replicas or external caches. Sharding is the write-scaling heavy hammer, and a CDN helps public static content but cannot cache these personalized dynamic queries.

title: scaling-reads
text:
What are the three key challenges in scaling reads? (Select all that apply.)
The key read-scaling considerations are cache invalidation, replication lag on read replicas, and hot keys for popular content.

title: scaling-writes
text:
What is the core strategy for scaling writes?
Scaling writes relies on horizontal sharding, vertical partitioning, and handling bursts with queues and load shedding.

title: scaling-writes
text:
What two properties should a good partition key satisfy?
A good partition key distributes load evenly across shards while keeping related data together.

title: scaling-writes
text:
What are two ways to handle bursty writes?
Buffer temporary spikes with write queues and use load shedding to prioritize important writes during overload.

title: scaling-writes
text:
Fill in the write-scaling strategy list.
Write scaling combines horizontal sharding, vertical partitioning, queue buffering or load shedding for bursts, and batching to reduce per-operation overhead.

title: large-blobs
text:
What is the large-blob pattern?
Generate presigned URLs so clients upload directly to blob storage and download from CDNs, keeping large files off your application servers.

title: large-blobs
text:
What is the key challenge in the large-blob pattern (direct client upload plus CDN download), and how do you mitigate it?
Because file bytes bypass the server, database metadata can drift from the real objects in storage, including after failed or abandoned uploads. The main fix is storage event notifications that let the backend update metadata state once an object lands; since events can be delayed or lost, a periodic reconciliation job acts as a backstop.

title: multi-step-processes
text:
Which approach best fits these constraints?
A workflow engine durably persists each step's state, resumes and retries automatically after failures, and keeps a full execution history. Activities are still at-least-once and may be retried, so end-to-end "no duplicate effects" relies on the activities being idempotent, which the scenario states.

title: multi-step-processes
text:
Without a central coordinator, how does event-driven choreography move a multi-step process forward?
In event-driven choreography each service emits an event when its step finishes, and downstream services subscribe and trigger the next step, so the chain advances without a central coordinator. This is a different layer from event sourcing, which stores state as an event log and derives the current state by replay; the two can be combined but are not the same thing.

title: multi-step-processes
text:
Fill in the key insight of the multi-step-process pattern.
The essence of the multi-step-process pattern is pulling state, retries, and recovery out of business code into a workflow engine (Temporal defines workflows in code, Step Functions as a declarative state machine). Because the engine retries steps, external side effects need idempotency (or compensation) to get exactly-once-like effects, and the execution history doubles as an audit trail.

title: proximity
text:
What is the key technology choice?
Proximity search relies on geospatial indexes, either extensions of general-purpose databases (PostGIS, Redis geospatial) or dedicated options (Elasticsearch geo-queries). They partition space into cells and index within cells, so a query first prunes large irrelevant areas and then filters by exact distance.

title: proximity
text:
What is the basic idea behind speeding up queries with a geospatial index?
Geospatial indexes divide the area into regions and index entities within them, letting queries quickly exclude vast irrelevant areas.

title: proximity
text:
At what scale does a dedicated geospatial index start to pay off?
With moderate query volume, a full O(n) distance scan over about a thousand entities is fast enough, so running a separate index service isn't worth its ops cost; at hundreds of thousands to millions, the index narrows candidates to nearby cells and finally pays off. High query rates lower the threshold, and a built-in database geo index (like PostGIS) is cheap enough to use earlier.

title: proximity
text:
For proximity queries, what geographic scope do most systems actually serve?
Most proximity systems serve users looking for entities local to them, not global queries.

title: pattern-selection
text:
Which patterns does this video-platform requirement combine? (Select all that apply.)
A video platform combines large blobs for uploads, long-running tasks for transcoding, realtime updates for progress, and multi-step processes to coordinate the workflow.

title: pattern-selection
text:
What is the general rule for choosing patterns?
Start with simpler approaches like polling and single-server orchestration, adding complexity only when specific requirements demand it.

title: pattern-selection
text:
What signal do you send by proactively recognizing and applying these patterns in an interview?
Proactively identifying patterns demonstrates architectural maturity and keeps you focused on the most important parts of the design.

title: contention
text:
Which mechanism holds the seat through the checkout window and prevents double-booking?
The requirement is "hold now, confirm minutes later", so you need a multi-step reservation with an expiry rather than a one-shot sold write. The reservation itself is usually claimed with a conditional write that succeeds only if the seat is available or the old hold has expired. Do not hold a database transaction or row lock for five minutes. The cost is that you own the TTL, release, and expiry cleanup.

title: contention
text:
With no concurrency control, how do these two requests corrupt the data?
Without concurrency control, two requests both read 'one left', both pass the check, and both write a booking, so the seat is sold twice and you must refund one customer.

title: difficulty-signal
text:
Compared with Easy problems, what extra technical judgment usually makes a Hard problem harder?
Hard problems are harder mainly because they stack extra cross-component tradeoffs like consistency, geography, or real-time constraints, not because they need more code.

title: easy-problems
text:
Which problem-to-core-judgment pairs are correct? Select all that apply.
Bitly's challenge is unique short codes plus a read-heavy redirect path; simplified Dropbox's is large-file upload and multi-device sync; News Aggregator is crawling plus a read-heavy feed. C copies Bitly's description onto Ticketmaster, whose real challenge is concurrent ticket sales: one seat must never be sold twice, which needs reservation locks or transactions.

title: practice-path
text:
Why start with an Easy problem like Bitly instead of jumping straight to Hard problems like ChatGPT or Payment System?
Easy problems isolate one technical judgment, so a beginner can first master the requirement-to-design flow before stacking on consistency and real-time constraints.

title: local-delivery-domain
text:
Compared with ordinary e-commerce shipping, what extra technical judgment does local delivery add?
Local delivery promises arrival within tens of minutes, so every availability query must find the nearby warehouses that cover the user's location and combine their inventory and delivery range in real time. Ordinary e-commerce also picks a warehouse, but with day-level delivery it does not need this real-time location-plus-inventory join on every query.

title: price-tracking-domain
text:
What is the core technical judgment for this kind of price tracking service?
Without an official push feed, the service has to collect prices itself: scheduled crawling is the main channel, optionally supplemented by client-side reports such as a browser extension. To support history and price-drop alerts, snapshots are stored as a time series and compared against thresholds.

title: medium-problems
text:
Which problem-to-core-judgment pairs are correct? Select all that apply.
Ticketmaster, WhatsApp, and the rate limiter each test a different judgment, while YouTube's real core is upload, transcoding, and global delivery, not ticket locking.

title: hard-problems
text:
Which problem-to-core-judgment pairs are correct? Select all that apply.
Uber tests geo-matching and dispatch over live locations; Google Docs tests merging concurrent edits (OT/CRDT); Payment System tests money correctness — idempotency, durable ledgers, and reconciliation, since you cannot get distributed strong consistency across an external gateway. Yelp's core is location-based proximity search, not collaborative-edit merging.

title: difficulty-contrast
text:
What core technical judgment does YouTube add beyond Dropbox?
Both need chunked large-file upload and object storage, and both can use a CDN for downloads. Dropbox's core is chunked sync and version metadata (concurrent edits resolve by last-write-wins, not content merging); YouTube adds a whole transcoding pipeline: segmenting, encoding into multiple bitrates/formats, and producing manifests so players can switch adaptively by bandwidth.

title: difficulty-contrast
text:
What core technical judgment does Instagram add beyond FB News Feed?
The feed part of both breakdowns is the same judgment: precomputed follow-graph feeds in reverse chronological order, with hybrid fan-out for celebrity accounts. What Instagram adds is media: large photos/videos uploaded directly to object storage via presigned URLs, resized into variants, and served globally through a CDN — which is why it sits one tier higher. B contradicts the stated reverse-chronological feed; C is wrong because the Instagram breakdown explicitly handles celebrity fan-out.

title: realtime-domain
text:
Which requirements are common to realtime communication or collaboration systems? Select all that apply.
All three rely on persistent connections for server push, and all must know which server a user/viewer is connected to, otherwise an update landing on another node can't be delivered. Conflict merging belongs only to collaborative editing like Google Docs: WhatsApp messages and live comments are append-only, with no concurrent edits to the same content, so C is not a shared requirement. D is an offline batch mindset.

title: geo-domain
text:
Which requirements are common to location or proximity-search systems? Select all that apply.
All three rely on spatial indexes for range queries and use distance in ranking or matching — those are shared. High-frequency location updates belong only to moving-entity systems like Uber and delivery; Yelp businesses barely move and the workload is read-heavy, so B is not shared. Storing query-result history is unrelated.

title: infra-domain
text:
Which problem-to-core-challenge pairs are correct? Select all that apply.
Each infrastructure problem has a distinct core challenge — sharding consistency, queue scheduling, and crawl dedupe — none of which is frontend styling.

title: meta-family-domain
text:
Which problem-to-core-technical-challenge pairs are correct? Select all that apply.
News Feed relies on fan-out ranking, Live Comments on high-concurrency realtime distribution, and Post Search on full-text indexing — three distinct challenges.

title: youtube-topk
text:
What technical judgment does the YouTube Top K prompt actually test?
YouTube Top K asks for the K most-viewed videos over windows like the last hour, day, month, and all time, computed from a massive view-event stream. The breakdown's baseline requires precise results; approximate structures like count-min sketch are a trade-off to discuss, not the default. It is unrelated to video storage or transcoding.

title: ai-product-domain
text:
Compared with a classic infrastructure prompt like Web Crawler, what extra technical judgment does a ChatGPT-style AI product add?
AI product design adds a model-serving layer of judgment — inference latency versus throughput, streaming token generation, and context management — that classic crawling problems don't have.

title: contention-domain
text:
When practicing contention over a limited resource, which two Medium problems are the best fit?
Ticket sales and auction bids both have many clients contending for the same limited resource, directly exercising locking, transactions, and serialization.

title: leetcode-domain
text:
What is the core technical judgment in Design LeetCode?
User-submitted code is untrusted, so it must run inside a resource-limited, network-isolated sandbox before results are collected.

title: location-domain
text:
What location-based judgment do Strava and Tinder share?
Both take the user's GPS coordinates as input: Strava samples coordinates at fixed intervals during an activity and uses the Haversine formula to accumulate distance and draw the route; Tinder uses the user's location to filter candidates by distance (that is where a spatial index for proximity queries comes in). The shared judgment is location capture plus geographic computation; proximity search is Tinder-specific.

title: finance-domain
text:
What financial consistency judgment do Robinhood and Payment System share?
Money and trades can't be wrong or counted twice, so both problems need strong consistency on the critical write path (balances, order state, ledger) and idempotency keys to absorb retries. Interactions with external PSPs or exchanges are usually asynchronous and converge through reconciliation, so this is not end-to-end strong consistency.

title: aggregation-domain
text:
What event-streaming judgment do Ad Click Aggregator and Metrics Monitoring share?
Both must aggregate a continuous event stream into windowed statistics in real time (stream processing). Note that ad clicks drive billing: the breakdown requires no lost clicks and accurate results, adding periodic reconciliation to correct the streaming layer, so approximate statistics are not the default here.

title: chat-domain
text:
When practicing a chat or messaging system, which breakdown is the closest match?
WhatsApp directly covers realtime message delivery and presence, the core judgments of a chat system, while the other problems test unrelated directions.

title: easy-problems
text:
Fill in the four Easy starter prompts from the Hello Interview catalog (use the catalog / breakdown product names):
Each easy problem isolates one core skill — redirect encoding, version metadata, geo-plus-inventory matching, or content aggregation — before stacking on more constraints.

title: realtime-domain
text:
What is the core technical judgment in Online Chess?
A two-player game needs moves to appear almost instantly and can't trust the client's reported move, so the core is low-latency sync plus server-side legality checks.

title: leaderboard-domain
text:
What is the core technical judgment in a Game Leaderboard?
A leaderboard needs live rank and top-N by score, so it uses an always-sorted, incrementally updated structure such as a Redis sorted set: score updates and rank lookups are O(log n), top-N is O(log n + N). The cost is keeping the whole set in memory; at larger scale you shard by score range or region, which makes global rank harder; durability comes separately from RDB/AOF snapshots.

title: notification-domain
text:
What is the core technical judgment in a Notification System?
One event fans out to several channels by preference and retries on failure, so the core is an async fan-out pipeline with dedup; the cost is at-least-once delivery, deduped by idempotency keys.

title: ci-domain
text:
What is the core technical judgment in GitHub Actions?
CI runs untrusted user code, so leftover files, processes, and secrets from one job must never reach the next; each job runs in a single-use isolated environment that is destroyed afterward — hosts may be reused, execution environments may not. Per-account concurrency quotas stop any account from hogging the runner pool. The cost is environment setup, usually hidden behind a warm pool.

title: definition
text:
What does contention mean in system design?
Contention happens when multiple processes compete for the same resource at the same time.

title: lost-update
text:
What is the core problem in a lost update?
A lost update occurs when concurrent read-modify-write cycles act on the same stale value and one write silently overwrites another.

title: race-condition
text:
Put the race that sells the last ticket twice in the correct order.
The race happens because both buyers act on the same stale seat count before either write closes the gap between it and the read.

title: conditional-write
text:
What is the simplest concurrency-safe way to enforce this rule in the database?
A conditional update makes the check and the write one atomic database operation, so the loser matches zero rows instead of overwriting a stale read.

title: conditional-write
text:
Which option best describes the concurrency behavior of this SQL?
The SQL encodes compare-and-set by updating only when the current row still satisfies the predicate, so a losing write matches zero rows instead of raising an error.

title: affected-rows
text:
What mistake is application code most likely to make when a conditional UPDATE matches zero rows?
A zero-row update usually succeeds without raising an error, so the application must check the affected count before continuing.

title: transaction
text:
Which SQL mechanism makes inventory decrement and ticket creation succeed together?
The insert is driven by the update's returned row, so no ticket is created unless the guarded update actually succeeded.

title: resource-granularity
text:
Why can protecting only the concert available_seats counter still sell seat A15 twice?
The guard must protect the actual contended resource, not just a derived aggregate counter.

title: resource-granularity
text:
Which resource should the condition guard so the database can prevent duplicate tickets?
When the specific seat is contested, the conditional write must target that seat's own row.

title: compare-and-set
text:
Which of these mechanisms all express this conditional-write semantics? (Select all that apply)
All four bind "check current state" to "write": SQL WHERE and DynamoDB ConditionExpression execute atomically inside the store; Redis SET NX is the special case where the expected state is "absent" (comparing an arbitrary old value needs Lua or WATCH/MULTI); HTTP If-Match is a protocol-level precondition that RFC 9110 requires the server to evaluate before applying the method, but atomic check-and-write still depends on the server mapping it to a conditional write like A or B.

title: pessimistic-locking
text:
Which concurrency control fits this read-decide-write case best?
Pessimistic locking fits read-decide-write logic that cannot be collapsed into one write predicate.

title: pessimistic-locking
text:
What does SELECT FOR UPDATE do inside a transaction?
SELECT FOR UPDATE locks the selected rows so other transactions cannot modify them until commit.

title: lock-failure-modes
text:
What are common failure modes of pessimistic locking?
Pessimistic locks bottleneck throughput when they are too broad, held too long, or acquired inconsistently across transactions.

title: lock-duration
text:
What is the better design principle while a database lock would cover a payment call?
Slow I/O inside a lock drags every transaction waiting on that row along with it, turning lock duration into the external call's latency. Database locks should cover the fewest rows for the shortest time; to "hold" a seat across payment, model it as a business state (held + expiry) rather than keeping the row lock. This is a design recommendation, not something the database enforces, but given queued waiters it is the best choice here.

title: deadlock
text:
Why can simultaneous Alice-to-Bob and Bob-to-Alice bank transfers deadlock?
Deadlock occurs when transactions acquire the same locks in opposite orders and end up waiting on each other.

title: deadlock
text:
What is the standard way to prevent this deadlock?
Consistent lock ordering prevents circular waits, and deadlock errors should still be caught and retried.

title: occ
text:
What is the basic assumption behind optimistic concurrency control?
Optimistic concurrency assumes conflicts are rare and detects them with a version check at write time instead of locking upfront.

title: occ
text:
Which concurrency control usually fits this low-conflict, read-heavy case?
OCC fits rare-conflict edits because the common path avoids blocking and only retries on the occasional conflict.

title: occ
text:
How does this SQL detect a concurrent conflict?
The version predicate detects stale writes because any intervening update changes the version.

title: occ-version
text:
Which values are safe to use as the version check for OCC?
A version token must reliably take a new value on every write to the row. A dedicated incrementing column is the safest default; updated_at or a monotonic business value is safe only if every write changes it and it never returns to an old value; an ordinary value that can round-trip suffers from ABA.

title: aba
text:
What exactly is the ABA problem in OCC?
The ABA problem occurs when a value changes away and back, fooling an equality-based optimistic check into missing the intervening write.

title: occ-vs-locking
text:
Why is pessimistic locking often a better fit than OCC under high contention?
Under high contention, optimistic retries can waste more work than simply locking up front and letting requests queue.

title: write-skew
text:
What kind of conflict is write skew?
Write skew happens when transactions write different rows but jointly violate an invariant based on overlapping reads.

title: isolation-levels
text:
Which mechanism lets the database catch write skew when no row is written by both transactions?
Serializable isolation catches write skew by ensuring the result matches some serial order of the transactions.

title: isolation-levels
text:
Which standard isolation levels do relational databases usually provide?
The common SQL isolation levels are read uncommitted, read committed, repeatable read, and serializable, with only serializable catching write skew.

title: serializable-cost
text:
Why should you not default every high-concurrency path to SERIALIZABLE?
SERIALIZABLE covers cross-row conflicts, but the database must detect extra conflicts: PostgreSQL tracks read/write dependencies with SSI, while MySQL InnoDB turns plain reads into shared-lock reads; either way a conflict aborts one transaction for the app to retry. Paths that only need single-row protection are usually cheaper with a conditional write, row lock, or OCC.

title: materialize-conflict
text:
What is the cheaper refactoring idea here?
Materializing a cross-row invariant onto one row turns it into a conflict the database can guard directly.

title: distributed-locks
text:
What is the key difference between a distributed lock and a database row lock?
A distributed lock is a lease with its own lifetime, unlike a transaction lock that ends the moment the database transaction does.

title: distributed-locks
text:
Which mechanism protects both user experience and data correctness?
Seat checkout needs a TTL reservation rather than a long-held database transaction lock.

title: redis-lock
text:
What are the two key elements in this Redis command shape?
Redis SET with NX and an expiration atomically creates a lock only if it does not already exist, and clears it automatically.

title: redis-lock
text:
What is the classic risk of a Redis TTL lock?
A TTL both cleans up dead locks and caps the lease, so a stalled holder can overrun it and two owners believe they hold the lock — the real guard is a fencing token or a conditional write at commit time.

title: db-reservation
text:
What is the key meaning of this SQL?
The database reservation succeeds only if the seat is free or the old hold has already expired.

title: coordination-services
text:
Compared with Redis or database reservations, what characterizes ZooKeeper or etcd locks?
ZooKeeper and etcd provide robust coordination through consensus, but they add operational complexity you should not default to.

title: technique-map
text:
Which cross-store technical mappings are correct?
The first three are the same concurrency ideas in different systems. D is wrong because most NoSQL stores do not give cross-item serializable transactions by default; you must use an explicit transaction API (e.g., DynamoDB TransactWriteItems) or materialize the conflict onto one item.

title: choosing-approach
text:
Order the contention tools from simplest to most complex.
Choose the simplest tool that protects the gap, escalating from conditional writes to locks, OCC, serializable, and reservations.

title: choosing-approach
text:
What is the best starting point for this rule?
A same-row status predicate is best handled by a simple conditional update, not heavier coordination.

title: choosing-approach
text:
Which mechanism should you consider first in this high-contention read-decide-write case?
High-contention read-decide-write paths usually favor pessimistic locking over repeated optimistic retries.

title: interview-signals
text:
Which interview scenarios should you recognize as contention risks and coordinate explicitly?
Contention signals include shared limited resources, double-booking risks, and concurrent writes to important shared state.

title: auction
text:
What is the common concurrency-control choice for this auction bidding case?
Auctions fit optimistic concurrency because the monotonically rising high bid is itself a natural version guard.

title: ticketmaster
text:
Which contention pattern best improves this experience while preserving correctness?
A short seat reservation shrinks the contention window and avoids checkout failures after payment entry.

title: banking
text:
When does a bank or payment contention problem become a distributed transaction problem?
Money movement becomes a distributed-transaction problem when it must atomically span multiple sources of truth.

title: ride-sharing
text:
What is a good approach for this short-term claim scenario?
A temporary pending-request status reserves the driver briefly and prevents simultaneous dispatches to the same person.

title: flash-sale
text:
Which techniques are often combined in a flash-sale inventory system?
Flash sales often combine guarded inventory updates, temporary cart holds, and queues for especially hot items.

title: reviews
text:
What concurrency control makes sense for concurrent writes to this aggregate field?
Restaurant aggregate updates fit OCC with a dedicated version column that avoids stale rating writes.

title: overcomplication
text:
Why should you not jump straight to a Redis distributed lock whenever you see concurrency?
Distributed locks add components and failure modes, so prefer database-native guards when they are already sufficient.

title: no-contention
text:
Does this scenario need complex contention coordination?
Single-user private state usually has no contention, so complex coordination machinery is unnecessary.

title: hot-resource
text:
Why do sharding, load balancing, and read replicas help only a little when everyone writes the same hot row?
When everyone writes the same resource, the bottleneck is the single source of truth, not the number of app servers.

title: queue-serialization
text:
When the resource really cannot be split, which strategy removes concurrent writes on it completely?
Queue-based serialization removes write contention by processing one hot resource's requests sequentially through a single worker.

title: queue-serialization
text:
What tradeoffs does queue-based serialization introduce?
Queue serialization improves stability but caps throughput and requires failure handling for the single worker.

title: source-of-truth
text:
Put the core reasoning for handling contention in the correct order.
Contention handling starts by identifying the true contested resource and guarding it at its source of truth with the simplest fitting tool.

title: isolation-levels
text:
Under REPEATABLE READ, how do these two transactions end up with nobody on call?
Under REPEATABLE READ, plain reads use a snapshot and only same-row write conflicts are caught; write skew lives in the read set, so both commit. To stop it, use SERIALIZABLE (MySQL turns reads into shared-lock reads, so one transaction deadlocks and aborts; PostgreSQL aborts one via SSI) or explicitly SELECT ... FOR UPDATE the rows you read.

title: replication-boundary
text:
Can the contention toolkit still handle a record that is writable in several places at once?
Every contention tool assumes one authoritative copy to guard, so once the same record is writable in several places you are into replication-level conflict resolution instead.

title: interview-signals
text:
What is the highest-scoring next move at this point in the interview?
The moment you write down a strong-consistency requirement is the moment to name the contention and the mechanism you will guard it with, rather than waiting to be asked.

title: hot-resource
text:
What should you try before reaching for queue-based serialization?
Queue serialization caps throughput and adds a single point of failure, so first ask whether the problem itself can change, which often removes the hot spot outright.

title: hot-resource
text:
What is the cheapest way to handle this hot write?
Nothing in the product needs this counter exact, so relaxing it to eventual consistency removes the hot write entirely at the price of a briefly stale number.

title: race-condition
text:
Why is a tiny race window not a reason to skip coordination?
The number of collisions scales with window times concurrency rather than the window alone, and growing further pushes you into coordinating across multiple nodes.

title: conditional-write
text:
What decides the shape of the failure Bob gets?
At READ COMMITTED Bob waits for Alice's commit, re-checks the WHERE clause, finds no seat left, and changes zero rows; at PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ or SERIALIZABLE his transaction aborts with a serialization failure instead. Either way it is one seat and one sale; what changes is your app code, which must either check affected rows or catch a serialization error and retry. (MySQL InnoDB still returns zero rows under RR, so this conclusion is database-specific.)

title: resource-granularity
text:
After the split, what role does that counter now play?
The guard now sits on the seat row that is actually contended, so the counter is only derived data. D is right that it cannot cause a double sale, but the scenario requires the displayed count to match the seat rows at every moment, and any asynchronous update leaves a mismatch window, so the counter must be computed on demand or maintained in the same transaction.

title: pessimistic-locking
text:
Which category do these two paths fall into, and what protects them?
Both decisions run in application code and cannot be expressed as one UPDATE predicate, and the rows you read are exactly the rows you will write (the account row, the item rows), so lock them with FOR UPDATE across the read-decide-write gap. The cost is that other writers on those rows wait for your commit.

title: lock-duration
text:
What does defaulting to row locks really cost on a low-conflict path?
Pessimistic locking is insurance against a collision that here almost never happens, so every transaction pays a premium for nothing while OCC plus a rare retry is cheaper.

title: coordination-services
text:
How does that seat become buyable again?
The process dies, heartbeats stop, the session times out, the ephemeral node vanishes and the seat frees itself, but you wait a full session timeout and you run a cluster to get it.

title: aba
text:
With no version column available, what is the OCC fallback?
Matching the whole row catches the review_count round trip through the other fields it changed, such as the average; even if every field happened to return to its old value, the row equals what you read, so a value computed from it is still correct. The cost is a long, brittle WHERE clause and retries from unrelated edits.

title: hot-resource
text:
How do you structurally remove this hot spot?
The ten pairs are interchangeable units, so ten separate auctions with one row each cut per-row contention to roughly a tenth and remove the hot spot structurally. B's read replicas can't take writes; C's ten partitions accepting bids independently can't guarantee each bid beats the global current high, and the displayed price diverges; D's lower isolation only adds dirty reads without reducing conflicts. The cost is that buyers pick one of ten auctions and final prices spread out.

title: definition
text:
What core problem does the Handling Large Blobs pattern solve?
The large-blob pattern moves bytes directly between clients, object storage, and CDNs while app servers orchestrate access.

title: when-to-use
text:
What design judgment does this rule of thumb support?
The 10MB line is a practical interview rule of thumb, not a hard database limit, so the real question is whether the file needs SQL queries.

title: database-vs-blob
text:
What problems come from storing a 100MB file directly in a database `bytea` column? (Select all that apply)
Postgres stores large `bytea` values out of line via TOAST, so queries that skip that column are mostly unaffected; but each video read pulls 100MB through the database, using I/O and buffer cache, every write goes through WAL, and backups and streaming replication balloon. Structured data and large files also can't scale separately. A database never comes with CDN distribution.

title: durability
text:
What design judgment does this durability level support?
Eleven-nines durability far exceeds what most self-built replication achieves, so object storage can own large-file persistence. Durability and consistency are separate guarantees (S3 is strongly consistent within a region, while cross-region replication is asynchronous), and durability does not protect against accidental deletes — use versioning for that and lifecycle rules for cleanup.

title: proxy-bottleneck
text:
What is the main problem with having the API server proxy large uploads and downloads?
Proxying large files turns app servers into bandwidth bottlenecks without adding business value.

title: direct-upload
text:
How should the upload path be designed?
For large uploads, the app server should authorize and issue a presigned URL, then let the client upload directly to storage.

title: direct-upload-flow
text:
Put a simple direct upload flow in the correct order:
The direct upload flow authorizes first, issues a scoped URL, uploads bytes directly, and then synchronizes metadata.

title: presigned-url
text:
What is a presigned URL really?
A presigned URL is a temporary signed permission for a specific operation on a specific object.

title: presigned-url
text:
Must you call S3 before generating an S3 presigned URL?
Generating a presigned URL is usually a local signing operation, with storage validating the signature later.

title: upload-restrictions
text:
Which limits should you encode into a presigned upload URL? (Select all that apply)
Whoever holds a presigned credential can use it, so scope it tightly: size limit, content type, specific key, plus a short expiry. Syntax differs by store (S3 POST policy uses content-length-range, presigned PUT can sign Content-Length / Content-Type; GCS uses x-goog-content-length-range). content-type only constrains the declared value; the real content still needs server-side scanning.

title: upload-restrictions
text:
What risk appears if a profile-picture upload URL has no content-length-range limit?
Without size constraints, a small-image upload URL can be abused to store unexpectedly large objects.

title: direct-download
text:
How can you design the download path?
For infrequent private downloads, a signed storage URL is simple and avoids proxying bytes through the app server.

title: cdn-download
text:
What is a better download path for this case?
CDNs cache popular objects near users while signed URLs or cookies preserve access control.

title: cdn-signature
text:
What is the key difference between an S3 presigned URL and a CloudFront signed URL?
Storage presigned URLs are validated by storage, while CDN signed URLs are validated by edge servers with public-key cryptography.

title: resumable-upload
text:
What design judgment does this upload-duration estimate support?
A multi-minute upload means restarting from scratch after a failure is expensive, which is exactly why resumable and multipart uploads exist.

title: multipart-upload
text:
What capability should you use for this upload?
Multipart or resumable upload lets the client retry only failed chunks instead of restarting the entire file.

title: provider-terms
text:
Which cloud-provider terms for chunked or resumable upload are mapped correctly? (Select all that apply)
AWS, GCS, and Azure use different names for the same broad chunked upload capability.

title: checksums
text:
What do per-part checksums or ETags do in multipart upload?
Part checksums or ETags let the client track successful chunks and complete the final object assembly.

title: resumable-upload-flow
text:
Put the resumable upload flow in the correct order:
Resumable upload creates a session, uploads parts, resumes missing parts, completes the object, and cleans up abandoned parts.

title: multipart-cleanup
text:
Why do incomplete multipart uploads need lifecycle cleanup?
Incomplete multipart parts still cost storage money, so lifecycle rules should remove abandoned uploads.

title: metadata
text:
How should file metadata be stored in a large-file system?
Store rich file metadata in the primary database and the file bytes in object storage.

title: metadata
text:
Which fields should a file metadata table usually include? (Select all that apply)
A file metadata row should track ownership, file attributes, storage key, and upload status.

title: metadata
text:
When is it better to create the database metadata row?
Create the metadata row before upload so storage events can reconcile the uploaded object to a known record.

title: client-complete-risk
text:
What problems come from trusting only a client-side "upload complete" call? (Select all that apply)
Trusting only the client creates orphan, malicious-completion, and notification-loss risks.

title: event-notifications
text:
What mechanism should be the primary path for this state update?
Storage event notifications are a trusted primary path for updating metadata after direct upload.

title: reconciliation
text:
If you already have storage events, why do you still need a reconciliation job?
Events are the primary update path, while reconciliation catches delayed, lost, or failed event processing.

title: state-sync-flow
text:
Put the state-sync flow after direct upload in the correct order:
The state sync flow creates pending metadata, uploads directly, processes storage events, and reconciles stragglers.

title: storage-key
text:
Which storage-key strategy is safer?
Server-generated storage keys prevent collisions and let events map objects back to metadata rows.

title: object-tags
text:
Why not store rich metadata only in S3 object tags or custom headers?
Object tags are limited and poor for rich queries, so business metadata belongs in a database.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Do you need the large-blob direct upload pattern here?
Small files usually do not justify the extra latency and complexity of presigned direct upload.

title: synchronous-validation
text:
Which upload path fits this validation requirement better?
Synchronous content validation requires the server or a controlled processor to see the bytes before accepting the upload.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Which cases should not default to direct blob upload? (Select all that apply)
Direct upload gives up synchronous control over the byte stream. Small files gain too little; synchronous validation needs the server to see the bytes; and because compliance forbids unscanned bytes from landing in any storage, a direct upload to a quarantine bucket followed by a scan is not allowed, so a controlled proxy pipeline is required. If compliance only required scanning before the file becomes visible, direct upload to a quarantine bucket plus an async scan would still work.

title: abuse-prevention
text:
What is the safer processing model?
A quarantine bucket plus scanning pipeline prevents uploaded content from becoming accessible before validation.

title: abuse-prevention
text:
What checks can a post-upload processing pipeline usually perform? (Select all that apply)
Post-upload processing can scan for viruses, unsafe content, and file type mismatches before release.

title: fast-downloads
text:
What is the most practical optimization?
A CDN addresses geographic latency: the first request at a PoP (cache miss) goes to origin, and later users in that region hit a nearby edge, with latency set by the distance to the PoP and typically far below the ~200ms trans-Pacific round trip; proper Cache-Control also lets browsers reuse the files locally.

title: range-requests
text:
How do HTTP range requests help with large-file downloads?
HTTP range requests let clients resume large downloads by fetching only missing byte ranges.

title: parallel-downloads
text:
What are the tradeoffs of parallel chunk downloads? (Select all that apply)
Parallel chunk downloads can help extreme cases but add client complexity and rarely beat total bandwidth limits.

title: interview-scenarios
text:
Which system-design prompts commonly trigger the large-blobs pattern? (Select all that apply)
Whenever a prompt involves video, photos, file sync, or chat media, reach for blob storage, presigned URLs, a CDN, and async processing. Sizes range from megabytes to gigabytes, but none of those bytes should flow through app servers or live in the database.

title: youtube
text:
What design best fits the large-blobs pattern?
YouTube-style uploads use multipart direct upload, storage-triggered transcoding, and CDN delivery.

title: instagram
text:
What is a reasonable design for this photo upload flow?
Instagram-style uploads direct originals to storage and use async workers for thumbnails, filters, and metadata.

title: dropbox
text:
What is the key upload design for this file-sync system?
Dropbox-style sync uses chunked direct uploads with metadata-driven state and sync workflows.

title: whatsapp
text:
How should the media path be designed?
The chat system passes a reference and permissions, not large bytes. Because a recipient may download much later, the server checks the recipient's identity at download time and issues a short-lived signed URL, so the media is not exposed through a long-lived public link.

title: provider-terms
text:
Which cloud-provider term mappings are correct? (Select all that apply)
Different cloud providers use different names for temporary access, events, multipart upload, and lifecycle cleanup.

title: end-to-end-design
text:
Put a production-grade large-file upload design in the correct order:
A production large-file design includes metadata, direct multipart upload, events, processing, CDN delivery, and reconciliation.

title: interview-trigger
text:
