What main design thread should you think of immediately?
The interview trigger is to bypass app servers for bytes while handling permissions, resumability, events, and CDN delivery.

title: resumable-upload
text:
Where should the upload progress bar get its data from?
Direct upload takes the server off the byte path, so progress has to come from the client: on a single PUT the platform's upload API exposes a bytes-sent callback, and with multipart you can also count completed parts. Multipart's main benefit is resumability, at the cost of extra initiate and complete calls.

title: presigned-url
text:
How should you set the expiry on that presigned URL?
S3 checks a presigned URL's expiry when the request starts, so an in-flight transfer is not cut off when the URL expires. The expiry therefore has to cover the window to start uploading plus retries with the same URL: too short and queued or retried requests fail, too long and a leaked URL stays writable. Fifteen minutes to an hour is common; larger or slower uploads should switch to multipart with short-lived per-part URLs.

title: resumable-upload
text:
How does the chunked-upload URL structure differ across the three clouds?
All three let you retry only the failed chunks; they differ in endpoint shape and commit step: S3 signs a URL per part and finishes with CompleteMultipartUpload, GCS hands out one session URI addressed by Content-Range, and Azure reuses a SAS URL with Put Block per blockid and then Put Block List. A cross-cloud client has to wrap all three behind one interface.

title: resumable-upload
text:
What must the client have persisted ahead of time?
The scenario says the backend keeps no session record, so the upload ID lives only in client memory, and once the app dies the uploaded parts can't be found. Persist the upload ID and key locally, then call ListParts on relaunch to resume. The cost is that orphaned uploads keep billing until lifecycle rules clean them up. If the backend recorded the upload ID in its metadata row, this state could live server-side instead.

title: cdn-delivery
text:
What happens if those CDN URLs are not signed?
A big reason to sign CDN URLs is anti-hotlinking, not just speed: the signature binds the link to an expiry and a key pair, so embedded links go stale — but your player must be able to re-request one.

title: file-sharing
text:
How should that share link be implemented?
The constraints are no account, automatic expiry, no revocation needed, and no bytes through the API servers; a signed URL (for example a CloudFront signed URL) encodes authorization and expiry in the link and serves bytes from the CDN. The cost is that an issued URL cannot be pulled back before it expires. If revocation were required, the share link would hit your API, validate a token, and 302 to a short-lived signed URL.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Should this use direct upload with async processing?
The constraint is content-based feedback while the user waits on one screen; the async chain adds event delivery and push with unpredictable latency, while a 2MB file is cheap to pass through the server. There is no fixed MB threshold — weigh size, request volume, and the need for synchronous feedback together. The cost is that bandwidth and processing for this path land back on your servers.

title: metadata
text:
How do you make the metadata atomic with the upload itself?
The case-id must live as the object's own metadata and cannot go in the key, so sign `x-amz-meta-case-id` into the presigned URL's SignedHeaders. Storage then rejects the write if the header is missing or different, making metadata and bytes atomic. The cost is that the client must reproduce those headers exactly. If metadata did not need to live on the object, a server-generated key or a pending database row would suffice.

title: download-optimization
text:
What breaks if the Range header is pinned by the signature too?
SigV4 hashes the value of every header in SignedHeaders, so once range is pinned only an identical Range passes, and both resuming with a new range and a whole-file request without Range get 403. By default a presigned GET does not sign Range, so clients can add it freely and receive 206. Sign the object path and expiry, not headers that resumption needs to vary.

title: definition
text:
What is the core idea behind the Managing Long-Running Tasks pattern?
The pattern splits work into immediate acknowledgment and asynchronous background processing.

title: sync-problem
text:
Why is a 45-second PDF generation job a poor fit for a synchronous HTTP request?
An average of 45 seconds already sits close to the 60-second gateway timeout, so tail requests fail outright; users also get no progress and may refresh or resubmit. An async job acknowledges immediately and exposes status.

title: trigger-signals
text:
Which operations should make you consider the long-running task pattern? (Select all that apply.)
Video transcoding, reports, exports, and bulk emails are classic long-running task triggers.

title: async-flow
text:
What should the API return for this report request?
The API should enqueue the work and immediately return a job ID for status tracking.

title: end-to-end-flow
text:
Put the basic async worker-pool flow in the correct order.
The web tier creates and enqueues the job, while workers fetch, process, and update its status.

title: components
text:
Which components do you usually need at minimum for the long-running task pattern? (Select all that apply.)
The core components are a queue, workers, and a durable job-status store.

title: queue-role
text:
What is the main role of the message queue in this pattern?
The queue durably holds pending job messages (usually just a job_id), so the web tier only enqueues quickly while transcoding workers consume at their own pace; peak overflow becomes a visible backlog instead of overwhelming workers, and the queue also supports retry and failure handling. C is wrong because messages are deleted once consumed — the authoritative job status still belongs in a database.

title: queue-payload
text:
What should you put in the queue message?
Keep the queue message small and stable and store the full context and status in the job DB. A large payload can hit the queue's per-message limit (SQS and others have one), and every retry or redelivery re-transfers the whole object; sending only the job_id also keeps the DB as the single source of truth, so there is no stale copy sitting in the queue.

title: queue-options
text:
Which statements about common queue choices are correct? (Select all that apply.)
Queue choices trade off durability, operations, routing flexibility, replayability, and scale.

title: queue-options
text:
Which queue option is common and quickest to get started with?
Redis with Bull or BullMQ is a practical startup-friendly queue choice, though durability must be evaluated.

title: worker-runtime
text:
What runtime should you prefer for these workers?
Long jobs often fit server or container workers because they avoid serverless execution limits.

title: worker-runtime
text:
Which tradeoffs about worker runtimes are correct? (Select all that apply.)
Match the worker runtime to job duration, resources, and ops headcount. Servers give the most control but you manage machines and idle cost; serverless removes ops but has execution-time, cold-start, and local-storage limits (30-minute jobs here may exceed some platforms' caps); containers sit in between. "Always best with no exceptions" is false.

title: independent-scaling
text:
How does the long-running task pattern handle this resource mismatch?
Async workers let web servers and GPU-heavy processing scale on different hardware.

title: benefits
text:
What benefits does the long-running task pattern provide? (Select all that apply.)
The pattern improves response time, independent scaling, and fault isolation, but adds monitoring and state complexity.

title: tradeoffs
text:
What new costs come with introducing an async worker pool? (Select all that apply.)
Async isn't free: you now maintain a queue, workers, and a job DB; the API only acknowledges receipt, so clients must handle the pending-to-terminal transition; and you need status queries, retries, DLQ, and monitoring. D is too absolute — with a status endpoint and notifications users can track progress.

title: user-feedback
text:
What product-facing support should you add for this async job?
Long-running tasks need status APIs and completion notifications so users understand progress.

title: status-model
text:
What minimum states does an async job status field usually go through?
A basic job state model is pending, processing, and then completed or failed.

title: worker-crash
text:
How does a queue system usually recover when a worker crashes mid-job?
Queues recover from worker crashes using heartbeats or visibility timeouts that allow another worker to retry the job.

title: heartbeat
text:
Why do many systems start this heartbeat timeout around 10-30 seconds instead of 1 second or 1 hour?
Ten to thirty seconds is a common starting point for the dead-worker timeout: too short mistakes GC pauses for crashes and causes duplicate work, too long delays recovery from real crashes. The heartbeat send interval is usually a fraction of that timeout, such as every five to ten seconds, so one or two lost heartbeats don't trigger a false failure.

title: timeout-terms
text:
Which mapping between queue products and liveness terms is reasonable?
SQS uses a visibility timeout (a message lease — if not deleted in time, it becomes visible again); RabbitMQ uses connection heartbeats, and unacked messages are requeued once the connection is declared dead; Kafka uses the consumer-group session timeout to detect dead consumers and rebalance (stuck processing is covered by max.poll.interval.ms). Same goal, different layers.

title: dlq
text:
What problem does a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) mainly solve?
A dead letter queue isolates repeatedly failing jobs so healthy work can continue.

title: dlq
text:
Why is the attempt limit before moving to the DLQ often around 3-5 instead of zero or unlimited?
Jobs commonly move to a dead letter queue after about three to five failed attempts, balancing transient-error tolerance against wasted worker time.

title: dlq
text:
Which signals should you keep monitoring in a DLQ design? (Select all that apply.)
A DLQ is a production failure signal, not a trash bin. Steadily growing depth means something is systematically broken; the failure-reason distribution points to a specific bug or bad data; redriven jobs failing again means the fix didn't work. All three deserve standing alerts — ignoring the DLQ lets failures snowball.

title: idempotency
text:
How do you avoid creating three jobs for the same business intent?
An idempotency key maps repeated submissions of the same operation to the existing job.

title: idempotent-work
text:
Why should the worker execution itself be as idempotent as possible? (Select all that apply.)
Workers should be idempotent because retries and at-least-once delivery can repeat side effects.

title: idempotency
text:
What is the key behavior in this submit_job pseudocode?
The idempotency key is persisted so repeated submissions return the same job instead of creating duplicates.

title: backpressure
text:
What does backpressure mean in an async worker system?
Backpressure slows or rejects new job intake when workers cannot keep up.

title: backpressure
text:
Which mitigations should you discuss first?
Use queue depth for autoscaling and apply rate limits or busy responses when the backlog is too deep.

title: autoscaling
text:
Why does worker-pool scaling usually watch queue depth instead of only CPU usage?
Queue depth better captures backlog and wait time, while CPU alone can lag the actual service-level problem.

title: mixed-workloads
text:
What goes wrong if 5-second PDFs and 5-hour annual reports share one FIFO queue?
Once annual reports occupy every worker, a 5-second PDF behind them in the FIFO queue must wait for some 5-hour job to finish, breaking the one-minute promise — that's head-of-line blocking. Mixed-duration jobs need separate queues, priorities, or splitting long jobs.

title: mixed-workloads
text:
How should you split the workers and queues?
Separate queues by job type or expected duration to keep short jobs responsive and tune workers independently.

title: job-dependencies
text:
How can you implement this simple chain of dependent jobs?
For simple chains, each worker can enqueue the next step with workflow context and retryable outputs.

title: workflow-orchestration
text:
What should you consider introducing next?
Complex branching or parallel job dependencies justify a workflow orchestrator.

title: monitoring
text:
Which metrics must an async worker system monitor? (Select all that apply.)
Async systems need monitoring for backlog, worker health, failures, retries, and dead-letter queues.

title: interview-signal
text:
How should you use those two numbers to derive an architecture conclusion?
Doing the throughput math shows image processing would saturate the web tier and should move to async workers.

title: interview-scenarios
text:
Which system-design prompts commonly use the long-running tasks pattern? (Select all that apply.)
Media processing, feed fanout, and file scanning are common long-running task scenarios.

title: payment
text:
How should you split the synchronous and asynchronous boundary in this system?
Users need to know immediately whether authorization succeeded, so authorization and the real-time fraud scoring it depends on stay synchronous; manual or deep fraud review, webhooks, and settlement can proceed in the background, tracked by persisted payment state. B fails because manual review and settlement can take hours or days — the user can't wait on that.

title: summary
text:
Fill in the one-sentence pattern for a long-running task.
The pattern is accept and enqueue, return a job ID, process in workers, and update job status.

title: queue-down
text:
How can these jobs stuck in pending get processed later?
If job creation can succeed while queueing fails, a poller or repair path must enqueue pending jobs later.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Should this scenario introduce a queue plus workers?
A 30-millisecond profile read should remain synchronous because queueing would add needless complexity.

title: failure-lifecycle
text:
Put the lifecycle of a failed job in the correct order.
A failed job is redelivered, retried with an attempt count, and eventually isolated in a dead letter queue.

title: notification
text:
What are good ways to proactively notify the user?
Async job completion should notify users through email, push, or realtime updates, or be visible through status polling.

title: interview-depth
text:
When you bring up the long-running task pattern in an interview, which deep dives should you be ready for? (Select all that apply.)
The common deep dives are crash retry, poison messages, idempotency, and backpressure.

title: long-running-vs-workflow
text:
Where is the rough boundary between a long-running task queue and a workflow orchestrator?
Use queues for simple async work and workflow systems for complex branching, retries, and compensation.

title: interview-answer
text:
Put the interview explanation for introducing long-running tasks in the right order.
A strong interview answer motivates async processing, proposes queue workers, explains UX, and covers failure modes.

title: idempotency
text:
How should you build the idempotency key for a user-initiated job?
The scenario asks for fixed-window dedup, so the rounding granularity is the window: clicks in the same window produce the same key and later windows separate naturally. The cost is exactly what the team accepts: two clicks straddling a boundary become two jobs. A strict "within five minutes of the last one" rule would instead use a time-free key stored server-side with a five-minute TTL.

title: mixed-workload
text:
Besides splitting into fast and slow queues, how else can you remove this head-of-line blocking?
Each small job writes one batch of followers, so a worker is occupied for seconds again; enqueuing batches one after another lets ordinary fanouts slip in between them, so no single big task owns the head of the queue. If you dumped every chunk into a FIFO queue at once, they would still sit ahead of ordinary jobs. The cost is tracking batch progress (a cursor) yourself and deciding which batch to redo on failure.

title: queue-semantics
text:
How does this hand-rolled queue break under concurrent consumption?
There is no lock between SELECT and UPDATE, and the UPDATE does not check that the row is still pending, so two workers can read the same row, both mark it processing, and both send the same email. Fixes: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, or a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status='pending'` plus an affected-row check. Mature queues hide a message at delivery time with a visibility timeout / message lock, at the cost of redelivery if that timeout is too short.

title: result-storage
text:
Where should each of these two kinds of result be stored when the job finishes?
Sending the artifact to object storage and keeping only a URL plus metadata in the database keeps queue messages and job rows small and predictable, at the cost of an extra S3 round trip and a cleanup policy you own.

title: mixed-workload
text:
Beyond longer waits for short jobs, what else does a mixed-duration workload cause?
When job duration is unpredictable the same queue depth can imply wildly different worker counts, so autoscaling thresholds cannot be tuned, and utilisation is badly uneven because some workers churn short jobs while others sit on a single long one.

title: dlq
text:
Which built-in configuration gives you a DLQ on SQS and on RabbitMQ respectively?
In both products the DLQ is queue-side configuration, not application code. An SQS redrive policy holds both the receive limit (maxReceiveCount=5) and the target DLQ. RabbitMQ splits the two: a quorum queue's delivery-limit counts to 5, and the dead letter exchange routes messages that exceed it or are rejected with requeue=false. Classic queues have no built-in delivery counter, so the consumer would have to count and reject.

title: dlq
text:
Why should a repeatedly failing message go to a DLQ instead of just being dropped?
Leaving the main queue keeps a poison message from killing workers on endless retries, but leaving is not deleting. Routing to a DLQ buys four things: data is preserved (failures are often just a transient downstream outage that can be replayed after recovery), the failures are diagnosable evidence of root cause, they can be re-driven back after a fix, and DLQ depth is an alertable signal. Dropping instead loses a real user request silently and permanently; it is only reasonable when the message itself is disposable, like a metrics heartbeat.

title: examples
text:
Should each of these two paths be synchronous or asynchronous?
Matching takes seconds but the rider needs instant feedback, so return a finding state and let the backend finish it. Location updates are high volume and tolerate a few seconds of lag, so they should use a write path separate from the main API (queue plus workers, or a dedicated location service writing an in-memory geo index).

title: failure-handling
text:
What should the worker do with the message it holds during those three minutes?
Normally the worker finishes, writes completed and acknowledges, but while the database is down it retries without acknowledging so the message stays queued until recovery; the cost is a deeper backlog and possible re-execution by another worker once the visibility timeout expires, which is why the work must be idempotent.

title: rate-limiting
text:
How do you respect that rate limit without dropping any notification?
The queue flattens the 200K burst into a steady rate the provider accepts. Workers share a rate limiter (e.g. a token bucket refilling 50 tokens/s) to control send speed; worker concurrency alone is only a coarse knob, since actual rate ≈ concurrency ÷ per-call latency. Any occasional 429 is retried with backoff and the message is not acked, so nothing is lost. The cost: the last message goes out after 200000 ÷ 50 = 4000 s (~67 min), and the product must accept that tail latency.

title: definition
text:
What problem does the multi-step processes pattern mainly solve?
Multi-step process patterns make long, failure-prone workflows across services reliable through durable state, retries, and compensation.

title: single-server
text:
What is the fatal flaw in implementing order fulfillment as one API server function?
A single in-memory function loses progress on crash, leaving the system unable to resume or compensate safely.

title: order-fulfillment
text:
Which steps can appear in an e-commerce order fulfillment workflow? (Select all)
Order fulfillment spans payment, inventory, shipping, human work, and notification steps.

title: callback-routing
text:
Why does a payment gateway webhook make in-memory orchestration on one server less reliable?
Webhook callbacks may land on a different host, so workflow state must be durable and addressable by ID.

title: saga
text:
What is the core definition of the saga pattern?
A saga is a sequence of local steps with compensating actions that undo completed work if a later step fails.

title: saga-vs-2pc
text:
Why do many cross-service business workflows use a saga instead of Two-Phase Commit?
Sagas avoid long distributed locks and work with external systems by compensating committed steps instead of atomically locking everything.

title: saga-compensation
text:
Put the compensation flow in order after inventory fails in an order saga.
If inventory fails after payment succeeds, the saga compensates by refunding the payment and marking the order failed.

title: compensation
text:
Which statements about compensating actions are correct? (Select all)
Compensations are business undo steps that must be retryable, idempotent, and observable.

title: choreography-vs-orchestration
text:
What is the main difference between saga choreography and orchestration?
Choreography coordinates through service reactions to events, while orchestration uses a central coordinator that owns the flow.

title: choreography
text:
Which saga coordination style fits this event-driven service setup?
Event-driven choreography fits moderately complex flows across independent services.

title: orchestration
text:
Which workflow coordination approach fits this complex stateful process?
Complex branching, waiting, compensation, and audit requirements fit workflow orchestration.

title: event-store
text:
What role does a durable log or event store play in event-driven choreography?
The durable event log stores history and drives workers that react to events and emit the next events.

title: choreography-benefits
text:
Which benefits does event-driven choreography provide? (Select all)
The event log gives fault tolerance (resume from offset), scaling (consumers in a group up to the partition count), and audit (an ordered, permanently retained event record). The audit trail is complete only because retention never expires and every state change is emitted. The flow is implicit, though, and inserting a step usually changes upstream/downstream contracts, so B is false.

title: choreography-limits
text:
What is the main problem with event-driven choreography in complex flows?
Choreography becomes hard to understand and change because the flow is implicit across many workers and contracts.

title: durable-execution
text:
What is durable execution?
Durable execution lets long-running workflow code survive crashes and resume from recorded progress.

title: workflow-vs-activity
text:
In Temporal, what is the difference between a Workflow and an Activity?
A workflow is deterministic orchestration code, while activities perform the external side-effecting steps.

title: determinism
text:
Why must durable-execution Workflow code be deterministic?
Workflow code must be deterministic because recovery replays it against recorded history.

title: activity-idempotency
text:
Why does an Activity need to be idempotent?
Activities need idempotency because retries can happen after ambiguous success reports.

title: replay
text:
Put Temporal crash-recovery replay in the correct order.
Replay re-executes workflow code but returns recorded activity results until execution reaches the point after the crash.

title: temporal-components
text:
Which core components are usually in a Temporal deployment? (Select all)
Temporal uses a server for bookkeeping, a history database, and worker pools that run workflow and activity code.

title: signals
text:
How should a workflow system wait efficiently for a long external step?
Workflow systems wait for external events with durable signals and timers without holding worker threads.

title: temporal-vs-step-functions
text:
What is the main modeling difference between Temporal and AWS Step Functions?
Temporal usually models workflows as code, while Step Functions models them as managed state machines.

title: workflow-tools
text:
Which statements about common workflow tools are correct? (Select all)
Workflow tool choice matters less than understanding the selected tool's recovery model and limits.

title: step-functions-limits
text:
What do these Step Functions limits imply for workflow state design?
These are fixed product limits rather than derived numbers, so state must carry references instead of large payloads and long flows must be resumable in segments.

title: when-to-use
text:
What is this stateful-process shape usually a signal to introduce?
A stateful multi-step process with waiting, compensation, and audit needs is a strong workflow signal.

title: interview-signals
text:
Which interview phrases strongly point to workflow or saga? (Select all)
Compensation, long waits, callbacks, and cross-service state are strong workflow signals.

title: payment-system
text:
Why is workflow or saga a reasonable choice for this payment flow?
Payment fulfillment fits sagas because it spans systems and needs compensation and crash-safe progress.

title: human-in-the-loop
text:
Why is this dispatch flow a workflow candidate?
Human-in-the-loop flows fit workflows because they wait durably for external signals.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Why should a single async email task not immediately use a workflow engine?
A workflow engine is overkill for simple one-step async tasks that a queue and worker can handle.

title: workflow-costs
text:
Which costs come with introducing a workflow system? (Select all)
Workflow systems add operational dependency, learning curve, and per-step orchestration overhead.

title: crash-recovery
text:
What information is most needed to recover this crashed fulfillment flow?
Crash recovery needs durable progress recording so the coordinator can resume or compensate correctly.

title: workflow-versioning
text:
What is the basic approach to workflow versioning?
Workflow versioning lets old executions keep their old definition while new executions use the new one.

title: workflow-migration
text:
How should a durable execution engine safely handle this workflow code change?
Durable engines use deterministic patch gates so workflow changes do not break replay for in-flight executions.

title: history-size
text:
Why is an oversized Temporal workflow history a problem?
Large workflow histories make replay slower and increase storage costs.

title: history-size
text:
Which methods control workflow history size? (Select all)
Keep histories small by passing references, storing large payloads externally, and using continue-as-new for long loops.

title: continue-as-new
text:
What is Temporal Continue-as-New?
Continue-as-New closes the current run and starts a new run under the same Workflow ID with empty history; the current state is carried over as input, so the new run executes the function from the top but logically continues. It suits long-running or looping workflows and prevents unbounded history growth in a single run. The old run's history is still retained per the retention policy, not deleted.

title: external-events
text:
How should the system route this external webhook event?
The webhook handler should signal the specific workflow execution using its workflow ID.

title: exactly-once
text:
What is the more accurate meaning of “exactly once” in workflow systems?
Attempts are often at-least-once; idempotency makes the effect exactly-once in practice.

title: idempotent-side-effects
text:
What is the more robust way to handle this side effect?
Use idempotency records with in-progress and completed states, and reconcile ambiguous in-progress side effects.

title: choosing-approach
text:
Put the multi-step process solution path in the right upgrade order.
Start with simple synchronous or queued work, then escalate to sagas and workflow engines as complexity grows.

title: interview-depth
text:
After introducing workflow in a Senior or Staff interview, which deep dives are common? (Select all)
Workflow deep dives test crash recovery, versioning, history size, and idempotent side effects.

title: summary
text:
Fill in the core sentence for a saga.
A saga uses local transactions plus compensating actions to achieve eventual consistency across services.

title: workflow-vs-cron-poller
text:
What is the key difference between a handwritten state table plus poller and a workflow engine?
A hand-rolled poller must implement the reliability machinery that workflow engines provide directly.

title: ai-pipelines
text:
Why does this AI agent pipeline fit workflow or durable execution?
AI agent pipelines fit workflows because they are long, stateful chains of flaky external steps.

title: interview-answer
text:
Put the interview answer structure for a multi-step workflow in the right order.
A strong answer motivates workflow complexity, chooses coordination, explains reliability, and covers operational deep dives.

title: saga
text:
In this choreographed order saga, who fires the refund compensation?
The team rule allows only events, no synchronous calls, so B is out; a Kafka broker has no business semantics and never undoes events (C is wrong); choreography can still compensate automatically (D is wrong). In choreography, compensation is a reverse subscription: the forward worker also listens for the downstream failure event and undoes its own step. The cost is that every worker maintains both forward and reverse handlers.

title: workflow-engines
text:
What is the essential difference between their recovery mechanisms?
Temporal recovers by replaying your workflow function with recorded activity results, which is why the code must be deterministic; Step Functions just resumes from a server-side position.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Should this request path be wrapped in a workflow engine?
Every activity costs an engine round trip plus history writes, and those milliseconds land straight in the user's latency budget.

title: versioning
text:
Will updating the state machine definition make in-flight executions take the new step?
Declarative systems save you migration code but cost you control: editing the definition only affects new executions.

title: external-events
text:
How should the timeout escalate instead of waiting forever?
A false return from condition is a timeout event you can chain into escalation: remind, give a short second window, then cancel.

title: single-server
text:
Why is this a structural design problem rather than a code-style problem?
Crashes, retries, and timeouts are system concerns; out-of-stock and refunds are business concerns — interleaving them scatters state and compensation across every app server.

title: single-server
text:
Without adopting a workflow engine, how should that callback be routed?
Once state lives in the database instead of memory, callbacks no longer depend on any one host — but you now hand-roll the poller, locking, and retries.

title: saga
text:
How should the system represent that window of inconsistency?
A saga trades cross-service atomicity for a brief inconsistency window, and a pending state makes that window explicit and queryable instead of an invisible bug.

title: choreography
text:
Where is the line between event sourcing and merely coordinating with a log?
Where truth lives sets the boundary: if the log is the source of truth you can rebuild any past state, whereas a coordination-only log leaves the table authoritative.

title: choreography
text:
How do the services' roles change?
The request returns as soon as the event is appended and subscribers take over — decoupled and scalable, but no single place spells out the whole flow.

title: choreography
text:
Which cost are they most likely to underestimate?
The log alone can't tell you why a PaymentFailed event had no consumer or what chain produced it — you have to build that tooling yourself.

title: durable-execution
text:
How do you explain what actually differs between them?
Readability comes from the code shape, reliability from how it's run: each activity result lands in history, and a new worker replays up to that point and continues.

title: durable-execution
text:
At that moment, which process actually calls the payment service?
The workflow worker only decides: it tells the server to schedule the activity, an activity worker makes the real call and reports back, and the workflow picks up where history ends.

title: step-functions
text:
What is the safer answer about maintaining the state machine definition?
At Amazon, mocking the ugly JSON reads as an AWS knowledge gap, since teams generate it with CDK anyway — the real limitation is expressiveness, not syntax.

title: versioning
text:
Why can't plain workflow versioning solve this?
By the definition in the scenario, versioning assumes you can wait for in-flight executions to finish on the old version. When the change must apply to running executions now, you need in-place migration such as a patch that deterministically picks the new or legacy path.

title: definition
text:
What problem does the Real-time Updates pattern solve?
Real-time updates deliver server-side events or data changes to clients with low latency.

title: two-hops
text:
Which two hops does a realtime update design usually need to solve? (Select all that apply.)
Hop one is the protocol between the client and the server holding its connection (polling / SSE / WebSocket); hop two is how the update travels from where it is produced (A) to the server holding the connection (B). The two choices are independent.

title: two-hop-flow
text:
Put the two-hop path of a realtime message in order.
A realtime update is produced, propagated to the right server, delivered over a client connection, and rendered by the client.

title: http-limits
text:
Why is standard HTTP request-response a poor fit for true server-initiated realtime push?
Request-response is client-driven: every response answers a request. Keep-alive only reuses the TCP connection; it does not let the server send unsolicited messages. To deliver later events you need repeated pulls (polling / long polling) or a persistent channel such as a streaming response (SSE) or WebSocket.

title: networking
text:
In realtime connection interviews, what key semantics does TCP provide compared with UDP?
HTTP/1.1, HTTP/2, classic WebSocket, and SSE rely on TCP's ordered, reliable byte stream; persistent connections lower latency but add server-side connection state. Note that HTTP/3 instead runs over QUIC, which is built on UDP and provides its own reliable, ordered streams.

title: load-balancers
text:
What is the key difference between L4 and L7 load balancers for realtime connections?
An L4 balancer doesn't parse application content, so it stays closer to a one-connection-to-one-backend model. An L7 balancer understands HTTP and can route by path or header, usually terminating the client connection and opening a separate backend connection. Mainstream L7 balancers do support WebSocket; you just need to account for idle timeouts and the split connection.

title: simple-polling
text:
What is the most pragmatic starting point?
If low latency is not critical, simple polling is a pragmatic baseline that avoids realtime infrastructure complexity.

title: simple-polling
text:
What are the pros and cons of simple polling? (Select all that apply.)
Polling's simplicity is valuable, but it costs latency (up to one extra interval versus push-based options) and many empty reads; it is one-way pull, not a full-duplex channel.

title: polling-scale
text:
What design judgment does this scale estimate most support?
One million clients polling every ten seconds is about one hundred thousand queries per second, so polling's simplicity can hide a real read-load problem that capacity planning must account for.

title: keep-alive
text:
How does HTTP keep-alive reduce simple polling overhead?
HTTP/1.1 reuses connections by default; as long as the server's (and any proxy's) idle timeout exceeds the polling interval, consecutive polls share one TCP connection and skip repeated handshakes and teardowns. The idle timeout is set by the server, not by the client.

title: long-polling
text:
What is the basic mechanism of long polling?
Long polling holds an HTTP request until data is available, then the client immediately issues the next request.

title: long-polling-flow
text:
Put the long-polling flow in order.
Long polling works by holding a request open, responding when data arrives, and immediately opening the next request.

title: long-polling
text:
Which option is simple and appropriate?
Long polling is a simple fit for infrequent status changes that should be shown as soon as they happen.

title: long-polling
text:
What are the main downsides of long polling? (Select all that apply.)
Long polling is compatible, but high update rates amplify request overhead and latency, and many hanging requests complicate monitoring. Under HTTP/1.1, browsers typically allow about 6 concurrent connections per host, so five tabs each holding a long poll eat most of that budget (HTTP/2 multiplexing mitigates this).

title: long-polling
text:
What tradeoff is this timeout window balancing?
A fifteen-to-thirty-second window balances avoiding too many repeated requests against getting cut off by a load balancer's idle timeout.

title: sse
text:
What are Server-Sent Events (SSE)?
SSE is an HTTP-based one-way event stream from server to client.

title: sse
text:
What connection option is usually the best fit?
SSE fits AI token streaming because the server streams one-way updates to the client.

title: sse
text:
What are the pros and cons of SSE? (Select all that apply.)
SSE is simple: native EventSource with automatic reconnection, and one response carries many events instead of re-issuing a request per update as long polling does. Downsides: the channel is one-way (client writes need separate HTTP requests), and it depends on infrastructure supporting streaming — proxies like nginx may buffer responses by default, so buffering must be disabled and timeouts raised.

title: sse-reconnect
text:
What does `last event ID` do when an SSE client reconnects?
The SSE spec only guarantees that EventSource puts the last received `id` into the `Last-Event-ID` request header on reconnect. Filling the gap is up to the server: here it buffers recent events, so it can replay everything after that ID. Without retained events, the header alone recovers nothing.

title: websocket
text:
What is WebSocket's key capability?
WebSocket provides full-duplex communication over a persistent connection.

title: websocket
text:
Put the WebSocket connection setup flow in order.
WebSocket starts with an HTTP upgrade handshake, then keeps a bidirectional message connection open.

title: websocket
text:
Which client connection protocol fits best?
Chat is a classic high-frequency bidirectional use case for WebSockets.

title: websocket
text:
What typical complexities come with WebSocket? (Select all that apply.)
WebSockets add stateful connection management, deployment, reconnection, and missed-message concerns.

title: websocket-service
text:
What is the common architecture choice?
A dedicated WebSocket service contains connection state so the rest of the backend can stay stateless.

title: webrtc
text:
What use case is WebRTC best suited for?
WebRTC fits peer-to-peer audio, video, screen sharing, gaming, or high-frequency collaboration.

title: webrtc
text:
Which components or concepts are usually involved in WebRTC setup? (Select all that apply.)
WebRTC setup involves signaling, ICE candidates, STUN, and often TURN relays.

title: webrtc
text:
What is the difference between STUN and TURN?
STUN helps peers discover routable paths, while TURN relays traffic when direct peer connections fail.

title: protocol-choice
text:
Which protocol choice is the better fit?
SSE is a good fit for one-way server-to-client dashboard updates.

title: protocol-choice
text:
Which protocol might you consider?
Interactive games need low-latency bidirectional communication, often with WebSockets or WebRTC.

title: protocol-summary
text:
Fill in the protocol-selection rule of thumb.
A useful protocol ladder is polling, long polling, SSE, WebSocket, and WebRTC as realtime demands increase.

title: server-side-propagation
text:
What core problem does server-side propagation solve?
Server-side propagation routes updates from their source to the server that can deliver them to the connected client.

title: pull-propagation
text:
How can server-side propagation be simplified?
With pull-based polling, updates are stored in a database and clients fetch changes after their last seen point.

title: persistent-connection-routing
text:
Why do updates need routing after you use persistent connections like WebSocket or SSE?
Persistent connections create server-side state, so updates must reach the server holding that user's connection.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
What is the basic idea behind using consistent hashing for realtime connection routing?
Consistent hashing assigns each user or entity to a predictable connection server while minimizing movement during scaling.

title: consistent-hashing-flow
text:
Put the flow for connecting a user to its consistent-hash owner server in order.
The client may connect anywhere first, then is redirected to the consistent-hash owner that stores its connection.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
What are the tradeoffs of managing realtime connections with consistent hashing? (Select all that apply.)
Consistent hashing makes ownership computable and moves only adjacent ring segments when scaling, which suits documents with expensive in-memory state. The cost is that every router must agree on the server list (often via ZooKeeper/etcd, but gossip or pushed config also work), and moving a document with tens of MB of state needs a migration process, so D is false.

title: consistent-hashing
text:
What server-side propagation approach is more likely here?
For heavy per-document connection state, consistent hashing keeps the state on a predictable owner server.

title: scaling-consistent-hash
text:
What mechanisms should you discuss when scaling consistent-hashing connection servers? (Select all that apply.)
Scaling consistent-hash connection servers needs coordinated migration, reconnects, and duplicate routing during transition.

title: pubsub
text:
What is the basic Pub/Sub model for propagating realtime updates?
Pub/sub moves routing into the pub/sub layer: the source just publishes to a topic, and whichever endpoint server holds the user's connection subscribes and forwards. Endpoints hold only connections and are interchangeable, so clients can connect to any of them.

title: pubsub-flow
text:
Put the pub/sub realtime push flow in order.
In pub/sub delivery, endpoints subscribe for their connected clients, updates publish to topics, and endpoints forward messages.

title: pubsub
text:
What server-side propagation approach fits better?
Pub/sub fits lightweight message forwarding where endpoint servers do not hold heavy per-user state.

title: pubsub
text:
What are the pros and cons of the Pub/Sub model? (Select all that apply.)
Pub/sub simplifies endpoint servers but can make the pub/sub service a bottleneck or critical dependency.

title: pubsub-latency
text:
What design judgment does this added-latency order of magnitude support?
In-region Redis Pub/Sub adds one or two in-memory hops, usually single-digit milliseconds; the real concerns are availability (Redis Pub/Sub does not persist, so disconnected subscribers miss messages) and sharding. Managed cloud pub/sub services have higher latency and must be estimated from their own docs.

title: load-balancing
text:
Which load-balancing strategy is the most direct fit?
Least-connections load balancing fits endpoint servers whose main resource is open connection count.

title: connection-failure
text:
What is a zombie connection in a realtime system?
A zombie connection is one side believing a connection is alive after the other side has lost or cleaned it up.

title: reconnection
text:
What capabilities does reconnect design usually need? (Select all that apply.)
Reliable realtime systems need heartbeats, reconnect backoff, and sequence IDs to replay missed updates.

title: missed-messages
text:
How should the server support this?
WebSocket does not store messages for you across a disconnect. The server needs a message log, retained long enough to cover the gap and readable from a position, plus the client's last-seen cursor, so it can replay from where the client left off.

title: celebrity-problem
text:
What is the celebrity problem in realtime systems?
The celebrity problem is massive fanout when one user's update must reach millions of clients at once.

title: celebrity-problem
text:
Which strategies can handle one update fanning out to millions of users? (Select all that apply.)
Extreme fanout needs layering, batching, or caching. Because the scenario says the display tolerates a 1–2 second delay and only the latest value matters, you can coalesce intermediate updates and push slightly later, trading a little freshness for stability; oversell protection lives in the server-side decrement at checkout. Fully synchronous one-by-one pushes create hotspots.

title: ordering
text:
Why do distributed realtime updates run into message ordering problems?
Distributed realtime systems can reorder messages when different servers or paths process them concurrently.

title: ordering
text:
What is the more pragmatic ordering strategy?
For product systems, funneling one entity's messages through one server or partition gives a simple total order.

title: vector-clocks
text:
When are vector clocks or logical timestamps more likely to come up?
Vector clocks are more common in deep infrastructure problems than in ordinary product realtime designs.

title: chat
text:
What is a reasonable main architecture path?
Chat commonly uses WebSockets for bidirectional delivery, pub/sub for routing, and a durable log for replay.

title: collaborative-editing
text:
What else must be discussed beyond realtime delivery?
Collaborative editing needs realtime delivery plus conflict resolution such as CRDTs or operational transforms.

title: live-comments
text:
What should the design focus on?
Live comments need batching and hierarchical fanout to preserve a realtime feel without delivering every event to every viewer.

title: interview-scenarios
text:
Which system design questions commonly trigger the Real-time Updates pattern? (Select all that apply.)
Chat, ride sharing, trading, and collaborative editing are common realtime update interview scenarios.

title: overengineering
text:
Why shouldn't you jump to WebSocket as soon as you see the word "updates"?
Do not jump to WebSockets unless the latency and bidirectional requirements justify stateful connection complexity.

title: deep-dives
text:
After proposing realtime updates, what common deep dives should you expect? (Select all that apply.)
Common realtime deep dives are reconnection, massive fanout, and message ordering.

title: interview-answer
text:
Put the interview answer structure for designing realtime updates in order.
A strong realtime answer clarifies requirements, chooses the client protocol, chooses propagation, and covers operational issues.

title: summary
text:
Complete the one-sentence summary of realtime updates.
Picking WebSocket alone is not enough; you must also explain how updates reach the server holding the connection. SSE is one-way server push, WebSocket is bidirectional; Pub/Sub broadcasts via subscriptions, while consistent hashing pins each user to one server so updates can be routed there.

title: long-polling-latency
text:
What design judgment does the 290 millisecond figure most support?
Ninety milliseconds for the first response to land, one hundred to re-issue the request, one hundred more for the reply: 290. The denser the updates, the more each one pays a full request round trip, and once that extra delay exceeds what the product tolerates, a persistent connection such as SSE or WebSocket is the better fit.

title: sse-plus-post
text:
Which client-server combination fits here?
When writes are far rarer than reads, a single POST covers them, so you skip operating a bidirectional WebSocket tier. SSE is still a long-lived connection, but it is just an ordinary HTTP response served by existing HTTP servers and load balancers; 200ms polling multiplies request volume across many users and still adds up to 200ms of display lag. Cost: every proxy on the path must stream rather than buffer the response.

title: initial-server-discovery
text:
What is the main cost of choosing option B?
Option B keeps topology knowledge server-side but pays an extra hop on every connect, and during a scaling event every client queries that central service at once.

title: networking-ip
text:
What delivery guarantee does IP at layer 3 actually provide?
IP is best-effort, so packets can be lost, duplicated, or reordered — reliability and ordering are what TCP adds at layer 4, and on UDP you must recover them yourself.

title: l7-sticky-session
text:
How do you pin one user to one backend?
A layer 7 load balancer parses the application protocol, so it can route on a cookie and keep a user on one backend — at the cost of more CPU spent inspecting every request.

title: short-update-window
text:
Which approach should push the verdict to the user?
With a one-second latency tolerance, no persistent-connection infrastructure, and a mandate for simplicity, simple polling works over plain stateless HTTP with no connection gateway, sticky routing, or reconnect handling, and the client simply stops once the verdict lands. The cost is up to one interval of delay and a few dozen empty requests.

title: sse-chunked
text:
What response header change tells the client the stream is not over?
Content-Length requires knowing the total byte count up front, and the response ends only when that many bytes are sent; SSE events are produced on the fly with unknown total length, so over HTTP/1.1 you switch to chunked encoding, writing chunk by chunk and ending with a zero-length chunk. The client recognizes SSE by Content-Type: text/event-stream, which must stay. HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 forbid chunked and stream via DATA frames instead. Cost: proxies that buffer responses will hold back the whole stream.

title: websocket-auth
text:
Why can the WebSocket handshake reuse that existing authentication?
WebSocket upgrades the layer 7 protocol on an existing TCP connection, so the handshake is still HTTP and its cookies and headers are available for auth.

title: webrtc-signaling
text:
How should the signaling server itself be built?
Peer availability and connection details keep changing, so clients must be pushed those updates: signaling is itself a realtime update problem nested inside WebRTC. WebRTC does not mandate a signaling transport; WebSocket is the common choice because it is bidirectional.

title: webrtc-persistence
text:
What must the design still account for?
Peer-to-peer solves transport, not durability — once the last peer leaves the state is gone, so you still need a path that writes it home.

title: consistent-hashing-failure
text:
What does the system go through after that crash?
The in-memory state has no replica, so a crash takes connections and state together; clients reconnect, the ring assigns the document to a new owner, and that owner replays the operation log before users can edit again, with unacknowledged operations resent by clients. D gets the granularity wrong: with virtual nodes the crashed server's different documents do spread across several servers, but each document still has exactly one owner, never several in-memory copies.

title: pubsub-topic-granularity
text:
At what granularity should topics be created?
Rooms are small (at most 10), so a per-user topic costs at most 10 publishes per message, and personal events ride the same channel with exactly one subscription per connection, so senders never need to know which machine holds the recipient. For a million-viewer live room, per-room topics win instead.

title: pubsub-blind-spot
text:
What does this blind spot cause?
Pub/sub knows who subscribed but not whether that connection is alive, so messages fall into a dead socket and you need heartbeats plus a last-event-ID catch-up to close the gap.

title: pubsub-cluster-fanout
text:
What new connection-management problem appears?
With sharded pub/sub each channel lives on one shard. Slots are computable, but one endpoint server holds thousands of users whose channels spread across all six shards, so every server connects to every shard: up to 200 x 6 = 1200 internal connections. Mitigate by keeping the cluster small or grouping users' channels onto fewer shards.

title: naive-hashing-failure
text:
What goes wrong with this modulo assignment when the fleet scales?
Changing N flips nearly every remainder at once, so consistent hashing exists specifically to move only a small ring segment instead.

title: tcp-handshake-teardown-cost
text:
What extra cost does this pay on every single poll?
TCP is connection-oriented: each new connection costs a three-way handshake before the request (one extra RTT), then a four-way close after the response — the close does not delay this response, but it adds packets and leaves the side that closes first in TIME_WAIT, which piles up ports and memory under frequent short connections. Keep-alive reuses the connection so these costs are paid once; over HTTPS it also saves a TLS handshake per poll.

title: websocket-redeploy-strategy
text:
How should the deployment handle those already-established connections?
The stem says connections hold no expensive state, clients can backfill, and reconnects already back off, so dropping and reconnecting only costs a reconnect burst that backoff smooths out, in exchange for the simplest deploy. B's seamless handoff is extra engineering worth it only when per-connection state is expensive to rebuild; C has no moment when everyone disconnects; D risks overloading half the fleet and relies on a manual cutover.

title: websocket-hotspot-offload
text:
Why do these servers still develop load hotspots?
Least connections counts every connection as one unit, but the stem says a few connections carry hundreds of times more messages, and validation and conversion CPU scales with messages, so servers holding those connections run hotter at equal connection counts. Common fixes are moving heavy processing into an independently scaled service or balancing on CPU or load metrics.

title: confirm-polling-with-interviewer
text:
What should you do first, before committing to the polling proposal?
Skipping the check risks spending your time on polling's architecture while the interviewer actually wanted to hear about WebSocket — one sentence of confirmation avoids that mismatch.

title: sse-vs-websocket-tradeoff
text:
From memory, write an SSE versus WebSocket comparison table and choose one for this scenario. Which five dimensions must the table include?
Downstream updates are frequent while upstream controls are sparse, so choose SSE plus REST: avoid a bidirectional connection tier and get native reconnect plus Last-Event-ID. Switch to WebSocket for frequent two-way traffic or binary payloads.

title: read-write-ratio
text:
Why do content-heavy apps usually hit read scaling before write scaling?
Opening the feed fires 100+ reads (photo metadata, user info, like counts, comment previews), while a person posts about once a day (one write). Each item is written once and read many times, so read traffic far exceeds write traffic in content-heavy apps, and the read side hits the database's capacity first.

title: read-write-ratio
text:
What does that order of magnitude imply for scaling priorities?
A hundred-to-one read-write ratio means most traffic is reads, so read-side techniques like indexing and caching pay off far more than write-path work.

title: bottleneck
text:
In this situation, why won't more SQL debugging fix the problem?
The scenario has already ruled out the query layer: hot queries use indexes and there are no N+1 patterns. What remains is a single machine's CPU, memory, and disk I/O ceiling; once you hit it, more SQL tweaks won't help, and you need architecture to offload reads — read replicas and caches. Note that a clean slow-query log alone isn't enough to conclude this: many fast but very frequent queries can also pin the CPU, so check top queries by total time first.

title: progression
text:
Put the standard read-scaling progression in the right order.
Read scaling progresses from optimizing within the database, to scaling horizontally with replicas, to adding external caching layers.

title: indexing
text:
What is a database index at its core?
An index is a sorted lookup table pointing to rows, like a book index that tells you exactly which pages to check.

title: indexing
text:
What is the complexity difference between a full table scan and an indexed lookup?
A B-tree index turns a linear scan into a logarithmic lookup: about 23 to 24 comparisons for ten million rows (only 3 to 4 page levels thanks to high fan-out), the cheapest big win in read optimization.

title: indexing
text:
Which statements about index types are correct? Select all that apply.
B-tree indexes are the general default, hash indexes suit exact matches but not ranges, and full-text or geo queries use specialized indexes.

title: indexing
text:
What should be the first read-scaling move?
EXPLAIN already shows both queries doing full table scans with no index on those columns. Indexing the frequently queried and sorted columns (such as hashtag and price) is then the cheapest first move: use up the headroom inside the single database before adding infrastructure like caches, replicas, or sharding.

title: indexing
text:
How should you handle the concern that too many indexes slow writes in an interview?
Every INSERT or UPDATE must maintain the related indexes, so the write cost is real; but at 100:1 reads to writes, an index serving a clear query pattern saves far more read work than it adds write work. In an interview, acknowledge the cost first, then justify it with the ratio; write-heavy tables call for more restraint.

title: hardware
text:
How should you position hardware upgrades for read pressure?
Hardware upgrades are boring but effective for buying headroom, worth mentioning in an interview but rarely what the interviewer wants.

title: hardware
text:
What does SSDs' random-I/O advantage over spinning disks imply for scaling?
SSDs have no mechanical seek: random-read latency drops from milliseconds to roughly a hundred microseconds, and the random-IOPS gap is even larger (hundreds to thousands of times, depending on SATA vs NVMe and queue depth). Treat these as order-of-magnitude anchors, not constants; the conclusion holds — swapping in SSDs is often the fastest way to buy read-scaling headroom.

title: denormalization
text:
What is the purpose of normalization?
Normalization splits data across tables so each fact is stored once: a rename touches one row, avoiding inconsistent copies (update anomalies), with storage savings as a side effect. The cost is that reads often need joins to reassemble an order summary.

title: denormalization
text:
What is the most direct read optimization?
Denormalization stores redundant copies so an expensive multi-table join becomes a simple single-table query, trading storage for read speed.

title: denormalization
text:
What happens after denormalization when a user changes their name?
Since pages must show the current name, a rename must update every redundant copy, which is acceptable because renames are rare compared to reads. (If orders only need a snapshot of the name at purchase time, no back-fill is needed.)

title: denormalization
text:
Complete the core denormalization tradeoff.
Denormalization trades extra storage and more complex writes for faster reads, so always check the read-write ratio first.

title: materialized-view
text:
What is the best technique here?
A materialized view precomputes an expensive aggregation once via a background job so every page load just reads the stored result.

title: materialized-view
text:
Which SQL statement is the right move?
The materialized view stores the join and group-by result so reads skip the computation entirely.

title: capacity
text:
What judgment does this read QPS level support?
40k out of 50k is 80% of this box's measured ceiling, so plan a cache or read replicas now. The ceiling must come from your own load test or monitoring: a single database's read capacity is often in the tens of thousands per second, but it varies several-fold with hardware, query complexity, row size, and buffer-cache hit rate — it is not a fixed threshold.

title: read-replicas
text:
In a read-replica architecture, where do reads and writes go?
Read replicas copy data from the primary, all writes go to the primary, and reads spread across the replicas.

title: read-replicas
text:
Besides spreading read throughput, what extra benefit do read replicas give?
Beyond spreading read load, replicas add redundancy because a replica can be promoted to primary if the primary fails.

title: replication
text:
Complete the standard replication architecture.
In leader-follower replication the leader handles writes and followers handle reads, with synchronous replication being consistent but slow and asynchronous being fast but possibly stale.

title: replication
text:
What is the core tradeoff between synchronous and asynchronous replication?
Synchronous replication guarantees consistency at the cost of write latency, while asynchronous replication is faster but replicas can serve stale data.

title: replication
text:
What is the classic user-visible symptom of replication lag?
With replication lag a user may not see their own change because the read hit a replica that has not caught up, mitigated with read-your-writes routing.

title: sharding
text:
How do read replicas and sharding differ on dataset size?
Replicas copy the full dataset to each server, while sharding splits the data so each database handles a smaller, faster subset.

title: sharding
text:
What does functional sharding split data by?
Functional sharding splits data by business domain, putting user data in one database and product data in another so each query hits a smaller database.

title: sharding
text:
Which sharding strategy fits best?
Geographic sharding stores each region's data near its users, cutting latency while spreading load across databases.

title: sharding
text:
How should sharding be positioned for read scaling?
200GB fits on one machine and the only bottleneck is read QPS; sharding adds cross-shard queries and re-sharding work that three engineers can't easily carry. Caching (when access has hot spots) and read replicas spread reads far more cheaply, so sharding waits until writes or dataset size outgrow one machine.

title: caching
text:
What access pattern makes caching so effective for read scaling?
Most applications have highly skewed access patterns where millions read the same rarely-changing data, which caches exploit by serving it from memory.

title: caching
text:
What is the response-time order of magnitude for a cache hit versus an optimized database query?
An in-datacenter cache hit is one memory lookup plus a network round trip, sub-millisecond. Even a well-indexed database query must parse and execute, typically taking milliseconds, and tens of milliseconds once it hits disk or gets complex. The gap ranges from several times to tens of times, which is the quantitative case for a cache.

title: caching
text:
What is the standard read flow for an application cache such as Redis or Memcached?
The application checks the cache first, and on a miss queries the database and populates the cache for future requests.

title: caching
text:
With TTL-based caching, how do hot and cold items naturally distribute?
TTL expires hot and cold entries alike; the difference is refill: a hot key is refilled by the very next miss, so it is almost always present, while a cold key goes unread after expiry and stays out. When memory fills, a maxmemory policy such as allkeys-lru likewise favors keeping hot data.

title: invalidation
text:
Fill in the five common cache invalidation strategies.
The five approaches trade off implementation complexity, staleness window, and write latency: TTL is simplest but has a fixed stale window; synchronous deletion on the write path minimizes staleness but adds write latency; asynchronous deletion via a queue or CDC keeps writes fast at the cost of brief staleness; tags invalidate a group at once; versioned keys let old entries age out. Write-through and write-behind are write policies (how data reaches cache and store), not names of invalidation strategies.

title: invalidation
text:
Which invalidation strategy fits best?
Plain TTL expiration is the simplest strategy and fits non-critical data with predictable update patterns like recommendation scores.

title: invalidation
text:
What is the core difference between synchronous and asynchronous invalidation?
Synchronous invalidation updates or deletes cache entries during the write path for consistency at the cost of write latency, while asynchronous invalidation queues events and briefly risks stale reads.

title: invalidation
text:
Which invalidation strategy fits best?
Tagged invalidation associates entries with tags so one change can invalidate every related entry, at the cost of maintaining tag relationships.

title: invalidation
text:
How do versioned cache keys work?
Versioned keys include a version number in the cache key and increment it on update, so old entries become unreachable instead of being deleted.

title: invalidation
text:
What combination is most common in production?
Production systems combine short TTLs of five to fifteen minutes as a safety net with active invalidation for critical data.

title: ttl
text:
How should you choose cache TTLs?
The staleness budget sets an upper bound on the TTL: at most 30 seconds for search and 5 minutes for profiles. If replication lag or additional cache layers also add staleness, subtract them from the budget and set the TTL a bit below it.

title: cdn
text:
Which statement about modern CDNs is correct?
CDNs started with static assets, but modern CDNs also cache dynamic content that changes yet is shared by many users, like this homepage that refreshes every 30 seconds and is identical for everyone, using a short TTL (Cache-Control: s-maxage) for freshness. Per-user personalized content is a poor fit for a shared cache.

title: cdn
text:
What latency change do you expect from a Virginia origin to a Tokyo edge node?
Edge caching cuts response times from around two hundred milliseconds cross-continent to under ten milliseconds locally.

title: cdn
text:
Roughly how much can a well-configured CDN reduce origin load in a read-heavy app?
Origin offload ≈ cacheable share × hit rate = 95% × 95% ≈ 90%. This is not a fixed property of a CDN; with lots of personalized or long-tail traffic it is far lower.

title: cdn
text:
What is the right CDN caching tradeoff?
A CDN pays off when many users read the same content, which fits posts, catalogs, and non-personalized search results. DMs and personal settings are read only by their owner, so a shared cache gains almost no hits and risks serving them to someone else; they are usually marked Cache-Control: private and cached in the app layer or on the client.

title: interview-method
text:
What is the strongest way to start the scalability discussion?
Strong candidates proactively flag high-volume endpoints, quantify the read load, and then work through query optimization before caching and replicas.

title: scenarios
text:
What caching strategy fits Bitly?
Bitly is a caching dream because the mapping never changes, so cache it aggressively with no expiration and let the CDN absorb global traffic.

title: scenarios
text:
Where should the caching boundary be?
Cache stable event details aggressively; seat availability can be approximate for display, but checkout must read authoritative inventory and reserve atomically.

title: scenarios
text:
What is the key read-scaling technique?
Pre-compute feeds for active users, cache recent posts, and paginate, because users typically only read the first few items.

title: scenarios
text:
What is a reasonable read-scaling mix?
Metadata rarely changes, so cache it aggressively; the prompt says view counts may lag, so make them eventually consistent with batched updates; thumbnails are static media, so serve them from a CDN.

title: when-not-to-use
text:
Which scenarios should not make read scaling the main focus? Select all that apply.
Skip read scaling for write-heavy systems, small-scale designs a single indexed database can handle, and real-time collaboration where caching actively hurts.

title: positioning
text:
What is the real goal of read scaling?
Read scaling is about reducing database load, and pure latency problems call for different solutions like edge computing.

title: indexing
text:
At 10 million users, email login takes 30 seconds and DB CPU is 100%; what is the likely cause?
The users table has only a primary key, so an email lookup has no usable index and each login sequentially scans ten million rows; with many concurrent logins the CPU pegs and queries stretch to tens of seconds. A (unique) index on email turns the lookup into O(log n).

title: indexing
text:
What is the right fix?
Creating an index on the email column turns the full table scan into a few index lookups, visible in EXPLAIN as the plan switches to an index scan.

title: indexing
text:
Which queries can a compound index on status and created_at speed up?
The index sorts by status, then by created_at within each status, so with an equality on status the created_at range filter and ordering follow index order; skipping status and querying created_at alone can't use the leftmost prefix. (Skip scan in some databases can partly use it when status has few values, but that isn't a general guarantee.)

title: hot-key
text:
A celebrity post pushes one cache key from 50k to 500k QPS and timeouts; what problem is this?
This is the hot-key problem: one key gets all the traffic and overwhelms a single cache server's CPU and network even though the data is in memory.

title: request-coalescing
text:
How far can request coalescing reduce backend load when a million users ask for the same key?
Request coalescing reduces backend load from potentially unlimited to exactly one request per application server doing the coalescing.

title: request-coalescing
text:
What role does the inflight map play in this request-coalescing code?
The inflight map tracks keys already being fetched so concurrent requests await the same future instead of issuing duplicate backend calls.

title: hot-key
text:
What should you do next?
Cache key fanout stores identical copies under multiple keys so clients randomly pick one, spreading the hot key's load across servers.

title: hot-key
text:
What is the cost of cache key fanout?
Fanout trades redundancy for availability: the hot item is stored nine extra times, and every update must invalidate (or wait out the TTL of) all ten copies. B is wrong because of "bound to": whether hit rate drops depends on memory headroom — under memory pressure the extra copies can evict other keys and each copy cold-misses once, so it may drop, but it is not guaranteed.

title: stampede
text:
What triggers a cache stampede?
Cache expiration is binary, so the instant this hot entry expires all 100k concurrent requests miss at once and each tries to run the ten-table join, a self-inflicted DDoS. The hotter the entry and the costlier the rebuild, the worse the stampede. (This is a single hot-key stampede, not an avalanche of many keys expiring together.)

title: stampede
text:
What is the main downside of using a distributed lock to stop a stampede?
With a distributed lock a slow or failed rebuild leaves thousands of waiting requests to time out, making the approach fragile under load.

title: stampede
text:
What is the smarter approach?
Probabilistic early refresh gives each request a growing chance to refresh the entry as expiry nears, spreading rebuilds over minutes instead of one instant.

title: stampede
text:
Which approach should you use?
A lock protects the database, but at expiry users still miss and queue behind the rebuild, which violates the no-waiting constraint; a longer TTL only postpones the stampede. A background refresher renews the entry before it lapses, so in normal operation user requests only read the cache. The costs are extra infrastructure, wasted refreshes of unread data, and the need to monitor the refresher itself, so reserve it for the most critical content.

title: invalidation
text:
What real problems does naive delete-cache-after-write create? Select all that apply.
Naive delete-after-write is unreliable here because caches live in several layers (app, CDN, browser), invalidations can fail, and a reader that fetched the old value before the write can put it back into the cache right after the delete. Deleting a cache key never locks a database table.

title: cache-versioning
text:
What is the read/write flow for cache versioning?
The idea is to reroute rather than delete: the version increments in the same transaction as the data, and reads fetch the version (which may itself be cached) to build the key. Old entries are never deleted, just unreachable until their TTL expires.

title: cache-versioning
text:
Why does versioning avoid a whole class of invalidation races?
Version changes are atomic in the database so keys never collide and readers move to the new key automatically, eliminating the whole class of invalidation races.

title: cache-versioning
text:
What costs come with cache versioning?
Versioning costs an extra version lookup per read (from the DB or a version cache), leaves old entries until their TTLs expire, and mainly fits single-entity caches; computed results like recommendation lists depend on many entities and have no single version to key on.

title: deleted-items-cache
text:
What is the efficient compromise?
A small deleted-items cache filters recently removed IDs at serve time so cached feeds stay usable while the expensive invalidation happens in the background.

title: cdn
text:
What extra challenge does cache invalidation have with a global CDN, and what is the response?
A one-hour TTL far exceeds one minute, so waiting is out; the stem says purges reach all nodes within tens of seconds, so an active purge on takedown meets the requirement, though it is not instant and its completion should be monitored. Only if the vendor's purge latency exceeded the requirement would you shorten edge TTLs or keep such pages out of the CDN.

title: cache-versioning
text:
Put the cache decision chain for venue address updates that must be visible immediately in order.
The chain runs requirement, choice, cost, mitigation: immediate visibility across cache layers leads to versioned keys, whose double lookup and accumulation are bounded by TTL cleanup.

title: scenarios
text:
Complete the reasoning for Bitly's cache strategy.
Because the mapping is immutable and read millions of times per write, Bitly can cache aggressively with no expiration at all.

title: strategy
text:
What is the right overall caching design principle?
Design caching around each data type's consistency needs instead of applying one approach everywhere.

title: strategy
text:
Which data should go to a cache versus a read replica?
Mappings never change and are read enormously, so aggressive caching has zero staleness and the best hit rate. Settings must be visible within one second, have modest reads, and the team wants no invalidation logic, so replicas with under-100ms lag meet the bar without any invalidation. B's 30-second TTL breaks the one-second requirement; C sends the huge mapping read volume to the database; D picks the wrong axis, since mutability and freshness requirements decide it.

title: strategy
text:
How should read-scaling patterns be positioned here?
Overselling is prevented on the authoritative path: deduct on the primary with an atomic conditional update (e.g. UPDATE ... SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE stock > 0), so slightly stale displayed numbers don't cause oversells. At 3:1 read scaling isn't the main problem; descriptions can still be cached normally and displayed stock can use a short TTL with write-time invalidation. B keeps both display and decisions stale for long; C refuses to cache even staleness-tolerant descriptions; D bases deductions on a lagging replica and oversells.

title: replication
text:
What breaks if Ticketmaster's purchase path also reads from a read replica?
After a seat sells the primary is updated but the replica lags 200ms; in that window a second buyer still reads "available" from the replica, and since the primary write doesn't re-check, the seat sells twice. The fix: the purchase path reads the primary and reserves with an atomic conditional update (WHERE status = 'available') or a lock/transaction, telling the buyer the seat is gone if it fails.

title: materialized-view
text:
When does a materialized view's average reflect a new review?
Here the view is fully recomputed by a background job on a schedule (like PostgreSQL's REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW), so reads between refreshes see the old aggregate and staleness is bounded by roughly the refresh interval plus one rebuild's duration. Fresher data means more frequent full recomputes. (Some databases offer incremental or on-commit materialized views; that is a different design.)

title: write-bottleneck
text:
When write throughput hits a single machine's ceiling, what are the three classic hardware bottlenecks?
Writes are bottlenecked by disk I/O, CPU, and network bandwidth, so confirm which wall you're actually hitting before proposing any redesign.

title: write-vs-read
text:
On the axis of "how hard is it to scale", why is scaling writes usually harder than scaling reads?
Reads scale with familiar tools like replicas and caching, while bursty, high-contention writes are much harder and invite interviewer probing.

title: strategy-overview
text:
Fill in the four write-scaling strategies:
