This is Hello Interview's four-layer framework: squeeze one machine, shard out, handle bursts with queues and load shedding, then batch to cut the number of writes. It's a useful order to escalate in an interview, not the only possible taxonomy.

title: vertical-scaling
text:
What should be your first move?
First do quick back-of-the-envelope math to check whether the write volume actually exceeds modern hardware before adding any architectural complexity.

title: vertical-scaling
text:
Which single-machine hardware baseline should you compare against so you don't prematurely conclude "we must shard"?
Compare against a large modern machine at order-of-magnitude level: 100+ cores, tens of Gbit or more of network, local NVMe. For writes, check storage separately — fsync latency, IOPS, transaction and index overhead often cap you before core count does. Tens of thousands of simple writes per second often fits on one such machine, so you avoid concluding "we must shard" too early.

title: vertical-scaling
text:
What's the right way to respond?
Make the case for vertical scaling once, but if the interviewer keeps raising the scale, move on to horizontal strategies instead of arguing.

title: database-choices
text:
Under write-heavy load Cassandra usually out-writes a B-tree relational database — what is the core mechanism?
Relational databases also have a sequentially written WAL; the difference is what follows: a B-tree must eventually write data pages back in place, causing random I/O. Cassandra only appends to the commit log and inserts into the memtable, then flushes it sequentially as an immutable SSTable — no in-place updates. That's why write-heavy throughput is usually much higher; the cost is merging multiple SSTables on reads plus background compaction.

title: database-choices
text:
On comparable commodity hardware, roughly how does Cassandra's write throughput compare to a traditional relational database's?
Cassandra uses LSM-style append writes and has no single-primary write bottleneck, so in append-heavy, horizontally-scaled workloads its cluster-wide write throughput usually far exceeds a single-primary relational database. Node for node on the same hardware, though, the gap depends on batching, indexing, transaction/fsync settings, and data model and may be only a few times. Treat it as an order-of-magnitude anchor, not a fixed benchmark.

title: database-choices
text:
Choosing Cassandra for high write throughput comes at what cost?
Cassandra trades read performance for write performance, since reads often check multiple files and merge results.

title: write-vs-read
text:
What does "write vs. read tension" mean?
Optimizing for writes usually degrades reads and vice versa, so identify which side is your bottleneck and optimize accordingly.

title: database-choices
text:
Which of these database types are built as trade-offs for write-heavy, sequential-write workloads? (select all)
Time-series databases are built for timestamped sequential writes plus compression; log-structured stores replace in-place updates with appends; column stores write very fast when inserts arrive in large batches (true here because the gateway batches), at the cost of being poor at row-by-row small writes. General-purpose OLTP databases target mixed workloads, not extreme writes.

title: database-choices
text:
Without switching databases, which of these can make this PostgreSQL write faster? (select all)
Disabling expensive features, tuning WAL flushing, and dropping indexes are all local "make room for writes" optimizations. WAL tuning has two levels: group commit (commit_delay) lets many transactions share one fsync without losing acknowledged data; synchronous_commit = off is faster but can lose the last few acknowledged transactions on a crash. Adding more indexes slows writes.

title: interview-method
text:
Which phrasing earns the most credit?
Do not just say use a faster database; explain why append-only writes beat B-tree updates or why a time-series store fits metrics.

title: sharding
text:
What's the basic promise of horizontal sharding?
Sharding promises near-linear scaling by spreading writes across servers so each handles a manageable portion, hidden behind one logical database.

title: sharding
text:
How does Redis Cluster decide which node a key gets written to?
Redis Cluster computes the slot as CRC16(key) mod 16384, and each slot belongs to one primary. A cluster-aware client caches the slot→node map and sends the write straight to the owner; if the map is stale, the node replies MOVED and the client refreshes. Only a `{}` hash tag makes multiple keys share a slot.

title: partition-key
text:
What's the most important sharding detail you must proactively spell out?
The most important sharding detail is selecting a partitioning key that spreads data evenly, which is what actually realizes the ten-times gain.

title: partition-key
text:
What happens if you use "user's country" as the partition key?
Partitioning by country skews load badly, overloading the China shard while the New Zealand shard sits idle.

title: partition-key
text:
Fill in the principle for choosing a partition key:
Pick the key that minimizes per-shard write variance, so each shard carries about total writes divided by shard count. Hashing a high-cardinality primary identifier usually achieves that, but check whether frequent reads then have to span shards.

title: partition-key
text:
Writes are perfectly spread out, but every read has to collect data from all shards — what's the consequence?
If every read must fan out to all shards, the network overhead can erase your sharding gains, so consider the read path when picking a key.

title: partition-key
text:
What two questions should you ask yourself?
Ask how many shards each request must hit and how often that request happens to decide whether your layout creates a bottleneck.

title: vertical-partitioning
text:
What's the difference between horizontal sharding and vertical partitioning?
Horizontal sharding splits rows across servers while vertical partitioning splits columns by access pattern.

title: vertical-partitioning
text:
What's the most sensible way to split it?
Split the monolithic table into content, metrics, and analytics tables so each access pattern stops interfering with the others.

title: vertical-partitioning
text:
After vertically partitioning into three tables and moving each to its own database instance, which "table → optimization" pairings are correct? (select all)
One payoff of vertical partitioning is that each table can move to a store suited to its access pattern: read-heavy content to B-tree indexes, high-frequency counters to in-memory counters, append-only analytics to columnar or time-series storage. D's "must stay on one instance" is false — keeping them together is only a simpler choice when traffic is low.

title: bursts
text:
If a peak can arrive at any time and the system must absorb 4x write volume when it does, what does that imply for normal-time capacity utilization?
If peaks can come at any time and you can't scale, queue, or shed in the moment, the capacity has to be standing: normal utilization ≤ 1 / peak multiplier, so a 4x peak means ≤ 25%. That cost is why many systems use queues or load shedding instead; when the peak is predictable (like Black Friday), the usual move is load-testing and pre-scaling ahead of time rather than idling year-round.

title: bursts
text:
Why isn't "autoscaling" a silver bullet for write bursts?
Autoscaling takes time and database scaling often means downtime or reduced throughput exactly when traffic is spiking.

title: write-queues
text:
Adding a Kafka/SQS queue to the write path fundamentally decouples what?
A write queue decouples write acceptance from write processing so the database drains at a steady rate while the queue absorbs bursts.

title: write-queues
text:
A queue is inherently asynchronous — what's the direct consequence for the client?
With an async queue the app only knows the write was enqueued, so clients often need a way to check back that it eventually reached the database.

title: write-queues
text:
If producers keep writing to the queue faster than the database can consume it, what happens?
A queue is a buffer, not capacity: a 70k/s gap adds roughly six billion messages of backlog a day and latency keeps climbing. The backlog isn't truly infinite either — it eventually hits retention (expired unconsumed messages are deleted) or disk limits (producers start erroring), turning "slow" into "data loss or rejected writes."

title: write-queues
text:
What's the right judgment on this proposal?
Use queues for short-lived bursts, not to patch a database that cannot handle the steady-state load.

title: write-queues
text:
Before adding a queue, what must you confirm at the requirements stage?
Before adding a queue, confirm at the requirements stage how much write delay and read inconsistency the system can tolerate.

title: load-shedding
text:
How should you handle the location writes while overloaded?
Deciding which writes to accept and which to reject under overload is load shedding. Here a dropped live position is superseded seconds later and the full track lives on the phone, so shedding high-frequency points only coarsens the live track; A just builds backlog under sustained overload, C takes everyone down, and D is slow and may cause a dip.

title: write-queues
text:
Under sustained overload, how does this write queue fail step by step?
When producers stay faster than consumers, the backlog keeps growing (until it hits retention or disk limits), write latency stretches out, and stored positions fall further behind. B is wrong: the default delete policy only removes the oldest segments by time/size, and even with compaction consumers still have to work through the backlog in order. Queues handle short bursts, not a steady-state throughput gap.

title: load-shedding
text:
Which event type should be shed first under overload?
Tiered shedding ranks writes by business value. The scenario says billing is per click and impressions are only for estimates without exact CTR, so every click must be kept while impressions can be sampled, recording the sample rate to scale estimates back up. A would also drop billable clicks; under CPM billing or an exact-CTR requirement the conclusion would change.

title: batching
text:
Without adding machines, which lever directly cuts the write overhead the database has to carry?
Sharding and queueing only move the same write volume around (and the scenario rules out more machines); batching collapses N round trips and transaction setups into one, even when every write has a different key. Repeated updates to the same key can additionally be pre-aggregated into one. The cost is extra buffering latency.

title: batching
text:
Why is this application-layer batching safe to adopt?
Whether batching is safe depends on who owns the source of truth: the data still lives in Kafka and the offset is committed only after the batch lands, so a crashed process re-reads from its last committed offset — at the cost of replays, so writes must be idempotent.

title: batching
text:
What happens if the process crashes before the batch commits?
The user already holds a success receipt while the write lives only in memory, so a crash leaves it neither committed nor replayable and the order simply disappears — never batch blindly when the app is the source of truth.

title: batching
text:
How many database writes land during that minute?
Database writes equal posts times windows, not likes: one post times one window is one write, so the compression ratio is 100 likes over 1 write — that ratio is what tells you whether batching is worth it.

title: batching
text:
How much benefit does batching deliver here?
Compression equals same-key events per window, so when arrivals fall below one per window the ratio is about one and you have bought only a minute of latency — validate arrival rate before batching.

title: batching
text:
How should you judge this database-layer batching?
Moving `appendfsync` from `always` to `everysec` pushes batching down into the storage engine: writes stop waiting for an fsync each, so throughput rises, but the whole instance now has roughly a one-second durability window — a crash can lose acknowledged writes to any key in that second. It cannot be scoped to hot keys, so it is the coarsest knob and comes after application-layer or intermediate batching.

title: hierarchical-aggregation
text:
Why does hierarchical aggregation apply here?
The premise for high-volume stream data is that downstream only needs the aggregate, so each stage can reduce volume before forwarding — each extra stage costs one more hop of latency.

title: hierarchical-aggregation
text:
How do you cut down the all-to-all fan-out on the read side?
All-to-all assumes every writer reaches every reader; writing to M broadcast nodes instead drops fan-out from N to M, with viewers assigned by consistent hashing, at the cost of one more hop.

title: hierarchical-aggregation
text:
How do you shed one more layer of write pressure upstream?
Events route by comment ID to a fixed write processor that aggregates that comment over a window and forwards batches, leaving the root to merely merge — at the cost of another hop of latency.

title: strategy
text:
Which strategy-to-cost pairings are correct? (select all)
All three reduce per-component throughput, each at its own cost: queues bring eventual consistency and delay (confirming a write needs polling or a notification), partitioning makes cross-partition reads fan out, batching adds latency and a moving part — name the cost before proposing.

title: resharding
text:
How does this naive resharding break on a large dataset?
Going from 8 to 16 under modulo, a key stays put only when `hash mod 16 < 8`, so exactly half the data moves — about 25 TB of 50 TB. With eight old shards each pushing 100 MB/s, that is roughly 8–9 hours with reads and writes unavailable, and it grows with dataset size. A non-doubling change (say 8 to 12) moves even more, about two thirds. That is why naive offline rehashing cannot ship to production.

title: resharding
text:
How should production migrate this data?
During dual-write each write lands on both old and new shards while history is copied in batches; reads prefer the new shard and fall back to the old, and dual-write stops once the copy completes — at double write cost and extra complexity.

title: hot-keys
text:
What problem does this single tweet create?
A partition key balances across keys, never inside one: 100,000 likes per second all hit the same counter row on a single shard, where row locks serialize updates at about 5,000 per second — 20x short — so adding shards changes nothing.

title: hot-keys
text:
What is the key difference between the two key-splitting schemes?
A fixed k-way split cuts per-key write volume to one k-th but multiplies dataset size and per-read lookups by k, while dynamic splitting confines that cost to hot keys at the price of hotness detection.

title: hot-keys
text:
For which kind of data does this trick not hold?
Splitting works when summing all sub-keys reproduces the truth, which holds for additive metrics like likes, views, and counts; balances can be summed on read too, but debits must additionally protect a non-negative total. A user profile is a whole record that must stay atomic and cannot be reassembled from sub-keys.

title: hot-keys
text:
Under these constraints, how do you keep readers and writers in agreement?
Any disagreement silently loses counts. With no coordination protocol allowed and a fixed read amplification accepted, readers unconditionally check every sub-key, so they see the count whether or not the writer split — at 100 extra reads each. A broadcast protocol only pays off when read QPS makes that amplification unacceptable.

title: Idempotent job creation
text:
Write the create-job request, success response, and conflict response.
Persist the key, request fingerprint, and job ID atomically. Replay the result for the original payload and reject a different payload.
